surprises.fact_evidence: The company doubled its estimated served addressable data center market to approximately $2 billion by adding Europe, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia and reflecting the shift toward liquid cooling.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management is pointing at a >$1B addressable market.

surprises.description: Q2 sales included about $20 million of demand pulled forward into the quarter, including early data center project shipments. That creates a timing-related qualification to the otherwise strong sales beat, although the preview had flagged data center order timing as a risk to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 results included roughly $20 million of pull-forward demand—about $10 million ahead of a June SAP implementation and about $10 million of data center projects shipped early across the Americas and APMEA.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flags “order-timing lumpiness” as something to watch in data center commentary.

surprises.description: APMEA organic sales grew 31%, led by China data center demand, whereas the preview modeled the segment at about $45 million with Saudi Cast contributing and the Middle East conflict as a headwind. The China-led growth was a stronger demand driver than that preview framing anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: APMEA organic sales grew 31% led by China data center demand.
surprises.expectation_evidence: APMEA Q2 estimate: ~$45M; “Saudi Cast contribution; conflict headwind concentrated here.”

surprises.description: The EPS beat included a favorable tax-rate effect from reversing a prior-year tax liability, making part of the reported earnings growth nonrecurring rather than purely operational.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EPS grew 18% year-over-year to $3.66, aided by a 210 bps favorable tax rate driven by a nonrecurring benefit from reversing a prior-year tax liability.

surprises.description: Year-to-date free cash flow was still lower than a year ago, rather than showing the catch-up the preview wanted after Q1’s weak result. The company attributed the decline to higher receivables and strategic inventory investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: Year-to-date free cash flow declined to $98 million from $105 million due to higher receivables and strategic inventory investment.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says the ≥90% conversion target requires a large H2 catch-up and that “a second weak FCF quarter would be a real negative.”

surprises.description: Residential and non-institutional new construction remained soft, as the preview expected, but single-family conditions were slightly worse than the prior quarter, adding some deterioration to the market backdrop.
surprises.fact_evidence: Residential and non-institutional new construction remain soft, with single-family conditions slightly worse than last quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says “Residential remains soft” and calls for watching whether the core is decelerating underneath data center growth.

in_line: Residential and non-institutional new construction remained soft, consistent with the preview’s expectation of continued softness; the incremental surprise was that single-family conditions were slightly worse than last quarter.

surprises.description: Intapp reported Q4 revenue of $152.5 million, above the preview’s $150.5 million estimate and $149.75 million consensus. The beat was positive but relatively modest against those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 total revenue was $152.5 million (up 13% YoY)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue … Consensus $149.75M”; “My estimate: $150.5M.”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP operating income reached $34.3 million, well above the preview’s roughly $28.9 million consensus estimate and $29.5 million estimate. That was a substantially larger profit result than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “non-GAAP operating income of $34.3 million versus $21.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income | ~$28.9M implied | … $29.5M (19.6% margin).”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP EPS was $0.41, above the preview’s $0.39 estimate and $0.36–$0.37 consensus range. It also reached the preview’s bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “non-GAAP EPS of $0.41 versus $0.27 a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS | $0.361 …; $0.37 elsewhere”; “My estimate: $0.39”; bull scenario: “≥$0.41.”

surprises.description: AI exceeded the preview’s bull-case booking threshold: AI accounted for more than 20% of Q4 net new bookings, even though Celeste Firm AI became generally available just after quarter-end. The preview had sought a quantified contribution and framed more than 20% as a bull outcome for post-GA bookings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI now represents over 20% of net new bookings in Q4, doubling sequentially”; Celeste Firm AI “reached general availability on July 15, just after quarter close.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Celeste >20% of net new bookings post-GA” in the bull scenario; the preview also said the buy-side wanted “Celeste % of net new bookings for the full quarter.”

surprises.description: FY27 non-GAAP EPS guidance has a $1.60 midpoint, above the preview’s $1.55 consensus and slightly above its anticipated $1.50–$1.58 guide range. The top of the actual range is also above the preview’s expected high end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 guidance calls for … non-GAAP EPS of $1.58-$1.62.”

in_line: Cloud ARR was $495.7 million, up 29%, within the preview’s expected roughly $495–$501 million and 29–31% growth range; total ARR of $590.5 million was also close to the roughly $588 million expectation.
Cloud net revenue retention held at approximately 123%, in line with the preview’s expectation for stable-to-up retention from 123%.
FY27 total revenue guidance of $656.5–$660.5 million, with a $658.5 million midpoint, was broadly in line with the preview’s $656.3 million consensus and expected $650–$660 million guide range.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $14.3 million, well above the preview’s roughly $10.5 million consensus and the $9.5–11.5 million company range. The beat included $1.3 million from a one-time legacy customer project, but management’s roughly $13 million normalized baseline still exceeds the preview’s expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $14.3 million”; management flagged “a normalized baseline of ~$13 million after excluding $1.3 million from a one-time legacy customer project.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$10.5M (guide midpoint)” and company guidance of “$9.5M – $11.5M.”

surprises.description: PAR raised both full-year guidance ranges beyond the preview’s existing ranges: revenue is now $516–523 million versus $500–515 million, and adjusted EBITDA is $50–53 million versus $44–47 million. The EBITDA outlook also exceeds the preview’s bull-case threshold of $47 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year 2026 guidance, lifting total revenue to $516-523 million (from $500-515 million) and adjusted EBITDA to $50-53 million (from $44-47 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 revenue guidance of “$500M – $515M” and FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$44M – $47M”; it said a raise, particularly EBITDA “toward/above $47M,” was the bull trigger.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $133 million exceeded the preview’s $124.63 million consensus and the company’s $122.5–127.5 million range. Subscription service revenue grew 16% to $83 million, alongside the overall 19% revenue increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 total revenue grew 19% year-over-year to $133 million, with subscription service revenue up 16% to $83 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $124.63M” consensus and company guidance of “$122.5M – $127.5M.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow turned positive at $3 million and improved $11.5 million year over year, a substantially better outcome than the preview’s concern about another material cash-burn quarter. The call did not provide operating cash flow, so this is a comparison with the preview’s broader cash-burn concern rather than its specific operating-cash-flow trigger.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow rose $11.5 million year-over-year to $3 million with cash of $77 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “another double-digit burn quarter” would be concerning and identified “Operating cash flow turning positive (or at least burn <$5M)” as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: Management said ARR growth could accelerate to the mid-to-high teens in the second half, a stronger forward-growth indication than the preview’s mid-teens target. Q2 ARR itself was about $338 million, within the preview’s expected range, with organic growth above its stated 11% threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: PAR exited Q2 with “approximately $338 million in ARR,” over 17% year-over-year growth and 12.3% organic growth; management guided to “meaningfully faster ARR growth (potentially mid-to-high teens) in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “mid-teens” growth target, estimated total ARR of “~$338–342M,” and said organic growth “needs to hold ≥11% and ideally re-accelerate.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating expense fell to 38% of revenue, down 1,000 basis points year over year, with the largest run-rate step-down occurring in Q2. That was stronger than the preview’s general expectation of continued sequential declines after Q1’s 650-basis-point year-over-year improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP OpEx as a percentage of revenue improved 1,000 basis points year-over-year to 38%,” and “the largest step-down in run rate” occurred in Q2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q1 non-GAAP opex was down “650bps YoY to 43.3% of revenue” and said management “guided to continued sequential opex declines.”

surprises.description: GAAP loss per share was $0.41, much worse than the preview’s cited $0.09 GAAP loss estimate, even though the net loss narrowed year over year. The preview cautioned that published EPS estimates conflicted across vendors, so the comparison is less reliable than the EBITDA comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $17 million ($0.41 per share) from $21 million ($0.52) a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “−$0.09 GAAP / +$0.12 non-GAAP” EPS consensus and warned that published EPS consensus was contradictory across vendors.

surprises.description: PAR Intelligence was on track to reach its 50,000-site FY2026 commitment, but meaningful add-on subscription monetization is now expected to start in 2027 rather than beginning in 2026 as the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: PAR Intelligence had “roughly 20,000 live sites” with “another 20,000 planned for Q3,” while “meaningful monetization” is expected “starting in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said PAR Intelligence was “targeted at 50,000+ sites in-year with SaaS monetization beginning in 2026.”

surprises.description: The newly acquired Bridg product secured more than $1.3 million in committed ARR from two customers with contracts through 2029, an unanticipated commercial win in the preview. The amount is small relative to PAR’s overall ARR base.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The newly acquired Bridg product added over $1.3 million in new committed ARR from two customers signed through 2029.”

surprises.description: Bridg temporarily reduced non-GAAP subscription margin to 65.1% from 66.4%, with management expecting a reversal over coming quarters. The preview did not flag this acquisition-related margin reset.
surprises.fact_evidence: Bridg “temporarily lowered non-GAAP subscription margin to 65.1% from 66.4%, a reset management expects to reverse over coming quarters.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP net income was $7.5 million, or $0.18 per diluted share, above the preview’s $0.12 non-GAAP EPS estimate. This was a smaller positive EPS surprise alongside the much weaker-than-estimated GAAP loss per share.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net income improved to $7.5 million ($0.18 diluted EPS) from $0.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “+$0.12 non-GAAP” EPS consensus.

surprises.description: Hardware revenue reached $35 million, its strongest quarter in at least a decade, but management expects it to normalize in the second half. That caution tempers the preview’s focus on ongoing hardware rollouts, although the preview had already noted low-20% hardware margins and the call gave a similar margin outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hardware revenue jumped 31% to $35 million in its strongest quarter in at least 10 years, but management expects this to normalize in the second half, with margins staying in the low-20% range due to tariff and supply chain pressures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted Burger King rollouts and said “Q1 hardware was +34% YoY to $29M at low-20s margins.”

surprises.description: Nearly all new Q2 engagements included multiple products, the average customer carried about two products, and management estimated a 3x cross-sell opportunity in the existing base. The preview did not flag this level of product attachment or quantify that opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Multiproduct attachment on new Q2 engagements was nearly 100%, with the average customer now carrying about 2 products (up from ~1.5), and management estimates a 3x cross-sell opportunity within the existing base.”

in_line: Q2 ARR was approximately $338 million, within the preview’s $338–342 million estimate; 12.3% organic growth also cleared the preview’s stated minimum of 11%.
PAR Intelligence’s site rollout remained on track for the preview’s 50,000+ in-year target, with roughly 20,000 sites live and another 20,000 planned for Q3.
Hardware margins were expected to be in the low-20% range based on the preview’s Q1 margin reference; management continued to expect low-20% hardware margins.

surprises.description: Operating cash flow exceeded $36 million, allowing SBDS to repay its revolver in full and finish the quarter with $35.4 million of cash. That is a much stronger liquidity outcome than the preview’s focus on the coming Q3 covenant tests and its cited $16.5 million of cash.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow exceeded $36 million during the quarter, enabling full repayment of the revolver” and the company ended with “$35.4 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Covenant and liquidity disclosure. Leverage, fixed-charge coverage and minimum-liquidity covenants begin testing in Q3 2026. Watch cash (was $16.5M), revolver availability (was $63.6M).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $13.5 million, above the preview’s roughly $12 million de facto whisper and the midpoint of its $10–14 million guide-math range, despite sales being essentially at the whisper.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 28.6% year-over-year to $13.5 million,” with a “15.3% adjusted EBITDA margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat ~$88M / ~$12M as the de facto whisper”; Q2 needs “roughly $85–92M of revenue and $10–14M adjusted EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Chubbies sales fell 8.6%, whereas the preview treated Q2 as its seasonal peak and said sales needed to reach at least about $44 million for the order-shift story to hold. The reported decline implies sales below that benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Chubbies declined 8.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If Q2 Chubbies isn't ≥ ~$44M, the ‘orders shifted to Q2’ story fails”; the base case assumed “Chubbies ~$44M flat.”

surprises.description: Water sports surged 59%, substantially stronger than the preview’s description of watersports as a growing piece at roughly 20% growth in Q1 and its Q2 base-case estimate of about $11.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The newly-separated water sports segment surged 59%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watersports/other (ISLE, Oru): the only growing piece (~$10.2M in Q1, +~20%)”; the base-case Q2 segment build was “$11.5M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 59.9%, near the top of the preview’s 57–60% recovery range and above its 56.5% base case. This was achieved despite a Mexico-facility raw-material write-off, with prior-period tariff refunds providing an offset.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined to 59.9% from 61.3%, pressured by channel mix and a $1.4 million Mexico facility raw material write-off, largely offset by $1.5 million of prior-period IEPA tariff refunds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin recovery toward 57–60%”; the base scenario assumed “GM ~56.5%.”

surprises.description: SBDS returned to adjusted profitability, reporting $3.9 million of adjusted net income, while the preview’s base case estimated slightly negative EPS. The GAAP net loss also narrowed to $4.4 million from $13.5 million a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income of $3.9 million, versus roughly break-even in the prior-year period,” and “narrowed its net loss to $4.4 million from $13.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario estimated “EPS (est.) −$0.20.”

surprises.description: International sales rose 46% to $9.8 million, supported by a Chubbies partnership in India and three new distributor contracts, including a European partner with Yeti experience. The preview did not identify this growth or these partnerships as an expected source of upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International sales grew 46% year-over-year to $9.8 million,” and the company “signed three new distributor contracts including a Yeti-experienced European partner.”

surprises.description: New products accounted for nearly half of Solo Stove DTC sales, and management described a robust fall and holiday pipeline. The preview asked investors to watch product sell-through and holiday setup but did not anticipate this reported share of sales from launches.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New product launches accounted for nearly half of Solo Stove's DTC channel sales in the quarter,” with a “robust fall/holiday pipeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch sell-through on Summit 27 / SteelFire 22 griddle” and noted that “Q2 commentary sets up the holiday guide.”

surprises.description: Management is consolidating U.S. distribution from five facilities to one by Q4 and shifting Oru manufacturing from Mexico to a sourcing model. The preview anticipated cost savings but did not describe this specific footprint and production restructuring.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidating its U.S. distribution footprint from five facilities in 2025 to just one by the fourth quarter,” closing a U.S. distribution center and shifting Oru manufacturing “from Mexico to a sourcing model.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referenced “cost saves ($8M payroll / ~$10M fully burdened, plus ~$3.5M operational)” but did not specify this consolidation or Oru change.

in_line: Net sales of $88.5 million were essentially at the preview’s ~$88 million de facto whisper and within its $85–92 million range for the quarter.
The Stove segment’s 14.7% decline was broadly consistent with the preview’s base-case Solo Stove assumption of about $32 million, or roughly 16% down year over year.

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA margin guidance fell to 21.3% excluding refunds, below the preview’s 22.2% guide. Q2 margin was 21.5% excluding refunds, also slightly below the preview’s 21.8% estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin was 23.5%, but only 21.5% excluding refunds, and full-year margin guidance was cut to 21.3% (ex-refunds).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin: ~22.2% (trimmed from 22.5%).” The preview also estimated Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin at “~21.8%.”

surprises.description: The EPS midpoint stayed at $10.60 rather than moving higher, and the new range includes a $0.57-per-share refund benefit. That makes the underlying outlook weaker than the unchanged midpoint alone suggests.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year sales guidance was held at $6.2 billion (4.5% growth) and adjusted EPS midpoint unchanged at $10.60, with the range narrowed to $10.35-$10.85 and a $48 million/$0.57 refund benefit now incorporated.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a raise was needed: “FY adj. EPS guide vs. $10.20–11.00 — a raise is needed, not just a reaffirm.” It also identified the standing midpoint as $10.60.

surprises.description: Free cash flow guidance was cut by $50 million to $600 million instead of remaining at $650 million. The company still expects leverage below 3x in the second half, but the lower cash-flow outlook weakens the expected deleveraging path.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow guidance was reduced by $50 million to $600 million as stronger AMC growth required incremental working capital, though the company still expects net debt leverage below 3x in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Free cash flow: $650M (unchanged).”

surprises.description: Management expects price/cost headwinds to continue through the second half, rather than reaching the expected mid-year dollar-cost neutrality on schedule. Faster inflation and price lag also contributed to the lower margin outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects modest price/cost headwinds to persist through the second half due to inflation lags”; the margin outlook was cut partly because “price lagging faster inflation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “targets dollar-cost neutrality by mid-2026 — i.e., this quarter” and called for confirmation that “the crossover happened on schedule.”

surprises.description: IPS and PES growth expectations were lowered: IPS moved to low-single-digit growth from mid-single digits, while PES moved to flat-to-slightly-down. IPS has a stronger 2027 shippable backlog, but metals and mining project roll-offs create a near-term revenue air pocket.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management shifted its segment growth outlook… lowering IPS to low single digits (from mid-single) and PES to flat-to-slightly-down.” The “IPS 2027 shippable backlog is up over 20%” but prior projects “roll off and create a near-term revenue air pocket.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “explicitly guided all three segments to sequentially higher sales and margins in Q2,” with IPS benefiting “on shippable backlog” and PES from “seasonality plus lighter residential HVAC pressure.”

surprises.description: AMC’s outlook was raised to low-double-digit growth from high-single digits, while reported organic sales grew 15.6%. This was stronger than the preview’s roughly 13% Q2 AMC sales build.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AMC was the standout segment with organic sales up 15.6% and orders up 17.1%”; management raised AMC to “low double digits (from high single digits).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s AMC build estimated sales at “~$465M” versus $411.1M, or “+13%.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS of $2.99 was well above the $2.58–$2.60 expected range, but the $32 million IEEPA tariff refund explains the gap: EPS excluding refunds was $2.60, essentially in line with expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EPS was $2.99, but excluding $32 million of IEEPA tariff refunds, EPS was $2.60, representing 5% underlying growth versus the prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 adjusted diluted EPS consensus was “$2.58 – $2.60.”

surprises.description: The company now expects an additional $15 million of ePod sales in Q4, an earlier revenue contribution than the preview’s framing of 2026 as a bridge year focused on 2027 shipments. The roughly 20% ePod margin expectation was in line with the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An additional $15 million of ePod sales (at ~20% margins) now expected in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “2026 is a bridge year — the revenue is 2027's story,” and called for confirmation of “20%+ ePOD margins.”

surprises.description: Commercial rare-earth magnet supply should be mostly mitigated this quarter, but defense applications remain constrained. The commercial improvement is reassuring, while the continuing defense constraint is a remaining supply issue not specifically anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rare earth magnet supply for commercial uses should be mostly mitigated this quarter but remains constrained for defense applications.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “rare earth magnet constraints” as a margin headwind, but did not distinguish commercial from defense supply.

in_line: Enterprise daily orders grew 8.8% (8.1% excluding data center), with July still positive at 7%; this was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of positive orders decelerating from the prior quarter’s surge.
The $6.2 billion full-year sales outlook and 4.5% growth rate were held, matching the preview’s standing sales guidance.
Switchgear revenue tracking to roughly $180 million this year and $240–250 million next year was consistent with the preview’s approximately $180 million and $240 million expectations.

First-half AMC orders were up over 25%, but nearly half reflected longer-cycle projects benefiting 2027–2028; the preview had highlighted strong AMC orders and the importance of assessing order durability.

surprises.description: WRAP reported $2.1 million of Q2 revenue, above the preview’s $1.7–1.9 million estimate and its roughly $2.0 million whisper. The 103% year-over-year increase also exceeded the preview’s modeled 75–85% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue increased 103% year-over-year to $2.1 million from $1.0 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue … Q2'26E (my base) $1.7–1.9M”; “Revenue vs. ~$1.8M (my base) / ~$2.0M whisper.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was approximately 75%, far above the preview’s 58–63% estimate and opposite its expectation of year-over-year compression. The preview had identified services mix as central to margin recovery, but the reported margin expanded even though subscription revenue was still ahead rather than realized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit rose 217% to $1.5 million with gross margin expanding to approximately 75% from approximately 48% a year earlier”; subscription revenue is “still ahead of the company rather than realized.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin … Q2'26E (my base) 58–63% (down Y/Y)”; “the entire margin-recovery thesis rests on services mix rising.”

surprises.description: The $2.3 million net loss was substantially narrower than the preview’s modeled $4.3–4.8 million loss. The year-over-year improvement is less pronounced after accounting for the prior-year warrant charge, but the reported loss still beat the preview estimate by a wide margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss improved 39% to $2.3 million from $3.7 million, though the prior year included a $0.9 million non-recurring noncash warrant fair-value loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net loss … Q2'26E (my base) $(4.3)–(4.8)M.”

surprises.description: Management identified a larger potential customer pool for BolaWrap than the preview described: the ATF classification was said to open access to more than 1.2 million licensed private security officers. The preview discussed the ruling mainly as easing agency procurement, not this private-security opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: The July ATF determination classified BolaWrap 150 as a restraint/rescue tool, “unlocking access to the private security market of over 1.2 million licensed security officers—larger than the entire U.S. law enforcement population.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the ruling’s “practical effect” was that “federal/agency procurement collapses from a weapons-appropriation path to a standard non-lethal/safety-equipment line.”

surprises.description: Management pointed to 11 active reopened DOJ grant programs that could fund BolaWrap and related offerings, an additional funding route not identified in the preview. The programs may help the company’s mostly small and midsized department customers, though no dollar amount or resulting orders were given.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management identified 11 active reopened DOJ grant programs that could fund BolaWrap, body cameras, de-escalation training, and virtual training for its predominantly small and midsized department customers.”

surprises.description: The company said Chile business is excluded from its 2026 growth forecast because of a Chilean government funding gap. The preview discussed the 100% growth target and the risk of order timing, but did not flag this specific funding constraint.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management reaffirmed roughly 100% revenue growth for 2026, “with Chile business excluded from the forecast due to a Chilean government funding gap.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the target implied “~$10.4M for FY26” and highlighted that it required a step-change in H2; it did not mention Chile funding.

surprises.description: Liabilities fell to $2.0 million from $3.9 million after WRAP terminated its former office lease, a balance-sheet improvement the preview did not discuss. Cash at $4.8 million was within the preview’s $4.5–5.5 million estimate, so the surprise is the liability reduction rather than the cash balance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents grew to $4.8 million at June 30, 2026 from $3.5 million at year-end 2025, while total liabilities fell to $2.0 million from $3.9 million after terminating the former office lease.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash (period end) … Q2'26E (my base) $4.5–5.5M.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed its roughly 100% revenue-growth target for 2026, consistent with the preview’s base case of a qualitative reaffirmation without a quantified H2 bridge; its warning that results depend on the timing of one or two large orders was also consistent with the preview’s flagged timing risk.
June 30 cash of $4.8 million was within the preview’s $4.5–5.5 million estimate.
The ATF ruling and exclusive U.S. and NATO sensing-technology rights supported the counter-UAS and defense-platform narrative the preview had already identified as a key commentary focus.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA came in at $2.1 million, well above the preview’s $1.4 million estimate. Adjusted net income was also $838,000, rather than the expected near-break-even to small loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated adjusted EBITDA rose 63% year-over-year to $2.1 million from $1.3 million,” and “adjusted net income” was $838,000 ($0.04 per share).
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 base estimate was “Adjusted EBITDA $1.4M”; its EPS estimate was “$(0.01) – $0.00.”

surprises.description: SPAR returned to GAAP profitability, reporting $0.02 per diluted share instead of the preview’s expected small loss to break-even. The preview had expected GAAP EPS of $(0.01) to $0.00.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SPAR Group returned to profitability in Q2 2026 for the first time since Q1 2025,” with GAAP net income of $409,000, or $0.02 per diluted share.

surprises.description: Quarterly revenue was $36.9 million, above the preview’s $34.5 million base estimate, even though revenue still declined year over year. The preview had modeled a 10.7% decline; the reported decline was 4.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net revenues declined 4.5% year-over-year to $36.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 base was “$34.5M (–10.7% YoY).”

surprises.description: Full-year gross-margin guidance was raised by one percentage point at both ends, to 21.5%–23.5%, from the previously stated 20.5%–22.5% range. This was a more favorable outlook than the preview’s cited company guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company maintained full-year gross-margin guidance of “21.5%–23.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company FY2026 gross-margin guidance of “20.5%–22.5%.”

surprises.description: Quarterly SG&A was higher than the preview expected: $6.8 million versus a $6.3 million estimate and a stated buy-side benchmark of no more than $6.5 million. The $543,000 of one-time costs partly explains the gap, but does not eliminate it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A fell to $6.8 million from $7.9 million year-over-year, including $543,000 in one-time costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 base estimate was “SG&A ~$6.3M,” and its buy-side benchmark was “SG&A ≤ $6.5M.”

surprises.description: Despite the quarterly SG&A coming in above estimate, the full-year SG&A range was cut substantially, to $21–24 million from the previously stated $25.5–26.5 million. Management also pointed to an underlying annual run rate of roughly $20 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company maintained full-year SG&A guidance of “$21–24 million,” while management guided underlying run-rate SG&A toward “roughly $20 million annually.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited FY2026 SG&A guidance of “$25.5–26.5M.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow deteriorated rather than normalizing: SPAR used $8.7 million in cash in the quarter, compared with $3.9 million used in Q1. The preview specifically flagged cash flow as a risk to watch and said Q2 needed to show working-capital normalization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash used by operating activities was $8.7 million for the quarter,” reflecting working-capital timing tied to merchandising-business growth.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q1 operating cash flow of “–$3.9M” and said “Q2 must show working-capital normalization.”

surprises.description: SPAR disclosed a new ongoing technology agreement with ReposiTrak costing $151,500 per month to re-platform its technology and develop a scan-based trading proposition. The preview focused on whether the partnership was generating revenue, not on this recurring cost commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SPAR entered an IT agreement with Repositrak costing $151,500 per month to re-platform its technology and develop a scan-based trading proposition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether the ReposiTrak partnership was “generating revenue yet” and discussed the share issuance and ownership stake.

surprises.description: The call disclosed ongoing legal matters involving Robert Brown, which were not specifically anticipated in the preview’s discussion of board and governance tensions. Management characterized the matters as non-material.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company disclosed “ongoing legal matters involving Robert Brown that management deemed non-material.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed governance concerns, the board reset, and founder Robert G. Brown’s public pressure on the board, but did not mention ongoing legal matters.

in_line: The full-year revenue guidance was cut to $130–138 million, as the preview identified a re-base as the most likely outcome and specifically described a clean re-base to roughly $130–138 million as possible.
Q2 gross margin was 22.8%, matching the preview’s base estimate of 22.8% and exceeding its 22.5% buy-side benchmark.

The revenue decline was attributed primarily to lower remodel volume as SPAR shifted toward higher-margin recurring merchandising work, consistent with the preview’s description of a deliberate remodel-to-merchandising pivot.
The Nasdaq delisting and move to OTCQB were already known and discussed in the preview; management said the change did not alter the company’s strategy.

surprises.description: The preview treated a clean FDA review as a bull case and flagged an additional-information request or clock stop as a key risk. Management reported that the FDA sent an additional information letter in July and requires an SIR alignment meeting before the data package can be resubmitted, although the company still targets authorization later in 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Since the March FDA submission, the company roughly tripled its collected study samples and received an additional information letter in July, requiring an SIR alignment meeting before resubmitting its data package.” Management continues to target authorization “later in 2026,” while cautioning that government review timing is not fully within its control.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a clean “on track, no AI request” would be a bull-case outcome, and that “any commentary on Additional Information (AI) requests, clock stops, or a shifted timeline” was the largest swing factor.

surprises.description: Management raised its expected second-half cash burn to about $8 million per quarter, rather than the roughly $6 million per quarter the preview said was the prior expectation. The increase reflects regulatory, registry, and commercial-launch costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its second-half cash burn guidance to approximately $8 million per quarter, up from a prior expectation of roughly $6 million per quarter, due to regulatory, registry, and commercial launch costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had guided H2 burn “back toward ~$6M/quarter” and highlighted reaffirmation of “~$6M/qtr H2 burn” as a key item to watch.

surprises.description: The call introduced a $2 billion estimate for the kidney-testing opportunity, with potential to grow through more frequent surveillance, therapy monitoring, and additional organ indications. The preview discussed reimbursement and the transplant revenue ramp but gave no comparable TAM estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company estimates a $2 billion total addressable market based on a conservative 2 tests per year per kidney patient, which grows further with higher surveillance frequency, therapy monitoring, and expanded organ indications.”

in_line: The company maintained its target of FDA marketing authorization for GraftAssureDx later in 2026, consistent with the preview’s stated baseline of “later in 2026, timing uncertain,” though the additional-information letter is a separate setback.
Q2 cash burn was $10 million and management called it the high watermark, broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of Q2 burn above $9 million and its characterization of Q2 as peak burn.

The preview already noted the MolDX coverage expansion and GraftAssureCore reimbursement of $2,753 per result; the call’s details about coverage rising from 8 to 14 kidney-surveillance tests in the first three years reinforce that expected development.

surprises.description: The preview implied roughly 7–8% same-park revenue growth, based on the fresh $914 million revenue estimate and the expected divestiture-related reduction. The call reported same-park net revenue growth of only 2%, to about $864 million, despite 44 fewer operating days.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Same-park basis, Q2 2026 attendance rose 4% … and net revenue increased 2% to approximately $864 million, despite 44 fewer operating days.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Flat reported revenue on a portfolio ~$65–75M smaller in Q2 revenue terms implies ~7–8% same-park revenue growth”; Guggenheim revenue estimate: “$914M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA and margin fell short of the preview’s bar: same-park adjusted EBITDA was $249 million, versus the preview’s $288 million estimate, while the implied same-park margin was about 29% rather than the preview’s roughly 31.5% estimate and expectation of more than 30%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Same-park adjusted EBITDA increased 7% to $249 million in Q2 2026, with margins expanding roughly 120 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Guggenheim adjusted EBITDA estimate: “$288M”; the preview estimated “$288M on $914M” revenue, or “31.5%,” and said “if EBITDA margin does not print north of 30%” the cost thesis would be in question.

surprises.description: Per-capita spending declined slightly rather than reaching the preview’s expected roughly 4% increase. Higher average prices on single-day and combined pass/membership products did not prevent the overall per-capita result from being weighed down by pass mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Both single-day and combined pass/membership products [were] yielding higher average prices, while per capita spending declined less than 1% due to pass mix effects.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “per cap ~$65 (+4%)” and flagged admissions yield as a key debate, noting that “admissions per cap” was +3% in Q1.

surprises.description: The divested parks removed more year-ago revenue than the preview’s estimated portfolio headwind: $86 million rather than roughly $65–75 million. That made the reported revenue comparison more exposed to the portfolio change than the preview had modeled.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The sale of 7 noncore parks removed approximately $86 million of Q2 2025 revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a portfolio “~$65–75M smaller in Q2 revenue terms.”

surprises.description: Management gave a constructive quarterly EBITDA outlook despite the preview’s emphasis on uncertainty around the July update: it expects year-over-year adjusted EBITDA growth in both Q3 and Q4, with the larger opportunity in Q4. The preview anticipated demand and trading commentary, but not this specific growth outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects adjusted EBITDA to grow year-over-year in both Q3 and Q4 2026, with the larger growth opportunity weighted toward Q4 from Halloween and Holiday in the Park events.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said there was “no formal FY2026 guidance” and that management had chosen to guide on “demand trends, per-caps, cost discipline and liquidity instead.”

surprises.description: The Q3 operating calendar provides a larger tailwind than the preview discussed: the company plans 66 more operating days than a year earlier. This is a favorable, unanticipated offset to the July holiday timing and wildfire disruptions, though the call did not quantify its financial effect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans 2,133 operating days in Q3 2026, 66 more than the prior year, primarily due to Labor Day timing adding an extra week of summer operations.”

surprises.description: Despite the preview’s concern about a weak or merely flat July, management cited a strong attendance day on days not affected by air quality: the company recorded its highest summer attendance day in five years. This is a limited positive datapoint, not a quantified July trend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company still delivered its highest summer attendance day in five years on unaffected days.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “July flat-to-slightly-up” was the base case and described a “hot start to July and air quality issues from Canadian wildfires” as an existing concern.

in_line: Same-park attendance increased 4%, broadly matching the preview’s cited Guggenheim expectation of about 4.4% same-park growth.
The active pass base grew 6%, in line with the preview’s report of approximately 6% same-park pass-base growth through May.
Wildfire-related air-quality disruption was a known concern in the preview; the call confirmed that it caused some park closures.

surprises.description: MEC reported Q2 sales of $163 million, above the preview’s $150.6 million consensus and the company’s $145–155 million guide. That is a clear upside surprise, though organic growth was 9.2% excluding AccuFab.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 net sales rose 23.2% year-over-year to $163 million, with organic sales up 9.2% excluding the AccuFab acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales (consensus) $150.6M”; “Company Q2 guide (sales) $145–155M.”

surprises.description: Q2 free cash flow was negative despite the preview expecting a positive quarter, and MEC cut full-year free cash flow guidance from $25–35 million to $7–15 million. This is a substantial deterioration from the cash outlook investors were given.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 free cash flow was a use of $6.6 million versus $12.5 million provided a year earlier, prompting the company to lower full-year free cash flow guidance to $7-15 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance … FCF $25–35M”; “Q2 FCF positive — Q1 was −$6.9M against a $25–35M FY target.”

surprises.description: MEC raised its full-year sales outlook to $620–650 million, above the prior $590–620 million range the preview expected it to reaffirm. The higher outlook is positive, although the company did not raise its adjusted EBITDA range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 net sales guidance was raised to $620-650 million while adjusted EBITDA guidance was maintained at $52-60 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year FY26 guidance … sales $590–620M, adj. EBITDA $52–60M”; “Reaffirmation of $590–620M / $52–60M is the base case.”

surprises.description: The preview expected launch costs to roll off after Q2 as the margin recovery progressed. Instead, the full-year outlook still includes $5–6 million of launch costs plus $2–3 million of outsourcing costs, with equipment lead times delaying the move of work in-house.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year outlook includes $5-6 million of launch-related costs and $2-3 million of outsourcing costs, with new equipment carrying four-to-six-month lead times before work moves in-house.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bridge management offers is real — launch costs roll off ($1.2M in Q1, similar guided for Q2)”; the preview also expected the H2 margin step-up to be supported by launch costs rolling off.

surprises.description: Net leverage was 2.9x, worse than the preview’s estimated 2.6–2.8x after the offering and above its 2.8x checkpoint. The offering reduced debt, but the reported leverage did not reach the expected post-offering level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt rose to $134.7 million from $71.8 million a year ago, pushing the bank covenant net leverage ratio to 2.9x versus a long-term target of 2.5x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Applying ~$93.9M of net proceeds implies roughly $125–130M net debt and ~2.6–2.8x”; “Net leverage ≤ 2.8x — the clearest available positive.”

surprises.description: MEC disclosed a substantial capacity expansion plan: about $50 million of incremental investment over two years, plus a possible $25–30 million Southeast facility, to expand beyond its prior $850 million revenue capacity. The preview noted capacity conversion and a possible greenfield as watch items, but did not anticipate this scale of investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans ~$50 million of incremental investment over two years (plus a potential $25-30 million new Southeast facility) to lift revenue capacity beyond the prior $850 million level, targeting 15%+ IRR and 2-3 year payback.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year FY26 guidance … capex $15–20M”; “Secondary: capacity conversion pace … any commentary on an eastern-seaboard greenfield.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed that a single new post-acquisition customer awarded MEC more than $55 million this year. The preview discussed pipeline and quarterly award expectations but did not flag a customer award of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “One new post-acquisition customer alone awarding over $55 million this year.”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin was 8.1%, modestly above the preview’s roughly 7.6% margin implied at the guide midpoint, though it remained below the prior-year 10.3%.
DCP added about $40 million of Q2 awards, meeting the preview’s $40 million checkpoint, and its qualified pipeline remained above $125 million as expected.
The expectation that DCP would contribute about one-fifth of full-year revenue was broadly consistent with management’s forecast that it would reach approximately 20% of 2026 revenue.
Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance remained $52–60 million, as the preview’s base case anticipated.

surprises.description: Purple reported Q2 revenue of $98.3 million, below the preview’s roughly $102.5–$103.9 million expectation. The shortfall was driven primarily by wholesale weakness.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net revenue declined 6.5% year-over-year to $98.3 million from $105.1 million, driven primarily by wholesale weakness.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net revenue: ~$103.9M”; the alternate feed was “~$102.5M.”

surprises.description: Purple cut its FY2026 revenue guidance to $420–$440 million from $465–$485 million, a substantial reduction where the preview described reaffirmation as the base case. It maintained adjusted EBITDA guidance despite the revenue cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to $420–$440 million while maintaining its adjusted EBITDA outlook, trimming the top of its prior range due to wholesale softness.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the “FY2026 guidance action” was “reaffirm / trim / withdraw,” and that the base case was “FY guide reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Wholesale revenue fell 19.1%, contrary to the preview’s expectation that the channel would inflect and help carry the second half. Even excluding $5.3 million in incremental customer payments, wholesale was down about 8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wholesale revenue fell 19.1% to $37.4 million, though excluding $5.3 million in incremental customer payments (co-op marketing and related-party transactions) the decline was approximately 8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said wholesale “needs to inflect to carry H2” and noted Q1’s “early traction.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was positive $2.1 million, above the preview’s roughly breakeven threshold and its base-case range of a $2 million loss to $1 million of profit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA improved $4.4 million year-over-year to a positive $2.1 million, versus a $2.4 million loss in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 EBITDA above roughly breakeven keeps the guide credible”; the base case projected “−$2 to +$1M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 45.2%, well above the preview’s roughly 38% watch level and its expectation that margins would return toward 40%. A $5.3 million tariff refund and sourcing-driven tariff mitigation helped produce the unusually strong result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP gross margin rose about 470 basis points to 45.2%, helped by a $5.3 million tariff refund (100% of applied amount) and sourcing-driven tariff mitigation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the EBITDA bridge above is impossible without margin back toward 40%” and flagged “Gross margin vs. ~38%.”

surprises.description: The early customer response to Purple’s mid-June price increases was worse than management expected, raising a demand concern not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management took an 8–10% price increase across mattresses and pillows in mid-June to offset input inflation, but noted early consumer demand reaction was more negative than expected, with elasticity not fully readable until after Labor Day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Early consumer demand reaction was more negative than expected.”

surprises.description: The GAAP loss was much smaller than the preview’s roughly $8 million implied loss: Purple reported a $3.2 million loss and a $0.74 per-share loss, versus the preview’s post-split consensus estimate of a $1.84 per-share loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss narrowed by $14.1 million to $3.2 million, or a loss of $0.74 per share versus $4.01 last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP EPS: −$1.84 post-split” and “Implied GAAP net loss: ~$8M.”

surprises.description: Showroom comparable-store sales were up 18%, a strong acceleration from the 7% Q1 comps cited in the preview, rather than merely another positive quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Showroom revenue jumped 16.6% to $18.4 million with comparable-store sales up 18%, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of positive comps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “+7% comps in Q1” and said a “fourth consecutive positive quarter matters for the narrative.”

in_line: Purple maintained its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook, as the preview’s base case expected the EBITDA guide to be reaffirmed.
Showrooms delivered a fourth consecutive quarter of positive comparable-store sales, as the preview highlighted as an important expected outcome.
E-commerce declined modestly, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of a still slightly negative quarter after a flat March exit rate.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $1.16, below the preview’s current consensus of $1.22, rather than meeting the roughly $1.25 working estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS was essentially flat at $1.16 versus $1.17.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 Adj. EPS $1.22”; “Working center of gravity: Adj. EPS ~$1.25.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $54.2 million, below the preview’s roughly $56 million level needed to keep the full-year bridge credible, although it fell within the preview’s $54–57 million base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA declined to $54.2 million from $56.2 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 adj. EBITDA needs to land at roughly $56M+ to keep the range credible without a back-half hockey stick.”

surprises.description: Applebee’s comps were negative 1.8%, a reversal from the preview’s expectation of continued momentum and its base case of positive comps. The preview had highlighted Applebee’s traffic as a risk, but the reported comp was weaker than its expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Applebee's posted negative 1.8% comp sales (hurt by a tough April comparison against last year's Sizzlin' Skillets).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Applebee’s as having “momentum” and gave a base case of “Applebee's +0.5–1.5%”; its bull case expected “+2.5–4%.”

surprises.description: Full-year guidance was maintained, but management said results were trending toward the lower end of the range. The preview expected the range to be maintained, while specifically warning that low-end language would effectively amount to a cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was maintained but management signaled results are trending toward the lower end of the range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Buy-side expects ‘maintained’” and that “anything like ‘toward the low end’ is functionally a cut”; its base case also anticipated “maintained-but-hedged guidance.”

surprises.description: First-half adjusted free cash flow was only $3.7 million, down from $48.7 million a year earlier, rather than showing the sharp recovery the preview said investors needed to see after Q1’s negative $3.0 million. That leaves the preview’s concern about cash generation and the buyback funding more acute.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted free cash flow collapsed to $3.7 million for the first six months of 2026 from $48.7 million a year earlier,” driven by “higher capex, marketing timing, and compensation/interest payments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “Adj. FCF recovery + Q2 buyback disclosure” and said “If Q2 FCF doesn't recover sharply, the buyback runway—and the entire EPS bridge—comes into question.”

surprises.description: Applebee’s commodity inflation was much higher than IHOP’s, adding a specific cost headwind not quantified in the preview: Applebee’s costs rose 8.2%, versus 1.6% at IHOP, with mid-single-digit full-year inflation still expected at Applebee’s.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Applebee's commodity costs rose 8.2% (driven by beef and lapping favorable contracts) versus just 1.6% at IHOP, with full-year guidance of mid-single-digit and low-single-digit inflation respectively.”

surprises.description: The Q2 buyback was slower than the Q1 pace the preview highlighted: the company bought back $7 million of shares in Q2 versus $22 million in Q1. The new $100 million authorization and $29 million of year-to-date repurchases provide continued capacity, so the signal is mixed rather than a halt to buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company returned $9 million to shareholders in Q2 ($7 million buybacks, $2 million dividends) and repurchased $29 million year-to-date—about 7% of shares outstanding—under a new $100 million authorization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “retired roughly 5% of shares outstanding in Q1 alone ($22M of buyback)” and flagged “Q2 buyback disclosure” as a key metric.

surprises.description: Management said the 136 company-owned restaurants are tracking near breakeven EBITDA, with AUVs in the low $2 millions versus about $3 million for the system, and is beginning to consider refranchising them. That raises a portfolio-quality and refranchising question beyond the preview’s stated roughly three-year timeline for refranchising acquired units.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company owns 136 restaurants (about 4% of the system) tracking near breakeven EBITDA, with AUVs in the low $2 millions versus a system average near $3 million, and management is beginning to consider refranchising.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed a “refranchising timeline on the acquired units (management indicated ~3 years).”

in_line: IHOP comps were positive 1.5%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that they would turn positive and within its stated 0% to +2% full-year range; the preview’s base case was −0.5% to +0.5%.

Revenue of $240.9 million exceeded the preview’s $236.1 million consensus, but the preview had already warned that the NRP restaurant takebacks could create an optical, lower-quality revenue beat. The result was consistent with its $238–248 million base-case range.
Dual-brand conversions were producing roughly 2x single-brand sales, within the preview’s expected 1.5–2.5x uplift, and management retained the year-end target of about 80 locations.

surprises.description: Longeveron reported a Q2 net loss of $6.1 million, above the preview’s $4.4–4.9 million estimate. The loss was therefore materially wider than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened 22% to $6.1 million for Q2 2026 versus $5.0 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net loss … $4.4–4.9M.”

surprises.description: Cash at June 30 was $10.1 million, below the preview’s $11.0–11.5 million estimate. The shortfall was roughly $0.9–1.4 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents were $10.1 million as of June 30, 2026.”

surprises.description: G&A rose to $3.2 million, well above the preview’s roughly $2.6 million estimate. The increase was attributed mainly to higher legal and personnel costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “G&A expenses rose 23% to $3.2 million, driven mainly by a $0.4 million increase in legal spend and $0.2 million in personnel costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “G&A … ~$2.6M”; the preview expected “asset-light” cuts to show.

surprises.description: R&D was $3.2 million, above the preview’s $2.2–2.6 million estimate, despite the preview expecting database-lock costs to be offset by trial wind-down.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D expenses rose 7% to $3.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “R&D … $2.2–2.6M”; “ELPIS II database lock costs offset by wind-down.”

surprises.description: Revenue was about $0.3 million, below the preview’s roughly $0.35 million estimate. Management attributed the decline to the absence of contract manufacturing revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Quarterly revenue declined 10% (about $29,000) to $0.3 million due to the absence of contract manufacturing revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue … Q2’26E ~$0.35M”; the preview described the base as “Bahamas Registry + contract mfg.”

surprises.description: ELPIS-2 topline is now expected in mid-September rather than the preview’s August expectation, a modest delay. Management attributed it to MRI and last-patient-visit scheduling, not unresolved FDA statistical-analysis-plan issues.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Top-line data … in mid-September 2026”; database lock is planned for “August 31st,” with the delay attributed to “MRI and last-patient-visit scheduling rather than any unresolved FDA statistical analysis plan issues.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The trial was “guided to ‘August 2026’ topline”; the preview said “any language other than August/early September is a negative.”

surprises.description: Management described an “auction” among major potential HLHS partners, suggesting stronger partnering interest than the preview’s watch for progress or a possible term sheet. Any deal remains contingent on positive ELPIS-2 data.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is pursuing an ‘auction’ among major potential partners for HLHS commercialization contingent on positive ELPIS-2 data.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “partnering progress” and noted that “a term sheet would change the financing calculus.”

surprises.description: Management said it may still pursue BLA or pivotal status even if the RVEF primary endpoint misses significance, relying on exploratory event-based outcomes. That is more optimistic than the preview’s warning that a clean RVEF result alone would not be sufficient and that transplant-free survival or MACE signal mattered.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Even if the RVEF primary endpoint misses statistical significance, management believes it can still pursue BLA/pivotal status using exploratory endpoints like all-cause mortality and transplant-free survival,” and said it had “sufficient blinded data to demonstrate significance on event-based outcomes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Even a clean RVEF result is not sufficient — FDA has said RVEF cannot demonstrate efficacy and no longer treats ELPIS II as pivotal”; a primary-endpoint headline without “a transplant-free survival or MACE signal” should be sold, not bought.

surprises.description: The call identified a second possible priority review voucher tied to the planned pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy program; the preview’s bull-case discussion centered on a voucher from HLHS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A second potential voucher [is] tied to the planned pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the success case as carrying “a Priority Review Voucher” and mentioned pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy as one of the programs to watch for licensing.

surprises.description: The call cited a recent value of around $215 million for the HLHS-related priority review voucher, above the preview’s $150–200 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: A successful HLHS approval “would come with a priority review voucher (recently valued around $215 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management values the voucher at “$150–200M.”

surprises.description: Beyond the already known XPRIZE finalist status and $1 million award, the call highlighted eligibility for a grand prize of up to $81 million in 2029, an additional potential source of funding not mentioned in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Longeveron was “named an XPRIZE HealthSpan finalist out of over 600 applicants, earning a $1 million award and eligibility for a grand prize of up to $81 million awarded in 2029.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted the “XPRIZE Healthspan finalist news and its $1M non-dilutive award,” but did not mention eligibility for the grand prize.

in_line: Management still expects the ELPIS-2 topline readout in the near term, rather than reporting results on the call; the preview also expected the call to confirm timing, not deliver the data.
The stated cash runway into the fourth quarter of 2026 matched the preview’s note that Q1 guidance already said operations would be funded “into Q4 2026.”
The XPRIZE finalist designation and $1 million award were already noted in the preview.

surprises.description: Total segment operating income grew 21%, well above the preview’s roughly 15% growth expectation and approximately $5.3 billion quarterly bogey. Company revenue grew 7%, broadly around the preview’s 7.5% consensus growth estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total segment operating income grew 21% and total company revenue rose 7% in fiscal Q3, exceeding the company's prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total segment OI ~$5.3B” and “~+15%”; revenue consensus was “+7.5%.”

surprises.description: Experiences produced $10 billion in revenue, up 10%, with record operating income and margin—stronger than the preview’s roughly $9.8 billion revenue and 9–12% OI growth build. The segment’s FY26 OI outlook was also raised to the high end of its previously provided high-single-digit growth range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Disney Experiences delivered record fiscal Q3 revenue of $10 billion, up 10% year-over-year, with record segment operating income and margin”; guidance was “raised to the high end of the previously provided high-single-digit growth for fiscal 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Experiences revenue at “~$9.8B” and OI growth at “+9–12%.”

surprises.description: Domestic parks attendance turned positive at 3%, with global guests up 4%, rather than merely improving without turning positive as the preview’s base case allowed. Per-capita spending rose 4%, alongside attendance growth rather than relying on discounting.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Domestic parks saw 3% attendance growth and 4% per capita spending growth, while global guests rose 4%, indicating volume growth was not achieved through discounting.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the base case could involve attendance “described as ‘improved’ without turning positive”; its bull case required domestic attendance to “turn positive.”

surprises.description: Disney reported a 13% SVOD operating margin in Q3, stronger than the preview’s stated full-year threshold of at least 10%. The full-year double-digit margin outlook itself remained on track, as expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Disney delivered a 13% SVOD operating margin in fiscal Q3 and remains on track for double-digit streaming margins in fiscal 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q2’s “~10.6%” Entertainment SVOD margin and management’s commitment to “≥10% for full-year FY26.”

surprises.description: The FY26 repurchase target rose to at least $9 billion, above the preview’s expectation of at least $8 billion. Management attributed the funding to cash freed by abandoning the OpenAI deal and expected proceeds from the A&E transaction announced overnight.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Share repurchases for fiscal 2026 were raised from an initial ~$7 billion to at least $9 billion, funded by cash freed from the abandoned OpenAI deal and expected proceeds from the A&E transaction announced overnight.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged a buyback of “≥$8B” and said a “buyback raised above $8B” was part of its bull scenario.

surprises.description: Disney disclosed plans for about $24 billion of FY26 content spending and $9 billion of Experiences CapEx as part of a $60 billion, 10-year parks investment cycle, rather than leaving capex and capacity questions for D23 as the preview said management might do. The scale of investment was not specified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans ~$24 billion in content spend and $9 billion in Experiences CapEx in fiscal 2026 as part of a $60 billion 10-year parks investment cycle.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “may deliberately defer capex and capacity questions” until D23.

surprises.description: Management disclosed underperformance from The Mandalorian and Grogu and the live-action Moana, titles the preview had not identified as a risk. It nevertheless reaffirmed double-digit adjusted EPS growth for FY26 and FY27.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reaffirmed double-digit adjusted EPS growth for both fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027 despite underperformance from titles like The Mandalorian and Grogu and live-action Moana.”

surprises.description: A roughly $100 million tariff refund boosted Experiences OI in the quarter, an unflagged one-off benefit. Management said the full-year tariff impact nets to essentially zero and did not drive the raised guidance, limiting the benefit to the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately $100 million in tariff refunds hit Experiences segment OI in the quarter, but the full-year tariff impact nets to essentially zero and did not drive the raised guidance.”

surprises.description: Upfront ad commitments were strong: total volume commitments rose double digits, sports volumes rose low teens, and Super Bowl inventory was sold out. The preview did not flag this demand strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Upfront advertising showed total volume commitments up double digits and sports volumes up low teens with Super Bowl inventory sold out.”

surprises.description: SVOD ad pricing faced pressure from rising streaming supply, a negative advertising detail not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SVOD ad pricing faced pressure from rising streaming supply.”

in_line: Revenue growth of 7% was broadly in line with the preview’s approximately 7.5% consensus growth estimate.
Management reaffirmed double-digit adjusted EPS growth for FY26 and FY27, matching the preview’s expected reaffirmation.
The company remained on track for double-digit streaming margins in FY26, consistent with the preview’s expectation of at least 10% for the year.

surprises.description: LOCL’s adjusted gross margin was 27%, versus the preview’s 29% estimate. Management attributed the decline to temporary packing inefficiencies while diversifying Georgia’s channel mix, which it said have since been resolved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin declined to 27% from 30% a year earlier and 29% in Q1, due to temporary packing inefficiencies from diversifying Georgia's channel mix that have since been resolved.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The estimates table forecast “Adj. gross margin” of “29%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA loss was $5.8 million, worse than the preview’s $5.2 million estimate and below its base-case range of $5.0–$5.4 million in losses. It also slightly worsened from Q1, rather than continuing the expected sequential improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss improved 17% year-over-year to $5.8 million”; Q1 adjusted EBITDA loss was $5.7 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The estimates table forecast adjusted EBITDA of “($5.2M),” and the base scenario expected “($5.0M)–($5.4M).”

surprises.description: Cash and restricted cash ended at $10.1 million, below the preview’s roughly $12 million estimate and near its sub-$10 million warning threshold. The preview expected a decline from Q1, but the actual balance was lower than its modeled runway estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash dropped to $10.1 million from $18.8 million in Q1, reflecting operating cash burn.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The estimates table forecast cash plus restricted cash of “~$12.0M”; the preview said “Any number below ~$10M” would dominate the results.

surprises.description: The sequential net loss widened to $19.8 million, well above the preview’s $15.0 million estimate. The preview anticipated another noncash warrant-related gain, but LOCL instead recorded a $1.4 million warrant-liability loss after a $5.2 million gain in Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss narrowed to $19.8 million from $21.6 million year-over-year but widened sequentially from $12.7 million, driven almost entirely by a noncash swing in warrant liabilities from a $5.2 million gain to a $1.4 million loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The estimates table forecast net loss of “($15.0M).” The preview also said the warrant liability “likely marked down again,” generating “another non-cash gain.”

surprises.description: After quarter end, LOCL received a $12.5 million follow-on investment from an existing strategic investor. The preview’s base case assumed no financing announcement, though it identified strategic-investor financing as a possibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received a $12.5 million follow-on investment from an existing strategic investor after quarter end, adding to a $15 million March investment and prior 2025 transactions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case listed “no financing announcement”; the preview also said a strategic-investor financing would be ideal.

surprises.description: Adjusted G&A was $4.1 million, slightly above the preview’s $4.0 million estimate and flat with Q1, rather than declining modestly.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted G&A expense fell 17% year-over-year to $4.1 million, remaining flat versus Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The estimates table forecast adjusted G&A of “$4.0M,” down 2% quarter over quarter.

surprises.description: LOCL disclosed a fall pilot relaunch of its single-serve salad kits across approximately 400 Mid-Atlantic stores with a major retailer, an initiative not identified in the preview’s expected catalysts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is relaunching its single-serve salad kit line via a fall pilot across approximately 400 Mid-Atlantic stores with a major retailer.”

surprises.description: Beyond the Harris Teeter rollout already discussed in the preview, LOCL reported new July and August retail launches: five SKUs across about 66 Mid-South stores and four SKUs across about 110 Rocky Mountain stores.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New retail launches include a 5-SKU rollout across ~66 Mid-South stores in July and a 4-SKU rollout across ~110 Rocky Mountain stores in early August.”

surprises.description: LOCL reported that more efficient seeding cut seed costs by roughly 20% year over year, a cost improvement not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “More efficient seeding cut seed costs roughly 20% year-over-year.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $13.9 million, matching the preview’s $13.9 million estimate, despite year-over-year growth of 14% versus the preview’s modeled 15%.

The Harris Teeter six-SKU rollout across 250+ stores was described as fully launched, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it would be a Q3 revenue event rather than a meaningful Q2 contributor.

Tower upgrades in Georgia, Texas, and Washington were running about 10% higher yield capacity, consistent with the preview’s cited roughly 10% run-rate yield from upgrades; California investments were targeting up to 20% yield improvement, as previewed.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $5.8 million, well above the preview’s roughly $4.0 million analyst-implied anchor and within its $5.3–6.0 million bull scenario. The preview cautioned that the estimate was derived rather than reliable published consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $5.8 million,” up sharply from $3.5 million in Q1, “driven by improved conversion and international deliveries.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Analyst-implied ~$4.0M (derived, see below)” for Q2 revenue; the preview also described $5.3–6.0M as the bull scenario.

surprises.description: The quarterly loss was much smaller than the preview’s EPS consensus implied: reported EPS was -$0.02 versus an expected -$0.10. The reported net loss was consequently far less severe than the preview’s estimate-derived loss of about $1.1 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net loss of $0.3 million ($0.02 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 EPS: -$0.10”; the preview derived this as approximately a “-$1.1M net loss.”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 59%, below the preview’s 60–64% base-case range despite revenue exceeding its anchor. That is a modestly worse margin outcome than expected, though it remained above the preview’s below-58% bear-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin compressed to 59% from 69% a year earlier,” reflecting lower revenue volume and increased content production investment.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “GM 60–64%”; the preview also said margin below 58% would imply mix or pricing damage.

surprises.description: Cash after the Orlando acquisition was lower than the preview’s approximate $17–18 million gross-cash expectation: it stood at $14.3 million. The reported decline reflected both inventory investment and the facility acquisition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and equivalents declined to $14.3 million from $18.6 million at year-end 2025, reflecting inventory investment and the Orlando facility acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “~$17–18M gross cash” after the purchase and called for confirmation of cash and financing details.

surprises.description: The Orlando campus acquisition was already known, but the preview did not mention that tenant leases were expected to generate rental income. This adds a potential income source that was absent from the preview’s discussion of the purchase.
surprises.fact_evidence: The acquired Orlando campus “includes tenant leases expected to generate rental income.”

surprises.description: VirTra produced about 10 new training scenarios in the quarter, above its historical level of production; the preview did not anticipate this higher content output.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “produced ~10 new training scenarios in the quarter, above historical levels.”

in_line: Bookings were $5.5 million, within the preview’s $5–6 million base-case range, though below its roughly $6 million-plus threshold for especially clear demand confirmation.
Backlog remained approximately $24.9 million, broadly around the preview’s expected $25–26 million level.
The U.S. Army Marketplace acceptance had already been flagged in the preview; the reported access across three categories expands opportunity access but is not reported as an order.

surprises.description: Q2 sales reached $721.3 million, above the preview’s $699.1–$708.9 million consensus range. The beat was mostly from FX, as the preview had flagged as a risk, but volume/mix and price recoveries also contributed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 sales rose 2.2% year-over-year to $721.3 million,” driven primarily by “favorable foreign exchange (~$10M)” with a smaller contribution from “volume/mix and price recoveries (~$5M).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Revenue consensus was “$699.1M (Zacks) / $708.9M (MarketBeat)”; the preview also said to watch whether growth was “again FX-manufactured with negative volume.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was well below the roughly $65 million estimate, and its implied margin was about 7.5%, below the preview’s roughly 9% benchmark. The preview expected about $63–66 million in its base case; the reported result was instead near its bear-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA fell to $53.9 million from $62.8 million,” hurt by “$10M higher material costs, $8M in wage/inflation, and $8M in higher duties and tariffs.”
