surprises.description: The company disclosed that $65–68 million of alternative investments remained under pressure from lower valuations, a portfolio headwind not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$65-68 million of alternative investments remained pressured by lower valuations.”

surprises.description: Skyward Specialty’s non-cat loss ratio rose 1.4 points to 61.3% because of a mix shift toward higher-loss A&H and agriculture, and management expects the full-year accident-year loss ratio to be up roughly 1% or more. This is a headwind, but broadly matches the deterioration anticipated in the preview’s loss-ratio estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Skyward Specialty non-cat loss ratio increased 1.4 points to 61.3% driven purely by business mix shift toward higher-loss A&H and agriculture, with management expecting full-year accident-year loss ratio up roughly 1%+ offset by lower acquisition costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Loss ratio | 62.3%” versus “61.3%” a year earlier, implying about 100 basis points of deterioration.

surprises.description: The company repaid $50 million of its term loan and reduced financial leverage by two points to 26%, a debt reduction not discussed in the preview. Management said it is targeting a low-20s debt-to-capital ratio.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repaid $50 million of its $150 million term loan, reducing financial leverage 2 points to 26% as it targets a low-20s debt-to-cap ratio.”

surprises.description: Book value per share was $28.55, below the preview’s estimated Q2 range of $28.75–$29.25, despite having risen 15% from year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Book value per share increased 15% from year-end to $28.55.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Estimated Q2 BVPS of ~$28.75–29.25.”

in_line: The $30–35 million full-year underwriting fee-income guidance was reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s base-case expectation that guidance would be reaffirmed rather than raised. The preview also said fee income was tracking at or above the high end; the call reported $23 million booked in the first half.

The preview highlighted the July doubling of the buyback authorization to $100 million and expected Q2 repurchase activity. The call reported approximately $10 million of repurchases during the quarter; the authorization itself was already known before the release.

surprises.description: H&P reported an adjusted EPS loss of $0.11 per share after excluding the Utica Square gain and select items, versus the preview’s expectation of adjusted EPS of $0.11. The underlying result was therefore a loss rather than the expected profit, despite reported EPS of $0.74.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 EPS was $0.74 per diluted share, but excluding the Utica Square sale gain and select items, the company recorded a loss of $0.11 per share.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $236 million, well above the preview’s implied midpoint of about $208 million. This was a substantial beat against the range derived from segment guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $236 million, coming in above the implied midpoint of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA … midpoint ~$208M”

surprises.description: North America Solutions direct margin reached $241 million, above the $230–240 million guide, and margins were $18,700 per day—higher than the preview’s roughly $17,500–18,000 base case and above its $18,000 inflection threshold. Average rigs of 142 were within the guided range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North America Solutions averaged 142 rigs with direct margins of $241 million and industry-leading margins of $18,700 per day, up over $1,000 sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “North America Solutions … Direct margin: $230–240M”; “~140 NAS rigs at $17.5–18.0k/day”

surprises.description: The Q4 NAS outlook was stronger than the preview’s threshold for an in-line bridge: H&P guided to $245–255 million of direct margin on 145–151 rigs. It also raised full-year NAS rig-count guidance to 140–144, rather than merely narrowing the outlook as the preview anticipated might happen.
surprises.fact_evidence: “H&P raised full-year North America Solutions rig count guidance to 140-144 rigs and set Q4 NAS direct margin guidance at $245-255 million on 145-151 rigs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “An FQ4 NAS margin guide below ~$230M materially damages that bridge”; “FY ranges narrowed rather than raised.”

surprises.description: Management expressed confidence in reaching at least $45 million of quarterly International Solutions direct margin run rate, with Argentina growth offsetting Middle East activity changes. The preview discussed a much wider FQ3 International margin range but did not anticipate this specific run-rate target; it is not directly comparable to the FQ3 range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company remains confident in reaching a quarterly International Solutions direct margin run rate of at least $45 million, driven by Argentina growth offsetting Middle East conflict-related activity changes.”

surprises.description: Saudi reactivations had not proceeded as planned: five of seven suspended rigs had restarted, and the remaining two were excluded from Q4 guidance. This leaves less near-term contribution from those rigs than the stated reactivation plan implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Saudi rig reactivations lagged plans, with only five of seven suspended rigs restarted … and the remaining two rigs excluded from Q4 guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Saudi rig reactivations lagged plans.”

surprises.description: H&P disclosed a sizeable Argentina expansion plan not raised in the preview: it has roughly 25% share in Vaca Muerta with nine rigs and plans to grow to 15 FlexRigs within six to eight months, at margins in line with the U.S. Lower 48.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In Argentina's Vaca Muerta, H&P holds roughly 25% market share with nine rigs and plans to expand to 15 FlexRigs within six to eight months, with margins in line with U.S. Lower 48 levels.”

surprises.description: Management laid out a more specific deleveraging path than the preview described: a target of $40 million in annualized corporate-cost reductions by end-2027 and more than $160 million of asset-sale proceeds, prioritizing repayment of the $350 million bond due at the end of 2027 and a 1x net-debt-to-EBITDA target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management targets reducing corporate costs by an annualized $40 million by end of 2027 and raising over $160 million from asset sales, while prioritizing paying down the $350 million bond due end of 2027 to reach 1x net debt-to-EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Focus now on the $350M bond maturing end-2027.”

in_line: Revenue exceeded $1 billion versus the preview’s $987.7 million consensus, a modest beat consistent with the preview’s bull scenario of $1.03–1.06 billion being well above the base case.

The $100 million annual dividend was maintained, and buybacks or expanded returns were indicated from 2028 onward, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the base dividend would be reaffirmed and incremental returns were a 2028 event.
NAS averaged 142 rigs, within the previewed Q3 guidance range of 137–143.

surprises.description: Americas operating income was a $10 million loss, far below the preview’s roughly $90–100 million recovery expectation. This was a large shortfall against the preview’s key test of whether the region was recovering.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Americas posting a $10 million loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Americas SOI” needs to be “>$100M”; the base scenario expected “Americas ~$90M.”

surprises.description: Goodyear now expects a $200–300 million free-cash-flow burn in 2026 and continued burn into 2027, rather than the preview’s hoped-for visible progress toward a year-end working-capital inflow. The Q2 cash-flow result itself improved substantially, but the outlook still points to a longer cash-generation recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow to be a burn of $200 million to $300 million in fiscal 2026 with continued but moderating burn into 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management targets a year-end working-capital inflow — needs visible Q2 progress or the FY story breaks.”

surprises.description: Q2 free cash flow was a $69 million use, an improvement of $318 million year over year and a substantial step toward the visible Q2 progress the preview was watching for. This is a positive quarterly result even though the full-year outlook remains a burn.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow improved $318 million versus the prior year to a $69 million use.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 FCF was -$893M” and the preview said Goodyear “needs visible Q2 progress.”

surprises.description: Unit volume declined 4%, materially better than the preview’s roughly 10% decline assumption. That points to less volume pressure than the bridge and scenarios had built in.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Unit volume declining 4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “units ~-10%” in its bridge and watched for volume “vs. the ~-10% guide.”

surprises.description: Sales of $4.3 billion were above the preview’s working consensus of about $4.15–4.20 billion, although near the high end of its cited vendor estimates. The beat was therefore positive but limited by the unusually wide estimate range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 sales were $4.3 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working consensus: revenue ~$4.15–4.20B”; the preview also cited estimates as high as “$4.33B.”

surprises.description: EMEA remained loss-making at $17 million, rather than reaching the preview’s roughly breakeven expectation. The gap was modest, and the loss was smaller than the prior-year $25 million loss cited in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EMEA a $17 million loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected “EMEA still ~breakeven.”

surprises.description: Management said raw materials could bring relief in 2027 as the 4–6 month lag works through and index resets take effect. The preview focused on the second-half headwind and did not flag this possible later-period relief.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A 4-6 month lag and index resets could bring relief in 2027.”

in_line: Non-GAAP EPS was a $0.61 loss, essentially in line with the preview’s working estimate of about a $0.60 loss and within its cited range; the unusually high regional-mix tax expense was the stated driver.
Total segment operating income of $36 million was within the preview’s implied $30–70 million range, albeit just below its $40–70 million base case.
The second-half raw-material headwind remained about $200 million, in line with the preview’s stated expectation; the preview had also identified a possible re-raise as a key risk.

The Fayetteville closure benefits and approximately $200 million of cash costs were consistent with the preview’s cited $90 million 2027 benefit, $270 million annual benefit from 2028, and $190–210 million cash-cost estimate.
The company reaffirmed full-year segment operating income guidance of about $600 million or slightly higher, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the FY framework would be reaffirmed.

APAC remained the bright spot, consistent with the preview; the preview also anticipated OE share gains and stronger premium mix, so the reported consumer OE growth, regional share gains, and 18-inch-and-above rim-size increase are broadly consistent with those themes.

surprises.description: SVV raised the low end of its full-year outlook even though the preview expected guidance to be reaffirmed or narrowed and viewed a raise as unlikely. The low end increased for sales, comps, adjusted EPS, and adjusted EBITDA, while the high ends stayed unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised the low end of its 2026 outlook” to net sales of “$1.77-$1.79 billion,” comps of “3-4%,” adjusted EPS of “$0.47-$0.53,” and adjusted EBITDA of “$265-$275 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance: ... Net sales $1.76–1.79B | Comps +2.5–4.0% ... Adjusted EBITDA $260–275M”; the preview said the base case was “FY guidance reaffirmed or narrowed, not raised” and called a raise “unlikely given FX.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA came in above the preview’s $71–73 million estimate, and the 16.6% margin also exceeded its roughly 16.0% forecast. The margin was slightly above the preview’s 16.5% year-ago reference as well.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA rose 8% to $75 million with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 16.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA (implied) ~ $71–73M”; “Adjusted EBITDA $72M” and “Margin ~16.0% vs 16.5% LY.”

surprises.description: U.S. comparable sales were stronger than the preview’s mid-single-digit base estimate: the reported 6.6% exceeded its 5.5% estimate and reached the level the preview described as a potential upside signal. Sales growth was also supported by both transactions and basket size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “US net sales grew 11.6% to $255 million with comparable store sales up 6.6%, driven by both higher average basket and transactions across regions, categories, and income cohorts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side is anchored on U.S. mid-single-digits”; the base case forecast “U.S. +5.5%,” and the preview said “Above +6% and the stock re-rates.”

surprises.description: Management gave a more ambitious longer-term margin trajectory than the preview discussed, targeting annual adjusted EBITDA margin expansion starting in 2027 and a return to high-teens margins within three years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management now targets 50 to 100 basis points of annual adjusted EBITDA margin expansion beginning in 2027 and a return to high-teens margins within the next three years.”

surprises.description: The Thrift IQ pilot produced better gross-profit-dollar growth than non-pilot stores while keeping average prices at the same or a lower level, an operating result the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The new Thrift IQ pricing platform, live in 58 stores, delivered gross profit dollar growth roughly 100 basis points higher than non-pilot stores while maintaining equal or lower average prices (40-70% off retail).”

surprises.description: Thrift IQ also appears to be improving store and labor productivity: grader training time was cut roughly in half, and more than half of the 2025 new-store class reached positive four-wall contribution in Q2, ahead of prior classes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Thrift IQ has cut new grader training time by approximately half and helped more than half of the 2025 new store class achieve positive four-wall contribution in Q2, ahead of prior classes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged new-store productivity and the back-half-weighted opening cadence as an issue to watch, but did not anticipate these results.

surprises.description: SVV reported a larger annualized interest-expense reduction than the preview’s modeled quarterly tailwind would suggest. The preview expected about $2 million per quarter from the prior refinancing; the call cited approximately $20 million of annualized savings from refinancing and repricing over the past year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Debt refinancing and repricing reduced annualized interest expense by approximately $20 million over the past year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Interest expense, net ~$12.5M” versus “~$14.6M”; the preview described a “~$2M/quarter interest tailwind from the 2025 term loan refi.”

surprises.description: Canada’s reported comp was slightly above the preview’s roughly 0.5% estimate, but the 70-basis-point Easter benefit means the underlying comp was close to flat rather than a clear improvement. That makes the reported positive sign less convincing than a clean Canadian turnaround.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Canada comps rose only 0.8% (including a ~70 bps Easter shift benefit).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base build estimated “Canada +0.5%” and said “A positive Canadian comp would be the genuine upside surprise here.”

surprises.description: SVV bought back 1.2 million shares at a weighted average price of $8.10, below the preview’s expectation of continued repurchases near $10–11. The repurchase continued as expected, but at a lower average price.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased 1.2 million shares at a weighted average price of $8.10 while holding net leverage at 2.4x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Continued repurchase near $10–11 is a modest confidence signal; a pause is a yellow flag.”

in_line: The third consecutive quarter of year-over-year adjusted EBITDA growth was consistent with the preview’s expectation if Q2 reached its roughly $72 million estimate.

Q3 adjusted EBITDA being modestly below Q2, with comps moderating as comparisons get tougher, was broadly consistent with the preview’s warning about back-half store-opening costs and tightening comparisons.
Canada’s segment-profit improvement was consistent with the preview’s expectation that productivity and processing-center efficiency could support profit despite weak comps.
The higher share of onsite donations plus GreenDrop fits the preview’s expectation of robust onsite donation growth and its focus on supply as a margin-supporting input.

surprises.description: Cipher reported Q2 revenue of $25 million, below the preview’s central estimate of about $29.3 million and also below its lower consensus alternative of $29.79 million. The decline reflected the Black Pearl mining shutdown during the shift to contracted data center revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $25 million, down from $35 million in Q1, reflecting the decommissioning of bitcoin mining at Black Pearl amid the transition to contracted data center revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $29.28M” (with alternatives of $29.79M and $32.52M).

surprises.description: The GAAP loss was substantially worse than the preview’s expected loss of roughly $0.21 per share: Cipher reported a $0.65 diluted loss per share. A $150.5 million noncash warrant remeasurement loss was the primary reason for the wider net loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 GAAP net loss of $268 million ($0.65 per diluted share), widening from a $114 million loss in Q1, primarily due to a $150.5 million noncash warrant remeasurement loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS: -$0.21” (with alternatives of -$0.11 and -$0.24).

surprises.description: Initial Black Pearl data center capacity was delivered two months ahead of schedule, and rent began in August rather than the preview’s expected October start. The early delivery was requested by the tenant, while the remaining delivery deadlines were unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cipher delivered initial data center capacity at Black Pearl two months ahead of schedule at the tenant's request, with rent commencing in August, though the remaining Black Pearl delivery deadlines stay unchanged.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Black Pearl rent commencement (AWS) | October 2026.”

surprises.description: Cipher added up to 1.1 gigawatts of potential Texas capacity, including the option-based Apollo site targeting 2031 and a Stingray expansion. The preview focused on possible leases at Reveille or Ulysses and did not flag these capacity additions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added up to 1.1 gigawatts of potential new Texas capacity this quarter, including a 900-megawatt site called Apollo (option-based, near San Antonio, targeting 2031) and a 200-megawatt Stingray expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A fourth lease — Reveille (70 MW, ERCOT-approved, Q3 2027) or Ulysses (200 MW, PJM-approved, Q4 2027).”

surprises.description: Management said it does not expect to need additional equity for near-term commitments, easing the dilution concern raised in the preview. Unrestricted liquidity was also $870 million versus $715 million at Q1, although total debt had risen above $6 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cipher ended Q2 with total assets of $7.5 billion (up 75% from year-end), $870 million of unrestricted liquidity, over $6 billion of total debt outstanding, and no cash borrowings on its $200 million revolver, and management does not expect to require additional equity for near-term commitments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The question: can Reveille/Ulysses be funded with project debt, or does equity/ATM come? Any signal of common equity issuance is a clear negative.” The preview cited “Unrestricted cash was $715M” at Q1.

surprises.description: An unexpected Texas interconnection queue audit delayed the expected ERCOT Batch Zero results and introduced timing uncertainty. Management said the delay could also increase the value of Cipher’s 477 megawatts available outside the batch process, making the development mixed rather than purely negative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Texas Governor Abbott issued a letter the day before the call requesting an interconnection queue audit, delaying the expected Friday ERCOT Batch Zero results and creating timing uncertainty, though management believes it increases the value of Cipher's 477 megawatts available in 2027 outside the batch process.”

surprises.description: The Stingray bond attracted unusually strong demand and priced tighter than prior bonds despite widening credit spreads. The preview already knew the bond had a 6% coupon, so the surprise is the reported oversubscription and relative pricing strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cipher priced an $810 million project-level senior secured bond for Stingray at a 6% coupon (its lowest to date), which was approximately 8x oversubscribed and priced tighter than prior bonds despite widening credit spreads.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “the $810M 6.000% Stingray notes due 2031” had been priced in June.

in_line: Average annualized NOI from the three executed data center leases was approximately $793 million, broadly matching the preview’s expected approximately $787 million.

The expectation of data center rental revenue beginning in the second half of 2026 remained broadly intact: the call said first rental payments would begin at Barber Lake and Black Pearl in that period.

Odessa’s 207 MW mining operation, approximately 11.6 EH/s at 17.2 J/TH, and an end-of-2027 conversion target were broadly consistent with the preview’s description of the site and planned mining exit. The call added that tenant discussions were early-stage and a conversion depends on renegotiating the PPA.

surprises.description: ROK’s sales growth was stronger than the preview’s 5.2% revenue-growth consensus: reported sales rose 8%, implying roughly $2.32B versus the $2.26B estimate. Organic growth was 10%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 fiscal 2026 reported sales rose 8% and organic sales rose 10%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $3.49 exceeded the $3.39 consensus and was also above the preview’s implied $3.24–$3.36 range from management’s earlier Q3 framing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $3.49, up more than 20% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS | $3.39 (Zacks) / $3.37 (S&P/Barchart)”; management’s Q3 framing “implies $3.24–$3.36.”

surprises.description: ROK raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to a $13.15 midpoint, up $0.35 from the prior midpoint and slightly above the $13.03–$13.06 consensus. The raise met the preview’s central requirement, though the new midpoint remained below its suggested $13.20+ threshold for a more forceful raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $13.00-$13.30 ($13.15 midpoint) … and up $0.35 from prior midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bar is a raise, not a beat”; FY26 adjusted EPS consensus was “$13.03–$13.06”; the preview said “Watch for a raise to $13.20+.”

surprises.description: Full-year sales guidance rose to an 8.5% midpoint from the prior 7% midpoint, putting the midpoint above the preview’s 7.5% consensus growth estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year fiscal 2026 organic and reported sales growth guidance to 7.5%-9.5% (8.5% midpoint), up 150 bps from prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 revenue consensus implied “+7.5%”; the preview said the bar was a guidance raise.

surprises.description: Software & Control organic sales growth of 18% was well above the preview’s 11.1% segment-sales growth estimate, and segment margin expanded 320 basis points rather than merely delivering the forecast 15.5% growth in operating profit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Software & Control organic sales grew 18% with segment margin of 34.8% (up 320 bps) and incrementals of about 50%, driven by strong double-digit Logix growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Software & Control sales | $698M | $628M | +11.1%”; “Software & Control op. profit | $230M | $199M | +15.5%.”

surprises.description: The enterprise margin held up better than the preview’s base-case expectation of a 50–100 basis-point sequential decline: it was 22.3%, only 20 basis points below Q2’s 22.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enterprise operating margin reached 22.3%, up 280 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “margin down ~50–100bps sequentially as flagged”; Q2 enterprise margin was 22.5%.

surprises.description: Book-to-bill slipped below 1.0, crossing the preview’s explicitly flagged threshold for reopening concerns about pull-forwards and future demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lifecycle Services organic sales fell 2% with a book-to-bill of 0.97.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If Q3 book-to-bill slips below 1.0, the pull-forward debate reopens immediately”; the preview also said below 1.0 would give the “orders were borrowed from FY27” bear case evidence.

surprises.description: Inflation and memory costs became a larger-than-anticipated second-half drag. The preview already expected a double-digit-million-dollar headwind, but the call described it as a higher double-digit-million drag, hitting Software & Control hardest; positive price/cost in Q4 and for the full year partly offsets it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inflation is an increasing headwind, now a higher double-digit-million second-half drag, hitting Software & Control hardest via memory costs, though price/cost is expected positive in Q4 and full year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged rising memory/DRAM costs as a “double-digit million-dollar” headwind and said to watch whether “the memory number got bigger.”

surprises.description: Growth was not solely dependent on data center demand: organic growth would still have been 8% excluding data center, with early double-digit recovery in Automotive and 10% growth in Life Sciences—stronger breadth than the preview’s emphasis on muted investment in other verticals suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding data center, organic growth would still have been 8% in the quarter, with early recovery signs in Automotive (up low double digits) and Life Sciences (up 10%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “capital investment remains muted in other key verticals” as management’s Q2 language and emphasized dependence on data center, semiconductor, and warehouse automation momentum.

in_line: E-commerce & Warehouse Automation sustained 30% growth, consistent with the preview’s cited Q2 growth of 30% and its expectation of continued momentum.

Lifecycle Services remained in organic decline, consistent with the preview’s warning that it was the segment still shrinking; the separate book-to-bill reading of 0.97 was weaker than the preview’s threshold expectation.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was slightly better than the preview’s company-cadence estimate: $125 million versus an implied roughly $122–125 million, and management said it was ahead of company expectations. The 14.7% margin was within the preview’s estimated 14.5–14.8% range, so the beat was modest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of approximately $125 million (14.7% margin) … ahead of company expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA (on ≥$530M) | $122M – $125M”; “Q2 adjusted EBITDA vs. ~$123M.”

surprises.description: Same-facility revenue growth was stronger than the preview’s estimated 3.5–4.5%, reaching 5%. The increase came almost entirely from rate, rather than stronger case volume.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Same-facility net revenue increased 5% in Q2 (4.8% from rate, 0.3% from case growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Same-facility revenue: *~+3.5–4.5% (est.)*.”

surprises.description: Case growth was weaker than the preview’s expected 0.5–1.5% base-case range and well below the 1.5–2.0% reacceleration the preview said the volume story needed. Management described a strategic shift toward higher-acuity procedures rather than volume growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Same-facility revenue included “0.3% from case growth,” reflecting “a strategic shift toward higher-acuity procedures rather than volume growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “SF revenue +3.5–4.5% on +0.5–1.5% cases”; “Volume needs to reaccelerate toward +1.5–2.0%.”

surprises.description: The Idaho Falls disclosure supplied more detail on what leaves with the hospitals: excluding them, Q2 revenue would have been about $660 million and adjusted EBITDA about $98 million, while pro-forma Medicaid exposure would be below 2%. The facilities also had substantial capital needs and limited distributions relative to EBITDA, making the cash economics of the divestiture more favorable than EBITDA alone suggests.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding Idaho Falls, Q2 revenue would have been approximately $660 million and adjusted EBITDA approximately $98 million, with pro-forma Medicaid exposure falling to less than 2% of the business”; the facilities averaged “approximately $17 million in annual capex” and distributions to Surgery Partners were “less than 50%” of adjusted EBITDA.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Retained EBITDA disclosure — the market cannot underwrite pro forma numbers without knowing what leaves with the hospitals.”

surprises.description: Commercial payer mix slipped below the roughly 50% level highlighted in the preview, to about 49%. The decline was about 350 basis points year over year and was concentrated in larger surgical hospitals.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial payer mix declined to approximately 49% of net revenue in Q2, about 350 basis points lower year-over-year,” driven primarily by shifts within larger surgical hospitals.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Commercial payer mix (~50% in Q1)”; the bear scenario flagged “commercial mix slips below 50%.”

surprises.description: Physician recruiting exceeded the preview’s roughly 140-per-quarter recruiting pace: Surgery Partners recruited 191 physicians in Q2. The new cohort’s initial revenue contribution was also up nearly 16% versus the prior-year cohort, with no specific growth rate anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recruited 191 new physicians in Q2 (330 year-to-date), with the 2026 cohort’s initial revenue contribution up nearly 16% versus the prior year cohort.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The ~140-physician/quarter recruiting engine converting to volume.”

surprises.description: Management made clear that Surgery Partners will not reach its stated $200 million annual M&A investment target in 2026, with only an immaterial amount of acquisitions completed year to date. The preview had already highlighted the slow pace, but the explicit confirmation rules out meeting the target this year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management confirmed the company will not reach its $200 million annual M&A investment target in 2026 … having completed only an immaterial amount of acquisitions year-to-date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Just $4M in Q1 against a stated ~$200M/yr target — a real drag on the growth algorithm.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of approximately $849 million was close to the $846.97 million consensus estimate and within the preview’s $830–850 million base-case range.
Adjusted EBITDA of approximately $125 million and a 14.7% margin were at the top end of the preview’s estimated ranges; year-over-year EBITDA was slightly lower, as expected.
The company reaffirmed 2026 revenue guidance of $3.35–$3.45 billion and adjusted EBITDA guidance of at least $530 million excluding Idaho Falls, as the preview expected.
The Idaho Falls sale agreement’s approximately $795 million gross proceeds matched the already-disclosed transaction terms in the preview.

surprises.description: Bitcoin production reached 932 BTC, above the preview’s 800–870 BTC base estimate and its 850 BTC bull-case threshold. This was a stronger production quarter than the preview’s expectation that volume would merely hold up.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 Bitcoin production reached a record 932 BTC, up approximately 14% from 817 BTC in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... ~800–870 BTC”; “Bull: ≥850 BTC mined”; “Volume should hold up.”

surprises.description: Bitcoin holdings finished the quarter at 8,002 BTC, above the preview’s expected 7,500–7,900 range and near the top of its expected 500–1,000 BTC additions. The preview had highlighted a sharp slowdown from Q1 accumulation, but additions from the 7,021 BTC Q1-end balance were about 981 BTC.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The strategic Bitcoin reserve grew nearly 1,000 BTC (about 14%) to 8,002 BTC at quarter end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “That implies Q2 additions of roughly 500–1,000 BTC vs. +1,620 in Q1 — a sharp deceleration”; “holdings ~7,500–7,900.”

surprises.description: Satoshis per share rose about 11% in the quarter instead of being roughly flat, while the share count grew only about 3% against 14% Bitcoin growth. The company also described the remaining ATM capacity as flexible and pausable when issuance would not be accretive, addressing the preview’s concern about below-NAV dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Satoshis per share rose about 11% quarter-over-quarter”; “Share count grew only about 3% versus 14% Bitcoin growth,” and “roughly 82% of ATM program capacity remains available, giving flexible capital that management can pause when accretion conditions are unfavorable.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “SPS roughly flat post-split-adjustment”; “Any disclosure of continued below-NAV issuance — versus a stated pause — will likely drive the reaction more than the P&L.”

surprises.description: Revenue per Bitcoin was about $71,900, substantially above the preview’s expectation that it would fall toward the low $60,000s. That stronger realized revenue per coin helped revenue rise despite the lower Bitcoin price.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue per Bitcoin was about $71,900, down 5% from $76,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Realized price per BTC likely drops toward the low-$60Ks.”

surprises.description: Revenue of roughly $67 million was below the preview’s cited aggregator estimates of $73.8–$75.3 million, although it exceeded the preview author’s own $50–$60 million base estimate. The comparison is uncertain because the preview called the aggregator figure undated and likely stale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue grew approximately 8% to roughly $67 million from $62.1 million in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: ~$73.8M–$75.3M cited by aggregators, no publication date verifiable”; “Base: Revenue ~$50–60M (my estimate)”; “That estimate looks stale.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed that President and Interim CFO Matt Prusak would depart effective August 4, with Head of Derivatives Paul Sacks taking over as Interim CFO. The preview did not flag a leadership transition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “President and Interim CFO Matt Prusak is departing effective August 4, with Head of Derivatives Paul Sacks stepping in as Interim CFO.”

in_line: Cost to mine held near $36,000 per Bitcoin, as the preview expected costs to remain near or below $36,000.
The digital-asset fair-value loss was $71.2 million, within the preview’s estimated $60–$90 million range for the mark-to-market hit; the preview also expected a large, mostly non-cash GAAP loss.
Gross margin compressed from 52% to 49%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that lower realized Bitcoin prices would pressure margins.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $3.5 million, well below the preview’s $4.55 million consensus estimate. Management attributed the decline to BARDA work moving into a cost-sharing phase and the completion of the MTEC contract.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 R&D revenue declined to $3.5 million from $5.1 million in Q2 2025,” driven by “the transition of BARDA work into a cost-sharing phase and completion of the MTEC contract.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 FY26 consensus | $4.55M.”

surprises.description: Cash at quarter-end was $14 million, versus the preview’s estimate of about $8 million after a similar quarterly burn. The company also reported access to more than $60 million of additional non-dilutive BARDA funding, a stronger liquidity picture than the preview’s cash-focused downside scenario anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “As of June 30, 2026, Spectral AI held $14 million in cash” and had “access to over $60 million of additional non-dilutive BARDA funding.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A similar Q2 burn puts cash near $8M” and “cash at 6/30” was estimated at “$8–9M” in the base case.

surprises.description: FDA clearance triggered a $6.5 million draw from the Avenue Capital facility, and the interest-only period was extended to 24 months with no principal due until March 2028. The preview flagged balance-sheet risk and possible new financing disclosures but did not anticipate these specific facility terms.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FDA clearance triggered the drawdown of the second $6.5 million tranche” of the facility and “extended the interest-only period to 24 months with no principal payments due until March 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch also for any new ATM, warrant inducement, or debt facility disclosed in the 10-Q.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a specific commercial structure: capital purchases or leases paired with recurring software and services on a minimum three-year term. A third-party pricing study also indicated that the market can support margins well above current development work, adding concrete pricing and margin evidence beyond the preview’s request for a pricing model.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The commercial model combines capital purchases or leases with recurring software and services revenue on a minimum three-year term,” and “a third-party pricing study indicated the market will support margins well above current development work.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for details on “the pricing/placement model (capital sale vs. per-scan vs. placement-plus-consumable).”

surprises.description: The company specified plans to deploy up to 30 systems through its BARDA CLIN II Project BioShield contract by June 30, 2027, with a longer-term opportunity across more than 200 high-value U.S. facilities. This is a concrete placement target that the preview had sought but did not identify in advance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to deploy up to 30 systems under its BARDA CLIN II Project BioShield contract through June 30, 2027,” with a “longer-term opportunity across over 200 high-value US facilities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said investors wanted “a number (LOIs, POs, units, sites)” and a “target number of US burn centers in year one.”

surprises.description: The company expects UKCA clearance in Q4 2026, which could enable initial sales in the UK, Australia, or Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The preview did not identify this international-market timing or opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects UKCA clearance in Q4 2026 to enable initial international sales in the UK, Australia, or Gulf Cooperation Council countries.”

in_line: FY2026 revenue guidance remained approximately $18.5 million, as the preview expected; the reported facts do not provide a new H2 bridge or a change to that guidance.

GAAP EPS of -$0.13 was within the preview’s cited estimate range of -$0.11 to -$0.15. The preview also warned that GAAP EPS could be distorted by non-cash warrant-liability changes; the reported narrowing in net loss was primarily due to a non-cash warrant fair value swing.

surprises.description: Tejon reported $0.10 per share versus the preview’s $0.02 consensus expectation. The Dedeaux land sale contributed $2 million of recognized profit, while another $3 million was deferred because Tejon retained an ownership interest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income attributable to common stockholders reached $2.6 million ($0.10 per share)” and the land sale contributed “$2 million of recognized profit, with an additional $3 million of profit deferred due to the company's retained ownership interest.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP) | Consensus | $0.02.” The preview’s base scenario also assumed “no land sale.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA grew approximately 47% year over year, stronger than the preview’s base-case expectation of modest EBITDA growth. The preview said there was no consensus estimate for this metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew approximately 47% year-over-year, and trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA rose 21% to $29.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA | n/a — not surveyed”; the base case anticipated “modest EBITDA growth on cost cuts.”

surprises.description: Liquidity ended at approximately $79 million, below the preview’s roughly $86 million Q1 level, despite the land sale and positive quarterly net income. That is a weaker cash trajectory than the preview’s roughly zero trailing free-cash-flow description suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with approximately $79 million of liquidity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Liquidity has been walking down” from “~$86M at Q1”; the preview also said “Free cash flow is roughly zero on a trailing basis.”

surprises.description: Joint venture equity earnings rose 21%, with gains attributed to TA/Petro and improved outlet results as well as the fully leased industrial portfolio. The preview highlighted full occupancy and outlet performance but did not set an expectation for this earnings growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Joint venture equity earnings rose 21% to $3.1 million, led by TA/Petro, improved outlet results, and a fully leased industrial portfolio.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described industrial as “100% leased” and Outlets at Tejon as “92%” leased, but provided no JV equity earnings growth expectation.

surprises.description: The board will shrink from nine directors to seven by next May, a governance change the preview did not anticipate. The preview focused on shareholder demands and management’s flexibility on alternatives rather than a board-size reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The board is reducing its size from 9 to 7 directors by next May.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed the “25% shareholder special-meeting right” and management’s statement that it would “consider all alternatives and look to remain flexible”; it did not mention a board reduction.

surprises.description: The industrial building was already expected to be developed through a Dedeaux JV, but the call specified that the 60-40 structure requires minimal net cash investment from Tejon. That financing detail is favorable and was not part of the preview’s stated expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is developing a 510,000 square foot Class A industrial building through a 60-40 joint venture with Dedeaux, targeting an early 2027 delivery with minimal net cash investment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the 510,385 sq ft Building 1B as targeting “early-2027 delivery” and identified the JV land contribution as a key potential swing item, but did not state that the project would require minimal net cash investment.

in_line: Terra Vista leasing crossed 80%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the project would confirm or remain on track with its summer 2026 stabilization target.
The preview expected cost discipline; the call reported core corporate expenses down 18% over the first six months.
The preview highlighted opportunistic water sales and water-asset monetization as key themes; management discussed pursuing opportunistic and strategic water sales and infrastructure investments.

surprises.description: The preview treated August 22 as the imminent PDUFA date, but Capricor said the FDA agreed to extend it after receiving a planned BLA amendment. The BLA remains under review, but the expected decision timing is now subject to a delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The BLA remains under review with a PDUFA target action date of August 22, 2026, though the FDA has agreed to extend that date upon receiving a planned BLA amendment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The August 22 PDUFA for deramiocel — nine days after the call — is the entire equity.”

surprises.description: Rather than continuing to pursue the preview’s cardiomyopathy-focused approval path, Capricor plans to amend the BLA for a refined indication focused on upper-limb skeletal-muscle function. That may build on the favorable upper-limb data, but it also represents a narrower proposed use than the cardiomyopathy indication at the center of the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capricor plans to submit a BLA amendment including 24-month open-label extension data from HOPE-3 to pursue a refined indication focused on upper limb skeletal muscle function rather than cardiomyopathy.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview centered on the August 22 PDUFA and described the advisory committee vote as being on “substantial evidence of effectiveness in DMD cardiomyopathy”; it noted that “the panel's upper-limb discussion was reportedly directionally supportive.”

surprises.description: A statistical-model correction weakened the all-patient left-ventricular-ejection-fraction result from the earlier 2.4-point, p=0.04 result to 1.8 points, p=0.09. The cardiomyopathy subgroup result remained significant, but results lower in the testing hierarchy are now only nominally significant.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A statistical model correction reverted the key secondary endpoint (LV ejection fraction in all patients) from a 2.4-point difference (p=0.04) at top line to a weaker 1.8-point difference (p=0.09) as published in The Lancet”; the subgroup result was unchanged at 2.8 points with p=0.02, while lower endpoints are “now only nominally significant.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the FDA briefing document reported that HOPE-3 “failed its prespecified primary and secondary endpoints,” but did not flag this subsequent model correction or its specific effect on the published result.

surprises.description: Q2 loss was worse than the preview’s estimates: net loss was about $40.7 million and EPS was $(0.70), versus an estimated net loss of about $35 million and EPS of $(0.60), with consensus EPS at $(0.58)–$(0.59). Higher operating expenses accompanied the miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss widened to approximately $40.7 million ($0.70 per share) … with operating expenses rising to $42.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS … $(0.58) – $(0.59)”; “My Estimate” was $(0.60), and “Net loss” was estimated at “~$35M.”

surprises.description: Capricor said it is slowing commercial-readiness spending and pacing capital deployment until it has more regulatory clarity, rather than maintaining an unchanged launch build. The preview had identified a spending pause as a possible response to regulatory uncertainty, but not as its base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is slowing commercial readiness spending and pacing capital deployment until it gains greater regulatory clarity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked, “Are they still spending into launch?” and described the base case as “no new information”; it listed commercial spend “paused” in the bear scenario.

surprises.description: Capricor withdrew its preliminary-injunction motion against NS Pharma and said rescission of the U.S. distribution agreement will instead proceed through arbitration expected this fall. The preview identified the litigation as important, but had looked for an injunction ruling, settlement, or reversion of rights rather than this stated route and timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capricor withdrew its preliminary injunction motion against NS Pharma and will pursue rescission of the U.S. distribution agreement through arbitration expected to begin this fall.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “any settlement, injunction ruling, or reversion of U.S. rights” would be a catalyst and listed “hearing dates, settlement posture, or reversion of U.S. commercial rights” to watch.

surprises.description: The company also put all work on its non-deramocel pipeline on hold, a broader cutback than the preview’s discussion of launch spending and manufacturing readiness anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “All non-deramocel pipeline work is on hold.”

in_line: The call reported no Q2 revenue, consistent with the preview’s $0 estimate and its warning that revenue consensus was unreliable.
Quarter-end cash and marketable securities of approximately $237.9 million fell within the preview’s estimated $232–248 million range and its base-case range of about $235–248 million.
The call’s report of the advisory committee vote—9 against and 3 in favor—matched the vote already disclosed in the preview.

HOPE-3’s upper-limb PUL 2.0 result was consistent with the preview’s account of the Lancet report: the call described a statistically significant 4.55% mean difference, p=0.029, while the preview cited a Lancet upper-limb result with p=0.03.

surprises.description: Matthews cut FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $158–162 million from the preview’s “at least $180M” expectation, a reduction of $18–22 million. This was a substantial weakening of the core earnings outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered its full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $158-162 million,” including its 40% share of Propelis adjusted EBITDA.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance (adj. EBITDA, incl. 40% Propelis) | ≥ $180M”; the preview expected a reaffirmation, possibly with hedges.

surprises.description: Industrial Technology adjusted EBITDA was a $5.4 million loss, well below the preview’s estimate of a $1 million loss to breakeven. Two anticipated engineering orders were lost, others were delayed, and another order’s scope was reduced, leading to a restructuring and strategic review.
surprises.fact_evidence: Industrial technology “swung to an adjusted EBITDA loss of $5.4 million versus a $9 million profit”; the engineering/OBRA business “lost two anticipated orders,” saw others delayed, and had an order scope immediately reduced, prompting a “$10 million annual cost-reduction restructuring and a strategic review.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Industrial Tech adjusted EBITDA at “~$(1)M to $0M” and said it “must inflect positive.”

surprises.description: The company reported a $0.75-per-share net loss, rather than the preview’s expectation of low positive or near-breakeven GAAP EPS. The reported loss reflected the absence of the prior-year SGK divestiture gain as well as weaker industrial results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 fiscal 2026 net loss of $23.7 million (-$0.75 per share), compared to net income of $15.4 million ($0.49 per share) a year ago,” largely reflecting “the absence of a prior-year SGK divestiture gain and weaker industrial technology results.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed expected GAAP EPS as “low positive / near breakeven.”

surprises.description: Revenue came in at $246 million, below both the preview’s roughly $257 million base estimate and the $264.5 million consensus figure. Divestitures reduced sales by about $85 million, partly offset by the Dodge acquisition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q3 sales fell to $246 million from $349 million,” driven by “roughly $85 million of divestiture impact” and partly offset by “$4.4 million from the Dodge acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave “Revenue | $264.5M” consensus and a “~$257M” base estimate.

surprises.description: Operating cash flow did not turn positive in Q3 as management had promised. Nine-month operating cash flow was still negative $69.5 million, compared with negative $67.4 million for the first half, implying a further outflow during Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nine-month operating cash flow was negative $69.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “explicitly promised positive OCF in Q3 and Q4” after a “$(67.4)M 1H outflow.”

surprises.description: Propelis synergy capture was delayed by SAP implementation timing, creating an estimated $5 million shortfall. This added a specific earnings headwind beyond the preview’s expectation of roughly $9.9 million for the quarter from Propelis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A delay in Propelis synergy capture caused by SAP implementation timing created an estimated $5 million shortfall.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Propelis 40% contribution” at “~$9.9M” and did not flag a SAP-related synergy delay.

surprises.description: Memorialization sales and adjusted EBITDA were below the preview’s estimates, with EBITDA also slipping year over year despite higher sales. Rising copper, steel, labor, and fuel costs outpaced price increases.
surprises.fact_evidence: Memorialization sales rose 2.1% to “$208.1 million” while adjusted EBITDA slipped to “$42.2 million from $42.8 million”; copper rose from “$4.50 to $6.60/lb,” steel was “+21% YoY,” and labor and fuel costs also increased.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Memorialization at “~$210M / ~$44M” and highlighted the need to watch price versus volume and input-cost commentary.

surprises.description: Matthews expects Propelis to reach an approximately $130 million annualized EBITDA run rate by its exit from calendar 2026 and plans to begin marketing a sale within the next 12 months. That is earlier than the preview’s 12–18-month exit window and its expectation of EBITDA heading to that level into 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: Matthews “still expects Propelis to exit calendar 2026 at a ~$130 million annualized EBITDA run rate, triggering a sale marketing process within the next 12 months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the exit had been guided at “12–18 months” and described EBITDA as “heading to ~$130M into 2027”; it said a narrowed window or banker mandate could be a positive surprise.

surprises.description: The CEO announced an intention to retire once a successor is hired, an unanticipated leadership transition with no timing or successor identified in the provided facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CEO Joe Bartolese announced his intention to retire once a successor is hired.”

surprises.description: The company reported record interest in its dry battery electrode technology, a more encouraging signal than the preview’s watchlist, which described DBE as an option with no contribution to current numbers and looked for customer developments.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company reported “record interest in its dry battery electrode (DBE) technology.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called DBE “pure option value, zero in numbers” and listed “any named customer” as something to watch.

surprises.description: Matthews announced a new strategic printing partnership with Lynx, a development not anticipated in the preview. The facts provide no financial contribution or timing, so its earnings significance is unclear.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company announced “a new strategic printing partnership with Lynx.”

surprises.description: Matthews plans an additional $5 million in corporate cost reductions next year, a concrete cost-cutting plan not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company announced “planned $5 million corporate cost reductions for next year.”

in_line: Matthews maintained a record full-year adjusted EBITDA target of approximately $175 million for Memorialization, broadly consistent with the preview’s view that the segment was already running at a $175 million-plus annualized EBITDA rate.

surprises.description: Rapid7 raised full-year non-GAAP operating income guidance to $129–133 million from the preview’s prior $112–118 million range, despite keeping its revenue outlook broadly unchanged. It also guided to a 20% Q4 operating margin, well above Q2’s 13.7%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided to a 20% non-GAAP operating margin in Q4 2026, up sharply from 13.7% in Q2, and raised full-year operating income guidance to $129-133 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance (reaffirmed June 1, 2026): Revenue $836–842M (–2% to –3%); non-GAAP operating income $112–118M; non-GAAP EPS $1.52–1.60; FCF $125–135M.”

surprises.description: Q2 earnings and revenue came in above the preview’s working estimates: EPS was $0.44 versus about $0.35 expected, operating income was $28.9 million versus roughly $25 million, and revenue was $210.9 million versus roughly $208.5 million. Revenue still declined year over year, but the reported quarter beat the expected ranges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP operating income of $28.9 million (13.7% margin) and EPS of $0.44 beat guidance”; “Q2 total revenue fell ~1.5% year-over-year to $210.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Use $208.5M / $0.35 as the working consensus”; Q2 company guidance was “$207–209M” revenue and “$24–26M” non-GAAP operating income.

surprises.description: The company gave a concrete plan to repay its $600 million convertible notes due in March 2027 using its cash and an undrawn credit facility, addressing a capital-structure issue the preview said lacked a clear plan. The preview specifically identified a refinancing announcement—or the absence of one—as a key catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $702.6 million in cash and short-term investments plus a $200 million undrawn credit facility to repay its $600 million convertible notes due March 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A refinancing announcement — or the conspicuous absence of a plan — is a real catalyst and is not in most models.”

surprises.description: Although Q2 exit ARR of $824 million was slightly above the preview’s roughly $820 million guide, growth in the core weakened rather than showing the stabilization bulls were looking for: Detection & Response grew about 5% versus the preview’s roughly 7% reference point, and core platform solutions grew only about 1% year over year versus about 2% in Q1. Exposure management underperformed and offset Detection & Response growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total ARR declined to $824 million in Q2 2026”; “core platform solutions (over 80% of ARR) grew only ~1% year-over-year”; “Detection and response… grew approximately 5% year-over-year, while exposure management underperformed and offset that growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Core platform ARR (>80% of total) grew only ~2% Y/Y in Q1”; “Detection & Response ARR growth (was ~7% Y/Y; ~55% of total).”

surprises.description: The company’s new Q3 outlook calls for ARR to fall further to about $812 million, with core solutions only roughly flat sequentially and the decline continuing in noncore offerings. The preview focused on Q2’s expected decline and whether ARR would stabilize, but did not provide a Q3 outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for ARR declining further to approximately $812 million, with core solutions roughly flat sequentially and the decline coming from noncore offerings.”

surprises.description: Rapid7 announced a workforce restructuring affecting about 12% of employees, a more specific and substantial action than the preview’s watch item about a possible cost-out program. The plan comes with $10–11 million in charges, so the operating reset has a near-term cost as well as a stated focus on core solutions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced a restructuring impacting approximately 12% of its workforce, incurring $10-11 million in charges, to refocus resources on core platform solutions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for: restructuring/cost-out program and any associated charge.”

surprises.description: Management said it expects free cash flow to improve in 2027 even with a lower ARR base, an additional forward-looking claim not addressed in the preview. The preview discussed only the 2026 free-cash-flow outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year free cash flow guidance was maintained at approximately $130 million (~15.5% margin), with management expecting free cash flow to improve in 2027 despite a lower ARR base.”

in_line: Full-year revenue guidance of $837–841 million was broadly in line with the preview’s prior $836–842 million range; management did not cut or raise it.
Full-year free cash flow guidance was maintained at approximately $130 million, within the preview’s $125–135 million range.
Q2 ARR remained in the neighborhood of the preview’s roughly $820 million expectation and still declined sequentially, as the preview anticipated.

surprises.description: Toast added 9,500 net locations, versus the preview’s estimate of about 8,400. That was a meaningful beat on the preview’s most-watched metric and set a new company record.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added a record 9,500 net new locations in Q2, roughly 1,000 above its prior high.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied net adds: ~8,400”; the preview called net location adds “the single most-watched line.”

surprises.description: Recurring gross profit growth exceeded the Q2 guide implied by the preview. Toast reported growth of over 28%, compared with the preview’s expected 24–26% growth range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Toast grew recurring gross profit streams over 28% year-over-year in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP recurring GP: $565–575M (guide) … +24–26%.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was well above the preview’s cited $185–195 million guidance range. The beat was partly helped by a roughly $10 million tariff refund that had not been included in guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 38% to $221 million with margins expanding 240 basis points to 37%, though this included an approximately $10 million tariff refund not contemplated in Q2 guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: $185–195M (guide).”

surprises.description: The reported 98-basis-point take rate fell short of the preview’s expectation that it would exceed Q1’s 103 basis points. Its year-over-year increase did not prevent a sequential miss against this explicitly watched threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total take rate reached 98 basis points of GPV (up 5 bps year-over-year).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Take rate above 103 bps + non-payment fintech GP above $51M”; the preview also said take rate was “expanding.”

surprises.description: Toast raised its full-year recurring gross profit growth outlook to 23–25%, above the prior 21–23% outlook referenced in the preview. That puts the midpoint above 23%, the level the preview identified as a stronger-than-base-case outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Toast raised its full-year 2026 outlook to recurring gross profit growth of 23%-25%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited prior FY26 guidance of “recurring GP of $2.29–2.32B (+21–23%)” and said the bull case required raising recurring GP growth “above 23%.”

surprises.description: Toast reported a $61 billion GPV, slightly above the preview’s $60.31 billion consensus estimate. The beat was modest relative to the expected level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GPV rose 22% to $61 billion.”

surprises.description: Toast said it would invest more aggressively to accelerate growth in international, enterprise, and retail, while those newer markets are on track to nearly double ARR to $200 million this year. The preview identified these as TAM extensions but did not anticipate this stated investment push or ARR trajectory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New TAMs (international, enterprise, retail) are on a path to nearly double ARR to $200 million this year, with the company choosing to invest more aggressively to accelerate growth in these segments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described international and enterprise as “credible TAM extensions” and noted enterprise bookings, but gave no $200 million ARR trajectory or expectation of more aggressive investment.

surprises.description: Toast IQ Grow appears to be gaining traction faster than the preview had quantified: management said it is on track to be the company’s fastest product to reach $10 million in ARR and already has positive, improving gross margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Toast IQ Grow, the company's new AI marketing agent, is on track to become its fastest product ever to reach $10 million in ARR and is already running at positive and improving gross margins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted the Grow agent’s early launch and pilots reporting “~8% sales lift,” but gave no $10 million ARR milestone or margin information.

in_line: GPV per location was flat year-over-year, within the preview’s base-case range of down 1% to flat.
The full-year adjusted EBITDA outlook was raised, but by less than the Q2 beat; the preview’s base case anticipated a modest raise rather than a larger run-rate uplift.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $49.8 million, above the $40–48 million company guide and roughly $7–8 million above the preview’s $41.6–42.4 million consensus range. The beat was partly supported by $4.9 million of previously deferred GM settlement revenue included in Thermal Barrier sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $49.8 million (up 32% sequentially)” and Thermal Barrier revenue “includ[ed] $4.9 million of previously deferred GM settlement revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 revenue guidance of “$40–48M” and consensus of “$41.6M … / $42.4M.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of $65–80 million was far above the preview’s base-case $46–52 million range and its $50 million quarterly breakeven threshold. The company also expects $7–15 million of adjusted EBITDA, signaling a return to positive EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue guidance of $65 million to $80 million represents 30% to 60% sequential growth, with adjusted EBITDA guided to $7 million to $15 million, signaling a return to positive EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case had Q3 revenue “$46–52M”; it said “Q3 guided ≥$50M” was part of the bull case and highlighted the “$50M quarterly revenue” H2 breakeven threshold.

surprises.description: Aspen raised its 2026 European Thermal Barrier outlook to $20–30 million from the preview’s expected $10–15 million. It had already generated $10.9 million in the first half, exceeding the full-year 2025 total.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its 2026 European Thermal Barrier revenue outlook from $10-15 million to $20-30 million, having already generated $10.9 million in the first half, surpassing all of 2025's $8.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “European TB $10–15M in FY26” as the expected outlook.

surprises.description: GM production assumptions were substantially higher than the preview’s 55,000–65,000 annualized expectation: production was about 100,000 annualized in Q2, and Q3 guidance assumes 90,000–125,000. This is a favorable change in the production backdrop despite the preview’s concern about weak GM sales and destocking.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GM production ran at roughly 40,000 vehicles annualized in Q1 and 100,000 in Q2, with Q3 guidance assuming 90,000-125,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said guidance assumed “GM production of 55,000–65,000 vehicles annualized.”

surprises.description: The Q2 gross margin of 7% was below the preview’s base-case expectation of roughly 11–13%. Excluding $5.3 million of explosion-related costs, adjusted gross margin was 17%, indicating the incident costs weighed heavily on the reported result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin was just 7% ($3.3 million), or 17% adjusted margin excluding $5.3 million of incident-related costs from the April East Providence explosion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “GM ~11–13% on disruption costs.”

surprises.description: Energy Industrial revenue was only $20.4 million in Q2, below the preview’s implied $26–28 million estimate from the Q2 revenue guide midpoint. That shortfall stands out against the overall revenue beat, although management expects a sharp segment rebound in Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $49.8 million … split between $20.4 million Energy Industrial and $29.5 million Thermal Barrier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the Q2 guide midpoint “implies EI of only ~$26–28M.”

surprises.description: The preview warned that the roughly 20% full-year Energy Industrial growth target was likely to be reset, but management retained it and guided to about $40 million of Energy Industrial revenue in Q3, roughly double Q2. The Q3 segment outlook is a substantial near-term rebound versus the Q2 result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Energy Industrial is guided to approximately $40 million in Q3 (roughly double Q2), targeting ~20% full-year 2026 growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the 20% target “the most likely thing to get quietly reset on this call” and said Q3 revenue needed to start with a “5” to preserve the breakeven thesis.

surprises.description: The East Providence outlook now specifies that full production capacity is not expected until the first half of 2027, while incident-related charges of $5–10 million continue through Q3. The preview had flagged the recovery timeline and insurance amount as uncertain; the expectation that costs would persist into Q3 was broadly consistent, but the stated restoration date extends the disruption outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full production capacity at the East Providence plant is expected to be restored in the first half of 2027, with incident-related charges of $5-10 million continuing through Q3 and largely recoverable via insurance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch the “timeline to full capability” and noted that an insurance recovery had “unknown size and timing”; it also expected disruption costs in “Q2–Q3.”

surprises.description: The Plant 2 asset sale has slipped from the preview’s expected Q4 2026 timing and is now likely a 2027 event, delaying the anticipated sale proceeds and debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Plant 2 asset sale is now likely a 2027 event.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the Plant 2 sale as “expected Q4 2026” with proceeds going to debt reduction.

surprises.description: Aspen added Jaguar Land Rover as a seventh European OEM customer and expanded its awarded pipeline to nine vehicle platforms worth up to $135 million at full production. The preview did not flag this customer win or pipeline expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Aspen added Jaguar Land Rover as its seventh European OEM customer, expanding its awarded pipeline to nine vehicle platforms worth up to $135 million at full production volumes.”

surprises.description: Management set a target to double Thermal Barrier revenue to $40–60 million in 2027 from the 2026 outlook, introducing a substantial segment-growth target not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management targets doubling Thermal Barrier revenue to $40-60 million in 2027 from the 2026 outlook, based on conservative volume assumptions.”

in_line: Management retained the approximately 20% full-year 2026 Energy Industrial growth target, which the preview said the company had promised, although it had expected a possible reset.
The expectation that LNG activity would more than double versus 2025 was consistent with the preview’s stated outlook.

surprises.description: RYAM reported $376 million of Q2 sales, about $14 million above the preview’s roughly $362 million consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales reached $376 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: ~$362 million.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA rose to $40 million from $8 million in Q1, a strong sequential improvement against the preview’s concern that a weak Q2 would make the full-year EBITDA bridge hard to credit. High Purity Cellulose generated $57 million of adjusted EBITDA, with margins rising to 19% from 9% in Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose to $40 million from $8 million in Q1”; “High Purity Cellulose adjusted EBITDA grew to $57 million with margins expanding to 19% from 9% in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Sequential EBITDA ramp — guidance implies a large H2-weighted build from Q1's $8M toward >$133M for the year; a weak Q2 makes the full-year bridge hard to credit.”

surprises.description: Cellulose Specialties pricing rose 8% sequentially, alongside a 19% volume increase from Q1, and management expects pricing to stay significantly above prior-year levels through H2. That was stronger than the preview’s concern about whether the previous price gain would hold as inventories normalized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cellulose Specialties pricing increased 8% sequentially and 21% year-over-year, with volumes up 19% from Q1”; management expects pricing to “remain significantly above prior-year levels through the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cellulose Specialties pricing/volume — whether the 17% price gain holds as customers normalize inventories, and any early 2027 pricing commentary.”

surprises.description: Paperboard and high-yield pulp lost $10 million of adjusted EBITDA, twice the $5 million loss in Q1 despite higher volumes. The preview already flagged losses in the segment, but the reported deterioration was worse than that general warning conveyed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Paperboard and high-yield pulp segment posted negative $10 million adjusted EBITDA, worsening from negative $5 million in Q1 and negative $2 million a year ago, despite higher volumes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Paperboard & High-Yield Pulp losses and tariff/FX headwinds, which drove last year's guidance cut.”

surprises.description: RYAM disclosed a new $13 million noncash impairment related to high-yield pulp, which the preview had not flagged as an expected Q2 item.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Loss from continuing operations narrowed to $33 million from $81 million in Q1, though it included a $13 million noncash asset impairment charge related to high-yield pulp.”

surprises.description: The announced Section 301 tariffs on Brazilian and Norwegian dissolving wood pulp were not anticipated in the preview; management said they could improve U.S. suppliers’ competitiveness if they remain in place.
surprises.fact_evidence: “USTR announced final Section 301 tariffs of 37.5% on Brazilian and 12.5% on Norwegian dissolving wood pulp imports, which management believes will improve competitiveness for U.S. suppliers if sustained.”

surprises.description: RYAM also highlighted newly announced tariffs on Canadian-origin products as a potential material risk to its paperboard business, with roughly 75% of paperboard volume sold in the U.S.; the preview had flagged tariff headwinds generally but not this specific exposure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly 75% of the company's paperboard volume is sold into the U.S., exposing the segment to potentially material impact from newly announced tariffs on Canadian-origin products.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Paperboard & High-Yield Pulp losses and tariff/FX headwinds, which drove last year's guidance cut.”

in_line: The preview expected an update on the strategic review; management said it expects to conclude the review and communicate a clear path forward during Q4 2026.
The preview expected positive full-year free cash flow; management said RYAM remained on track for positive full-year free cash flow.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $23.2 million, above the preview’s roughly $21.5 million consensus and the $21–23 million base case, though below its $25–27 million bull case. The result beat the consensus bar by about 8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 22% year-over-year to $23.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$21.5M”; the base scenario anticipated “$21–23M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $11.4 million, far above the preview’s implied $4–6 million expectation. The result was also a record, rather than merely another quarter of positive EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached a record $11.4 million (up ~300%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$4–6M (implied).”

surprises.description: EPS was $0.15, well above the preview’s $0.03 consensus, alongside record net income. This was a substantially stronger earnings result than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income hit a record $8.9 million ($0.15 EPS).”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 73%, far exceeding the preview’s expected 55–57% range. The increase was much larger than the preview’s anticipated licensing-mix-driven improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded to 73% from 53% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~55–57%”; the preview said a print below about 54% would suggest the mix shift stalled.

surprises.description: Management raised full-year guidance to $77–82 million of revenue and $18–22 million of adjusted EBITDA, versus prior company guidance of $75–80 million and $16–20 million. The revenue range also straddles the preview’s $77.71 million analyst consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance calls for revenue of $77 million-$82 million and adjusted EBITDA of $18 million-$22 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 co. guidance $75–80M rev / $16–20M adj EBITDA”; the preview flagged whether guidance would be “reaffirm[ed], raise[d], or trim[med].”

surprises.description: Despite the higher full-year EBITDA guidance, the $6–10 million second-half EBITDA outlook implies a step-down from Q2’s $11.4 million and is below the roughly $9–15 million second-half range implied by the prior full-year guidance and preview’s expected H1 EBITDA. Management attributed the cautious outlook mainly to conservative licensing assumptions and more rev-share agreements.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Second-half adjusted EBITDA guidance of $6 million-$10 million implies a step-down from Q2's $11.4 million, attributed mainly to conservative licensing assumptions and more rev-share agreements.”
