surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited prior FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$16–20M” and expected Q2 adjusted EBITDA of “~$4–6M” against Q1 actual of $0.9 million, implying H1 of roughly $5–7 million.

surprises.description: Operating expenses fell 24.1% year over year, and management expects a further 18–20% reduction in the second half versus the first half. The preview did not anticipate this scale of realized and planned cost reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total operating expenses fell 24.1% year-over-year, with management guiding to an additional 18%-20% cost reduction in the second half versus the first half.”

surprises.description: The call highlighted an 880-billion-token private code corpus and 17 productized off-the-shelf video data sets as assets supporting AI-training licensing growth. The preview discussed AI licensing and potential counterparties but did not anticipate these specific data assets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its 880-billion-token private code corpus and 17 productized off-the-shelf video data sets support AI-training licensing growth.”

in_line: Licensing revenue was $14.1 million, essentially matching the preview’s estimate that roughly $13–14 million was needed for Q2.
Subscription revenue of $8.9 million was within the preview’s expected $8.7–9.0 million range and was roughly flat year over year, consistent with its stabilization watch.
Q1 and Q2 revenue totaled $38.4 million, within management’s H1 guide of $35–41 million cited in the preview.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $30.5 million, well below the preview’s $37.04 million consensus, despite growing 16% year over year excluding the non-recurring Spanish work. The reported total was essentially flat year over year rather than the expected 20% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $30.5 million, essentially flat versus $30.8 million a year earlier,” and “excluding $4.3 million of non-recurring Spanish scooper return-to-service work, revenue grew 16% year over year.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $8.1 million, materially below the preview’s estimated $12–14 million range and down from $10.8 million a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA declined to $8.1 million from $10.8 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | No published consensus (my est. $12–14M) | $10.8M | +11–30%”

surprises.description: The earnings result was weaker than the preview’s implied expectation of roughly $1 million in net income: Bridger reported a $0.5 million net loss, while loss attributable to common stockholders was $0.13 per diluted share versus the preview’s -$0.03 estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported a Q2 net loss of $0.5 million,” with “loss attributable to common stockholders of $7.6 million ($0.13 per diluted share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus EPS of -$0.03 is therefore consistent with positive net income of roughly $1M.”

surprises.description: Management reiterated rather than raised full-year guidance, missing the preview’s stated preferred outcome even though reiteration was also described as the likely base case. The unchanged outlook is $135–145 million of revenue and $55–60 million of adjusted EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bridger reiterated full-year 2026 guidance of $135-145 million in revenue and $55-60 million in adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bar is a raise, not a reiteration”; the preview’s bull case called for “$150M+ / $62M+ EBITDA,” while its base case anticipated a reiteration.

surprises.description: Cash fell further to $7.2 million instead of showing the seasonal Q2 improvement the preview expected. That leaves cash below the preview’s cited $9.0 million Q1 balance and far short of the more than $25 million rebuild described in its bull case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents fell to $7.2 million from $31.4 million at year-end 2025 due to seasonal working capital use, aircraft slot investments, and fleet readiness spending.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 should be the seasonal inflection to positive cash generation”; the bull case specified “cash rebuilt >$25M.”

surprises.description: The two newest Super Scoopers were committed to the Portugal deployment later than expected, and management plans to reposition them to the U.S. after the season unless stronger European commitments emerge. This is a less favorable near-term European deployment outlook than the preview’s account of the Portugal lease as a Q3-weighted opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The two newest Super Scoopers leased to Europe's DaVinci for Portugal were committed later than expected,” and management plans to “reposition them to the U.S. after the season for higher-value opportunities absent stronger European commitments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Portugal is a lease to Avincis ... through mid-October — capital-light and high-margin, but finite and Q3-weighted.”

surprises.description: The U.S. Forest Service awarded four Super Scoopers two 160-day task orders, described as the longest guaranteed task orders in Bridger’s history. The preview emphasized unusually strong fire activity and asked for Q3-to-date color, but did not anticipate these specific long-duration guaranteed orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The U.S. Forest Service awarded two 160-day task orders covering four Super Scoopers—the longest guaranteed task orders in Bridger's history—with activation on a staggered basis into October and November.”

in_line: The Texas A&M award’s three-aircraft, three-year delivery schedule and limited contribution to 2026 margin-generating revenue matched the preview’s expectation that the contract was largely a FY27–29 revenue opportunity.

surprises.description: Flotek’s Q2 revenue approached $100 million, far above the preview’s $69.5 million consensus and its $71–73 million inferred whisper. The 70% year-over-year increase also made this the company’s strongest quarter in 10 years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue approached $100 million, up 70% year-over-year, marking Flotek's strongest quarterly performance in the last 10 years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 Consensus” revenue of “$69.5M” (with another feed at $68.4M); the preview’s inferred “working whisper” was “$71–73M revenue.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA of $16.8 million substantially exceeded the preview’s expected Q2 range of roughly $9.5–10.5 million. The result was also much stronger than the preview’s implied first-half-to-full-year guidance math.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total company adjusted EBITDA grew 109% year-over-year to $16.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “$9.5–10.5M” of Q2 adjusted EBITDA; its guidance math used approximately “$9.5M” for Q2.

surprises.description: GAAP EPS was $0.26, twice the $0.13 consensus and well above the preview’s $0.14–0.15 inferred whisper. This is a notable reversal from the preview’s concern that tax and other costs could again keep EPS weak despite stronger revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income rose to $10 million ($0.26 per share) from $1.8 million ($0.05 per share) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 GAAP diluted EPS consensus was “$0.13”; the preview’s inferred whisper was “$0.14–0.15 EPS.” It also flagged “EPS quality / tax rate” as a key issue.

surprises.description: Flotek raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $340–350 million, far above the preview’s expected range of roughly $280–295 million and the $285.2 million consensus. The new adjusted EBITDA range of $47–51 million also exceeds the preview’s expected $39–43 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised 2026 guidance to revenue of $340-350 million and adjusted EBITDA of $47-51 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected a raise “to ~$280–295M / EBITDA $39–43M” and listed FY2026 revenue consensus of “$285.2M.”

surprises.description: Chemistry Technologies grew much faster than the preview’s anticipated Q2 inflection: revenue rose 53% despite a 5% decline in North American frac fleet count, and June alone contributed nearly $31 million. International chemistry also accelerated to $10.6 million from $1.9 million in Q1 as Jafurah expanded to four fleets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Chemistry Technologies revenue grew 53% year-over-year despite a 5% decline in North American frac fleet count,” marking its “strongest chemistry quarter since 2017”; “International chemistry revenue reached $10.6 million, up 172% year-over-year and up from $1.9 million in Q1,” with four Jafurah fleets.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said external Chemistry revenue was expected “to increase from Q2 onward” as completions stabilized and Middle East deployments accelerated, while warning that continued external erosion would be a concern.

surprises.description: The preview anticipated sequential Data Analytics growth, but the reported gross-profit share was 51%, only slightly above Q1’s 50% and below the preview’s greater-than-55% bull-case marker. The segment did set a quarterly revenue record and became the largest gross-profit contributor, so the result was strong but did not reach that upside marker.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Data Analytics achieved record quarterly revenue, up 223% year-over-year, and accounted for 51% of company gross profit versus 26% in the prior year quarter, becoming the largest segment contributor to gross profit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Above ~$13M with GP share >55% validates it”; it also reported Q1 Data Analytics at “50% of gross profit.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Montana contract mobilization to support Data Analytics growth and cited approximately $12 million of expected 2026 revenue. The call instead said guidance conservatively excludes any Q4 revenue from the unrenewed Montana Power Services contract, a newly disclosed risk to the expected contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guidance conservatively excludes any Q4 revenue from the unrenewed Montana Power Services contract (~$6 million/quarter).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described sequential Data Analytics growth as driven by mobilization of the “Montana utility disaster-recovery contract” and cited “~$12M expected 2026 revenue.”

surprises.description: Digital valuation measurement devices deployed or contracted reached 89, up 56% sequentially, and management expects proprietary analyzers on more than half of active North American e-frac and gas-powered fleets by year-end. That provides more concrete deployment scale than the preview’s request for signs of additional power-services unit wins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Digital valuation measurement devices deployed or contracted grew 56% sequentially to 89 units,” and Flotek expects analyzers on “over 50% of active North American e-frac and gas-powered fleets by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “naming new Power Services unit orders beyond the 27-unit and 15-unit wins” as a bullish signal, but gave no deployment target.

surprises.description: Management described a power-services opportunity substantially broader than the PREPA contract already discussed in the preview: a pipeline exceeding $1 billion and expected measurement or control over roughly 5 gigawatts by Q1 2027. These are pipeline and deployment expectations, not reported revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management cited a total power services pipeline exceeding $1 billion and expects to have measurement or control over roughly 5 gigawatts of power by Q1 2027.”

surprises.description: General and administrative expense fell below 8% of revenue, the lowest quarterly rate in at least a decade. The preview did not forecast this degree of overhead leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “G&A expenses fell to under 8% of revenue from nearly 12% a year ago, the lowest quarterly rate in at least a decade.”

surprises.description: Leverage was below 1x and ABL borrowings had been reduced to zero, better than the preview’s roughly 1.0x leverage estimate. This is a modestly stronger balance-sheet position than the preview’s baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Leverage remained below 1x and ABL borrowings were reduced to zero as of the call date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Net leverage ~1.0x” and flagged leverage as a metric to watch.

in_line: The PREPA contract’s 10-year term, approximately $400 million of potential revenue backlog, and lack of 2026 financial impact were consistent with the preview, which had already discussed the contract and emphasized that it would contribute essentially no 2026 revenue.

The preview expected a Data Analytics mix shift and continuing growth; the reported record quarter and 51% share of gross profit were consistent with strong segment performance, although the preview’s bull-case marker was above 55%.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $32.9 million, about 14% below the $38.06 million consensus and below the preview’s $36.5–38.0 million range based on management’s May framing. The shortfall was broad-based.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 revenue was $32.9 million, roughly $3 million (9%) below the guidance provided in May, with the shortfall described as broad-based across the business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus” Q2 revenue was “$38.06M”; management’s Q2 framing implied “$36.5–38.0M.”

surprises.description: The company cut FY2026 revenue guidance to $142–148 million, about $26–27 million below the prior range’s midpoint. This was a much deeper reset than the preview’s bear case of roughly $158–166 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was slashed to $142-$148 million from the prior range of $169-$174 million, a cut of roughly $26-27 million at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed prior FY2026 guidance of “$169–174M” and described a bear-case cut to “~$158–166M.”

surprises.description: Revenue fell 23% year over year pro forma, rather than being roughly flat as the preview expected. The 34% growth in reported revenue reflects the acquisition comparison and does not offset the underlying decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On a pro forma basis (including pre-acquisition Akoya revenue), total revenue declined 23% year-over-year, while as-reported revenue grew 34%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described FY guidance as “roughly flat pro-forma” and called the headline reported growth “inflated by the Akoya comp.”

surprises.description: The expected second-half ramp was pushed out: Q3 revenue is expected to be flat to slightly above Q2, and management said the sales-force changes would drive material improvement only in 2027 and beyond. That contrasts with the preview’s expectation that the FY plan depended on a substantial 2H 2026 step-up.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 revenue is expected to be flat to slightly above Q2, with commercial changes expected to drive material revenue improvement only in 2027 and beyond.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the FY guide required “~$95–100M in 2H, or a ~29% half-over-half step-up,” and that execution depended on “lead generation, new commercial hires” and other self-help efforts.

surprises.description: Cash-flow break-even was pushed from Q4 2026/year-end 2026 to 2027, later than the preview’s stated expectation. This extends the period before the company is expected to fund itself from operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company now expects cash flow break-even to slip to 2027 (versus year-end 2026 previously).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “cash-flow breakeven by Q4 2026” and highlighted a possible slip into 2027 as a bear-case tell.

surprises.description: Expected year-end cash fell to roughly $80 million from the prior outlook of about $100 million, a material deterioration in the projected cash cushion.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “projects ending 2026 with roughly $80 million in cash, down from about $100 million guided earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited year-end cash of “~$100M, no debt.”

surprises.description: The company recorded a $26.9 million non-cash goodwill impairment related to Akoya. The preview flagged further impairment as a risk, but did not forecast that a sizable goodwill write-off would occur in this quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recorded a $26.9 million non-cash goodwill impairment write-off tied to the Akoya acquisition, driven by macro factors and company performance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “any further impairment” and noted that another write-down would worsen the Akoya narrative.

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP gross margin was 47.9%, below the preview’s 49–53% expected range, and full-year margin guidance was also lowered to 48–50%. The 600-basis-point year-over-year improvement did not prevent the result and outlook from coming in below expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin improved 600 basis points year-over-year to 47.9%, though full-year non-GAAP gross margin guidance was lowered to 48-50% from 49-53% previously.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 adjusted gross margin at “~49–53% (guide)” and FY2026 adjusted gross margin guidance of “49–53%.”

surprises.description: Q2 cash usage was substantially lower than the preview’s estimate: $5.7 million reported, or $4 million adjusted, versus expected adjusted usage of about $10–12 million. The quarter ended with $96.9 million in cash and no debt.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 cash usage was $5.7 million (or $4 million adjusted), ending the quarter with $96.9 million in cash and no debt, reflecting better-than-planned cash preservation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adj. cash usage ~–$10 to –$12M” for Q2.

surprises.description: Management said diagnostics revenue was tracking ahead of its prior $10 million reference, a stronger near-term indication than the preview’s description of diagnostics as a small current business with 2027+ optionality. The announced coverage and CMS pricing themselves were already expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diagnostics revenue tracking ahead of the prior $10 million reference.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said diagnostics was “only ~$2.9M/quarter today” and framed it as “2027+ optionality.”

in_line: Anthem Blue Cross coverage and CMS pricing of $897 for Lucent AD Complete were already noted in the preview; the coverage took effect July 1 as anticipated.
FDA clearance was anticipated in the second half of 2026 in the preview; management’s expectation of clearance around year-end remains within that timing.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $783 million, below the preview’s $795 million base case and roughly $804 million published consensus; management also said the result was below its own expectations. Revenue was only marginally above Q1’s $781.5 million, rather than delivering the more meaningful sequential growth the preview centered on.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was approximately $783 million, essentially flat with Q1 and explicitly acknowledged as below the company's own expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Street has set it at ~$804M”; the preview’s base case was “$795M (+1.7% q/q).”

surprises.description: Total Tyvaso revenue was $453 million, below the preview’s roughly $463 million base-case estimate. The call also described nebulized Tyvaso as pressured by intensifying competition, consistent with the preview’s concern about erosion but adding no actual nebulized revenue figure to assess against its threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Tyvaso revenue for the quarter was $453 million, with nebulized Tyvaso remaining pressured by intensifying competition in the inhaled prostacyclin category.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case estimated “Tyvaso total ~$463M”; it flagged nebulized Tyvaso as a key metric and said “Stabilization near $120M” would indicate a one-time channel shift.

surprises.description: Management did not reaffirm or update prior 2026 revenue-growth guidance, leaving the near-term outlook less definite than the preview’s focus on a return to sequential growth. It did say it expects the second half of 2026 to be stronger than the first half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management declined to reaffirm or update any prior 2026 revenue growth guidance, while stating they expect the second half of 2026 to be stronger than the first half.”

surprises.description: The $4 billion revenue run-rate target by the end of 2027 was described as achievable, but management said the path has narrowed and now requires contributions from IPF and ralinepag launches. That is a qualification of the target the preview expected management to reaffirm, rather than an unqualified bridge from the existing portfolio.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The prior $4 billion revenue run-rate target by end of 2027 from the existing portfolio was described as still achievable but with a path that has ‘certainly narrowed,’ now requiring contributions from IPF and ralinepag launches.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Reaffirmation of the ‘$4B run-rate by end of 2027’ target” as a catalyst and referred to the “$4B run-rate by end of 2027” from the existing portfolio.

surprises.description: The planned 2027 IPF launch will initially include nebulized Tyvaso only; DPI and SMI still need bridging data and further FDA engagement. The preview discussed an IPF launch in 2027 but did not flag this formulation limitation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The IPF launch in 2027 will initially be limited to nebulized Tyvaso only, as DPI and SMI formulations still require bridging data and further FDA engagement before approval in that indication.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected a “launch by Q2 2027 on standard review” but did not specify that the initial launch would be limited to nebulized Tyvaso.

surprises.description: The company roughly doubled its sales force, a more specific and substantial expansion than the preview’s general expectation of a mid-year commercial-infrastructure build. This adds launch preparation but also implies a larger operating investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company roughly doubled its sales force, with new representatives entering the field around July 1 to expand reach into the community setting ahead of the IPF and ralinepag launches.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said IPF commercial infrastructure was being built “mid-year” and to “expect further build,” without anticipating a roughly doubled sales force.

surprises.description: Management reported record patient starts, referrals, total patients, and commercial patients exiting the quarter—an underlying-demand signal the preview did not identify, despite the nearly flat revenue result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record levels were reached in patient starts, referrals, total patients, and commercial patients exiting Q2, which management cited as evidence of underlying momentum despite flat reported revenue.”

surprises.description: TETON-1 results were said to surpass the prior TETON-2 readout. The preview noted both positive studies but did not anticipate this favorable comparison between them.
surprises.fact_evidence: “TETON-1 results surpassed the prior TETON-2 readout.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described both TETON-2 and TETON-1 as positive readouts, including TETON-1’s “+130.1 mL FVC,” but did not say TETON-1 would surpass TETON-2.

surprises.description: TETON-PPF enrollment was already over 95% complete and nearly finished ahead of schedule, with a Phase III readout expected in the second half of 2027. The preview did not discuss this trial’s enrollment progress.
surprises.fact_evidence: “TETON-PPF enrollment is over 95% complete (nearly finished ahead of schedule) with a Phase III readout expected in the second half of 2027.”

surprises.description: Management said the PPF opportunity could be at least twice the size of IPF, introducing a potentially larger opportunity than the preview’s discussion of IPF and ralinepag. The preview did not quantify a PPF opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management framed both IPF and ralinepag as multibillion-dollar opportunities, and stated the PPF opportunity could be at least double that of IPF.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said IPF and ralinepag could “each independently exceed current total revenue,” but did not mention PPF as a larger opportunity.

surprises.description: The nebulized Tyvaso IPF sNDA was filed in late June, ahead of the preview’s expected filing timing of by the end of summer. This advances a key pipeline milestone relative to the timing investors were told to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An sNDA for nebulized Tyvaso in IPF (filed late June).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for TETON sNDA filing confirmation “by the end of summer 2026.”

in_line: The ralinepag NDA submission was confirmed, consistent with the preview’s expectation of an NDA by 2H 2026; the preview also anticipated a launch around mid-2027, consistent with the call’s potential 2027 approval timing.

surprises.description: TTEC reported $455 million of Q2 revenue, well below the preview’s $478.2 million consensus estimate. The 11.3% year-over-year decline was also steeper than the expected 6.9% decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue fell 11.3% year-over-year to $455 million from $525 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $478.2M” and “YoY | -6.9%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $39 million, far below the preview’s $50–52 million estimate. That misses the preview’s stated $50 million level needed to keep the full-year EBITDA guidance arithmetically achievable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA declining to $39 million (8.7% margin) from $52 million (10.1%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA (my est.) ~$50–52M”; “A Q2 adjusted EBITDA below ~$50M makes the FY EBITDA guide arithmetically very hard.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was just $0.03 versus the preview’s $0.253 estimate. The preview described $0.253 as a fair bar, so the reported result was a substantial miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS collapsed to $0.03 from $0.22 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS | $0.253.”

surprises.description: Engage weakened enough that TTEC cut its full-year outlook: the midpoint now implies an 8% revenue decline rather than a 4.1% decline, and the margin outlook fell from 10.6% to 10.1%. That conflicts with the preview’s highlighted expectation that Engage would return to improved profitable year-over-year growth starting in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Engage segment saw revenue drop 12.1% to $351 million, with full-year Engage guidance cut so revenue now declines 8% (from 4.1%) at the midpoint and EBITDA margin lowered to 10.1% from 10.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management explicitly promised Engage returns to improved profitable YoY growth starting in Q2.” The preview also listed FY26 Engage revenue guidance of “$1,585–1,615M / EBITDA $164–176M.”

surprises.description: Management said second-half Engage weakness was concentrated in two clients, mainly one large public-sector client affected by an unaffiliated third party’s underperforming technology. That adds a specific client and technology problem to the preview’s expected Engage recovery, rather than a broad-based improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Second-half Engage weakness was concentrated in two clients, primarily one large public sector client whose issue stems from an unaffiliated third party's underperforming technology.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management explicitly promised Engage returns to improved profitable YoY growth starting in Q2.”

surprises.description: The normalized tax rate was 82.8%, far above the preview’s 38–42% FY26 tax-rate guidance. Management said a U.S.-loss valuation allowance drove an $0.08 negative EPS impact, adding to the earnings shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A higher normalized tax rate of 82.8% (versus 43.4%) driving an $0.08 negative EPS impact largely due to a valuation allowance against U.S. losses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Tax rate 38–42%.”

surprises.description: TTEC initiated a strategic-alternatives review for Digital, with a sale among the possible outcomes and no set timeline. The preview raised this as a possible bear-case development, but it was not presented as the expected outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management initiated a review of strategic alternatives for the T-TECH Digital segment via advisor PJT Partners, with outcomes ranging from a sale to keeping Digital within T-TECH and no set timeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bear-case scenario mentioned “any reference to reviewing strategic alternatives for Digital,” while its catalyst checklist flagged “any capital-structure language — amendment, waiver, asset sale, or Digital divestiture.”

surprises.description: Digital revenue fell 8.5% and its operating margin compressed to 11.7% from 16.1%. Although management reiterated the segment’s full-year guidance, the reported quarterly contraction and margin decline add to the Digital weakness behind the preview’s concern about sub-1.0 book-to-bill.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Digital revenue declined 8.5% to $104 million (4.6% adjusted for a prior-year one-time IP software sale), while operating margin compressed to 11.7% from 16.1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “Digital bookings / book-to-bill,” noting it “ran 96% in Q1 (below 1.0),” and listed FY26 Digital guidance of “$420–440M / EBITDA $56–64M.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow was $39 million, down from $86 million a year earlier, despite cash generation being a key part of the preview’s deleveraging thesis. TTEC attributed part of the comparison to a prior-year $21 million aged VAT collection and said capex was $5 million higher to get ahead of H2 price increases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow fell to $39 million from $86 million, partly due to a prior-year $21 million aged VAT collection and a $5 million increase in capex to pre-empt H2 price hikes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Offshore mix and free cash flow” were listed as key metrics; “Cash generation is the only organic deleveraging lever.”

surprises.description: TTEC obtained covenant flexibility through a credit-facility amendment, an actual capital-structure step the preview had identified as a possible catalyst. The amendment provides flexibility, though its need underscores the company’s financing pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company obtained covenant flexibility through a credit facility amendment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “any capital-structure language — amendment, waiver, asset sale, or Digital divestiture” and described “amendment/waiver language” as part of its bear scenario.

surprises.description: Management said high-single-digit underperforming Engage clients are being renegotiated, while Digital deals are closing smaller and more slowly as customers cautiously assess AI-driven CX investments. This points to additional commercial pressure beyond the reported quarterly results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is renegotiating economics with high-single-digit underperforming Engage clients, and Digital deals are closing smaller and slower as customers cautiously evaluate AI-driven CX transformation investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected the Engage recovery to produce “improved profitable YoY growth starting in Q2” and described Digital as having a “healthy pipeline” in its base-case call scenario.

surprises.description: Net debt fell to $767 million, $36 million below the preview’s roughly $803 million figure, and management reported a $58 million year-to-date reduction. That is a better debt balance than the preview’s covenant discussion assumed, despite the weak EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reduced net debt by $58 million year-to-date to $767 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Net debt: ~$803M” and used “$800M net debt” in its leverage scenarios.

in_line: The reported 3.85x net leverage ratio was at the top of the preview’s 3.75–3.85x base-case range, rather than outside the range it described as on track.

surprises.description: Duke reported adjusted EPS of $1.43, well above the preview’s effective $1.30 whisper and above even its bull-case range of $1.36–$1.42. This was a substantially stronger quarter than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EPS rose to $1.43”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat $1.30 as the effective whisper”; bull scenario adjusted EPS: “$1.36–$1.42.”

surprises.description: Duke reached a North Carolina DEC rate-case settlement that sets the ROE and equity capital structure, whereas the preview said those items remained unresolved and would go to hearing. The settlement also includes an earnings-sharing mechanism allowing ROE up to 10.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reached a North Carolina DEC rate case settlement featuring a 9.8% ROE, 53% equity capital structure, and an earnings sharing mechanism allowing up to 10.3% ROE.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ROE and capital structure remain unresolved and go to hearing.”

surprises.description: Duke identified $5 billion to $10 billion of potential capital spending beyond its current five-year plan and said it is on track to add 15 GW of generation by 2031. The preview cited a roughly $103 billion plan with about 14 GW of new generation, so the potential expansion is larger than the stated plan, though it depends on signing ESAs and raises funding needs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$5 billion to $10 billion of potential upside to the current 5-year capital plan for additional generation and transmission, primarily in Indiana and Florida, triggered when ESAs are signed”; “on track to add 15 gigawatts of generation capacity by 2031.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $103B 2026–2030 plan” and “~14 GW of new generation by 2031”; “Utilities frequently raise mid-year — an increase is rate-base positive but re-opens the financing question.”

surprises.description: The preview listed $300 million of ATM equity as in flight, while Duke reported pricing $600 million under the program. Management said no large-block equity is planned within the five-year plan, but the reported ATM amount is larger than the preview indicated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company priced $600 million under its ATM equity program to settle at the end of 2027” and “no large block equity is planned within the 5-year plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$300M ATM equity (Dec 2027 settlement)”; “Any increase in the equity component of the funding plan is a direct negative.”

surprises.description: Duke gave a target to convert the remaining 15.4 GW data-center pipeline into electric service agreements by the first half of 2027. The preview highlighted the pipeline and possible revenue-ramp timing but did not provide this conversion timetable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expects to convert the remaining 15.4 gigawatt pipeline to ESAs by the first half of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “15.4 GW high-confidence pipeline” and said to watch for “any pull-forward of the H2 2027 revenue ramp,” without specifying when the remaining pipeline would convert to ESAs.

surprises.description: Management detailed when tax-credit flowbacks that benefit near-term customer costs are expected to reach parity, and said investment returns should then support cash-flow growth into the late 2030s. The preview discussed tax-credit monetization but did not set out this customer-cost and cash-flow timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Accelerated tax credit flowbacks benefiting near-term customer costs will reach parity around 2028-2029 for nuclear PTCs, after which investment returns are expected to sustain durable cash flow growth into the late 2030s.”

surprises.description: Duke reported $5 billion of economic-development investment and support for more than 9,000 jobs in the first half of 2026, an unanticipated positive operating and community-development update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Secured $5 billion of economic development investment supporting over 9,000 jobs in the first half of 2026.”

in_line: Duke reaffirmed 2026 EPS guidance of $6.55–$6.80, as the preview’s base case expected; management’s confidence in reaching the top half beginning in 2028 did not pull forward the timeframe the preview cited.
Data-center ESAs reached 7.8 GW versus 7.6 GW entering the quarter, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the signed total would edge up modestly.
Duke said it is on track for its 14.5% FFO-to-debt target in 2026 and expects 15% longer term, matching the preview’s stated balance-sheet targets.

surprises.description: Sezzle’s $149.7 million of Q2 revenue substantially exceeded the preview’s $130.30 million consensus estimate and the higher $135.09 million panel estimate. Revenue grew 51.7% year over year, versus the preview’s expected 32.0%–36.9% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue rose 51.7% year-over-year to $149.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | $130.30M”; “Revenue (alt. panel) | $135.09M”; respective expected YoY growth: “+32.0%” and “+36.9%.”

surprises.description: GMV reached $1.3 billion, ahead of the preview’s roughly $1.25 billion base case and its expected 35% growth. It also set a new record, surpassing the prior Q4 holiday-season peak.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 GMV grew 37.9% year-over-year to a record $1.3 billion, exceeding the prior Q4 2025 holiday season peak.”

surprises.description: Subscriber growth was much stronger than the preview’s watchpoint of re-accelerating beyond the prior quarter’s 44,000 additions: Sezzle added a record 140,000 net new subscribers and reached 854,000 total subscribers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Active subscribers reached 854,000, up 76.4% year-over-year, with a record 140,000 net new subscribers added—the largest quarterly gain since the subscription program launched.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether subscriber adds re-accelerate above the +44K Q1 pace.”

surprises.description: Management raised full-year guidance rather than merely reiterating it: adjusted EPS increased from $5.10 to $5.25 and adjusted net income from $180 million to $185 million. Revenue growth guidance is now targeted at 35%, the upper end of the previous 30%–35% range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year guidance, now targeting revenue growth of 35% (upper bound of prior 30%-35% range), adjusted net income of $185 million (up from $180 million), and adjusted EPS of $5.25 (up from $5.10).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “With the stock at 32.7x that $5.10, a mere reiteration is likely read as a disappointment. The buy side is positioned for another raise.”

surprises.description: The preview expected marketing spend to rise again, but management characterized the large spend increase as a one-time test rather than a new run rate and expects lower core marketing spend in Q3. That points to less ongoing spend pressure than the preview’s expected continued ramp suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marketing spend surged to $19.4 million (more than double year-over-year), described as a deliberate one-time test rather than a new run rate, with management expecting lower core marketing spend in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Marketing spend | more than doubled YoY | up again QoQ (explicit mandate).”

surprises.description: SezzleCash showed early customer uptake that the preview did not discuss: nearly 10% of eligible new subscribers used it as their first transaction. This is an early product traction signal beyond the preview’s listed engagement watchpoints.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Newly launched SezzleCash shows early traction with an average advance size of ~$165 and nearly 10% of eligible new subscribers using it as their first transaction.”

in_line: Average purchase frequency was 7.2x, broadly in line with the preview’s expectation that it would hold at or above 7.1x.
Full-year credit loss provisions were guided to 2.5%–3% of GMV, matching the preview’s cited target range and expectation of seasonal increases in the second half.
Management still plans to submit the bank charter application this quarter, consistent with the preview’s expectation that submission was due around this time.

surprises.description: Consolidated sales growth was 6.7%, well above the preview’s 3.6% consensus-implied growth. That makes the top-line result materially stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated net sales grew 6.7% in Q2 2026 (adjusted for tariff refund accounting).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The consensus table showed revenue implying “+3.6%” year-over-year growth.

surprises.description: Temperature Control sales rose 15.7% to $152 million, far above the preview’s roughly $137 million base estimate. The preview expected preseason orders to shift into Q2, and management said that timing helped the result, so the sales beat does not necessarily signal equally strong end-demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Temperature Control sales surged 15.7% to $152 million” and “the gain was aided by preseason order timing shifting into Q2 rather than end-demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base build estimated Temperature Control sales of “~$137M” (+4.3%); it also said preseason orders had shifted into Q2 and set a threshold of about $132 million.

surprises.description: Vehicle Control sales fell 1.6%, versus the preview’s estimate of roughly 3.6% growth and its expectation that the segment would decelerate to mid-single-digit growth. Customer point-of-sale remained up only in the low single digits and was weighted toward pricing, while the wire-set category was a major drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vehicle Control sales fell 1.6% to $198.6 million,” driven largely by “secular decline in the wire set category”; customer POS was “up in low single digits with strength weighted toward pricing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base build estimated Vehicle Control sales of “~$209M” (+3.6%) and said growth “should decelerate to mid-single digits.”

surprises.description: Engineered Solutions sales grew 16.8%, substantially above the preview’s roughly 3.8% base estimate. Management also said this was the segment’s last quarter of easy comparisons and expects its growth rate to slow for the rest of the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Engineered Solutions sales rose 16.8%,” but this was “the last quarter of easy comparisons,” and management expects growth “to slow through the remainder of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base segment build estimated Engineered Solutions sales growth of “+3.8%.”

surprises.description: Consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin reached 12.1%, slightly below the preview’s roughly 12.3% consensus-implied margin, even though adjusted EBITDA was a record $63.5 million. The margin therefore fell short of the preview’s key threshold for validating consensus expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record $63.5 million in adjusted EBITDA in Q2, representing 12.1% of net sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “~$63M / ~12.3% margin” and said margin needed to be “≥12.3% to validate consensus.”

surprises.description: Nissens’ adjusted EBITDA margin reached 19%, above the preview’s cited 18.0% prior-year Q2 margin and contrary to the concern that Q1 currency transaction losses might repeat. Sales growth was 4.8%, slightly above the preview’s 3.9% base estimate, though local-currency growth was only 2.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nissens (European aftermarket) sales grew 4.8%,” including “2.3% local currency growth and favorable currency conversion,” with adjusted EBITDA at “19% of net sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base build estimated Nissens sales growth of “+3.9%”; it highlighted Q1 margin of 12.5% versus 18.0% in Q2’25 and asked whether currency transaction losses would repeat.

surprises.description: The tariff refund detail was not laid out in the preview: SMP received IEEPA refunds but expects to share part of them with customers, while replacement Section 301 tariffs reduce total exposure only nominally. This makes the refunds less clearly a lasting net benefit than a simple refund headline might suggest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received IEEPA tariff refunds in Q2 that it expects to partly share with customers,” while replacement Section 301 tariffs “net to only a nominal reduction in total tariff exposure.”

in_line: Adjusted diluted EPS was $1.40, within the preview’s $1.39–$1.42 consensus range.
Full-year guidance was maintained, consistent with the preview’s base case of a reaffirmation, although the preview also noted that some investors wanted a raise.

Cash generation and deleveraging moved in the direction the preview said was needed: first-half operating cash flow was positive, net debt declined, and management reaffirmed the 2x year-end leverage target.

surprises.description: Vital Farms’ Q2 adjusted EBITDA loss was $26.6 million, materially worse than the preview’s expected negative mid-to-high teens and below the preview’s -$20 million downside threshold. Management called it the year’s financial trough.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $26.6 million,” including $21.8 million in peak supply management costs and $3 million in one-time feed program professional fees.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management explicitly guided Q2 adjusted EBITDA to negative mid-to-high teens ($ millions)” and “worse than -$20M signals supply-management costs are running above the $32M plan.”

surprises.description: Gross margin came in at 6.6%, far below the preview’s mid-to-high-teens expectation. The shortfall reflected $28.1 million of discrete costs, including the excess-breaker-sales impact and butter wind-down costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit fell to $10.9 million (6.6% of net revenue), burdened by $28.1 million of discrete costs including a $19.5 million excess breaker sales impact and $7.8 million in butter wind-down exit costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 reported GM should be mid-to-high teens on the supply-management load.”

surprises.description: Liquidity was tighter and the company took on substantially more financing than the preview’s starting position suggested: cash was $21.2 million, with $30 million drawn on the revolver, and Vital Farms added a fully drawn $125 million term loan plus a $60 million ABL facility. The facilities increase debt capacity, but the company now has significant new borrowing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with only $21.2 million in cash and $30 million drawn on its revolver, then secured a new $125 million term loan (fully drawn) and $60 million ABL facility, boosting debt capacity to $185 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$51.4M cash & investments at Q1-end” and “No debt today,” while flagging a revolver draw as a liquidity risk to watch.

surprises.description: Full-year supply-management costs are now expected in the mid-$30 million range, above the initial $32 million estimate. The increase is modest relative to the original estimate, though breaker-channel reliance is expected to fall sharply in the second half after peaking in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year supply management costs are now modeled in the mid-$30 million range versus an initial $32 million estimate,” with breaker-channel reliance expected to drop sharply in the second half after peaking in Q2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “~$32M of ‘supply management’ costs absorbed” and said costs were “concentrated in Q2.”

surprises.description: Despite industry oversupply and falling category pricing, Vital Farms gained more than 200 basis points of year-over-year retail dollar share in Shell Eggs. That is positive evidence for the volume-response strategy the preview identified as a key test.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vital Farms gained more than 200 basis points of year-over-year retail dollar share in the Shell Egg category during Q2 despite industry-wide oversupply and falling category pricing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called Q2 “the first clean quarter to test” the volume-response strategy and said to watch “Circana/Nielsen dollar and unit share.”

surprises.description: The average price gap to branded competitors narrowed by only $0.15 from Q1 and remained above management’s targeted $1-to-$2 range. This is progress toward the price-gap objective, but the reported gap had not yet reached the target range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average price gaps to branded competitors narrowed from approximately $2.51 in Q1 to $2.36 in Q2, moving toward the targeted $1-to-$2 range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted the “price-gap strategy” and described the thesis as “buy the gap down, get the volume back,” but gave no expected Q2 gap.

surprises.description: Vital Farms incurred $3 million in one-time professional fees for its feed program, an unanticipated item that added to the larger-than-expected quarterly EBITDA loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Q2 adjusted EBITDA loss included “$3 million in one-time feed program professional fees.”

surprises.description: Vital Farms plans to pause VXR construction by year-end, a project-specific deferral not identified in the preview, although the company reaffirmed its existing full-year CapEx range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “VXR construction will be paused by year-end within reaffirmed CapEx guidance of $70-$75 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “further capex deferral” as something to watch, but did not identify a VXR construction pause.

in_line: Q2 revenue of $166 million was within the preview’s stated $165–172 million consensus band, despite being below the $171.1 million Zacks estimate.
Management reaffirmed FY2026 revenue guidance of $775–800 million and adjusted EBITDA guidance of $0–10 million, as the preview’s base case expected.
The company reiterated an approximately 30% Q4 gross-margin run rate, matching the recovery target the preview highlighted.
The 2026 distribution outlook of 150–160 total distribution points, with 170–175 in Q4, remained on track with the distribution growth plan discussed in the preview.
The preview flagged a formal buyback pause as a possibility; the board terminated the 2026 repurchase program, citing the new loan terms.

surprises.description: Constant-currency ARR growth accelerated to 12%, above the preview’s 11.5% baseline and at its thesis-changing threshold, but ARR of $1.536 billion came in below the roughly $1.550 billion estimate. The growth rate was better than expected while the ending ARR balance was lower.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 ARR growth accelerated to 12% year-over-year on a constant currency basis, reaching $1.536 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Fundamentals have been remarkably steady — constant-currency ARR growth has printed exactly 11.5%”; consensus ARR was “~$1,550M”; “≥12.0% cc → thesis-changing.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $411 million, slightly below the $412.8 million consensus and further below the preview’s alternative $416.3 million survey. That is a modest shortfall against an expectation of roughly 13.4% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 revenues were $411 million, up 12.8% year-over-year (12.2% constant currency).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $412.8M (alt. survey: $416.3M)”; implied y/y growth was “+13.4%.”

surprises.description: The Q2 AOI-less-SBC margin was 28.3%, below the preview’s roughly 29–30% estimate and the 28.9% year-ago margin. The first-half margin also trailed the prior year, with management attributing the pressure to front-loaded investments and platform go-live costs rather than reporting an inflection.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AOI less operating SBC was $116 million (28.3% margin) in Q2 and $257 million (30.8% margin) in the first half, with first-half margins trailing prior year due to front-loaded investments and new finance/Quote-to-Cash platform go-live costs absorbed within margins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “AOI less op. SBC margin | ~29–30%”; it said the guide was for “~+100bp y/y improvement” and identified “AOI-less-SBC margin direction” as a key show-me item.

surprises.description: Management said it will not monetize AI/MCP-server agentic consumption until 2027, prioritizing adoption and validation first. That is later and less commercially immediate than the preview’s hoped-for early API-consumption revenue proof.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management does not plan to monetize AI/MCP-server agentic consumption until 2027, prioritizing adoption, exploration, and validation first.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case needed “the Virtuoso SMB and API-consumption motions to show early revenue” and listed “API consumption-based pricing rollout” and “any framing of AI as TAM expansion” among the items to watch.

surprises.description: Management described reaching the high end of the ARR range as dependent on sustained momentum, completing an acquisition, and closing lumpy Asset Analytics deals. That adds specific execution dependencies to the high-end outcome rather than making it sound like a straightforward continuation of current performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reaching the high end of the ARR range would require sustained momentum plus completing an acquisition and closing lumpy Asset Analytics big deals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case described “continuation” and expected the 11.5% streak to hold; its bull case called for the “cc ARR range [to be] raised/narrowed upward.”

surprises.description: The call warned that unfavorable FX could reduce second-half revenue by another $8–10 million versus outlook assumptions. This contrasts with the preview’s emphasis on a weak dollar as a revenue tailwind that could make a dollar-guide increase relatively easy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Unfavorable FX could reduce second-half revenue by an incremental $8-10 million versus outlook assumptions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the dollar has been weak” and that “the FX tailwind makes a revenue raise close to automatic,” while describing a raise as “nearly free.”

surprises.description: The company reported substantially increased share repurchases—$155 million in the first half—and said the fully diluted share count had fallen to 319 million. The preview did not flag this level of buyback activity as an expected result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased 3.1 million shares in Q2 and $155 million in buybacks in the first half (up meaningfully year-over-year), reducing fully diluted share count to 319 million.”

surprises.description: Power Line Systems’ revenue outside the U.S. has grown to equal the entire PLS business at its 2022 acquisition, a specific international expansion milestone not called out in the preview’s discussion of resources-sector strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Power Line Systems' revenue outside the U.S. is now as large as the entire PLS business was at its 2022 acquisition.”

in_line: Subscription revenue grew 13.6%, essentially matching the preview’s 13.7% consensus estimate.
Net revenue retention remained at 109%, matching the preview’s stated Q1 level and expectation of stability.
Resources remained the fastest-growing sector, as the preview anticipated.
The company reaffirmed its $500–$570 million full-year free-cash-flow outlook.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $24.3 million, about 29% below the preview’s roughly $34.0 million consensus and below its $33.0 million segment-based estimate. The preview modeled $14.0 million of Heavy Fabrications revenue, while the company classified Heavy Fabrications as discontinued operations after exiting wind tower manufacturing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue rose 67% year-over-year to $24.3 million”; the company “exited wind tower manufacturing, reclassifying Heavy Fabrications as discontinued operations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 FY2026 Consensus | ~$34.0M”; the segment model estimated “Heavy Fabrications: $14.0M” and total revenue of “$33.0M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was positive, but at $1.6 million it came in below the preview’s $2.4 million estimate and below the preview’s $2.2–2.6 million base-case range. The preview’s bear case had projected $1.0–1.6 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA swung to a positive $1.6 million from a $1.1 million loss in the prior year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA” estimate: “$2.4M”; base case: “$2.2–2.6M.”

surprises.description: Industrial Solutions revenue substantially exceeded the preview’s $10.0 million estimate, reaching $13.2 million. The preview expected growth and a record backlog, but not this level of quarterly revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Industrial Solutions revenue jumped nearly 80% to a record $13.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The segment model estimated “Industrial Solutions | $10.0M.”

surprises.description: Orders and backlog across Gearing and Industrial Solutions were stronger than the preview’s already-positive threshold: their combined orders were $33.4 million, above the preview’s $25 million benchmark, and combined backlog was up 93% year over year with a 1.5x book-to-bill. Gearing orders also exceeded the prior-quarter level used in the preview’s model.
surprises.fact_evidence: Combined backlog “increased 93% year-over-year” with “a book-to-bill ratio of 1.5x”; Gearing orders were “up 138% year-over-year to $16.2 million,” and Industrial Solutions orders were “up 24% year-over-year to $17.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said combined orders above “$25M” would support the story, cited Q1 combined backlog of “$73.8M,” and expected Gearing to sustain its Q1 order surge of “$13.2M.”

surprises.description: Although Industrial Solutions delivered a margin near the preview’s roughly 19% expectation in Q2, management said margins should normalize downward going forward. That is a less favorable outlook than the preview’s bull case of holding the margin at higher volume and base case of the trajectory continuing.
surprises.fact_evidence: Industrial Solutions had “EBITDA margin near 19%, though management expects margins to normalize downward going forward.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case required Industrial Solutions to “hold its ~19% segment EBITDA margin at higher volume” and that the base case assumed “the Q1 trajectory simply continues.”

in_line: Management did not reinstate guidance, consistent with the preview’s base case; it said it would wait until the Abilene wind-down completes in Q3 2026.
Industrial Solutions achieved the record backlog the preview was watching for, extending its streak to eight consecutive quarters of growth.

The company reported more than $40 million of total cash and credit availability and is pursuing bolt-on acquisitions, broadly matching the preview’s focus on post-Abilene financial flexibility and capital redeployment.

surprises.description: NAV rose to $8.25 from $7.90, above the preview’s roughly $7.85–$7.95 implied range and its $7.80–$8.00 base case. The $0.35 increase included $0.17 of accretion from below-NAV repurchases and $0.08 of unrealized appreciation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net asset value per share rose $0.35 to $8.25,” including “$0.17 of accretion from below-NAV share repurchases” and “$0.08 of unrealized appreciation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “NAV/share: no formal consensus (~$7.85–7.95 implied)” and the base scenario projected “NAV roughly flat” at “$7.80–8.00.”

surprises.description: NII was $0.15 per share, essentially matching the published $0.153 consensus but below the preview’s stated realistic whisper of $0.18–$0.22. Thus, the result met the formal estimate but missed the higher expectation the preview said was more realistic.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AFC generated Q2 2026 net investment income of $0.15 per weighted average share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The whisper on NII is realistically $0.18–0.22, above the printed $0.153.”

surprises.description: Investment income of $8.7 million beat the preview’s $8.00 million consensus, but came in below its $9.5–$10.5 million base-case range and declined from Q1’s $9.8 million. The call attributed the sequential decline largely to $1.8 million of non-recurring Q1 other income, including a $1.5 million Bloom exit fee.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total investment income declined to $8.7 million from $9.8 million in Q1, largely due to $1.8 million of non-recurring other income including a $1.5 million exit fee from the Bloom repayment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Revenue (total investment income) … Q2 2026 Consensus $8.00M,” but also said revenue “should be flat-to-up” and gave a “Base” scenario of “$9.5–10.5M.”

surprises.description: The pipeline was reported at $1.3 billion, below the preview’s previously quoted level of more than $1.5 billion, and management described originations as lumpy: about $80 million in Q1 versus less in Q2. That is weaker evidence of steady deployment than the preview’s expected deployment pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pipeline stands at $1.3 billion”; year-to-date commitments were “approximately $102 million,” with originations “lumpy—about $80 million in Q1 versus less in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the pipeline “was quoted at >$1.5B” and its base scenario anticipated “deployment steady.”

surprises.description: Debbie’s reported principal recovery had risen to $58 million, far above the $20.8 million cumulative recovery cited through Q1, and AFC had a binding term sheet to sell two assets for $12.5 million with a $2 million hard deposit. This is substantially more recovery and a firmer resolution step than the preview highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Debbie has recovered $58 million of principal to date and signed a binding term sheet with a $2 million hard deposit to sell two assets for $12.5 million (AFC holds ~80% participation).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “cumulative $20.8M through Q1, incl. a $6.2M Q1 paydown” and said to watch “continued Debbie Holdings recoveries.”

surprises.description: Two of DMA’s three dispensaries closed in July, an adverse development in the legacy cannabis portfolio that the preview did not flag. The provided call facts do not quantify the effect on AFC’s recovery or valuation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Two of three DMA dispensaries closed in July.”

surprises.description: AFC did not provide a specific Justice Grown mark in the supplied call facts; instead, it reported that the loan remained in maturity default and that it had started Article IX foreclosures and hired an advisor to market the collateral. The enforcement path was among the preview’s anticipated outcomes, but the absence of a valuation leaves its central NAV-credibility question unanswered.
surprises.fact_evidence: The loan “matured May 1, 2026 and is in maturity default,” prompting AFC to “commence Article IX foreclosures and engage SFC Advisors to market” the assets; no specific mark is reported in the supplied call facts.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “a specific mark, a forbearance/restructuring, or a foreclosure path” and that “absence of a specific mark is itself a mild negative.”

in_line: NII was essentially in line with the published $0.153 consensus, despite coming in below the preview’s higher $0.18–$0.22 whisper expectation.
The $0.05 quarterly distribution matched the preview’s stated Q2 expectation.
The Justice Grown foreclosure path was one of the possible outcomes the preview explicitly identified.
The repurchase program was active: AFC bought about 839,000 shares for roughly $2.8 million, consistent with the preview’s expectation that buyback execution would be a key signal.

surprises.description: The preview expected Managed Services bookings of $7.0–7.5 million and a recovery from the prior-year $5.6 million level. Instead, bookings fell 19% year over year to $4.5 million, with softer enterprise demand and delayed contracting.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Managed services bookings declined 19% year-over-year to $4.5 million amid softer enterprise demand and delayed contracting.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Managed Svcs bookings” estimate: “$7.0–7.5M”; the preview said the expected recovery was “the whole ballgame” and that bookings “inflect positively YoY.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated revenue of $6.9 million, while reported Managed Services revenue was $5.8 million. That is a substantially weaker result than the preview’s expected 24% year-over-year decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Managed services revenue fell 36% year-over-year to $5.8 million from $9.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue” estimate: “$6.9M (-24% YoY)” (with published consensus of $8.00M).

surprises.description: Operating expenses were lower than the preview’s roughly $4.1 million quarterly expectation: they fell 18% year over year to $3.3 million. The reduction was attributed to lower commissions, headcount, and payroll costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses fell 18% year-over-year to $3.3 million, with G&A down roughly 20%, driven by lower commissions, headcount, and payroll costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the CFO had guided opex to “remain relatively stable through the balance of this year” at “~$4.1M/qtr.”

surprises.description: IZEA reported a net loss of $0.7 million, or $0.04 per share, slightly worse than the preview’s expected $0.03 loss per share and the published $0.02 loss consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company swung to a net loss of $0.7 million (negative $0.04 per share) versus net income of $1.2 million ($0.07 per share) in the prior year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed GAAP EPS estimates of “$(0.03)” and published consensus of “$(0.02).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was a $0.4 million loss, a little worse than the preview’s expected $0.3 million loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA turned negative at negative $0.4 million compared to positive $1.3 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adj. EBITDA” of “$(0.3)M.”

surprises.description: IZEA had repurchased $1.8 million of shares under its $10 million authorization, above the preview’s estimate that about $1.4 million had been used. It also reported roughly $0.5 million of repurchases since the plan adopted in May.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Under its $10 million buyback authorization, the company has repurchased about 658,000 shares for $1.8 million,” including “roughly 135,000 shares for $0.5 million since the current plan was adopted in May.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to “only ~$1.4M of the $10M authorization used to date” and flagged resumption of buybacks under the post-May plan as a catalyst.

surprises.description: Management said its acquisition pipeline was its most active ever. The preview expected M&A discussion and described the environment as “target-rich,” but did not anticipate this specific level of activity; no completed acquisition was reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “cited its most active acquisition pipeline ever.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had called the environment “target-rich” and identified “any concrete M&A framing” as a live issue.

in_line: Gross margins remained relatively consistent with the prior year, as the preview had highlighted margin confirmation as important.
Cash ended at $46.6 million with no debt, close to the preview’s $45–46 million cash expectation.

surprises.description: Q2 EPS of $2.51 and adjusted EBITDA of $324 million were far above the preview’s $0.50–$0.51 EPS consensus and $185–$197 million base-case EBITDA, largely because Core recognized $125 million of Leer South insurance proceeds in Q2. The $155 million total settlement also exceeded the preview’s expectation of approximately $100 million of additional proceeds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income rose to $126 million ($2.51 per diluted share) … with adjusted EBITDA jumping to $324 million … aided by insurance proceeds”; “settled the Leer South insurance claim for $155 million total, recognizing $125 million in Q2 EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) $0.50 – $0.51”; base-case “Adj. EBITDA $185–197M”; “approximately $100M of additional insurance proceeds … expected in Q2.”

surprises.description: High CV thermal cash costs were $38.58 per ton in Q2, better than the preview’s $39–$40 base case and below its $39 threshold for a clear win. Despite that strong quarter, Core raised full-year cost guidance by $1 per ton to $39–$40.50, reversing the preview’s expectation that guidance would be reaffirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HCV thermal cash costs dropped to $38.58 per ton from $42.56 in Q1, though full-year guidance was raised $1 to $39-$40.50 per ton due to persistent inflationary pressures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case: “High CV cost lands $39.00–40.00”; “buy-side expects reaffirmation”; the preview also said “Below $39.00 is a clear win.”

surprises.description: Metallurgical cash costs fell to $85.65 per ton, beating even the preview’s bull-case assumption of roughly $88, and Core lowered its full-year met cash-cost guidance by $2.50 per ton. This was a stronger cost improvement than the preview’s already-expected sharp improvement from Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Metallurgical segment cash costs fell nearly $7 per ton quarter-over-quarter to $85.65, prompting management to lower full-year met cash cost guidance by $2.50 to a range of $86-$91 per ton.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case assumed “met cost at low end (~$88)”; it also noted Q1 cash costs had improved “to $92.35 from $103.49.”

surprises.description: PRB sales were 10.2 million tons, below the preview’s 12.2-million-ton base-case assumption and down from Q1’s 11.9 million. The call attributed the decline to weak shoulder-season demand and low gas prices.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PRB coal sales fell to 10.2 million tons from 11.9 million in Q1 due to weak shoulder-season demand and low gas prices.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case assumed “~12.2Mt PRB” for the quarter; it listed the FY PRB volume framework as “47.0–50.0Mt.”

surprises.description: Core reported that more than 50 million PRB tons remain committed for 2026 delivery, above the preview’s stated full-year PRB guidance range of 47–50 million tons. The average committed price of $14.27 per ton indicates substantial volume coverage, though the preview had highlighted PRB’s very thin margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Over 50 million tons remain committed for 2026 delivery at an average price of $14.27 per ton.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed PRB full-year guidance as “47.0–50.0Mt” and described PRB margins as “wafer-thin.”

surprises.description: Core disclosed a DTA terminal outage affecting its 35% ownership interest, an operational issue the preview did not flag. Management said the impacts were already reflected in netback realizations and the outage was being managed, so the incremental financial effect is unclear.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Core's DTA terminal outage (35% ownership) is being managed with impacts already reflected in netback realizations.”

surprises.description: Core reported that its HCV thermal segment is nearly fully contracted for 2026 at more than 31 million tons and is already more than half contracted for 2027, with disclosed pricing. The preview did not flag this level of forward contracting or pricing visibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The HCV thermal segment is now nearly fully contracted for 2026 at over 31 million tons at approximately $58 per ton, and is more than 50% contracted for 2027 with India tons near $60 and West Elk in the upper $40s to low $50s.”

surprises.description: The marketing team secured approximately 16 million tons of contracted volume through 2030 at attractive prices, adding long-dated commercial visibility that the preview had not discussed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The marketing team secured ~16 million tons of contracted volume through 2030 at attractive prices.”

in_line: Core returned $68 million to shareholders in Q2, up from $47 million in Q1, and signaled further buyback increases in Q3 and Q4—consistent with the preview’s expectation that repurchases would step up.

Domestic coal demand remained weak, with coal burn down about 10% year to date, in line with the preview’s warning about soft thermal demand; the call also cited outages and hot weather as reasons to expect a stronger second half.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $224.2 million, about 2.2% above the $219.33 million consensus and above the company’s $218–220 million guide. The preview said revenue beats had usually been small, so this was a notably stronger print than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $224.2 million, up 20.1% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 consensus $219.33M”; “Q2'26 company guide $218–220M”; “Revenue beats have been consistent and small (<1%).”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin reached 19.3%, far above the preview’s 11.5–12.5% guide and roughly $25–27 million implied EBITDA. The preview viewed a margin of at least 12% as the key test, making the reported result a much larger outperformance than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $43.3 million or 19.3% of revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin” company guide “11.5–12.5%”; consensus “~$25–27M implied”; “Adj. EBITDA margin ≥12% in Q2” was a catalyst checklist item.

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA margin guidance rose to 13–14% from 12–13%, exceeding the preview’s stated FY26 range. This was a stronger profitability outlook than the preview’s expected guidance bridge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year adjusted EBITDA margin guidance to 13%-14%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance … adj. EBITDA margin 12.0–13.0%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.58 per diluted share, versus the preview’s consensus of a $0.04 loss. The preview cautioned that EPS submissions mixed GAAP and adjusted figures, but the reported positive result was still substantially above that stated consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS improved to net income of $0.58 per diluted share versus an adjusted net loss of $0.32 per share in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 consensus” EPS “($0.04)”; “Treat the ($0.04) EPS line with care — the vendor consensus mixes GAAP and adjusted submissions.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 72.8%, above the preview’s roughly 71%+ expectation and the 71.5% threshold used in its bull case. The preview had highlighted gross-margin progress as important to the 2027 profitability bridge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin reached 72.8%, up 160 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin … ~71%+”; the bull case included “GM ≥71.5%.”

surprises.description: The company raised FY2026 revenue guidance, but the new $880–890 million range has an $885 million midpoint—below the preview’s roughly $890 million buy-side expectation and at the low end of its base-case range. The raise was real, but less ambitious than the market framing in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $880 million-$890 million (18%-19% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buy-side is positioned for a raise to roughly $890M”; base case: guidance “raised modestly to $885–893M”; “failing to raise FY to ≥$890M would itself read as a negative.”

surprises.description: iRhythm agreed to acquire Vital Connect, which has an approximately $65 million annual revenue run rate, with contribution to growth expected from 2027. The preview discussed sleep-diagnostics pilots and capital deployment but did not anticipate an acquisition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “iRhythm agreed to acquire Vital Connect, currently at an approximately $65 million annual revenue run rate … with the deal expected to close by year-end and positively contribute to revenue growth beginning in 2027.”

surprises.description: The Vital Connect purchase will be partly funded with $50 million of equity, adding just over 420,000 shares. The preview raised capital deployment as an open question but did not forecast this equity issuance; management said the resulting dilution would be less than 1.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Vital Connect deal will be funded partly with $50 million in equity, equating to just over 420,000 shares or less than 1.5% dilution.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any capital deployment commentary against the $549.6M cash balance.”

surprises.description: The company agreed to settle the Baxter/Welch Allyn/Bardy Diagnostics litigation for $50 million, rather than proceeding toward the preview’s scheduled March 2027 jury trial. The settlement resolves the pending case but entails a substantial cash payment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company agreed to settle its Baxter/Welch Allyn/Bardy Diagnostics litigation for a $50 million settlement payment on July 31.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted a “5-day jury trial set March 22, 2027” and said to “Watch for any accrual or settlement language.”

surprises.description: The third-generation algorithm had been expected by the preview to receive clearance later in 2026; the call reported FDA clearance and reiterated substantial technician-time and cost-saving potential. That is an earlier clearance milestone than the preview anticipated, while the stated savings are broadly in line with its estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FDA clearance of the third-generation algorithm is expected to reduce clinical technician review time by as much as 50% and generate approximately $100 million of cumulative cost savings over five years upon its first-half 2027 launch.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Next-gen deep-learning algorithm 510(k) — clearance expected later in 2026”; the preview cited “~50% reduction in technician scan time” and “>$100M cumulative five-year benefit.”

in_line: Q2 free cash flow was positive, as the preview expected an inflection to positive after Q1’s seasonal outflow.
Management reaffirmed the 15% adjusted EBITDA margin target for 2027, in line with the preview’s expectation that the framework would be reaffirmed.
