surprises.fact_evidence: “The target market comprises approximately 20 million U.S. adults with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension, with commercial focus on roughly 50,000 physicians controlling third-line-or-later prescribing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “They are targeting the physicians who control ~50% of third- and fourth-line hypertension prescribing.”

in_line: The $200 million Tanabe payment drove the large reported loss: the preview explicitly warned that expensing it could produce a roughly $247 million net loss and an optically very poor EPS result. The reported $241.1 million net loss is close to that warned-about case.
The Tanabe royalty buyback and its $200 million upfront payment, up to $100 million in commercial milestones, and the financing package were already detailed in the preview.
Cash of $661.4 million and the expectation that it funds operations into 2028 are consistent with the preview’s $620–670 million cash range and expected runway.

Management said baxdrostat rebate levels were consistent with its expectations and lorundrostat is expected to have parity access on a non-specialty tier, in line with the preview’s expectation that payer coverage was achievable. Pricing remains undisclosed until around approval or launch, as the preview anticipated pricing signals might be limited.

surprises.description: Revenue was $14.5 million, about 9% above the preview’s $13.26 million consensus and also above its $13.8–14.2 million bull case. The preview had highlighted a risk that consensus required unusually strong GMV or added FFL-transfer revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net revenues rose 22.1% year-over-year to $14.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $13.26M”; bull case “$13.8-14.2M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $7.9 million, above the preview’s $6.3–6.9 million base case and its $6.5 million catalyst threshold. Trailing-12-month EBITDA was also about $27 million, ahead of the $25 million run-rate goal the preview emphasized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA jumped 152% to $7.9 million” and reached “~$27 million on a trailing-12-month basis, above the $25 million run-rate goal.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case adj. EBITDA “$6.3-6.9M”; catalyst checklist: “Adj. EBITDA ≥$6.5M”; the preview describes the “$25M annualized run-rate.”

surprises.description: GMV grew 18.1%, exceeding the preview’s 9–12% base case and even its 15%+ bull-case threshold. That was well above the preview’s roughly 5.5% NICS backdrop and its threshold for meaningful share gain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GMV grew 18.1% to $223.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case: “GMV +9-12%”; bull case: “GMV +15%+”; the preview says “Anything at +8% GMV or better is genuine share gain.”

surprises.description: The take rate rose to 6.47%, well above the preview’s 6.0–6.1% base-case range and the prior-quarter 6.06%. The new FFL transfer service contributed 39 basis points, countering the preview’s concern that this less-profitable service could weigh on monetization.
surprises.fact_evidence: The FFL transfer service “contributed $0.9 million in revenue and 39 basis points to the 6.47% take rate in its first quarter of operation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case: “take rate 6.0-6.1%”; the preview says FFL transfer services are “less profitable than the core marketplace” and identifies “Take rate ≥6.06%” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: EPS was positive $0.02 rather than the preview’s consensus loss of $0.01. The preview expected a clean quarter to produce only about $0.01, so the reported result also exceeded that clean-quarter estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income from continuing operations swung to $3.6 million from a $5.9 million loss” and diluted EPS was “$0.02.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus EPS “$(0.01)”; the preview says “A clean quarter mathematically produces ~+$0.01.”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 84.5%, substantially below the preview’s roughly 87% framing and the prior-quarter 87.6%. The reported explanation—non-recurring FFL start-up costs—was a margin headwind not quantified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined ~260 basis points to 84.5% due to non-recurring FFL start-up costs,” with management expecting it to “stabilize above 85%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview frames the marketplace as having “~87% gross margins” and says the base case involves “reaffirmation of the $25M run-rate and ‘87% gross margin’ language.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses fell about 45%, including lower legal and professional fees as litigation, SEC, and audit matters concluded. This was a favorable cost and below-the-line outcome versus the preview’s identified risk that legal or indemnification charges could resurface.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total operating expenses fell about 45% ($7.4 million) to $8.9 million,” including “$3.7 million lower legal/professional fees as Delaware litigation, SEC and audit matters concluded.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists as a bear-case risk that a “legal or indemnification charge resurfaces” and flags the “remaining Arizona class action / shareholder derivative matters.”

surprises.description: Management said part of the quarter’s demand was a temporary Virginia buying surge and warned that demand pulled into Q1 should not be assumed to recur in Q2. The preview did not identify this state-specific pull-forward risk; management also reported slowing June velocity and a continuing July seasonal slowdown.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management called the Virginia high-capacity firearm ban buying surge a “temporary, non-recurring tailwind,” warned that “demand pulled into Q1 is not assumed to repeat in Q2,” and said June velocity slowed while July continued the seasonal summer slowdown.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $2.37, far above the preview’s roughly $1.91–$1.92 expectation. The beat was about 24% versus consensus and exceeded the preview’s bull-case EPS range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS rose 13% year-over-year to $2.37.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS $1.91”; management framed “~$1.92 adj. EPS for Q2.”

surprises.description: ICU raised full-year adjusted EPS and EBITDA guidance above the prior ranges, rather than merely narrowing or reaffirming them. The new EPS range of $8.60–$9.00 is entirely above the prior $7.75–$8.45 range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $8.60-$9.00 (from $7.75-$8.45) and adjusted EBITDA to $415M-$435M (from $400M-$430M).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said buyers expected “a narrowing toward the upper half ($8.10–$8.45)” and described a flat reaffirm as a risk; its bull scenario anticipated a raise or narrowing to “$8.10–$8.45.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $548 million exceeded the preview’s $533.4–$538 million estimate range and grew 1% reported, rather than declining 2%–3% as the preview’s reported-growth estimates implied. Organic growth was 6% despite the reported comparison being affected by the Otsuka JV deconsolidation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $548 million, up 6% organically but only 1% reported due to the mid-2025 Otsuka JV deconsolidation of IV Solutions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $533.4M”; the preview also described consensus as implying “‑2% to ‑3% reported.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $110 million, above the preview’s estimated $103–$108 million range, though by less than the EPS beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 10% to $110 million at a 20% margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$103–108M (est., not formally polled).”

surprises.description: The full-year adjusted gross margin outlook moved up to around 41.5%, better than the preview’s modeled margin range of roughly 40.5%–41%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted gross margin guidance was raised to around 41.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “Adj. gross margin ~40.5–41%” and said to watch for “adj. GM ≥40.5%.”

surprises.description: The record IV Systems quarter came partly from installations occurring earlier than expected, which management said will reduce growth later in the year. The preview expected the record run to continue but did not anticipate this pull-forward caveat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “IV Systems grew 12% organically to a record pump quarter, but this was inflated by earlier-than-expected installations that will reduce later-year growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q1 as “a record pump quarter” and said to watch “whether the record run continues into a tougher sequential comp.”

surprises.description: Management said the pump upgrade and replacement cycle has not begun in earnest and is expected more in 2027. That means current systems strength is coming mostly from competitive wins, rather than from the replacement-cycle contribution investors might associate with the pump momentum.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pump upgrade/replacement cycle has not yet begun in earnest (expected more in 2027), meaning current systems strength stems mostly from competitive wins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “the pump cycle” and asked for commentary on “installed-base conversion and dedicated-set attach,” but did not expect the upgrade/replacement cycle to be deferred until 2027.

surprises.description: Despite repaying $50 million of debt, net leverage was 2.3x, above the preview’s stated Q1 level of about 1.5x and its expectation that the company was already within its ≤2.0x target. Management still expects to reach roughly 2x by year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ICU repaid $50 million of debt in Q2, lowering net leverage to 2.3x and remaining on track to reach its ~2x leverage target by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “net leverage was ~1.5x at Q1 — already inside target” and called for confirmation of the “≤2.0x leverage target.”

surprises.description: The company received $20 million in tariff refunds, an unanticipated cash-flow benefit, although the refunds were excluded from non-GAAP results. Management said smaller additional refunds may follow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $20 million in tariff refunds (excluded from non-GAAP results but included in free cash flow), with potential for smaller additional refunds later.”

surprises.description: Management described $30–$40 million of annual incremental tariffs still facing the company, a less favorable cost picture than the preview’s expectation of modest Q2–Q3 tariff relief. The preview did note the earlier $40–$50 million annual tariff framing, but expected lower rates to provide some relief.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ICU still faces $30-$40 million in annual incremental tariffs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the 10% rates “were expected to give modest Q2–Q3 relief versus the original $40–50M annual framing.”

surprises.description: Management quantified an additional roughly $60 million negative currency impact over four years from the Costa Rican colon, Mexican peso, and Japanese yen, an adverse headwind not raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A roughly $60 million negative currency impact over four years from the Costa Rican colon, Mexican peso, and Japanese yen.”

in_line: Consumables grew 5% organically, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Q2 would return to mid-single-digit organic growth.
IV Systems did post a record pump quarter, as the preview expected; the earlier-than-expected installation timing and resulting later-year growth effect were the unexpected caveats.

surprises.description: MicroVision reported Q2 revenue of $1.5 million, 50% above the preview’s primary $1.0 million consensus estimate, though within the preview’s $1.2–$1.6 million base scenario and below the $1.82 million alternate estimate. Most revenue came from IRIS long-range sensors.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $1.5 million,” with “the predominant portion from IRIS long-range sensors.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 Consensus” revenue was “$1.00M (alt: $1.82M)”; the base scenario expected “$1.2–1.6M.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin reached 44%, above the preview’s 35–40% guide range, and management attributed the result to favorable product mix and supply-chain efficiencies. The preview had questioned whether margins could hold as volume shifted toward newer builds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin reached 44% (42% year-to-date),” driven by “favorable product mix and supply chain efficiencies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed gross margin at “~35–40% (guide)” and asked “whether 35–40% holds as volume mixes toward newer builds.”

surprises.description: MicroVision raised its full-year gross-margin guidance to 40–45% from 35–40%, rather than merely maintaining the prior range as the preview expected it to defend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its full-year 2026 gross margin guidance from 35%-40% to 40%-45%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY2026 gross-margin guidance was “35–40%” and listed “35–40% (guide)” for Q2.

surprises.description: The cash position was weaker than the preview’s expected $30–34 million quarter-end balance: MicroVision reported $27.2 million in cash and investments. It also disclosed a $17.5 million minimum-liquidity covenant, while the preview had highlighted funding needs and convertible notes but not that specific cash floor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $27.2 million in cash and investments” and “must maintain minimum cash liquidity of $17.5 million under its convertible notes covenants.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Absent financing, Q2 should end near $30–34M.”

surprises.description: First-half cash use was higher than the preview’s roughly $32 million expectation, at $36 million. Management still guided to about $60 million for the full year and expected burn to decline in the second half, so the higher first-half burn makes that back-half reduction more important.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash used in operations plus capex was $19.5 million in Q2 ($17.4 million adjusted) and $36 million for the first half,” with “approximately $60 million full-year burn” and “declining burn in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “H1 consumes ~$32M” and cited the approximately $60 million annual burn guide.

surprises.description: Management raised its 2026–2030 booking-opportunity projection by 50%, from $500 million to $750 million, and reported more than 130 customer engagements versus the preview’s 100-plus figure. The larger opportunity is driven mainly by industrial and defense rather than automotive, but it is an opportunity projection rather than reported revenue or backlog.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its 2026-2030 booking opportunity projection by 50% from $500 million to $750 million across over 130 customer engagements (up ~30% from the prior 100), driven mainly by industrial and defense rather than automotive.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “100+ active customers/prospects” across industrial, security/defense, and automotive.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a near-term MOVIA S launch and substantial customer interest: launch is planned for October, with more than 25 active engagements, capacity being built for about 15,000 units annually, and management expecting a meaningful revenue contribution in 2027. The preview had not identified this product ramp as a specific catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The MOVIA S short-range sensor launches in October 2026 with more than 25 active customer engagements,” and the company is building “capacity for roughly 15,000 units annually,” expecting it “to be a meaningful revenue contributor in 2027.”

surprises.description: Semiconductor engineering services were already contributing revenue: approximately 15% of Q2 sales came from those services. The preview had explicitly questioned whether the new semiconductor unit would produce revenue or become an added cost center.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately 15%” of Q2 revenue came “from semiconductor engineering services.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked of MicroVision Semiconductor: “Is this a revenue line or an added cost center?”

surprises.description: Management said it integrated the acquired Luminar business in roughly one quarter and reconstituted about half of the roughly 30 inherited customer accounts. That is a concrete integration and account-recovery update, although 70–80% of first-half revenue still came from sales of acquired IRIS inventory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company integrated the acquired Luminar business within roughly one quarter, reconstituting about half of the ~30 inherited customer accounts,” while “70-80% of first-half revenue” came from acquired IRIS inventory sales.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 opex was inflated by “Luminar/Scantinel acquisition and integration costs” and that a drop in opex would signal “integration is done”; it also noted 75% of Q1 sales came from Luminar-acquired sensors.

surprises.description: The call described recent IRIS defense orders for military unmanned ground vehicles and unmanned aircraft, including use of the 1550nm sensor technology, beyond the defense reorder already noted in the preview. The orders add program detail, but no order values were provided in the facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received recent defense orders including IRIS sensors from a prime contractor for military UGVs” and “from a defense/aerospace contractor for unmanned aircraft.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted an April defense reorder of “200 additional Movia L units” and asked for “any quantification” of the defense program.

surprises.description: MicroVision launched MOVIA Air with nine prelaunch evaluation partners, a new product and partner update not anticipated in the preview. The information establishes evaluations, not yet commercial orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company was “launching MOVIA Air with 9 prelaunch evaluation partners.”

surprises.description: Although the full-year revenue range was reaffirmed, the supplied call facts do not provide the quantified PO values, backlog, or shipment schedules that the preview identified as important proof for the required second-half ramp. The new defense-order descriptions add some detail, but do not quantify that revenue path.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management reiterated “full-year revenue guidance of $10 million to $15 million, with the bulk expected in the second half”; the supplied facts give no PO values, backlog figure, or shipment schedule.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “A reaffirmation without named programs, PO values, and shipment schedules should be discounted heavily” and called for “any quantification of the mining/construction MDA or the defense program.”

in_line: Full-year revenue guidance remained $10–15 million, with most revenue expected in the second half, as the preview anticipated.
Full-year cash use of approximately $60 million was reiterated, matching the preview’s cited burn guide, although first-half cash use was higher than its estimate.

surprises.description: Park’s Q2 RevPAR rose nearly 7% excluding Royal Palm, well above the preview’s roughly 1.5% company-guidance midpoint and even its +5% bull case. Growth also accelerated to over 11% in June, and July RevPAR was up 8.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 RevPAR increased nearly 7% year-over-year excluding Royal Palm,” with monthly growth accelerating from “~4% in April to 5% in May and over 11% in June,” and “July RevPAR up 8.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q2 RevPAR as “~+1.5%, including ~100bps of Miami drag”; its bull scenario was “+5.0%.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA and adjusted FFO both came in well above the preview’s estimates: EBITDA was $204 million versus about $185 million, and FFO was $0.70 per share versus an estimated $0.60–$0.62.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 hotel adjusted EBITDA rose nearly 9% to $204 million” and “adjusted FFO was $0.70 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adjusted EBITDA ~$185M” and “Adjusted FFO/share ~ $0.60–0.62 (est.).”

surprises.description: Park raised its full-year RevPAR guidance midpoint by about 225 basis points, more than twice the preview’s 100-basis-point threshold for a meaningful raise. The new 3%–4.5% range also exceeds the preview’s bull-case range of 2.5%–4.0%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 RevPAR guidance by ~225 bps at the midpoint to a new range of 3% to 4.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a raise of “less than ~100bps at the midpoint” would be negative and set its bull case at “FY RevPAR to 2.5%–4.0%.”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA and FFO guidance were raised more than the preview’s base case anticipated: EBITDA midpoint increased by about $25 million, versus an expected $5–$10 million increase, and FFO guidance rose by $0.13 per share.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance was increased by ~$25 million at the midpoint to $617–$637 million, and adjusted FFO guidance rose ~$0.13 to $1.90–$2.00 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “EBITDA mid +$5–10M”; it listed prior FY guidance of “Adj. EBITDA $587–617M” and “Adj. FFO/sh $1.74–1.90.”

surprises.description: Hawaii performed much better than the preview’s uncertain setup suggested: Hilton Hawaiian Village RevPAR was up nearly 12% and EBITDA increased over 13%, despite the preview noting HHV had been only +1% in Q1 and flagging Hawaii as a key debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hilton Hawaiian Village RevPAR up nearly 12% and EBITDA up over 13%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “HHV was only +1%” in Q1 and described Hawaii as “genuinely mixed,” with “any progress” on the HHV index a key disclosure.

surprises.description: The non-core hotel sale program advanced far beyond the preview’s concern that only $31 million had closed year-to-date and the program might not finish in 2026: Park has sold 10 of 19 identified hotels for nearly $200 million, leaving less than 5% of portfolio value in non-core assets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Since its 2025 exit plan, Park has sold 10 of 19 identified non-core hotels for nearly $200 million at ~12.5x EBITDA, with remaining non-core assets now less than 5% of portfolio value.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Only $31M of the planned pipeline has closed year-to-date” and noted Barclays’ view that “the program won’t finish in 2026.”

surprises.description: The reopened Royal Palm showed much stronger balance-of-year pricing than the preview’s delayed-ramp concern implied: group ADRs were up 21% and transient ADRs up 53% versus pre-renovation. The July 22 reopening itself was expected, but these pricing figures were not.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $100M+ Royal Palm South Beach redevelopment reopened July 22” and balance-of-year “group and transient ADRs up 21% and 53% versus pre-renovation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the reopening was “pushed into Q4/2027” for the ramp and described “a ramp pushed into Q4/2027.”

surprises.description: Forward group demand was strong beyond the preview’s Q2 focus: full-year group pace was nearly 6% higher, Q3 pace was over 15% higher, and 2027 core group pace was over 6% higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 group pace is up nearly 6%, Q3 group pace is up over 15%, and 2027 core group pace is up over 6%.”

surprises.description: Leverage improved rather than remaining above the preview’s 6.3x concern: net debt-to-EBITDA was 6.1x, down about 0.2x from the prior quarter. Park also gave a specific plan to repay the $1.27 billion Hilton Hawaiian Village mortgage in September.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt was ~$3.7 billion (6.1x net debt-to-EBITDA, down ~0.2x from prior quarter) with $2.6 billion liquidity,” and Park plans to “fully repay the $1.27 billion Hilton Hawaiian Village mortgage in September.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “6.31x net debt / TTM comparable EBITDA” and described leverage as a concern, with its bear case including “leverage above 6.3x.”

surprises.description: Hotel EBITDA margin expanded 80 basis points to nearly 32%, a stronger result than the preview’s margin discussion—which highlighted Host’s 60-basis-point expansion and Park’s need to control costs—would suggest.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 hotel adjusted EBITDA was $204 million “with margin of nearly 32% (up 80 bps).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “Host expanded 60bps on rate-led growth” and said Park’s opex guidance was “+2.4%–3.4% against ~5% wage growth, offset by lower insurance premiums.”

in_line: Q2 group rooms revenue grew 9.5%, broadly in line with the preview’s report that management had preannounced group revenue up about 10%.
Royal Palm reopened on July 22, as the preview anticipated after saying it “reopened July 22, 2026”; the missed World Cup window and delayed reopening were also already flagged.
The approximately $28 million Royal Palm stabilized EBITDA potential was already identified in the preview as the “promised $28M stabilized EBITDA.”

surprises.description: July net sales grew about 18% year over year, well ahead of the preview’s roughly 10% Q3-to-date reference point and above its low-teens bull-case signal. This marked a clear acceleration from Q2’s 12% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “July net sales increasing approximately 18% year-over-year, a 6-point acceleration from Q2's growth rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything below ~+10% Q3-to-date breaks the reacceleration story”; the bull case called for Q3-to-date growth in the “low-teens.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 56.6%, above the previewed 54.1%–54.6% guide. Even excluding roughly 160 basis points from tariff refunds, underlying gross margin rose about 90 basis points year over year, exceeding the preview’s expected flat-to-50-basis-point improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin was 56.6%, but excluding roughly 160 basis points of tariff refund benefit, underlying gross margin rose about 90 basis points year-over-year on AI-driven markdown recalibration.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | 54.1–54.6% (co. guide) | ... flat to +50bps.”

surprises.description: Tariff refunds delivered an unmodeled benefit, including 6 cents per share and $5.6 million of adjusted EBITDA. That helped lift reported EPS to 26 cents versus the 22-cent estimate, but backing out the EPS benefit implies 20 cents, below consensus; the preview had identified refunds as a possible one-time upside excluded from guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS rose to 26 cents ... including a 6-cent benefit from IEPA tariff refunds,” and adjusted EBITDA was $27 million “including a $5.6 million tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Tariff refunds filed April 20 with 60–90 day timing were explicitly excluded from guidance — a possible unmodeled one-time benefit.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed that it plans to invest about two points of adjusted EBITDA margin in 2026, including 150 basis points in marketing and 50 basis points in G&A. The preview anticipated substantial marketing spend and watched for cost overruns, but did not flag an investment of this stated size, which pressures near-term profitability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is investing approximately two points of adjusted EBITDA margin in 2026 (about 150 bps in marketing and 50 bps in G&A) to seed long-term initiatives, pressuring near-term profitability.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited marketing at “~15.7% of sales (FY 15.3–15.8%)” and warned that “marketing above 15.8%” could indicate that growth was being bought.

surprises.description: Active-customer growth accelerated to 11%, above the preview’s expected 8% range, and the company exceeded 3 million trailing 12-month active customers. The quarterly increase of 115,000 was also described as the highest in four years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month active customers accelerated to 11% growth year-over-year, surpassing the 3 million milestone with a 115,000 quarterly increase—the highest quarterly growth in four years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Active customers (TTM) ~2.95–3.00M” and said sustaining “≥8% active growth” was important.

surprises.description: International sales grew 16%, above the preview’s watchpoint of roughly 15%, while the Middle East rebounded to strong double-digit growth despite the expected continued slowdown. The international mix also reached a record high.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International sales grew 16% year-over-year and reached nearly 23% of total net sales—the highest mix ever—with the Middle East rebounding to strong double-digit growth despite a weak start.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the Middle East slowdown “persisted into Q2” and asked whether international sales would “decelerate below ~15%.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow was negative $11 million and inventory rose 25% year over year, a working-capital and inventory build that the preview did not identify as an expected Q2 issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 free cash flow was negative $11 million on unfavorable working capital and inventory rose 25% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: The company repurchased nearly 500,000 Class A shares for about $10 million, more than 1% of the Class A stock. The preview discussed the company’s cash position but did not flag a repurchase as an expected capital-allocation action.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased nearly 500,000 Class A shares at an average price of $19.98 (about $10 million, over 1% of Class A stock).”

surprises.description: The Cardi B Grow Good venture showed strong repeat purchasing and social-media traction, and its gross margins are accretive. The preview noted prior sellouts and expected more inventory, but the call said inventory constraints still limited sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Cardi B Grow Good beauty joint venture sold out within hours across its first drops, achieved a repeat purchase rate approaching 40%, generated 670,000 Instagram followers, and carries gross margins accretive to the business, though inventory constraints limited sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted GrowGood had “sold out in under an hour, gated on inventory” and that management had flagged “a big wave of inventory coming.”

in_line: Q2 net sales were $347 million, up 12% year over year, at the top of the preview’s $343–347 million consensus range and within its expected 11%–12% growth.
Full-year gross-margin guidance was maintained at 53.5%–54.0%, as the preview expected.

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EPS was $0.35, well above the preview’s $0.21 estimate. The 67% gap was much larger than the preview’s expected 11% year-over-year increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS rising to $0.35 from $0.19 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS: $0.21”; implied y/y “+11%.”

surprises.description: Q4 total segment EBITDA reached $423 million, substantially above the preview’s estimated $355–365 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total segment EBITDA surged 31% to $423 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total Segment EBITDA ~$355–365M (est., not a published print).”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $2.3 billion, about 4% above the preview’s $2.21 billion estimate, rather than merely matching the roughly 5% year-over-year growth expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue rose 11% to $2.3 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue: $2.21B”; implied y/y “+5%.”

surprises.description: Digital-only subscription net adds were about 194,000, far above the preview’s self-set expectation of notably higher adds and its warning that anything below 60,000 could be a soft miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Digital-only subscriptions up 9% to nearly 6.3 million and the highest sequential net adds (~194,000) in over two years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management guided to “notably higher” Q4 net adds; “Sub-60k would read as a soft miss.”

surprises.description: Digital Real Estate Services delivered especially strong growth, with revenue up 19% and EBITDA up 46%; realtor.com revenue grew 13% despite the preview’s concerns about housing and rate headwinds and its warning that forward commentary was a risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Digital Real Estate Services delivered standout Q4 results with revenue up 19% to $553 million and EBITDA up 46% to $222 million, as realtor.com posted its seventh straight quarter of revenue growth (+13%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described realtor.com as “the clearest bear vector,” citing falling existing home sales and higher mortgage rates, and said “the forward commentary is where this bites.”

surprises.description: FY2026 revenue and EBITDA finished above the preview’s derived expectations: revenue was $9 billion versus about $8.90 billion, and EBITDA exceeded $1.6 billion versus an estimated $1.55–1.60 billion range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year revenue grew 7% to $9 billion and total segment EBITDA rose 15% to over $1.6 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Derived FY2026 revenue of “~$8.90B, +5.3%” and total segment EBITDA of “~$1.55–1.60B.”

surprises.description: The Meta AI licensing deal was already signed, but it was contributing to Q4 results across Dow Jones and News Media, rather than remaining mostly a future-facing narrative as the preview suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Meta AI licensing deal is now contributing to Q4 results across both Dow Jones and News Media, with more deals in the pipeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview characterized AI licensing as “narrative >> numbers this quarter” and said the Meta and OpenAI deals were signed.

surprises.description: Dow Jones raised the WSJ digital subscription full price for new customers from $39.99 to $44.99, a pricing action the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The WSJ digital subscription full price [was raised] from $39.99 to $44.99 for new customers.”

in_line: FY2026 buybacks totaled $643 million, close to the preview’s expectation that a Q4 repurchase near $200 million would put the full-year total around $650 million; the preview also noted the roughly $380 million Foxtel loan repayment.
The preview expected strong Q4 free cash flow, and the call reported FY2026 free cash flow of $811 million, up 42%, though it did not provide a Q4-only figure.

Management’s expectation of benefiting from its share of the Anthropic settlement is consistent with the preview’s view that the settlement benefit would come later in the calendar year, rather than in Q4.

surprises.description: Peloton guided to FY27 revenue of $2.3–2.4 billion, down 3.9% at the midpoint, rather than the roughly flat revenue the preview said the Street expected. Management also framed FY27 as a transition year, with new-category launches not expected to drive acceleration until fall 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 revenue guidance of $2.3-2.4 billion implies a 3.9% year-over-year decline at the midpoint,” with acceleration from new-category launches “starting fall of calendar 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street: roughly flat revenue (~$2.43B)” and UBS “models revenue −1%.” The preview also said to watch for a date for the revenue inflection.

surprises.description: FY27 adjusted EBITDA guidance was below the preview’s $504 million consensus midpoint: the company’s $435–525 million range has a $480 million midpoint. The top of the range is near consensus, but the midpoint is about 5% lower.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $435-525 million reflects a 7% increase at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$504M” for FY27; the preview’s base scenario expected “$495–520M.”

surprises.description: Q4 net churn reached 2.2%, materially above the preview’s 1.4% level for reopening the bear case. Management attributed about half of the increase to a since-reverted payment reactivation algorithm change and half to lingering price-increase effects; FY27 churn is expected roughly flat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 net churn rose 37 basis points year-over-year to 2.2%,” with roughly half attributed to a “one-time payment reactivation algorithm change” and half to “lingering price-increase effects”; “full-year FY27 churn is expected roughly flat.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 churn was 1.2%; anything ≥1.4% reopens the bear case.”

surprises.description: FY27 gross margin guidance of about 54% was higher than the preview’s roughly 52.5% full-year guide assumption, by about 150 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 gross margin is expected around 54%, up roughly 140 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY gross margin guide of ~52.5% requires a meaningful Q4 step-up.”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $608 million, above the $597 million consensus and $6 million above the high end of the implied company range. The beat was modest, but it exceeded the preview’s upper implied-guide threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue of $608 million beat the high end of implied guidance by $6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q4 revenue consensus was “$597.0M” and company implied guidance was “$581.6–601.6M.”

surprises.description: Peloton recorded a $23.8 million Q4 legal contingency accrual for a patent-infringement jury verdict, an unanticipated charge. Management said it does not expect a material ongoing royalty impact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company booked a $23.8 million legal contingency accrual in Q4 tied to a jury verdict over third-party media player patent infringement,” though it “does not expect material go-forward royalty impact.”

surprises.description: Peloton reported its first full fiscal year of positive net income and operating income, an annual profitability milestone the preview did not specifically anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its first full fiscal year of positive net income ($63 million) and positive operating income ($161 million).”

surprises.description: Peloton IQ engagement and interest were stronger than the preview’s unquantified discussion of IQ as a possible conversion driver: it engaged more than half of monthly active users in Q4 and ranked as the top feature of interest among prospective customers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Peloton IQ engaged more than 50% of monthly active users in Q4 and is now the #1 feature of interest among prospective customers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case required “Peloton IQ converting existing members at higher attach.”

surprises.description: The number of members owning multiple connected-fitness products reached 316,000, up 20,000 year over year, and these members churn at lower rates. The preview identified higher attach as a possible driver but did not give an expected ownership figure or churn comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “316,000 members now own multiple connected fitness products (up 20,000 YoY) and churn at lower rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case cited “Cross Training Series and Peloton IQ converting existing members at higher attach.”

in_line: Peloton began a refinancing process and said excess cash could support buybacks once refinancing is complete, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of refinancing and buyback consideration; no buyback authorization was reported.

The new Peloton Commercial bike and treadmill series is expected to launch in the coming months and support commercial growth, consistent with the preview’s focus on the Commercial Series as a potential FY27 growth driver.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.52 versus the preview's $0.36 consensus, but $0.17 per share came from tariff refunds; excluding that benefit, EPS was about $0.35, slightly below consensus and down year over year. The headline beat was therefore large, but the underlying result did not beat expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was flat year-over-year at $0.52, including a $0.17 per share benefit from $44 million in tariff refunds, meaning underlying EPS declined absent the refund.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS: $0.36.”

surprises.description: Management said Q3 revenue would decline sequentially and Q3 earnings would be below Q2 levels excluding the tariff-refund benefit, with investment benefits not visible until Q4. That pushes visible benefits later than the preview's expectation that tariff mitigation would land in Q2–Q3 and transformation benefits would accelerate in H2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Q3 2026 revenue to decline sequentially on seasonality and Q3 earnings to fall below Q2 levels (excluding the $0.17 tariff benefit), with investment benefits expected to become visible starting in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management explicitly told the Street that tariff mitigation lands in Q2–Q3 and that transformation benefits accelerate in H2.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $898 million beat both preview estimates, but the constant-currency decline was 6.3%, slightly worse than the preview's roughly 4%–6% range. The reported decline of 4.1% was flattered by currency; adjusting for Byte and the planned dealer inventory reduction, the constant-currency decline was 3.6%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $898 million, down 4.1% as reported and 6.3% on a constant currency basis, or a 3.6% constant currency decline when adjusting for Byte and an ~$8 million planned dealer inventory reduction.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales $883.9M” and an alternative estimate of “~$893M”; the preview also described the base case as “cc still −4 to −6%” and warned that FX could make reported revenue beat while constant-currency results remained weak.

surprises.description: The underlying OIS picture remained weak: implants declined mid-single digits and SureSmile ortho fell double digits on U.S. weakness. That fell short of the preview's highlighted possibility that core implants could stabilize, although the 5.7% OIS decline excluding Byte was close to the preview's roughly 6% bull-case decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OIS revenue fell 13.2% as reported (5.7% excluding Byte), with SureSmile ortho revenue of $40 million declining double digits driven by U.S. weakness, while implants (IPS) of $157 million declined mid-single digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Core implant stabilization is the most under-appreciated potential positive”; the preview's bull case also required the OIS decline to halve to “~−6%.”

surprises.description: Cash from operations more than doubled to $99 million, a stronger cash-flow result than the preview's concern about another weak cash quarter suggested. The improvement was partly supported by tariff refunds and working-capital management, so it does not by itself establish a comparable improvement in free cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow more than doubled to $99 million from $48 million a year earlier, aided by tariff refunds and improved working capital management.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 FCF was −$12M” and “A second consecutive negative-FCF quarter puts capital-allocation questions … into the Q&A.”

surprises.description: The company restarted share repurchases, buying 1.3 million shares for about $12 million, its first buyback since Q3 2024. The preview raised buyback pace as a capital-allocation question amid cash-flow concerns, but did not anticipate a resumption.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased 1.3 million shares for approximately $12 million at an average price below $10 per share, marking its first buyback since Q3 2024.”

surprises.description: CTS showed a pronounced regional split: Americas revenue was down nearly 10% constant currency as customers deferred CAD/CAM capital spending, while APAC grew at a double-digit rate, including in milling systems. The preview did not flag this segment or regional pattern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CTS Americas was down nearly 10% constant currency driven by CAD/CAM CapEx deferrals, while APAC posted double-digit growth including double-digit growth in milling systems.”

in_line: Full-year 2026 guidance remained at $3.5–$3.6 billion in sales and $1.40–$1.50 adjusted EPS, as the preview expected the existing guidance to be reaffirmed.

EDS weakness was attributed largely to European distributors reducing inventory rather than to softer demand, consistent with the preview's focus on dealer destocking and the debate over whether it was transitory or structural. No EDS sales figure was provided to determine whether its trend beat the preview's range.

surprises.description: The preview expected FY26 guidance to be reaffirmed at $730–750 million of revenue and $91–93 million of adjusted EBITDA, while noting that a raise was possible. Management raised the ranges to $740–755 million and $92–95 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to $740-$755 million in revenue and $92-$95 million in adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company guidance (reaffirmed May 5, 2026): FY26 revenue $730–750M, adj. EBITDA $91–93M”; the preview said investors wanted “a narrow to the top half ... or an outright raise.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS came in above the preview’s $0.25 anchor and the top of its $0.23–$0.27 analyst range. GAAP EPS also exceeded the preview’s derived estimate of about $0.14–$0.16.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP EPS was $0.23 and non-GAAP EPS was $0.28.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS (ex-special items) $0.25 (range $0.23–$0.27, 3 analysts)” and “GAAP diluted EPS ~$0.14–$0.16 (my est.).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA exceeded the preview’s roughly $25.0 million estimate, and the reported margin was slightly above the preview’s 13.2% base-case scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record second-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $25.8 million, up 7% year-over-year, with adjusted EBITDA margin expanding 30 basis points to 13.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$25.0M (my est., no published consensus)”; the base scenario projected “$25.0M (13.2%).”

surprises.description: Revenue was above the preview’s $189.2 million consensus estimate, delivering 4.2% year-over-year growth versus the preview’s expected 2.0%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 4.2% year-over-year to $193 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $189.2M” and “Y/Y +2.0%.”

surprises.description: Aerospace & Defense grew only 13.2%, below the preview’s expectation that growth markets stay comfortably above roughly 20%. Infrastructure and Power Generation did clear that bar, but A&D fell short of the stated threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Aerospace & Defense up 13.2% ($3.2 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said A&D, Infrastructure, and Power Generation “must stay comfortably north of ~20% to offset O&G.”

surprises.description: Operating income rose much faster than revenue, with management reporting nearly 60% conversion of incremental revenue into operating income and calling that rate sustainable. The preview expected margin expansion but did not forecast this degree of operating leverage or management’s sustainability claim.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating income increased 53.6% to $12.9 million, converting nearly 60% of incremental revenue into operating income, a rate management called sustainable and slightly higher on a full-year basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called margin momentum “the strongest part of the story” and said margins “need[]” to expand, but gave no operating-income conversion estimate.

surprises.description: Management disclosed plans to nearly triple in-lab testing capacity by the end of 2027, backed by visible customer demand. The preview discussed recent lab expansions but did not anticipate this larger capacity buildout.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is investing to nearly triple its in-lab testing capacity by the end of 2027, supported by visible customer demand, with new investments typically taking 9-12 months to come online.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted the Los Angeles aerospace lab expansion and a similar Houston expansion, but did not mention a plan to nearly triple total in-lab testing capacity.

in_line: Oil & Gas revenue fell 8.2%, within the preview’s expected high-single- to low-double-digit decline. The reported decline included exited programs and deferred maintenance; after adjusting for turnarounds and exited work, revenue was up 1%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that much of the weakness would reflect deliberate exits and timing.

Infrastructure grew 76.5% and Power Generation grew 26.4%, both above the preview’s roughly 20% threshold for growth markets; the preview also cautioned that the prior quarter’s especially high growth rates would moderate.
Adjusted EBITDA margin of 13.3% was close to the preview’s 13.2% base-case scenario.
Leverage fell from 2.4x to approximately 2.2x, consistent with progress toward the preview’s stated 2.0x year-end target.

Management reiterated that cash flow should return to historically favorable levels in the second half, in line with the preview’s expectation of H2 improvement. The reported $23.9 million quarter-over-quarter FCF improvement does not provide an H1 total to compare with the preview’s H1 benchmark.

surprises.description: Cisco’s FY27 revenue guide of $72.2–73.4 billion implies roughly 15% growth at the midpoint, well above the preview’s estimate of about 9.5% growth and $68.7–69.0 billion. This was a substantially stronger outlook than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 guidance calls for revenue of $72.2-$73.4 billion (roughly 15% growth at midpoint).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street models ~9.5% FY27 revenue growth (≈$68.7–69.0B).”

surprises.description: FY27 non-GAAP EPS guidance of $5.05–5.11 was above the preview’s roughly $4.80 consensus and above Evercore’s expected $4.80–5.00 range. The earnings outlook therefore exceeded even the preview’s cited upper-end expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “non-GAAP EPS of $5.05-$5.11.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street models … ~$4.80 EPS”; “Evercore ISI expects management to guide $4.80–5.00 EPS.”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue of $17.3 billion exceeded the roughly $16.83 billion consensus and the preview’s inferred $17.0–17.2 billion whisper range. The revenue beat was stronger than the preview’s already-above-consensus expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue reached a record $17.3 billion, up 18% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue … $16.82–16.85B”; “Inferred whisper … revenue ~$17.0B.”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP EPS of $1.22 beat both the $1.17 consensus and the preview’s inferred $1.19–1.20 whisper range, and exceeded the high end of company guidance. The beat was larger than the preview’s expected narrow, roughly 2% pattern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS of $1.22 up 23%, exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS $1.17”; “Inferred whisper … EPS ~$1.19–1.20”; Cisco had beaten “by a narrow, consistent ~2%.”

surprises.description: Security revenue grew 14% in Q4, far above the preview’s expected 4.7% growth and breaking from the recent flat trend. Management said unusually large, longer-duration on-prem Splunk deals benefited the quarter, which qualifies the strength but does not erase the sizable beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Security revenue grew 14% in Q4 … though management noted the quarter benefited from unusually large on-prem Splunk deals with longer duration.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Security … +4.7%”; “Security was flat Y/Y in Q3 and has missed repeatedly.”

surprises.description: Cisco set its FY27 AI infrastructure revenue target at $7.5 billion, above the preview’s expected $6.5–7 billion range. That implies a stronger AI revenue outlook than investors were led to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guiding to $7.5 billion in AI infrastructure revenue for FY27 versus $4 billion in FY26.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Morgan Stanley expects an FY27 AI revenue target of $6.5–7B.”

surprises.description: FY26 hyperscaler AI infrastructure orders totaled $9.3 billion, slightly surpassing the preview’s $9 billion target. The preview’s implied Q4 requirement was about $3.7 billion, so the result indicates a modest overachievement rather than a major step-up.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI infrastructure orders from hyperscalers totaled $9.3 billion in FY26.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cisco raised the FY26 hyperscaler AI order target to $9B”; “implying ~$3.7B needed in Q4.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP gross margin was 66.3%, about 40 basis points above the preview’s roughly 65.9% model despite the year-over-year decline. The preview had expected margin pressure from AI mix, but the reported margin level was better than modeled.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin fell 210 basis points year-over-year to 66.3%, driven by higher hardware mix and memory costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP GM (implied) ~65.9%”; “Street models ~65.9% in Q4.”

surprises.description: The FY27 core business excluding AI is implied to grow about 10%, a stronger outlook for non-AI demand than the preview’s concern that growth outside AI was only around 4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The core business ex-AI [is] implied to grow about 10%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue growth of ~7% collapses to roughly 4% ex-AI”; campus/traditional networking saturation was described as “the core bear argument.”

surprises.description: Cisco guided to roughly 35% FY27 operating margin, above the preview’s cited expectation of about 34%. This suggests the much stronger growth outlook is not accompanied by the degree of operating-margin pressure the preview contemplated.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management guided to “~35% operating margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Evercore ISI expects management to guide … on ~34% EBIT margin.”

surprises.description: Cisco reported three new hyperscaler design wins in Q4 and visibility to multiple additional AI design wins over the next six months. The preview focused on orders, revenue conversion, and the AI target, but did not anticipate this specific expansion of the design-win pipeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured three new hyperscaler design wins in Q4 … with line of sight to multiple additional AI design wins over the next six months.”

surprises.description: Networking product orders grew 40%, with campus networking orders up 20%, giving stronger evidence of continuing campus demand than the preview’s question of whether the refresh cycle would merely sustain. This was a positive demand signal beyond the preview’s stated concern about traditional networking saturation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Networking product orders grew 40% in Q4 marking the eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, with Campus Networking orders up 20%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether the campus refresh cycle (a Q3 strength) sustains”; “Campus/traditional networking saturation is the core bear argument.”

surprises.description: FY26 revenue of $63.3 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $4.33 both exceeded the company’s full-year guide ranges of $62.8–63.0 billion and $4.27–4.29. Full-year operating margin also expanded 40 basis points to 34.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year FY26 revenue was a record $63.3 billion … with non-GAAP EPS of $4.33 … and operating margin improving 40 basis points to 34.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 full-year guide: revenue $62.8–63.0B; non-GAAP EPS $4.27–4.29.”

in_line: Total Q4 product orders grew 35% year-over-year, matching the preview’s reference to Q3 product-order growth of 35% and its description of a very hard compare.

The Q4 gross-margin decline was 210 basis points year-over-year, in line with the preview’s stated expected decline of roughly 210 basis points; the reported margin level nevertheless came in above the preview’s modeled 65.9%.

surprises.description: Harmony reported diluted EPS of $1.28, well above the preview’s working expectation of about $1.05–$1.10. The preview identified Q2 expenses as the key uncertainty, but the reported EPS was roughly 16%–22% above that bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income more than doubled to $75.4 million ($1.28 per diluted share)” in Q2 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A fair working bar is ~$1.05–1.10.”

surprises.description: WAKIX added about 450 patients, described as its highest Q2 increase in brand history. The preview expected demand-led sequential growth to be confirmed, but did not anticipate a record Q2 patient gain.
surprises.fact_evidence: WAKIX “added approximately 450 patients in Q2” and this was “the highest Q2 increase in the brand's history.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “demand-led QoQ growth confirmed”; the preview also said to watch whether the sequential jump reflected “demand/new patient starts” rather than gross-to-net or channel effects.

surprises.description: Cost of product sold rose to 24.2% of revenue, above the preview’s estimate based on Q1’s 20.7% ratio. Management attributed the increase primarily to new royalties under the Novitium license, making product costs less favorable than the preview’s build assumed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cost of product sold rose to 24.2% of net revenue from 19% a year ago, primarily due to new royalties tied to the Novitium license agreement signed in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview applied Q1 margins to Q2 revenue and estimated “COGS ~$54M”; Q1 COGS was listed as “20.7%.”

surprises.description: The reported WAKIX protection date was March 2030 including pediatric exclusivity, shorter than the preview’s stated July 2030 protection with pediatric exclusivity. That leaves a shorter stated protection period than investors were led to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “WAKIX exclusivity is protected to March 2030 including pediatric exclusivity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “July 2030 with pediatric exclusivity.”

surprises.description: The BP-205 SAD readout included a notably detailed favorable profile: once-daily-supportive half-life, high orexin-2 selectivity, a wide projected margin over the maximum predicted efficacy dose, and no serious adverse events in the volunteers studied. The preview expected the data as a credibility checkpoint but did not specify or set expectations for these characteristics.
surprises.fact_evidence: BP-205 showed a “~25-hour half-life supporting once-daily dosing,” “over 600-fold selectivity for orexin-2 over orexin-1 receptors,” a “projected 140-fold margin over the maximum predicted efficacy dose,” and no serious cardiovascular, hepatic, or visual adverse events across 72 volunteers.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “BP-205 Phase 1 SAD PK/safety data” as “the credibility test for Harmony's own orexin answer.”

in_line: Q2 WAKIX revenue was about $261 million, matching the amount preannounced before the release; the preview explicitly said the top line was already known.
FY2026 revenue guidance remained $1.00–$1.04 billion, as the preview expected when it said reaffirmation was the base case.
The BP-205 SAD data arrived in the period the preview had identified, and the planned Q3 Phase Ib start falls within the preview’s expected second-half 2026 timing.

surprises.description: McDonald’s adjusted EPS was $3.38, above the preview’s $3.32–$3.34 consensus range. The reported 5% constant-currency growth was stronger than the roughly 4.1% growth implied by the preview’s comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $3.38, up 5% in constant currency, including a $0.03 foreign currency benefit.”

surprises.description: The U.S. exit rate remained weak: management said same-store sales were slightly negative in July, rather than describing an improving trend or a July acceleration. That adds evidence of continued pressure entering Q3, though the preview had identified the exit rate as uncertain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. same-store sales were slightly negative in July, signaling weak momentum entering Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If management frames May/June as sequentially improving and quantifies a July acceleration, the quarter gets forgiven”; the preview also identified the “June and July exit rate” as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: Management said the launch of the under-$3 EDAP menu coincided with pulling back digital offers and removing Buy One Add One for $1, a “bad trade” that accounted for about two-thirds of U.S. traffic underperformance. The preview worried that value offers might not restore traffic, but did not anticipate this specific promotional trade-off.
surprises.fact_evidence: “About two-thirds of the U.S. traffic underperformance” came from a “‘bad trade’” in which the EDAP menu launched while digital offers were pulled back and Buy One Add One for $1 was removed.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If comps are positive on price/mix alone with traffic down mid-single digits, the value strategy is not working as advertised.”

surprises.description: Only 60% to 65% of the U.S. system followed the recommended EDAP pricing architecture, and management said inconsistent execution contributed to lower incrementality. The preview discussed the value menu’s potential traffic and margin effects but did not flag this limited franchisee execution as a risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Only about 60% to 65% of the U.S. system executed the recommended EDAP pricing architecture, contributing to inconsistent results and lower incrementality.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $3 menu (launched April) and $4 breakfast deal are margin-dilutive by construction; franchisee P&L commentary matters as much as the corporate line.”

surprises.description: The June FIFA marketing campaign underdelivered against expectations, accounting for about one-third of U.S. underperformance. That contrasts with the preview’s potential upside case that World Cup-related marketing and the value menu could drive traffic.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The remaining one-third of U.S. underperformance was tied to the June FIFA marketing campaign underdelivering versus expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “World Cup cups + $3 menu drive real traffic.”

surprises.description: McDonald’s reduced its expected 2026 forex tailwind to about $0.15 from the preview’s $0.20–$0.30 framework. That is a meaningful reduction in the expected currency support to full-year results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company cut its full-year 2026 forex tailwind estimate to about $0.15, down from a prior range of $0.20 to $0.30.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A $0.20–0.30 FY EPS FX tailwind.”

surprises.description: The 50,000-restaurant target moved from the end of 2027 to 2028, with management citing pressured consumers and higher cumulative development costs. The preview expected about 2,600 openings in 2026 but did not anticipate this delay to the longer-term target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “McDonald’s pushed its 50,000-restaurant target from end of 2027 to 2028, citing pressured consumers and cumulative inflation on development costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The only standing framework is FY26 operating margin in the mid-to-high 40% range, ~2,600 openings (~2,100 net new).”

surprises.description: The beverage platform was already exceeding expectations, with more than half of its traffic after lunch and average checks on those orders about 50% above the full-day average. The preview had called for beverage datapoints as proof of the platform’s potential but did not anticipate these strong reported usage and check figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The new beverage platform is exceeding expectations, with more than half of traffic coming after lunch and average checks on those orders running about 50% above the full-day average.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Beverage platform datapoints. McCafé Refreshers, crafted sodas, energy entry, plus Germany/Canada platforms. Any hard mix or attach-rate numbers would be the first real proof point.”

surprises.description: McDonald’s announced an immediate change in U.S. leadership, with Sky Anderson replacing Joe Erlinger, who is leaving after more than two decades. The announcement came alongside Q2 declines in customer satisfaction and service times—operating and leadership developments not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sky Anderson was named U.S. President effective immediately, replacing Joe Erlinger who is leaving after over two decades, amid Q2 declines in customer satisfaction and service times.”

in_line: Global comparable sales grew 1.3%, matching the preview’s 1.3%–1.4% consensus range.
U.S. comparable sales grew 0.8%, near the preview’s 0.9%–1.1% published consensus and within its cited 0.5%–0.8% whisper range.
The company still targeted about 2,600 gross openings in 2026, consistent with the preview’s expected ~2,600 openings.

surprises.description: Cibus reported Q2 revenue of about $1 million, well below the preview’s $1.70 million consensus estimate and $1.8 million model. The shortfall was roughly 40% versus consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue of approximately $1 million”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue Q2 2026E: $1.70M”; the preview’s model was “$1.8M.”

surprises.description: Cibus pushed its Latin American rice commercial launch from the preview’s 2027 target to 2028. That is a further delay to a major anticipated rice opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Delayed rice commercial launch guidance in Latin America from late 2027 to 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Ecuador/Colombia launch is targeted 2027.”

surprises.description: Cash was slightly below the preview’s roughly $21 million estimate, and management described runway only into early Q1 2027, earlier than the prior late-Q1 wording. This points to financing needs sooner than the preview’s already-cautious runway expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents were $20.4 million as of June 30, 2026, projected to fund operations only into early Q1 2027, signaling potential near-term financing needs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled cash of “~$21M” and said Q1 had indicated runway “into late in the first quarter of 2027.”

surprises.description: Net loss was worse than the preview’s $20.6 million model, and GAAP loss per share of $0.29 was also below the $0.26 loss consensus. The per-share miss was less severe against the preview’s own $0.27 model.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $22.1 million ($0.29 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “Net loss $(20.6)M” and “EPS $(0.27),” and listed GAAP EPS consensus of “–$0.26.”

surprises.description: The company’s stated exit-2026 net cash usage run rate target was about $35 million, above the preview’s approximately $30 million annual burn target. Although cash usage declined, the stated target implies a higher burn level than investors were watching for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Quarterly cash usage fell approximately 19% sequentially and 31% year-over-year, with the company targeting a net cash usage run rate of about $35 million exiting 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to a “stated ~$30M/yr burn target” and said cash usage “must trend to ~$7.5M/qtr to hit the $30M/yr target.”

surprises.description: Cibus expanded the Interoc rice framework from two traits to five, adding breadth to the opportunity beyond the preview’s description of the existing two-trait framework. A definitive commercial agreement is still being pursued, so the expansion is progress but not a conversion to a signed deal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expanded its Interoc framework from two rice traits to five in August, shifting toward a multi-trait pipeline model as it works toward a definitive commercial agreement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the January LOI as non-binding and focused on the “LOI → definitive” step; it characterized the base case as Interoc “still ‘negotiating in good faith.’”

surprises.description: In addition to the EU decision already highlighted in the preview, Cibus cited favorable edited-crop determinations across several other jurisdictions. The preview had identified the EU rule as the known regulatory tailwind but did not anticipate these additional determinations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Regulatory tailwinds strengthened as the EU finalized rules in June treating most non-GMO edited crops as conventional, while Ecuador, Peru, USDA APHIS, and the FDA granted favorable determinations across three continents.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted the June EU decision and said “No dates or dollars have been attached”; it asked whether a named EU seed partner would emerge.

surprises.description: Non-cash royalty liability interest expense was $9.5 million, slightly above the preview’s $9.3 million estimate. The preview already expected this to be the largest single item in net loss, so the difference was limited.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A large non-cash royalty liability interest expense of $9.5 million (up from $8.7 million) remains the primary driver of the gap between operating loss and net loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “Royalty liability interest (non-cash) $(9.3)M” and described it as “the largest single item in net loss.”

in_line: Cash of $20.4 million was within the preview’s expected $20–22 million base-case range, although the runway wording was less favorable.
The US rice launch target remained 2029, as the preview expected after the partner herbicide-registration delay.
Biofragrance scale-up orders were still expected in the second half of 2026, consistent with the preview; the call did not report a signed order or its dollar value.
Interoc was still working toward a definitive commercial agreement, consistent with the preview’s base-case expectation that negotiations would continue.

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EPS was $8.91, well above the preview’s reconstructed $7.24 consensus and the $6.78–$7.46 guidance-implied range. The call noted that the year-over-year comparison is affected by an unusually low prior-year tax provision, but the reported quarter still substantially exceeded the preview’s benchmarks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 adjusted EPS of $8.91 grew only 6.1% due to a much lower prior-year tax provision.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | ~$7.24”; guidance-implied range “$6.78 – $7.46.”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EPS reached $29.83, above both the preview’s $28.16 Street estimate and its $27.70–$28.38 guidance range. The preview had highlighted ARKA-related interest expense as a headwind, but EPS rose 12.7% despite $120 million of additional interest and tax expense.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted diluted EPS rose 12.7% to $29.83 despite $120 million in additional interest and tax expense.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 adjusted diluted EPS: guidance “$27.70 – $28.38”; Street “$28.16.” The preview also noted “a full year of ARKA interest expense … is a real EPS drag.”

surprises.description: Q4 EBITDA margin was 13%, far above the preview’s roughly 11.5% consensus and 11.4%–11.7% implied range, despite the warning that Q4 would be softer than Q3. About 30 basis points came from a UK divestiture gain, but the reported margin still cleared the expected range substantially.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fourth quarter … EBITDA margin of 13%, up 150 basis points, though about 30 basis points came from a UK divestiture gain.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EBITDA margin | ~11.5%”; guidance-implied range “11.4% – 11.7%.” The preview said management had pre-warned Q4 margin would be “softer than Q3.”

surprises.description: FY26 EBITDA margin was 12.3%, above the preview’s 11.8%–11.9% full-year guidance. This was a favorable full-year margin outcome in addition to the stronger-than-expected Q4 margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CACI delivered fiscal '26 … EBITDA margin of 12.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 EBITDA margin guidance: “11.8% – 11.9%.”

surprises.description: FY27 revenue guidance has a $10.75 billion midpoint, modestly above the preview’s $10.67 billion Street estimate. The range also includes about $500 million of acquired revenue, so the headline growth rate includes a material acquisition contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For fiscal '27, CACI guided revenue of $10.65-$10.85 billion (11.3%-13.4% growth including ~$500 million acquired revenue).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY27 Street revenue: “$10.67B (+11.8%).”

surprises.description: The FY27 EBITDA margin outlook in the high-12% range is above the preview’s FY26 margin baseline of 11.8%–11.9% and indicates margin expansion rather than a flat or dilutive outcome. The preview specifically identified the ARKA mix and margin bridge as an issue to assess.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For fiscal '27, CACI guided … EBITDA margins in the high 12% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “FY27 EBITDA margin guide vs. FY26's 11.8–11.9%” and said “flat-to-down implies dilution.”

surprises.description: FY27 free cash flow guidance of at least $900 million is a strong step-up from the preview’s FY26 floor of $725 million, with management indicating roughly 22% per-share growth. However, the FY27 figure includes substantial tax-related cash benefits, including a Section 174 benefit that was larger than previously discussed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow of at least $900 million (~22% per-share growth)”; FY27 FCF “includes a delayed $40 million tax refund and a $115 million cash benefit from Section 174 R&D tax credit changes, which was larger than previously discussed due to the ARKA acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 FCF guidance as “≥ $725M” and said the FY27 FCF guide and deleveraging path were a key swing factor, but gave no FY27 FCF estimate.

surprises.description: CACI accelerated its deleveraging timeline: it reduced pro forma leverage to 3.7x in one quarter and now expects to reach the low 3s by June 2027, a quarter earlier than previously communicated. The preview expected a return to the low 3s within six quarters, so the earlier timing is favorable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reduced pro forma leverage to 3.7x, a full turn reduction in one quarter, and now expects to reach the low 3s by June 2027, a quarter earlier than originally communicated.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management projected “4.2x net debt/EBITDA returning to ‘low threes’ within six quarters.”

surprises.description: FY26 book-to-bill was 1.1x, avoiding the sub-1.0x Q4 outcome the preview identified as a genuine negative signal. CACI also won more than $10 billion in awards, broadly meeting the preview’s focus on a strong year-end award quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CACI won more than $10 billion in awards in fiscal '26 (book-to-bill of 1.1x).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “a sub-1.0x Q4 book-to-bill would be a genuine negative signal into FY27” and tracked FY26 total awards against FY25’s “$10B.”

surprises.description: Funded backlog grew 29% year over year, faster than the 19% growth cited in the preview’s Q3 snapshot, while total backlog grew only 2%. The funded backlog result is stronger than the prior update, but the modest total-backlog growth is a weaker headline than the preview’s latest 6% total-backlog growth figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Funded backlog grew 29% year-over-year while total backlog of over $32 billion grew only 2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q3 “backlog $33.4B (+6%), funded backlog +19% (+10% organic).”

surprises.description: Bids under evaluation rose from $4 billion to nearly $11 billion, with about 75% new business. The preview anticipated $22 billion of bids to be submitted over the next two quarters, but did not flag this sharp increase in the current evaluation pipeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bids under evaluation surged from $4 billion to nearly $11 billion (about 75% new business).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “$22B of bids planned across the next two quarters, ~75% new business,” but did not give an expectation for bids already under evaluation.

surprises.description: CACI disclosed a separate $500 million Domestic Shield counter-drone award and export approval for most of its counter-UAS systems already delivered to 17 countries. The preview watched counter-UAS deployment and international expansion but did not anticipate these specific award and export developments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CACI received a separate $500 million Domestic Shield counter-drone award, holds export approval for the majority of its counter-UAS systems already delivered to 17 countries.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “counter-UAS deployment detail” and “international expansion” as strategic items to watch, without quantifying an award or export approval.

surprises.description: The value of CACI’s OTA awards in FY26 exceeded the combined value from FY24 and FY25, an acceleration not anticipated in the preview’s strategic discussion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its OTA award value in fiscal '26 exceeded the combined value of fiscal '24 and '25.”

in_line: Q4 revenue was $2.7 billion, close to the preview’s approximately $2.69 billion consensus and within its $2.641–$2.741 billion implied range; reported growth of 17.6% was also within the preview’s 15%–19% implied growth range.
FY26 free cash flow of $735 million modestly exceeded the preview’s FY26 floor of at least $725 million.

The preview expected $22 billion of bids to be submitted over the next two quarters, with roughly 75% new business; the call maintained the $22 billion outlook and reported about 80% new business for those planned submissions.

surprises.description: Revenue was $0.9 million, below the preview’s $1.1–1.4 million base case, although it rebounded from Q1’s $0.16 million. Management said deferred offshore projects contributed to the shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $0.9 million,” up $0.7 million sequentially but down $1.2 million year-over-year, “reflecting deferred offshore projects.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 base case” revenue: “$1.1–1.4M”; the preview also said revenue of “≥ ~$1.0M” was the minimum threshold to validate the seasonal rebound.
