surprises.fact_evidence: “The life insurance segment's six-month net investment income dropped 14% to $33.4 million, driven mainly by a $2.8 million year-to-date decline in homebuilder profit-share income and roughly $1.1 million lower construction lending income.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Ask for the split between (i) lower funeral-funding case counts, (ii) net investment income, (iii) DAC/acquisition-cost strain.”

surprises.description: SNFCA deliberately increased land and residential subdivision investments by about $24 million, but those investments suppress current income because GAAP profits are recognized only when lots are sold or construction starts. The preview did not flag this near-term income tradeoff.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company deliberately grew its land and residential subdivision investment to approximately $122 million as of June 30 from about $98 million at year-end, suppressing current income since GAAP profits are recognized only upon lot sales or construction starts.”

surprises.description: Cash and cash equivalents rose about 60%, while the added cash was earning below-market lending rates and management was still seeking deployment opportunities. This excess liquidity and its low current return were not raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents rose about 60% (roughly $61 million) since December 31, 2025 due to lower loan production, earning below-market lending rates as management seeks deployment opportunities amid a 40.6% decline in Utah new home starts.”

surprises.description: Mortgage originations remained down 11% year over year, but improved 12% sequentially and lifted industry market share from 9 to 10 basis points. The preview flagged origination volume as a key issue but did not give an expected direction or anticipate the sequential and share gains.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Mortgage origination volume fell 11% year-over-year to $548 million in Q2 (from $617 million) but rose 12% sequentially, lifting SNFC's industry market share to 10 basis points from 9.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Mortgage sustainability. Origination volume, gain-on-sale margin, and headcount.”

surprises.description: The debt-to-equity ratio improved to 2.72x from 2.81x at year-end as assets and stockholders’ equity grew. The preview noted book-value growth but did not highlight this improvement in leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total assets grew 3% to $1.61 billion and stockholders' equity rose 5.5% to $433 million, improving the debt-to-equity ratio to 2.72x from 2.81x at year-end.”

in_line: Consolidated revenue fell 6.3% for Q2 and 5% for the first half while after-tax earnings rose 7.3% and 8.1%, respectively; these figures were already reported in the preview, which also said there was no usable consensus.
Mortgage returned to a small Q2 pretax profit after a year-earlier loss, consistent with the preview’s reported $71,000 profit and its description of the segment’s cost-driven improvement.
Cemetery/Mortuary revenue and headline pretax earnings growth matched the preview’s reported figures, and the investment-income tailwind was already identified there.

surprises.description: Backlog rose 17.4% sequentially to $246.1 million, well above the preview’s $215–235 million base-case range and its bullish threshold of more than $235 million. The year-over-year decline was expected to look weak, but the sequential rebuild was stronger than the preview’s scenarios suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated backlog fell 8.8% year-over-year to $246.1 million” but “rose 17.4% sequentially from Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base scenario: “backlog $215–235M”; bull signal: “Backlog rebuilds to >$235M.”

surprises.description: Net sales of $138.6 million beat the $134.49 million consensus and declined 3.5% year over year, a milder decline than the preview’s expected 6.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales declined 3.5% year-over-year to $138.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Q2 2026 Consensus | $134.49M” and “Implied Y/Y | −6.3%.”

surprises.description: Gross margin rose 80 basis points to 22.3%, rather than staying roughly flat as the preview anticipated amid accelerating freight and fuel costs. The improvement came despite a charge for exiting two UK product lines.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin improved 80 basis points to 22.3% on favorable business mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “margins roughly flat as fuel offsets UK savings”; the preview also flagged that “elevated fuel costs in Infrastructure freight would accelerate into Q2.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a £15 million UK rail order and expects at least 80% of current backlog to convert to revenue by year-end, providing specific order and conversion visibility beyond the preview’s base-case expectation of qualitative order commentary without new backlog quantification.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects “at least 80% of the current backlog to convert to revenue by year-end” and disclosed “a ~£15 million UK rail order.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the base signal was “qualitative ‘strong bidding activity’ language and no new backlog quantification”; an explicit statement that H2 revenue is “largely covered by backlog” was listed as a bull signal.

surprises.description: Q2 operating cash flow reached $17.9 million, the highest Q2 level since 2017, and net debt fell to $42.2 million with gross leverage at 1.0x—better than the preview’s cited $55.7 million of net debt and 1.2x leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 operating cash flow reached $17.9 million,” the “highest Q2 level since 2017”; net debt fell “to $42.2 million,” and gross leverage fell “from 2.2x to 1.0x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net debt $55.7M, gross leverage 1.2x.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a $2.1 million charge for exiting two non-core UK product lines. The preview discussed annualized UK Rail restructuring savings but did not anticipate this exit charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: Gross margin improved “despite a $2.1 million charge related to the exit of two non-core UK product lines.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said UK Rail restructuring savings were “$1.5–2.0M annualized.”

surprises.description: Global friction management sales grew 18.1% and technology services and solutions sales grew 66.9%, strengths not quantified or specifically anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Global friction management sales grew 18.1% and technology services and solutions sales grew 66.9% in Q2.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was $11.7 million, within the preview-derived estimate of roughly $11.5–12.5 million, despite declining 4.7% year over year.

The consolidated book-to-bill ratio was 0.96:1, close to the preview’s 0.95:1 base case and just below the 1.0x benchmark; Rail at 1.03 and Infrastructure at 0.85 were also close to the preview’s 1.03 and 0.84 estimates.
Management reaffirmed full-year guidance, as expected. The $15–25 million free-cash-flow outlook (midpoint $20 million) and capital spending of approximately 2.7% of sales matched the preview.

surprises.description: The preview said SINTX had not issued forward guidance and emphasized that investors wanted quantified timing for the backlog. Instead, the company guided to Q3 revenue of about $900,000–$1.1 million and Q4 revenue of about $1 million–$1.3 million, implying a sharp step-up from Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company guided to Q3 2026 revenue of approximately $900,000 to $1.1 million and Q4 2026 revenue of approximately $1 million to $1.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No forward guidance has been issued by SINTX; the company does not guide.”

surprises.description: The preview’s implied Q2 net-loss estimate was about $3.4–$3.6 million, while SINTX reported a $2.3 million loss. The reported loss was materially smaller than the preview’s estimate, even though the preview cautioned that EPS could be noisy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss was flat at $2.3 million for Q2 2026 versus a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net loss (implied) ~$3.4–3.6M.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged the risk that a contract-manufacturing ramp could dilute gross margin because that work was expected to carry lower margins than proprietary implants. Instead, Q2 gross margin reached 61.5%, with the company citing higher-margin sales, favorable mix, and improved OEM pricing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to approximately 62% (61.5%) from 37.7% a year ago, driven by higher-margin sales, favorable mix, and improved OEM pricing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Contract-manufacturing ceramics is structurally lower margin than proprietary implants; a big 2H26 CM ramp is revenue-positive but mix-negative.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2-end cash of roughly $3.8–$4.5 million after the June financing. Reported cash was $3.6 million, alongside higher first-half operating cash use and a more-than-doubling of inventory that tied up working capital.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents declined to $3.6 million at June 30, 2026 from $4.1 million at year-end 2025”; “Net cash used in operating activities increased to $5.3 million for the first half of 2026 versus $3.7 million a year earlier”; “Inventory more than doubled to $2.3 million from $1 million at year-end, tying up working capital ahead of anticipated customer demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pro forma for the ~$4.7M net raise, Q2-end cash should be roughly $3.8–4.5M.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $452,000, close to the $460,000 consensus and just above the preview’s $380,000–$450,000 base case range.

The previously announced contract-manufacturing purchase orders of more than $3.2 million were consistent with the preview’s expectation that production would ship in the second half of 2026 and continue into 2027.

surprises.description: Q2 EPS was $0.10, above the preview’s $0.08 consensus and $0.09 base case; net income of $21.3 million also exceeded its estimated $16.5–18.5 million range. The preview cautioned that a one-cent difference was noisy, but the reported result was above both cited EPS expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 earnings rose to $21.3 million ($0.10 per share)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY26 Consensus” EPS “$0.08”; “My base sits at $0.09”; net income “~$16.5–18.5M.”

surprises.description: Bakken East precedent agreements reached nearly 1.2 Bcf/day, materially above the roughly 40% of the 1.4 Bcf/day open-season interest that the preview said was under agreement. The negotiated option could bring contracted volumes close to the full original interest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Executed precedent agreements totaling nearly 1.2 Bcf/day,” with an option that “could raise contracted volumes to nearly the full original binding open season interest.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “~40% under precedent agreements” and that the percentage “needs to move materially above 40% to de-risk FID.”

surprises.description: The Bakken East FERC filing moved from the expected third quarter to the fourth quarter of 2026 because precedent-agreement negotiations took longer. The preview had also targeted a Q3 filing; the call says the FID is expected before the filing but does not give a new FID date.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Bakken East FERC 7(c) filing has been pushed … to the fourth quarter of 2026 due to longer precedent agreement negotiations”; FID is expected “ahead of that filing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management targeted “a Section 7 application in Q3 2026” and listed a Q3 filing as the expected timing.

surprises.description: Natural gas distribution’s seasonal loss was smaller than expected: it lost $3.9 million versus the preview’s estimate of about $6 million. New rates, higher retail sales volumes and customer growth helped, though higher interest expense partly offset them.
surprises.fact_evidence: The segment “narrowed its seasonal loss to $3.9 million from $7.4 million,” aided by new rates, “a 6.7% increase in retail sales volumes and 1.6% customer growth,” partly offset by higher interest expense.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The segment model estimated natural gas distribution net income of “~($6)” for Q2 FY26.

surprises.description: Pipeline segment earnings fell short of the preview’s estimate, at $14.4 million versus about $16 million, as lower other income and higher depreciation and amortization weighed on results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pipeline segment filed a FERC rate case … but segment earnings dipped to $14.4 million from $15.4 million on lower other income and higher D&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The segment model estimated pipeline net income of “~$16” for Q2 FY26.

surprises.description: Oregon’s pending gas case was resolved for a $12.2 million settlement, below the $16.4 million case increase cited in the preview. The settlement is about $4.2 million lower than the preview’s stated amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: Pending gas cases included “Oregon ($12.2M settlement).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “OR +$16.4M case pending.”

surprises.description: MDU filed a pipeline FERC rate case seeking a $31 million annual revenue increase, a pipeline rate-case development the preview did not identify. The requested increase is subject to refund, so the ultimate amount is not certain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pipeline segment filed a FERC rate case seeking a $31 million annual revenue increase” with rates effective December 1, 2026, “subject to refund”; about 30% is tied to new depreciation and amortization rates.

in_line: MDU reaffirmed full-year 2026 EPS guidance of $0.93–$1.00, as the preview’s base case expected; it also maintained the 6%–8% long-term EPS growth objective.
Electric utility earnings of $14.7 million were close to the preview’s estimate of about $14 million, with the expected Badger Wind, Montana interim-rate and Wyoming-rate contributions.
Signed data-center ESAs exceeded 1 gigawatt, consistent with the preview’s expectation of an updated tally around 1,010 MW after the Applied Digital Polaris Forge 3 agreement.
Bakken East Phase 1 and Phase 2 in-service dates remained late 2029 and late 2030, respectively, consistent with the preview’s late-2029 phased-service expectation.
The North Dakota electric rate case and Washington gas case were among filings the preview expected; a Minnesota gas filing later in the year also remained planned.

surprises.description: FTC Solar guided Q3 revenue to $30–35 million, well below the roughly $48–50 million per quarter H2 pace the preview said was needed to support the FY2026 growth target. With the 40%+ annual target reaffirmed, the guidance leaves a much larger share of the ramp to Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 revenue guided to $30-35 million (midpoint growth of ~24%) and an even stronger Q4 expected”; full-year growth guidance of at least 40% was reaffirmed.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “H2 would need ~$96–100M, i.e. ~$48–50M per quarter” to reach approximately $140 million of FY2026 revenue.

surprises.description: Bookings were reported at close to $60 million per quarter over the last three quarters, far below the preview’s stated run rate of about $55 million per month. That suggests a materially slower bookings pace than investors were led to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bookings have averaged close to $60 million per quarter over the past three quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~$55M/month bookings run-rate over the prior seven months.”

surprises.description: Despite Q2 revenue coming in above guidance, non-GAAP gross loss widened sequentially and the margin was still negative at a revenue level near $25 million. This fell short of the preview’s positive-margin proof point and landed near the low end of the company’s gross-margin guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross loss widened to $1.3 million (-5.1% of revenue) versus a $0.4 million loss (-2.2%) in the prior quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Sustained positive gross margin at ~$25M of revenue is the proof point that the cost structure has been fixed”; company guidance was “(6.4%) – 4.0%.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a $20 million equity line of credit that had not been announced before the release. It provides a potential liquidity source, although it had not yet been drawn.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured a $20 million equity line of credit (ELOC) with an institutional investor to bolster liquidity, though it has not yet been utilized.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “There was no announced equity raise between the May 5 print and Aug 5”; the preview also said to watch for “any financing announcement.”

surprises.description: Beyond the cash covenant shortfall, FTC Solar also breached its direct-margin covenant, and the breaches caused all credit-agreement borrowings to be classified as current liabilities. The waivers mean the debt is not callable, but the current classification and additional covenant breach were not spelled out in the preview’s base-case scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Also breached its minimum direct margin covenant, requiring lender waivers”; “all outstanding credit-agreement borrowings were reclassified as current liabilities as of June 30th, though waivers meant the debt is not callable.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged the “step-up quarterly revenue and EBITDA covenant tests” and described a base case of “cash short of $15M but paired with a waiver”; it did not identify a direct-margin breach or current-liability reclassification.

surprises.description: FTC Solar reported several significant commercial wins not anticipated in the preview: a 400 MW order tied to a top-five EPC and developer, plus a first-time 1P order from an existing 2P customer. These add concrete large-project wins beyond the preview’s general backlog and booking discussion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FTC received a new 400 MW purchase order from a top-five EPC for a top-five developer, plus a first-time ~100 MW 1P order from an existing 2P East Coast customer.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed “$543M contracted backlog,” the bookings run rate, and monitoring conversion of the “1 GW safe-harbor award”; it did not mention these orders.

surprises.description: The company reported entering India with multiple wins and securing substantial Australian projects, including a 330+ MW project starting deliveries in H2. The preview did not anticipate these geographic expansions or project awards.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has entered India with multiple wins up to 100+ MW and secured new Australian projects (~90 MW plus a 330+ MW project starting deliveries in H2).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted backlog, bookings, and the 1 GW safe-harbor award, but did not mention India or Australian projects.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $26.2 million, slightly above the top of the company’s $22–26 million guidance range and above the $24.39 million consensus estimate. The beat was positive but small relative to the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $26.2 million … coming in slightly above the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue was “$24.39M”; company guidance was “$22.0M – $26.0M.”

in_line: Cash ended Q2 below the $15 million covenant and lenders granted waivers; the preview made this the central risk and described a base case of cash below $15 million paired with a waiver.
Management reaffirmed FY2026 revenue growth guidance of at least 40%, as the preview specifically flagged reaffirmation of approximately 40% growth as a key outcome.
The $9.8 million adjusted EBITDA loss was within the company’s Q2 guidance range of $(10.5) million to $(7.4) million and near the roughly $(9.0) million midpoint discussed in the preview.

surprises.description: Mastech reported non-GAAP EPS of $0.08, below the preview’s $0.09–$0.10 estimate and the $0.12–$0.13 consensus range. GAAP EPS was also a loss of $0.01 versus the preview’s $0.02 estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net income fell to $1 million ($0.08/share)” and GAAP results were “a net loss of $0.1 million (negative $0.01 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (non-GAAP, diluted) $0.12 – $0.13”; my estimate was “non-GAAP EPS $0.09–0.10” and “GAAP EPS $0.02.”

surprises.description: Total bookings reached $13.6 million in TCV, substantially above the preview’s $5–$7 million base-case bookings assumption. The preview focused especially on Data & AI bookings, while the reported figure is total-company TCV, so the segment-specific bar cannot be checked from these facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 bookings rose to $13.6 million in total contract value, up from $9 million in the prior-year period, marking a second consecutive strong bookings quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “bookings $5–7M”; the preview also said Data & AI bookings of “≥$7M again = the trend is real.”

surprises.description: Data & AI revenue was $13.5 million, above the preview’s roughly $13 million base estimate, and rose 7.2% sequentially. That was its first sequential growth since 2024, a more encouraging turn than the preview’s base case implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Data and AI segment grew 7.2% sequentially to $13.5 million, marking its first quarter of sequential growth since 2024.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “Data & AI ~$13M”; the preview described Q1 revenue as still falling and said the bull case required Data & AI revenue of “≥$14M.”

surprises.description: Talent revenue was slightly below the preview’s stabilization estimate and still declined sequentially: $28 million versus an expected roughly $28.5 million. The preview had anticipated top-client insourcing risk, but the reported figures show the segment had not yet stabilized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Talent segment declined 1.9% sequentially … to $28 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “Talent stabilizes ~$28.5M.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed three new logos and a strategic AI engagement with a major convenience-store chain, a specific commercial win not anticipated in the preview. The facts do not give the engagement’s contract value or revenue contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added three new logos across multiple verticals and won a strategic AI engagement with a major U.S. convenience store chain operating over 10,000 stores globally.”

in_line: Consolidated revenue was broadly in line: $41.4 million versus the preview’s $40.8 million aggregator estimate and $41.8 million model estimate.
Average bill rates continued to rise to a new high, consistent with the preview’s expectation of continued increases.
The preview had flagged top-client insourcing as a Talent risk; management attributed nearly 90% of the headcount reduction to insourcing by one top-10 client.

surprises.description: CMP reported FY27 highway de-icing bid-season price increases of roughly double digits, above the preview’s expected committed-price increases in the mid-to-high single digits. That is a stronger pricing indication than the preview’s base expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2026-27 highway de-icing bid season is delivering price increases of roughly double digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “What Good Looks Like” for FY27 bid-season commentary: “Committed price up mid-to-high single digits”; the preview also described the buy-side assumption as “high-single-digit-plus price.”

surprises.description: CMP raised its FY26 consolidated adjusted EBITDA midpoint to $230 million from $224 million, rather than reaffirming the prior range as the preview expected. The increase was driven by Plant Nutrition, whose guidance rose to $49–57 million from $43–47 million as Q3 EBITDA increased 32% despite lower revenue after the Wynyard asset sale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year consolidated adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoint to $230 million (range $218-242 million), driven by Plant Nutrition outperformance”; “Plant Nutrition segment guidance was raised to $49-57 million from the prior $43-47 million, with Q3 adjusted EBITDA up 32% to $15 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the FY26 guide was expected to be “Reaffirm $212–236M, or narrow to upper half,” and listed Plant Nutrition guidance at $43–47 million.

surprises.description: Salt’s FY26 guidance moved lower at the top end, to $225–236 million from $225–240 million, with management citing Goderich production and distribution costs that were higher than expected. The preview had flagged salt costs as the key execution risk, but also identified year-over-year cost improvement as the favorable outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Salt segment adjusted EBITDA fell 15% to $38.9 million and guidance was narrowed lower to $225-236 million (from $225-240 million) due to higher-than-expected production and distribution costs at Goderich.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the favorable outcome would be “Cost/ton down Y/Y; Goderich throughput improving,” and called Salt cost per ton/mining execution the key metric to watch.

surprises.description: Q3 consolidated adjusted EBITDA was $39.9 million, slightly below the preview’s approximately $41 million estimate. The gap was small, but the quarter came in below the stated expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total company Q3 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $39.9 million, down slightly from $41 million a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA (derived) ~$41M”; the preview also described consensus as “essentially flat versus the $41.0M posted in Q3 FY25.”

surprises.description: Highway salt sales volumes fell 6% even as highway pricing rose 8%. The preview had highlighted tight implied second-half volume math and warned that light Q3 shipments could make the full-year volume guide difficult to achieve.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Salt segment pricing rose 9% overall (highway up 8%, C&I up 6%), but highway sales volumes declined 6% while C&I volumes rose 3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “The volume math is tight” and that “If Q3 shipments run light, the full-year volume guide gets hard to hit in a seasonally dead Q4.”

surprises.description: Management said it expects to commit to a reduced salt demand profile for FY27 under normalized winter conditions, prioritizing per-unit margin over volume. That is a more explicit volume trade-off than the preview’s hoped-for confirmation of larger tender sizes, though the preview had also flagged the possibility of walking away from low-price tonnage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects to commit to a reduced salt demand profile for fiscal 2027 assuming normalized winter weather, prioritizing per-unit margin expansion over volume.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s “What Good Looks Like” included “tender sizes up”; it also described the volume issue as a test of “value over volume” and discussed the possibility of walking away from tonnage.

surprises.description: CMP disclosed that Canadian tariffs taking effect August 19 expose it mainly through Goderich highway de-icing salt shipped to the U.S. The preview did not identify this tariff exposure; management said contract pass-through provisions meaningfully reduce the risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Canadian tariffs on goods shipped to the U.S. take effect August 19th with most exposure tied to Goderich highway de-icing salt, though the company believes pass-through contract provisions meaningfully reduce this risk.”

surprises.description: The Board is considering expanded capital-allocation options after the credit upgrade and lower leverage, but the call did not announce a specific capital-return framework. The preview identified a return-of-capital path as a potential positive development, so this is progress on the topic without a concrete commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage improved to 2.8x from 4.3x a year ago, with net debt down $85.6 million (to $660.3 million) and a recent S&P credit upgrade, prompting the Board to consider expanded capital allocation options.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Any framing of a capital-return path (buyback/dividend) is a genuine narrative unlock” and identified capital allocation after deleveraging as a catalyst.

surprises.description: Leverage and net debt were modestly higher than the specific figures cited in the preview: 2.8x and $660.3 million versus 2.7x and $638.9 million. The company was still substantially deleveraged year over year, but its reported position was not quite as strong as the preview’s reference figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage improved to 2.8x from 4.3x a year ago, with net debt down $85.6 million (to $660.3 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Net debt $638.9M (-16% Y/Y), leverage 2.7x from 4.6x.”

surprises.description: CMP disclosed that COO Patrick Marin had departed and been replaced by Brandon Reisner; the preview gave no indication of a leadership change. The departure is an unanticipated management development, though the provided facts do not state its cause or effect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “COO Patrick Marin departed and was replaced by Brandon Reisner.”

surprises.description: The planned Goderich mill project is being delayed, with an updated timeline not expected until early next year. The preview focused on Goderich operating costs and throughput but did not flag a project delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The planned Goderich mill project is being delayed with an updated timeline expected early next year.”

in_line: Management confirmed historically low industry inventories after a strong winter, consistent with the preview’s description of depleted system inventories as a bullish setup for the FY27 bid season.

surprises.description: TACT reported Q2 net sales of $13.9 million, essentially at consensus, but said sales would have been $14.9 million, up 8% year over year, without an approximately $1 million tariff-refund reduction. The reported headline therefore concealed stronger underlying sales than the preview’s roughly flat-to-low-single-digit growth setup suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total net sales were $13.9 million, roughly flat versus $13.8 million a year earlier, but would have been $14.9 million (up 8% YoY) excluding an approximate $1 million tariff refund reduction to sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Q2'26 Consensus | $13.97M”; “My Base Est. | $14.1M.”

surprises.description: Casino and gaming revenue was $7.3 million, below the preview’s $7.6 million level that would confirm the run-rate and its roughly $7.8 million base estimate. Excluding the tariff impact, however, the segment would have been $8.3 million, above those expectations—so the reported decline was not reflective of the underlying comparison described on the call.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Casino and gaming revenue was $7.3 million, down 4% YoY and down 13% sequentially, but would have been $8.3 million (up 9% YoY) excluding the $1 million tariff impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything ≥$7.6M confirms the new run-rate”; “Base is simply ... Casino ~$7.8M.”

surprises.description: The Board initiated a formal strategic review of the casino and gaming business and hired B of A Securities, opening the possibility of a sale or divestiture. The preview discussed the segment’s cyclicality and cash contribution but did not anticipate a review of this business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board initiated a formal strategic review of the casino and gaming business and engaged B of A Securities as financial advisor, signaling a potential sale or divestiture of that segment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management called the segment ‘highly cyclical’ but a positive cash contributor through 2026.”

surprises.description: Recurring FST revenue reached $3.4 million, up 13% year over year—below the preview’s $3.6–3.8 million expectation and below its 20–25% growth watch range. The growth rate also fell below the preview’s specifically flagged 15% deceleration threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring FST revenue reached $3.4 million in Q2, up 13% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for $3.6–3.8M (+20–25%). Deceleration below +15% is the most damaging single data point.”

surprises.description: FST software revenue grew 47% year over year and 25% sequentially, with management attributing the growth primarily to price increases after ending free software bundling. That was concrete evidence of software monetization, which the preview identified as a key question but had not yet observed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FST software revenue grew 47% year-over-year and 25% sequentially, driven primarily by price increases as the company ended its prior practice of bundling software for free.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any concrete evidence of price realization on that gap is the highest-torque disclosure on the call.”

surprises.description: TACT grew its online BOHA base to nearly 22,000 units, up about 33% year over year, from the 19,959 units cited in the preview. That provided a stronger installed-base adoption update than the preview’s prior-quarter baseline alone established.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company sold 1,900 BOHA units in Q2 (3,270 in the first half of 2026) and grew its online installed base to nearly 22,000 units, up about 33% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Online terminals were 19,959 (+1,062 QoQ) ... Watch installed-base conversion more than gross unit sales.”

surprises.description: TACT raised its full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance rather than merely reaffirming it or nudging it toward the prior range’s high end. The preview expected a raise was likely, but the stated increase was more favorable than its base-case guidance action.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance was raised to a range of $1.5 million to $2.0-2.2 million, backed by $1.9 million of adjusted EBITDA in the first half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base ... FY guide reaffirmed, EBITDA nudged to high end”; “The FY EBITDA guide is very likely raised.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin was 50.2%, above the preview’s 49.5% base estimate and just above its 50% level that would suggest the annual margin outlook was conservative. Management nevertheless continued to guide to a mid-to-high-40% full-year range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin improved to 50.2% from 48.2% a year earlier, though management still guides to mid-to-high 40% range for the full year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Base Est. | Gross margin | 49.5%”; “A print at 50%+ again suggests the FY margin guide is also conservative.”

surprises.description: TACT posted a $50,000 net loss, or breakeven per share. That was better than the -$0.01 consensus but below the preview’s +$0.03 base estimate and its expectation that the stale consensus understated likely EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company posted a Q2 net loss of $50,000 (breakeven per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) | Q2'26 Consensus | -$0.01”; “My Base Est. | +$0.03”; “Whisper is almost certainly positive.”

surprises.description: Despite a $3 million buyback authorization and $19.4 million in cash, TACT did not repurchase shares. The preview had flagged buyback execution as an important item and noted that no repurchases would signal a lack of conviction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ... holds a strong balance sheet with $19.4 million in cash and minimal revolver debt, but did not repurchase any shares.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buyback execution. $3M authorized in May = ~5% of the market cap”; “Zero repurchases ... would read as a lack of conviction.”

in_line: Reported Q2 net sales of $13.9 million were essentially in line with the $13.97 million consensus, although the tariff-refund reduction meant the headline did not capture the stronger sales excluding that impact.
Management reaffirmed full-year net-sales guidance, consistent with the preview’s base case.
The full-year gross-margin outlook remained in the high-40% range, consistent with the preview’s description of management’s annual guidance.
Management reiterated the long-term target of $100–$200 per machine per month in recurring software revenue, a target already identified in the preview.

surprises.description: Appian reported $203.3 million of Q2 revenue, about 5% above the $193.4 million consensus and above the preview’s $200 million bull-case threshold. The quarter was materially stronger than the preview’s base-case revenue range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue rose 19% to $203.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 Consensus” total revenue: “$193.4M”; bull scenario: “Revenue | ≥$200M.”

surprises.description: Cloud subscription revenue reached $131.7 million, above the roughly $127 million consensus and the preview’s $131 million bull-case threshold. It was within the preview’s $130–132 million whisper range, but still represented a notably stronger result than consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 cloud subscription revenue grew 23% year-over-year to $131.7 million,” with “22%” constant-currency growth.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cloud subscriptions” consensus: “~$127M”; catalyst checklist: “~$127M consensus / whisper ~$130–132M”; bull scenario: “≥$131M.”

surprises.description: Total subscription revenue was $157.7 million, above the preview’s estimate of roughly $151–152 million. The preview expected about 14% growth, while Appian reported 19% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Subscriptions revenue [was] up 19% to $157.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Subscriptions (total)” consensus: “~$151–152M”; implied growth: “+14%.”

surprises.description: Professional services revenue reached $45.6 million, well above the preview’s roughly $41 million estimate and its expectation of high-single-digit growth. Appian reported 20% growth instead.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Professional services revenue [was] up 20% to $45.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Professional services consensus: “~$41M”; company guide: “high-single-digit” growth.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $16.2 million was more than double the preview’s roughly $7 million consensus and far above the $5–8 million company range; it also exceeded the preview’s $12 million bull-case threshold. Appian raised its FY26 adjusted EBITDA range to $104–110 million from $97–105 million, with management attributing the Q2 result partly to expense timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $16.2 million, roughly double the $8.1 million a year ago and well above the guided range of $5 million to $8 million, driven by higher revenue and expense timing.” Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance is now “$104–110 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 adjusted EBITDA consensus: “~$7M”; bull case: “adj. EBITDA ≥$15M and FY EBITDA raised”; FY guidance: “$97–105M.”

surprises.description: Appian raised FY26 cloud subscription guidance to $525–529 million, above its prior $515–521 million range and reaching the preview’s $525 million-or-more bull-case trigger. The increase is a clear step above the prior range, though the new midpoint is only modestly higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Appian raised full-year guidance, now expecting cloud subscription revenue of $525–529 million (20% growth at midpoint).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY2026 cloud subscriptions guidance: “$515–521M”; catalyst checklist: “a raise is required”; bull trigger: “cloud subs to $525M+.”

surprises.description: FY26 non-GAAP EPS guidance increased to $1.04–1.12 from $0.94–1.05, putting the full new range at or above the prior high end. The preview specifically highlighted a full-year EPS raise as an item to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year non-GAAP EPS of $1.04–1.12 (~77% growth at midpoint).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY2026 non-GAAP EPS guidance: “$0.94–1.05”; catalyst checklist: “FY adj. EBITDA / non-GAAP EPS raise.”

surprises.description: AI adoption indicators were stronger and more concrete than anecdotes: customer AI usage was 20 times the year-ago level, and 85% of new Q2 logos bought AI offerings. However, the preview wanted AI ARR or another dollarized monetization metric, and none is provided in the reported facts, so the evidence of adoption does not fully resolve the monetization question.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Customer AI usage was 20x greater than the prior-year Q2, and 85% of Q2 new logos purchased Appian's AI offerings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview sought “a durable metric (AI ARR, attach rate, agent consumption) rather than anecdotes” and said the buy-side wanted “dollars”; its bull case called for “AI attach >45% with a hard ARR number.”

surprises.description: Management said foreign exchange has turned from a tailwind into a modest headwind for the second half, an added drag not flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FX has flipped from a tailwind to a modest headwind in the second half,” and management said constant-currency trends are a more stable indicator than reported growth.

surprises.description: Appian refinanced its credit facility and expects to cut annual interest expense by about $4 million, a benefit not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Appian refinanced its credit facility, cutting annual interest expense by approximately $4 million.”

surprises.description: Appian is pulling some 2027 sales hiring into 2026 because of an unusually strong pipeline. That signals stronger near-term pipeline confidence than the preview’s base-case framing that the sales-org rebuild would not have a dramatic impact on this year’s numbers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[Appian] is pulling forward some 2027 sales hiring into 2026 on the strength of an unusually strong pipeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base-case operational tell: management “reiterates that the 2026 sales-org rebuild ‘won't have a dramatic impact on this year's numbers.’”

in_line: Cloud net ARR expansion was 115%, matching the preview’s expected range of roughly 114–115%; it did not reach the preview’s ≥116% threshold for a new acceleration story.
Q3 revenue guidance of $214–218 million was within the preview’s implied $212–218 million range.

Buybacks appeared consistent with the preview’s expectation that the $100 million authorization would be used during the year: Appian had repurchased $65.7 million cumulatively, leaving $34.3 million.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.40, above the preview’s $0.32–$0.35 consensus range. The call attributed the stronger result partly to lower interest expense, a lower tax rate, and a reduced share count.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS rose 24% to $0.40, aided by lower interest expense, a lower tax rate, and reduced share count.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. Diluted EPS: $0.32 – $0.35.”

surprises.description: Component Repair Services fell short of the preview’s growth and margin expectations: revenue grew 9.2% to $195 million versus a modeled ~$202 million and +13% growth, while its margin fell to 26.3% instead of the expected 29.5–30%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Component Repair Services revenue grew 9.2% to $195 million, but segment adjusted EBITDA margin fell 270 basis points to 26.3% due to work migration, labor ramp-up, and military input delays.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Component Repair Services rev … ~$202M … +13%”; “CRS EBITDA margin … 29.5–30%.”

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year 2026 guidance, whereas the preview’s base case anticipated only a nudge toward the high end rather than a material raise. The new ranges are higher for revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS, with management saying the EPS increase was driven mostly by earnings rather than the amortization change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance was raised: revenue to $6.375-$6.5 billion (up $50 million), adjusted EBITDA to $885-$910 million, and adjusted EPS to $1.50-$1.57, with the EPS raise driven mostly by earnings (amortization change contributing only ~5%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case … FY guide narrowed toward high end but not materially raised”; “buy-side expects revenue/EBITDA/EPS nudged toward the high end.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow was positive in Q2 rather than becoming a second consecutive cash outflow, the preview’s key concern after the Q1 burn. The full-year FCF outlook was maintained, not cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was a positive $50 million inflow in a seasonally cash-use quarter, though full-year adjusted free cash flow guidance was maintained at $270-$300 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A second consecutive outflow makes the FY FCF guide arithmetically strained”; “leaving it untouched while Q2 burns cash invites skepticism.”

surprises.description: Commercial aerospace grew at a mid-teens rate excluding the planned pass-through revenue elimination, above the preview’s estimate of roughly 11% ex-pass-through growth. The reported growth rate was only 6% because of the pass-through reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding the elimination of $300-$400 million of low/no-margin material pass-through revenue in 2026, commercial aerospace grew mid-teens versus the reported 6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Engine Services rev … +2.5% (~+11% ex-pass-through).”

surprises.description: StandardAero signed a sizable OEM license expansion with staged incremental EBITDA contributions through 2029. The preview did not flag this agreement or its potential earnings contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed a $180 million license expansion with an OEM partner expected to add roughly $25 million in incremental annual adjusted EBITDA at full run rate ($10 million in 2027, $20 million in 2028, $25 million in 2029+), with 80% recognized in Engine Services.”

surprises.description: Military and helicopter revenue declined 3% in the quarter because of input delays, a quarterly setback not described in the preview. Management nevertheless maintained its low-double-digit full-year military growth outlook, weighted to the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Military and helicopter revenue declined 3% in the quarter due to input delays, but full-year guidance maintains low double-digit military growth weighted to the back half.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed that LEAP is expected to reach $1 billion in annual revenue by the end of the decade and several billion by the mid-2030s. The preview focused on near-term profitability and induction mix, not these longer-term revenue targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LEAP … expected to hit $1 billion in annual revenue by decade's end and several billion by the mid-2030s.”

surprises.description: Moody’s and S&P upgraded the company’s ratings, an additional positive credit development not anticipated in the preview. Net leverage was 2.6x, the same level the preview cited at Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt to adjusted EBITDA improved to 2.6x from 3.0x a year ago, the company received ratings upgrades from Moody's (Ba2) and S&P (BB).”

in_line: Revenue of $1.6 billion was broadly in line with the preview’s $1.58–$1.59 billion consensus range.
Adjusted EBITDA of $230 million was at the top of the preview’s ~$225–$230 million estimate, consistent with the expected double-digit growth; reported growth was 12.3%.
The 14.4% adjusted EBITDA margin was within the preview’s estimated 14.2–14.5% range.
LEAP and CFM56 both reached profitability, as the preview expected them to do in H1 2026.

surprises.description: The preview expected sales of $129–132 million and flagged a sequential decline as a risk; PRTS reported $135.6 million, up from $132.0 million in Q1. The year-over-year decline was also smaller than the preview’s 15.1% consensus decline, at 10.7%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net sales declined 10.7% year-over-year to $135.6 million”; Q1 sales were $132.0 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Our estimate: Rev $130M”; the base scenario expected “$128–132M”; the preview flagged that a “sequential decline” would mean marketing cuts were still biting.

surprises.description: The preview described the IEEPA tariff claim as a possible upside but said management was not building the forward plan around it. PRTS had received $4.4 million and recognized $2.2 million in Q2, with the remaining $2.2 million expected to benefit COGS in future quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $4.4 million in IEEPA tariff claims, recognizing $2.2 million in Q2”; “the remaining $2.2 million” is to flow through COGS in future quarters.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said PRTS was pursuing “up to $4.3M” in claims and that “any recognition is upside not in numbers.”

surprises.description: Gross margin came in above the preview’s modeled range: 33.2% versus an implied 32.5–33.0% range and the preview’s 32.8% estimate. The increase occurred despite the tariff and freight cost pressures noted on the call.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded to 33.2%,” up 70 basis points sequentially and 40 basis points year-over-year, driven by “favorable product mix and freight optimization despite tariff and freight cost pressures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated gross margin at “~32.5–33.0% (implied)” and gave “GM 32.8%” in its own estimate.

surprises.description: Operating expenses were higher than the preview’s base-case assumption of roughly $43–44 million. They fell substantially year over year, but the reported $48.3 million was also above Q1’s $46.0 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total operating expenses fell 22% year-over-year to $48.3 million from $62.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “opex holds near $43–44M” and the preview described the cost base as “embedded.”

surprises.description: The preview wanted a dollar contribution from JC Whitney on Amazon, but did not provide a current run-rate expectation. PRTS reported a $2.5 million annualized run rate for the 7,000 live SKUs, an expected near-term tripling, and an exit-2026 target of about $7.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “JC Whitney's 7,000 live Amazon SKUs are running at a $2.5 million annualized run rate,” expected to “roughly triple short-term,” with an “exit-2026 target of ~$7.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to look for “a SKU count and a dollar contribution” and noted that vague qualitative language would be a tell.

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was positive for a second consecutive quarter, as the preview’s base case expected; $1.8 million was within its $0.5–2 million base-case range and close to the $1.5 million estimate.
A-Premium’s annualized run rate was approaching $50 million, in line with the preview’s near-term expectation of about $50 million.
Cash ended the quarter at $38 million, above the preview’s $35 million threshold for validating the balance-sheet outlook.
Management reaffirmed the target to be free cash flow positive in 2026, as expected.

surprises.description: Outset reported Q2 revenue of $31.6 million, above the preview’s $28.8–$29.0 million consensus, and grew 1% year over year rather than declining the expected 8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $31.6 million, up 1% year-over-year” and beat analyst consensus.

surprises.description: Console revenue was $9.5 million, well above the roughly $6.4 million analyst expectation cited on the call. The preview had flagged whether product and console revenue would inflect, making this a substantially stronger console result than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Actual console revenue of $9.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Product/console revenue inflection” and the call’s cited analyst expectation of “roughly $6.4 million” for consoles.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP gross margin was 42.2%, below the preview’s expected range of roughly 43–45%, even as it improved substantially year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin reached 42.2%, up over 380 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP GM ~43–45% (guide: low-to-mid 40s).”

surprises.description: The call described a broader refresh-cycle opportunity of roughly 3,000 consoles and up to $150 million in console revenue over several years, beyond the already-known $40 million HCA agreement. The preview discussed the HCA agreement but did not flag this broader opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The broader refresh cycle over the next several years may include roughly 3,000 consoles and up to $150 million in console revenue opportunity”; the HCA agreement “does not include potential expansion into additional HCA facilities not yet equipped with Tableau.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses increased only 1% year over year, and the non-GAAP operating loss improved 7%. That was better than the preview’s concern that analysts were modeling more operating expense and launch spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating loss improved 7% year-over-year to $12.4 million, with non-GAAP operating expenses of $25.8 million up only 1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the EPS drift meant “the sell side is modeling more opex/launch spend, not less revenue.”

in_line: Outset reiterated FY26 revenue guidance of $125–130 million, as the preview’s base case expected the range to be reaffirmed unchanged.
The company remained on track to use less than $40 million of cash for the year, consistent with the preview’s stated FY26 burn target.

Recurring revenue was broadly flat: consumables fell 12% year over year while service/other revenue rose 17%; management attributed the consumables decline to timing rather than weaker utilization. This fits the preview’s expectation that recurring revenue had stopped compounding.

surprises.description: Commercial Foodservice revenue was about $631 million, with 8.3% organic growth, above the preview’s 3–7% guide and its base case of roughly 5–6%. Middleby also raised full-year organic growth guidance for the segment to 6–8% from its initial 4–6%, with growth driven mainly by volume.
surprises.fact_evidence: Commercial Foodservice delivered Q2 revenue of ~$631 million with organic revenue growth of 8.3%; management raised full-year Commercial Foodservice organic growth guidance to 6%-8%, up from an initial 4%-6%, driven predominantly by volume rather than pricing.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Commercial Foodservice organic growth vs. the 3–7% guide” and used a base case of “CFS ~$615M, +5–6% org.”

surprises.description: The ice and beverage platform grew faster than expected, but its lower margins and new-product manufacturing ramp-up weighed on Commercial Foodservice profitability: the ramp created a 150-basis-point margin drag. The preview discussed ice and beverage growth but did not anticipate this specific margin burden.
surprises.fact_evidence: The ice and beverage platform was “growing faster than expected,” carries margins “~400 basis points below” the established cooking platform, and created a “150 basis point margin drag in Q2 from new product manufacturing ramp-up.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described ice and beverage as a growth area, including QSRs “adding beverage products… powered by Middleby,” but gave no expectation of a 150-basis-point ramp-up drag or the platform’s margin gap.

surprises.description: Management now expects $10–15 million of additional inflationary margin pressure in the second half, and pricing benefits will not arrive until Q4. That is worse and later than the preview’s expectation that a low-single-digit price increase would land in Q3 and that tariff headwinds would be lapped in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company expects incremental inflationary margin pressures of “~$10 million to $15 million in the second half versus prior expectations,” with pricing benefits “not materializing until Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “low-single-digit price increase” was “landing in Q3” and expected confirmation that “the tariff headwind laps in H2 as guided.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA of about $193 million edged above the top of the company’s $180–192 million guide, although the difference was small.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 total company adjusted EBITDA was “~$193 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company guidance of “$180–192M” adjusted EBITDA.

surprises.description: The post-spin leverage figure was 2.7x pro forma at the spin, below the preview’s expected 2.8x for RemainCo. The year-end deleveraging target remained about 2.5x, but management said debt paydown would be the primary use of second-half capital, rather than the preview’s expectation of aggressive continued repurchases.
surprises.fact_evidence: Leverage was “2.4x at quarter-end (2.7x pro forma at spin),” with a target of “~2.5x by year-end via debt paydown as the primary use of second-half capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Middleby RemainCo 2.8x, deleveraging to 2.5x by year-end” and called for “aggressive continued repurchase” as the most direct support.

in_line: Q2 adjusted EPS of $2.35 was within the preview’s expected $2.27–2.39 range; the preview also cautioned that the headline comparison depended on whether estimates included Food Processing.
Full-year post-spin adjusted EPS guidance of $6.73–6.89 was in line with the preview’s expected recast range of approximately $6.60–6.90 and its cited $6.77 KeyBanc estimate.

Commercial Foodservice adjusted EBITDA margin of 25.8% was close to Q1’s 25.7%, consistent with the preview’s expectation of continued Q2 margin pressure rather than the bull-case threshold of 26% or higher.

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 54.7%, below the preview’s 57–59% estimate and its 58% watch level. The reported decline reflected the wholesale mix shift, repacking labor, and a $187,000 increase in inventory reserves.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin contracted sharply to 54.7% from 61.5%,” driven by “the wholesale mix shift, repacking labor, and a $187,000 increase in inventory reserves.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “57–59%” gross margin and flagged “Gross margin ≥ 58%” as a key catalyst.

surprises.description: Profitability was substantially weaker than expected: adjusted EBITDA loss was $507,000, worse than the preview’s expected $100,000–$300,000 loss, while the operating loss widened to about $1.1 million against a $450,000 loss estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating loss widened to approximately $1.1 million from $905,000,” while “adjusted EBITDA loss” was about “$507,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated an operating loss of “($0.45M)” and adjusted EBITDA of “($0.1–0.3M)” in its base case.

surprises.description: Revenue was slightly below the preview’s $5.7 million base estimate and essentially flat versus Q2’s $5.64 million, so the expected third consecutive sequential increase did not materialize. It was nevertheless above the preview’s modeled $5.2–$5.3 million consensus range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net sales grew 20% year-over-year to $5.6 million in Q3 FY2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave a “$5.7M” base estimate, said a third consecutive sequential increase was “the whole bull narrative,” and modeled consensus at “~$5.2–5.3M.”

surprises.description: Management announced a new cost-reduction program targeting $100,000–$150,000 in monthly cash savings, a substantial initiative not anticipated in the preview. The savings could help cash generation, though the plan also underscores the need to reduce costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management launched a program targeting “$100,000–$150,000 in monthly cash savings” through payroll cuts, warehouse lease renegotiation, and vendor exits.

surprises.description: Oasis distributor demand accelerated sharply after the quarter: July depletions were a record and August was pacing at more than double the Q3 average. The preview expected Oasis retail expansion but did not anticipate this pace of depletion growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Oasis THC brand distributor depletions hit a record in July, up 35% over the Q3 average, with August pacing to more than double,” while a Texas distributor switch “quadrupled store access.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Oasis retail expansion” as a Q3 driver and flagged Alabama restrictions as an offset.

surprises.description: A Senate proposal could temporarily exempt cannabinoids through December 11, after the preview centered on the November 12 Section 781 deadline. This offers a possible short-term reprieve, but it is only a proposal and does not remove the underlying regulatory risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: Section 781 is “scheduled to take effect November 12, 2026,” though “a Senate proposal could temporarily exempt cannabinoids through December 11, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview emphasized the November 12 effective date and discussed legislative proposals, but did not mention this proposed December 11 temporary exemption.

in_line: Cash ended the quarter at $2.1 million, within the preview’s expected $2.0–$2.6 million range.
Management put cash-flow breakeven at a low-to-mid-$6 million quarterly revenue run rate, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the threshold was below $7 million.

surprises.description: SMCI’s Q4 non-GAAP gross margin was 17.6%, above the 15%–17% range already pre-announced and above the preview’s 16% base case. The gap to the preview’s expected range was small, even though the result was far above the original 8.2%–8.4% guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 non-GAAP gross margin surged to 17.6%,” with roughly 75% of the gain from favorable customer/product mix and 25% from lower tariffs and inventory reserves.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP and non-GAAP gross margin: 15%–17%”; the preview’s base model assumed “16%.”

surprises.description: The FY27 revenue outlook of $65–72 billion exceeded the preview’s roughly $60 billion working whisper and its $55–65 billion base scenario. Even the low end is above the whisper, while the high end reaches the preview’s bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided FY27 revenue to $65-72 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working whisper … an FY27 revenue guide of ~$60B”; the base scenario was “Rev $55–65B.”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP EPS of $1.70 was above the preview’s $1.40–$1.60 working whisper and slightly above its $1.67 high-end model. The preview cautioned that published consensus was stale, so the gap to the preview’s own estimate is relatively modest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 non-GAAP EPS came in at $1.70 versus guidance of $0.65-$0.79,” driven primarily by the gross margin beat.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working whisper … Q4 non-GAAP EPS of ~$1.40–1.60”; the preview’s high-end model was “~$1.67.”

surprises.description: Management gave a FY27 revenue outlook but no FY27 gross-margin outlook, leaving unanswered the margin question the preview identified as the central event risk. Q1 gross-margin guidance of 10.4%–10.8% points to a normalized near-term margin, but does not provide an annual FY27 margin assumption.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call facts report FY27 revenue guidance of $65–72 billion and Q1 FY27 gross-margin guidance of 10.4%–10.8%, but no FY27 gross-margin guidance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2027 gross margin guidance. This is the whole event”; the preview also gave a FY27 gross-margin whisper of “11–13%.”

surprises.description: Q1 FY27 revenue guidance of $14.5–15.5 billion cleared the preview’s $14 billion bull-case conversion threshold. That is a stronger near-term cadence signal than the preview’s base case specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY27 guidance calls for revenue of $14.5-15.5 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull scenario included “Q1 FY27 rev ≥$14B.”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue mix shifted sharply away from AI solutions: AI solutions were about 60% of revenue, down from over 80% in Q3, while enterprise and channel reached 50% of revenue. The preview emphasized AI backlog and AI-related orders but did not anticipate this large near-term mix shift; management attributed it to project timing and expects AI’s share to rise again.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI solutions fell to about 60% of Q4 revenue (from over 80% in Q3) due to large AI project timing”; enterprise and channel revenue was “$5.6 billion, or 50% of Q4 revenue,” up from 28% in the prior quarter.

surprises.description: Net debt fell to $1.2 billion from $7.5 billion, and management said it currently has no plans to use the ATM. This is a more favorable balance-sheet and issuance update than the preview’s concern that continued cash burn could make further ATM issuance an issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company raised $5.6 billion in equity, “cutting net debt to $1.2 billion from $7.5 billion,” and “stated it currently has no plans to use its ATM program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said that if Q4 showed another multi-billion cash burn, “further ATM issuance is on the table,” and flagged “signaling on the remaining ATM capacity” as a risk.

surprises.description: The call quantified customer concentration: one CSP customer accounted for 28% of FY26 revenue. The preview flagged concentration and sought disclosure about the large customer relationships, but did not provide an expected concentration figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Customer concentration remained high with one CSP customer at 28% of FY26 revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Customer concentration and order quality” and asked, “How much of the $60B and of the margin uplift is SpaceX/xAI?”

surprises.description: FY26 non-GAAP EPS of $3.63 exceeded the preview’s implied estimate of about $3.36, though that annual figure was itself a model rather than published consensus. FY26 revenue of $39.1 billion, by contrast, matched the preview’s implied figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year FY26 revenue reached a record $39.1 billion … with non-GAAP EPS of $3.63.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview implied FY26 non-GAAP EPS of “~$3.36” and revenue of “~$39.1B.”

in_line: Q4 revenue of $11.1 billion was near the low end of the $11–12.5 billion guidance, as the preview expected after the pre-announcement.
Q4 orders exceeded $60 billion and backlog reached record levels, matching the preview’s pre-announced order figure.
FY26 revenue of $39.1 billion matched the preview’s implied FY26 revenue of about $39.1 billion.
Q1 FY27 gross-margin guidance of 10.4%–10.8% was consistent with the preview’s expectation of normalized margins around 10%–12%.

surprises.description: GXO reported Q2 revenue of $3.4 billion, below the preview’s expected $3.45–$3.46 billion; revenue growth of 4% and organic growth of 3.4% also fell short of the preview’s implied 4.6%–4.7% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $3.4 billion, up 4% year-over-year and 3.4% organically.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS edged above the preview’s $0.58 consensus at $0.59, a modest beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS of $0.59.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS | $0.58.”

surprises.description: New business wins were notably strong: GXO reported $410 million in Q2 wins, up more than 30% year over year, and called it its strongest commercial quarter in three years. The preview anticipated a comparable disclosure but did not suggest this level of performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New business wins reached $410 million in Q2, up more than 30% year-over-year, marking the company's strongest commercial quarter in three years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 FY2026 cited a record $2.7B sales pipeline and $227M of new annualized contract wins; a comparable disclosure is likely in Q2.”

surprises.description: GXO disclosed substantial business already secured for future years: over $1 billion of incremental new business revenue for 2026 and about $353 million for 2027. The preview did not anticipate these bookings or this added forward-growth visibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management secured over $1 billion of incremental new business revenue for 2026 and approximately $353 million already secured for 2027, underpinning confidence in accelerating growth.”

surprises.description: Management gave a stronger forward margin outlook than the preview discussed, forecasting expansion in the second half of 2026 that accelerates into 2027 and targeting EBIT margin above 6%, versus a current 3.5%–4%. Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin itself was flat year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin held flat at 6.4% versus a year ago, but management guided to margin expansion in the back half of 2026 accelerating into 2027, targeting EBIT margin above 6% from the current 3.5%-4%.”

surprises.description: North American commercial indicators were particularly strong: pipeline was up 34% year over year, first-half wins were up 85%, and strategic-vertical wins were nearly three times last year’s pace. The preview identified organic growth and new-business wins as issues to watch but gave no expectation for this regional performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North America, cited as the largest growth opportunity, saw Q2 pipeline up 34% year-over-year and first-half wins up 85%, while strategic vertical wins ran at nearly 3x last year's pace.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic growth trajectory — Q1 FY2026 organic growth was 4.1%, within the 4%–5% full-year guided range; watch whether Q2 tracks toward the high or low end.”

surprises.description: GXO resumed share repurchases, buying back $21 million year to date and citing an undervalued stock; the preview did not flag a resumption of buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company resumed share repurchases, buying back $21 million year-to-date with approximately $280 million remaining under authorization, citing an undervalued stock.”

in_line: The 2026 organic revenue growth guidance remained 4%–5%, as previously stated. The EBITDA and EPS guidance midpoints also stayed at the levels implied by the preview’s prior ranges, although the new ranges were narrower.
Wincanton integration progress was flagged as a likely call topic; management said integration was roughly 90% complete and remained on track for $60 million in run-rate cost synergies by year-end.

surprises.description: DraftKings was expected to trim its FY26 EBITDA outlook toward roughly $625–750 million, but it maintained the $700–900 million range and said the core business alone is on track for about $1 billion of adjusted EBITDA. The maintained revenue range also contrasts with the preview’s base case of narrowing revenue guidance to the low end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company maintained its full-year 2026 guidance of $6.5 billion to $6.9 billion in revenue and $700 million to $900 million in adjusted EBITDA, with its core business alone on track to deliver approximately $1 billion in adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base ... FY revenue narrowed to low end, EBITDA trimmed to ~$625–750M”; the preview also said to “watch for a cut to a ~$600–750M range.”

surprises.description: Sportsbook handle grew 11% year over year in Q2, above the preview’s mid-single-digit-plus threshold, and accelerated to 20% growth in July even after the World Cup ended. That is stronger than the preview’s demand test and eases its concern that handle might be flat or down.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sportsbook handle rose 11% year-over-year in Q2 and accelerated to 20% growth year-over-year in July even after the World Cup ended, easing prior concerns about prediction-market cannibalization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If structural hold holds up and handle grows mid-single-digits+, the miss is outcome noise”; the bear case cited “Handle flat/down.”

surprises.description: Monthly unique payers grew 9% year over year, rather than the slight decline implied by the preview’s MUP estimate. Growth remained above 6% even excluding World Cup-only customers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Monthly unique payers grew 9% year-over-year (6%+ excluding World Cup-only customers).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “MUPs 3.26M” versus “3.30M” a year earlier, or “−1.2%.”

surprises.description: Net revenue per unique customer rose 14% year over year, substantially stronger than the preview’s expectation for a slight decline in ARPMUP. The reported measure is trailing-12-month net revenue per unique customer, while the preview’s estimate was ARPMUP.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month net revenue per unique customer grew 14% year-over-year in H1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “ARPMUP $149.78” versus “$151.00,” or “−0.8%.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $115 million, below even the low end of the preview’s $120–150 million whisper range and below its $130–150 million stated real bar. The call attributed the result to customer-friendly sports outcomes and higher-than-expected acquisition spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DraftKings generated $115 million of adjusted EBITDA in Q2 2026, which was dampened by customer-friendly sport outcomes (an ~$80 million revenue headwind) and higher-than-expected customer acquisition spend.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The real bar is $130–150M, not $173M”; the preview also gave a buy-side whisper of “$120–150M.”

surprises.description: Customer acquisition grew nearly 75% year over year while acquisition costs were about 25% better than anticipated, despite spending around 10% more than planned. The preview did not anticipate this combination of sharply higher acquisition and improved cost efficiency.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Customer acquisition grew nearly 75% year-over-year in Q2 at the best enterprise-wide CAC since Q1 2025, with acquisition costs coming in approximately 25% better than anticipated despite spending about 10% more than planned.”

surprises.description: Predictions showed substantial early engagement: annualized volume traded grew nearly fivefold from April to July, reaching $11 billion, with more than 600,000 customers engaging year to date. The preview wanted evidence of engagement but did not anticipate these reported scale and growth figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Predictions annualized total volume traded grew nearly 5x from $2.3 billion in April to $11 billion in July, with over 600,000 customers engaging year-to-date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “DKNG needs to show it's competing, not just spending.”

surprises.description: Management said 80%–90% of Predictions volume in Sportsbook states comes from professional syndicates and institutional traders, with only about 1% customer overlap. This offers specific evidence against the preview’s concern that prediction markets could cannibalize Sportsbook demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management estimates 80% to 90% of prediction market volume in Sportsbook states comes from professional syndicates and institutional traders, with only ~1% customer overlap, supporting the view that Predictions is incremental rather than cannibalistic.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned that “if handle is flat-to-down, the prediction-market cannibalization thesis gets real evidence for the first time.”

surprises.description: iGaming share stabilized after several quarters of losses, rather than continuing the slippage the preview identified as a key concern. Management credited the Lightning Link and Flex Spins launches.
surprises.fact_evidence: “iGaming share stabilized after several quarters of losses, aided by the Lightning Link and Flex Spins launches.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s key metrics included “iGaming/iCasino share” and noted, “DB flagged slippage.”

surprises.description: Combos already account for nearly 20% of Predictions volume, an adoption milestone that took years to reach in Sportsbook. The preview did not call out this level of product mix or adoption.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Combos already represent nearly 20% of Predictions volume, a milestone that took years to reach in Sportsbook.”

in_line: Predictions’ expected incremental 2026 investment of $200–300 million was within the preview’s anticipated $200–300 million range, centered around roughly $250 million; the call said it was embedded in maintained EBITDA guidance.

surprises.description: RCAT reported Q2 revenue of $20.2 million, below the preview’s $22.3 million Zacks estimate and $22.65 million broader Street estimate. The result was also below the preview’s $21–24 million base-case range, despite strong year-over-year growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached a record $20.2 million” and was “up approximately 30% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue was “$22.3M (Zacks) / $22.65M (broader street)”; the base scenario projected “$21–24M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 16.1%, below the preview’s expected range of roughly 18–22% and below the 18% level the preview said was needed to keep the year-end margin path credible. Management nevertheless continued to target 30% gross margin by year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to 16.1% in Q2”; management “targets 30% gross margin by the end of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “~18–22%” and said “Anything below ~18% and the year-end 30% target is functionally withdrawn.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses were about $41.9 million, substantially above the preview’s expectation of roughly $30 million or more. R&D alone was $14.2 million, roughly double sequentially, pointing to heavier spending and losses than the preview’s operating-cost assumptions implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 operating expenses totaled approximately $41.9 million, including R&D of $14.2 million (roughly double sequentially).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 “Opex” at “~$30M+” and discussed an operating-loss model assuming opex “near $29–30M.”

surprises.description: Blue Ops generated its first revenue from Variant 7 and moved the vessel into mass production, whereas the preview expected USV revenue in Q2 to be “likely near zero.” Management also said fewer than 10 boats could make the division profitable if Q4 internal targets are met.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Blue Ops moved its Variant 7 uncrewed surface vessel into mass production and received first revenue”; management said “fewer than 10 boats would make the division profitable if Q4 internal targets are met.”
