surprises.description: Management said July and August sales and traffic accelerated significantly, implying Q1 Chili’s comps are already running above Q4’s 6%. That is stronger early-quarter momentum than the preview’s mid-single-digit FY27 comp framing and its base-case expectations suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “July and August sales and traffic significantly accelerated, implying Q1 Chili's comps are running above the 6% reported in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described FY27 guidance as assuming “mid-single-digit comps” and its base case expected FY27 EPS guidance of $11.90–$12.30; it said a QTD figure would be the cleanest tell on early FY27 momentum.

surprises.description: Chili’s Q4 same-store sales growth was 6%, above the 5.4% consensus estimate, though it was at the upper end of the preview’s cited 5.5–6.0% buy-side chatter. The call facts do not give Q4 traffic, so whether the preview’s positive-traffic expectation was met cannot be assessed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Chili's delivered Q4 same-store sales growth of 6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Chili's comp sales: +5.4%” consensus; “buy-side chatter +5.5–6.0%.” The preview also said management guided Q4 to “mid-single-digit comps with positive traffic.”

surprises.description: FY27 revenue guidance implies growth above the preview’s 3–5% long-term revenue algorithm, based on the FY26 revenue guide of $5.78–$5.82 billion. The call’s FY27 range is $6.15–$6.27 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal '27 guidance calls for revenue of $6.15-6.27 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s long-term algorithm was “3–5% revenue” growth; its FY26 revenue guide was “$5.78–5.82B.”

surprises.description: Q4 restaurant operating margin was 18%, below the preview’s 18.2–18.5% estimate, although it cleared the preview’s 18.0% catalyst threshold. The result was therefore weaker than the estimated margin level, but not a miss of that stated threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 Brinker restaurant operating margin was 18%, up 20 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “~18.2–18.5%” and flagged “Restaurant operating margin ≥18.0%” as a catalyst threshold.

surprises.description: The Big Crispy sandwich continued to build after launch: sales reached 55 per restaurant per day from 20 before launch, a 175% increase. The preview cited a 161% increase after two weeks and questioned whether the product would add traffic or cannibalize the value anchor; the call reported continued sales growth but did not quantify cannibalization or traffic attribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Big Crispy chicken sandwich drove sales from 20 sandwiches per restaurant per day pre-launch to 55 by the end of Q4, a 175% increase that continues to build.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the sandwich was “at +161% vs. pre-launch sales after two weeks” and described Q4 as the first full read on “whether that's incremental traffic or mix cannibalization.”

surprises.description: Chili’s average annual unit volumes reached $5 million, up from just over $4.5 million, while restaurants were still operating at only 80% of historical guest capacity. The preview discussed reimages and unit-growth economics but did not anticipate or quantify this AUV and capacity update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Chili's average annual unit volumes rose from just over $4.5 million to $5 million year-over-year, with restaurants still operating at only 80% of historical guest capacity.”

surprises.description: Brinker said the Maggiano’s turnaround was slower than planned and FY27 guidance assumes flat revenues and profits. The preview highlighted the risk of further deterioration and the possibility of stabilization, but did not forecast a flat FY27 outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Maggiano's turnaround has been slower than planned… with fiscal '27 guidance assuming flat revenues and flat profits year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Any sign of stabilization is a quiet margin tailwind; further deterioration invites strategic-review questions.”

surprises.description: The company raised its total share-repurchase authorization to $750 million, which was not specifically anticipated in the preview. The reported $100 million of Q4 repurchases and nearly $400 million for the year add context, but the larger authorization is the distinct new capital-allocation update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased $100 million of stock in Q4 (nearly $400 million for the year), raised total buyback authorization to $750 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “$108M repurchased in Q3” and discussed the planned bond call, but gave no expectation for a higher repurchase authorization.

in_line: Q4 adjusted diluted EPS was $3.07, matching the preview’s $3.07 consensus estimate and falling within its stated $3.08–$3.09 Street-composite range.
The planned $350 million redemption of 8.25% bonds in FY27 was already flagged in the preview; the call confirmed the redemption and described the resulting interest savings as an FY27 benefit.
FY27 restaurant-margin guidance of 20–40 basis points of improvement overlaps the preview’s expected 30–40-basis-point annual expansion range, with up to 50 basis points including the 53rd week.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted free cash flow was $1.7 billion, below the preview’s estimated $1.8–$2.0 billion. That is a modest shortfall against the preview estimate, although the call did not explain the gap.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 generated $1.7 billion in adjusted free cash flow.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “I estimate Q2 FCF of ~$1.8–2.0B.”

surprises.description: Q2 capital spending was $1.3 billion, above the preview’s modeled $1.15–$1.25 billion. It was still 2.4% below the company-guidance midpoint, so the miss against the preview estimate was limited rather than a company-guidance overrun.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 capital of $1.3 billion coming in 2.4% below the guidance midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “I model ~$1.15–1.25B” for Q2 capex.

surprises.description: Devon completed its full $1.25 billion 2026 debt-reduction target by July, earlier than the preview’s expectation of completing that amount over the year. The amount was expected; the early completion was the positive difference.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its full $1.25 billion 2026 debt reduction target,” including “the remaining $750 million term loan in July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$1.25B of 2026 debt retirement.”

surprises.description: Management reaffirmed the $1 billion annual synergy target for year-end 2027, as expected, but added that more than 350 initiatives have been identified to support it. That supplies more execution detail than the preview’s base case, which expected no new synergy number or detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reaffirmed at least $1 billion in annual synergy targets by year-end 2027, now backed by more than 350 identified initiatives.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base — ‘on track,’ reaffirmed FY ranges, no new numbers”; the preview also described the target as “$1.0B run-rate by YE2027.”

surprises.description: Devon disclosed a New Mexico federal lease sale adding 400 Delaware locations, an acquisition the preview did not flag. Management framed the $6.5 million headline cost per location as about $4 million per premium location after adjusting for the lower royalty burden; the added inventory is positive, while the upfront price makes the news mixed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The New Mexico federal lease sale added 400 top-tier Delaware locations at a headline $6.5 million per location,” which management said “equates to an effective ~$4 million per premium location after accounting for the lower 12.5% royalty burden.”

surprises.description: The call offered stronger and more specific operating-efficiency evidence than the preview anticipated: Delaware drilling costs were already $800 per foot before most synergies, and second-half capital efficiency was described as 24% better than the peer average. The preview watched unit costs and spending discipline but did not anticipate these benchmarks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Delaware D&C costs are already at $800 per foot on a 9-12 month trailing basis before most synergies are captured”; “second-half capital efficiency is claimed to be 24% better than the peer average on a 20:1 basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Unit costs vs. FY guide” and said “G&A is where synergies show up first,” but gave no expectation for these Delaware D&C or peer-efficiency benchmarks.

surprises.description: Devon disclosed encouraging results from surfactant trials and the scale of its automated gas-lift program, neither of which the preview anticipated. The reported well uplift and existing deployment suggest operational upside, although the call did not quantify the resulting financial impact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “90% of tested wells” had “material uplift exceeding 15% at 180 days,” prompting expansion to “more than 50 wells this year”; AI-enabled closed-loop gas lift “autonomously optimizes 1,000 wells with over 2,000 more targeted in the Permian.”

in_line: Q2 total production reached the top of the 1,315–1,360 MBoe/d guide, and oil production of 503,000 barrels per day was within the 485,000–505,000 guide. This matched the preview’s expectation for volumes to land in range and its focus on a high-end oil result.
The $0.32 quarterly dividend was in line with the preview, which listed $0.32 per quarter as the expected dividend.
The $4.8–$5.0 billion full-year capital range and the $1 billion year-end 2027 synergy target were reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s base case.

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 revenue at about $31.95 million; ARS reported $33.7 million, about 5% above that estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 revenue was $33.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $31.95M (6 analysts)”

surprises.description: The preview’s cost build assumed roughly $8 million of COGS and a Q1-like gross margin near 72%. Q2 gross margin was about 62%, with short-dated product reserves, manufacturing inefficiencies, and ex-U.S. launch costs cited as pressures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin was about 62% in Q2 and over 64% year-to-date, pressured by reserves for short-dated product, manufacturing inefficiencies, and ex-US launch costs, but expected to improve in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My EPS build: revenue $32M, COGS ~$8M (Q1 gross margin ~72%).”

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 SG&A at about $70 million, while reported SG&A was roughly $77.6 million. That was a material cost overrun against the preview’s quarterly expense build, separate from the weaker gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total operating expenses were $95.1 million, including $12.8 million in cost of goods sold and roughly $77.6 million in SG&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My EPS build: revenue $32M, COGS ~$8M, SG&A ~$70M, R&D ~$5M.”

surprises.description: The preview modeled Q2 cash near $155–160 million; ARS ended the quarter with $143.8 million, roughly $11–16 million below that estimate. The company nevertheless continued to project cash-flow break-even by the end of 2027, as the preview expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ARS ended Q2 with $143.8 million in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments and projects reaching cash flow break-even by the end of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 burn of ~$40–45M puts cash near ~$155–160M at 6/30/26”; the preview also flagged “the 2027 breakeven reaffirmation.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the CSU Phase 2b interim readout in Q4 2026. Management pushed it to Q1 2027 because patients need time to log three separate flare episodes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The CSU Phase 2b interim data readout has been delayed from end of 2026 to Q1 2027 due to the time required for patients to log three separate flare episodes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “CSU Phase 2b interim, Q4 2026.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated a soft or absent formal guide and emphasized cost discipline generally. Instead, ARS gave a specific H2 cash-based SG&A and R&D range of $100–110 million and said cash-based SG&A would fall more than 40% from H1, with the trend continuing through 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company guided second-half 2026 cash-based SG&A and R&D expenses to $100-110 million, driven by a more than 40% reduction in cash-based SG&A from the first half, with the trend expected to continue through 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario anticipated “soft/no formal FY guide”; the preview described the bull case as “deeper opex cuts extend runway.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 U.S. net product revenue of about $27–29 million. ARS reported $26.2 million, slightly below that estimate, though within the preview’s $26–29 million base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 U.S. net product revenue was $26.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026E … neffy U.S. net product … ~$27–29M (my est.)”; the base scenario gave “neffy U.S. | $26–29M.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on whether the company would make cost and strategic changes, but did not anticipate a specific move away from broad direct-to-consumer TV advertising. ARS said it was shifting toward lower-cost, targeted provider-focused channels such as social media and search; the savings goal is positive, while the effectiveness of the new approach is not yet established.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is pivoting away from broad direct-to-consumer TV advertising toward lower-cost, targeted provider-focused channels like social media and search to improve SG&A efficiency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the call would outline “updated strategic priorities” and highlighted cost discipline and sales-force sizing, but did not identify this advertising shift.

surprises.description: The preview did not provide a specific market-share expectation. ARS reported that total U.S. NEPI share reached 5%, double the prior-year quarter, and that share in the targeted sales-force universe rose to 8% from 4%, compared with roughly 1% in non-targeted areas.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total U.S. NEPI market share reaching 5%, doubling from 2.5% in the prior-year quarter”; “Within the field sales targeted universe, NEPI market share rose to 8% from 4% a year ago, versus roughly 1% share in non-targeted areas.”

surprises.description: The preview did not forecast a prescriber count. ARS said unique NEPI prescribers exceeded 16,000 in Q2, more than tripling from the year-earlier quarter, a concrete sign of adoption beyond the revenue estimates in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Unique NEPI prescribers exceeded 16,000 in Q2, representing more than a three-fold increase versus the same period last year.”

in_line: The preview’s base case put Q2 U.S. net product revenue at $26–29 million; the reported $26.2 million was within that range, although below its separate $27–29 million estimate.
ARS continued to project cash-flow break-even by the end of 2027, consistent with the preview’s expectation that management would reaffirm 2027 break-even.

surprises.description: Heritage earned $2.05 per diluted share, well above the preview’s functional whisper of $1.40–$1.50 and even above its bull-case range of $1.70–$1.85.
surprises.fact_evidence: Heritage reported Q2 net income of $61.7 million, or $2.05 diluted EPS.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat $1.40–$1.50 as the functional whisper”; the bull scenario projected “$1.70–$1.85.”

surprises.description: Underwriting results were much stronger than the preview’s already favorable base case: the combined ratio was 64.9% versus an estimate of about 74.6%, and the net loss ratio was 30.4% versus about 40%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The combined ratio improved to 64.9% from 72.9%, and the net loss ratio improved to 30.4% from 38.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case projected a “~74.6%” combined ratio and “~40%” net loss ratio; even the bull case projected a 68–71% combined ratio.

surprises.description: Favorable prior-period reserve development was substantially larger than the preview’s bull-case assumption, adding to the unusually strong quarter’s underwriting result.
surprises.fact_evidence: Heritage reported “$23.4 million of favorable prior period reserve development (versus $2.3 million a year earlier).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull case assumed “favorable PYD >$8M”; the base case assumed “minimal PYD.”

surprises.description: Premium momentum did not turn as the preview hoped: gross premiums written fell 5.5% rather than reaching the expected roughly $400 million or turning positive, while premiums in force also remained down. Net premiums earned were below the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross premiums written fell 5.5% to $380.4 million,” premiums in force “declined 1.4% to $1.41 billion,” and net premiums earned were $201.1 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated gross premiums written at “~$400M,” said a positive print would validate the growth-inflection thesis, and estimated net premiums earned at “~$205M.”

surprises.description: Heritage disclosed plans for Florida rate reductions of 3%–5%, while the preview had identified how much of the reinsurance savings might be passed through to policyholders as an unresolved issue. Management expects other states’ increases to roughly match claims inflation and keep margins flat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Florida rate reductions in the 3%-5% range driven by lower reinsurance costs, while other states should see modest rate increases roughly matching claims inflation to keep margins flat.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said it was unknown “how much drops to the bottom line vs. gets passed to policyholders in rate filings.”

surprises.description: Book value per share finished above the preview’s estimate, at $19.09 rather than about $18.40.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Book value per share rose to $19.09.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 book value per share at “~$18.40.”

in_line: The new reinsurance program generated about $63 million of annualized savings, close to the preview’s expected $63.2 million.
The expected Q3 ceded-premium ratio reduction was consistent with the preview’s expectation of a roughly 42% ratio and a stronger run-rate benefit beginning in Q3.
The Texas E&S platform launch was consistent with the preview’s discussion of Heritage standing up the Texas business and preparing new product launches.

surprises.description: Tandem’s implied U.S. sales were about $180 million ($255 million worldwide less $75 million international), above the preview’s roughly $175 million expectation and at its $180 million bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: Worldwide Q2 sales were $255 million and international sales were $75 million, implying about $180 million of U.S. sales.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists U.S. sales of “~$175M” and says “If US comes in at $178M+, the PayGo drag is proving smaller than feared”; its bull case uses “US Rev | $180M+.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 57%, above the preview’s 55–56% consensus range and its 56% threshold for de-risking the full-year margin ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: Gross margin reached 57%, improving 5 percentage points year-over-year and 2 points sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gives “Gross margin … ~55–56%” consensus and says “A Q2 print ≥56% de-risks that.”

surprises.description: International sales were $75 million, below the preview’s roughly $80 million expectation, even though international pump shipments grew 19%. The company cited distributor inventory buyback headwinds.
surprises.fact_evidence: International sales rose 7% to $75 million, with approximately $3 million of distributor inventory buyback headwinds; shipments grew 19%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists international sales at “~$80M” and “+13.5%” year-over-year, and flags distributor destocking as a risk.

surprises.description: Pharmacy adoption was ahead of the preview’s stated penetration checkpoints: pharmacy shipments and sales each reached about 10% of the U.S. total, above the preview’s >8% sales checkpoint and its sub-5% Q1 pump-order baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: In the first full PAYGO quarter, pharmacy pump shipments and pharmacy sales each reached approximately 10% of the U.S. total.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gives Q1 baselines of “6% of US sales” and “<5% of pump orders via pharmacy,” and lists “pharmacy % of US sales >8%” as a catalyst checkpoint.

surprises.description: Formulary coverage reached about 45%, improving from the preview’s roughly 40% baseline but short of its >50% checkpoint. Coverage across the top three PBMs is in place, but the preview’s numerical milestone was not yet reached.
surprises.fact_evidence: Formulary coverage was approximately 45%, already approaching the high end of the company’s target range for the year, with contracts in place across the top three PBMs.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gives a Q1 baseline of “~40% formulary coverage” and says to watch whether coverage “crosses 50%”; its catalyst checklist says “Pharmacy coverage >50%.”

surprises.description: International direct-channel sales more than doubled to about 13% of international revenue, showing substantial channel progress despite the distributor transition and buyback headwind the preview expected to weigh on near-term results.
surprises.fact_evidence: Direct-channel sales more than doubled to approximately 13% of international revenue, despite approximately $3 million of distributor inventory buyback headwinds.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says the “distributor→direct in Europe” transition depresses reported revenue near-term and flags distributor destocking as a risk.

surprises.description: Net favorable pricing contributed more than half of sales growth despite an approximately $8 million initial pharmacy-pump headwind, a better offset to the transition drag than the preview’s discussion of near-term revenue pressure implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: The initial pharmacy pump headwind was approximately $8 million in Q2, but net favorable pricing still drove more than half of total sales growth.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says the PayGo pharmacy transition depresses reported revenue near-term and asks whether its headwind scales with adoption; it gives no pricing contribution estimate.

surprises.description: Stock-based compensation fell materially and the full-year expectation was reduced to about $65 million from about $80 million, helping operating margin improve by 8 points to negative 5%. This cost reduction was not part of the preview’s stated margin expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: Stock-based compensation fell to $16 million, or 6% of sales versus 11%, and full-year expectations were lowered to approximately $65 million from approximately $80 million, helping drive an 8-point improvement in operating margin to negative 5%.

in_line: Worldwide sales were $255 million, matching the preview’s approximately $255 million consensus and company guide.
Full-year sales, gross-margin, and adjusted EBITDA-margin guidance was reaffirmed at $1.065–$1.085 billion, 56–57%, and 5–6%, respectively, as the preview expected.
The company submitted the Mobi Tubeless 510(k) in Q2 and continued to target a scaled launch in the second half of 2026, matching the preview’s expected submission and timing.

surprises.description: The preview derived a Q3 revenue guide midpoint of about $33.9 million, but Blend guided to $31.5–33.5 million, a midpoint of $32.5 million. Management cited weaker macro conditions, making the outlook meaningfully softer than the preview’s bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q3 revenue of $31.5-33.5 million (negative 4% to positive 2% year-over-year)”; the guide reflects “a weaker macro.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Derived bar for the Q3 guide: ... implying a Q3 revenue guide midpoint of ~$33.9M (+3% Y/Y).”

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP operating income was $7 million, above both the preview’s roughly $6 million consensus and the top of Blend’s $5.5–6.5 million guide. That was a stronger profitability result than expected even though revenue was only modestly above consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income of $7 million exceeded the top of its $5.5-6.5 million guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income | ~$6.0M (guide mid)” and “OI above $6.5M on in-line revenue ... [would] prove[] the 80% gross margin is structural.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $33.8 million beat the preview’s $33.08 million consensus, although it remained within Blend’s guidance range rather than reaching the preview’s bull-case threshold. The beat was positive but relatively small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $33.8 million, up 7% year-over-year and near the high end of the $32-34 million guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $33.08M” consensus; the preview’s bull case was “$34.3M+.”

surprises.description: Blend now expects Q4 funded loan volume to fall 10–15% year over year to 180,000–190,000 loans. The preview noted a large-customer roll-off risk and cited a market-growth forecast, but did not anticipate a contraction of this size in Q4 volume.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 funded loan volume is expected to decline approximately 10-15% year-over-year to 180,000-190,000 loans,” reflecting “a projected 11% market contraction and the final roll-off of a previously disclosed large customer.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited management’s anchor of “Fannie Mae's ~19% Y/Y market volume growth forecast” and said to watch for confirmation that the large-customer “volume roll-off” was contained.

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP gross margin was 78.3%, below the roughly 80% level the preview treated as structural. The year-over-year improvement was positive, but the reported margin did not reach that expected level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin improved to 78.3% from 76.1% a year earlier despite growing Autopilot model costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “OI above $6.5M on in-line revenue proves the 80% gross margin is structural.”

surprises.description: Autopilot had six paying contracts, including Onity, and had processed more than 45,000 loans, ahead of the preview’s reference to five commercial customers and 25,500-plus loans. Blend also disclosed quantified early customer gains in pull-through, cycle time, and task automation, beyond the preview’s general expectation of faster, higher-converting loans.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Autopilot became commercially available July 1st, has processed over 45,000 cumulative loans since February, activated 65+ lenders, and already signed six paying contracts including major servicer Onity.” Early data showed “10-15% improvement in pull-through rates, 2-4 days of cycle time improvement, and automation of roughly 4.5 hours” of tasks per loan.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “first five commercial customers” and “25,500+ loans” processed, and said Autopilot loans “moved faster and converted at higher rates”; it wanted “a dollar number or a paying-customer count.”

surprises.description: The company reported more churn notices, with some customers moving to lower-cost or free point solutions. The preview did not flag this competitive pressure, though management characterized the revenue impact as manageable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported an uptick in churn notices this quarter, with customers moving to lower-cost or free point solutions, estimated to have a manageable low-single-digit impact on annual revenue.”

surprises.description: Engineering throughput rose 3.6 times since January with roughly unchanged headcount, materially exceeding the 1.5-times level reported in May. The preview did not anticipate this internal productivity disclosure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The engineering team increased its throughput (pull requests) 3.6x since January 2026 with roughly the same headcount, up from 1.5x in May,” with management “targeting 10x by year-end.”

in_line: Q2 evPFL was $79, within the preview’s $79–80 expectation; Q3 guidance of $80–81 was also broadly in line with that range.

Blend reported overall pipeline growth of more than 40% year over year, consistent with the preview’s expectation that pipeline growth and deal activity could be the main qualitative Autopilot and demand disclosures.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $12.9 million, below the preview’s $14.45 million consensus anchor and roughly $15.0 million model, while the net loss widened to $6.2 million, or $0.32 per share, versus the modeled $4.0 million loss and consensus loss of $0.17 per share. A customer-directed hold pushed treatment revenue into the second half even though related personnel and operating costs had already been incurred in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 revenue fell to $12.9 million” and “net loss widening to $6.2 million (-$0.32 per share)”; the primary driver was “a customer-directed hold on waste processing that pushed treatment revenue into the second half while related personnel and operating costs were already incurred in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview used “$14.45M” as the revenue anchor and modeled “~$15.0M” revenue and a “~−$4.0M / −$0.20” net loss/EPS.

surprises.description: The going-concern qualification remained in the 10-Q despite the preview expecting the May offering to support its removal. Cash ended at $20.5 million, slightly above the preview’s $18–20 million estimate, but the company still cited reliance on non-guaranteed government-directed waste shipments.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “disclosed a going concern qualification in its 10-Q due to reliance on non-guaranteed government-directed waste shipments”; it ended the quarter with “$20.5 million cash and only $2.1 million total debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the offering “should support removal” of the going-concern paragraph and described removal as “likely but not certain”; it modeled “$18–20M” of cash at June 30.

surprises.description: The call supplied a much larger prospective grouting scale than the preview’s discussion of 4.2 million gallons per year by October 2027: DOE’s target is 9 million gallons per year by 2030, and Perma-Fix is expanding its permit from 1.2 million to over 9–10 million gallons annually. The upgrades are expected to be operational by Q2/Q3 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is expanding its grouting permit from 1.2 million to over 9-10 million gallons annually to serve DOE's target of 9 million gallons per year by 2030, with upgrades expected operational by Q2/Q3 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted maintaining “100,800 gallons/week” and a “4.2M gallons/year by October 2027 target,” and noted the existing 1.2M-gallon annual permit.

surprises.description: Management described DOE’s dual glass-plus-grout strategy as potentially delivering up to 300% more throughput while reducing treatment and disposal costs from roughly $1,200 per gallon to under $50 per gallon versus vitrification. The preview did not anticipate this scale of throughput or cost advantage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DOE's dual glass-plus-grout strategy is projected to deliver up to 300% more throughput while cutting treatment and disposal costs from roughly $1,200 per gallon to under $50 per gallon versus vitrification.”

surprises.description: The call gave a specific DOE feedstock schedule: roughly 60,000 gallons per month could be available for grouting as early as Q4 2026, rising to about 130,000 gallons per month by 2028. The preview emphasized that no company volume was guaranteed and sought quantified task-order color, but did not include this schedule.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DOE estimates roughly 60,000 gallons per month will be available for grouting as early as Q4 2026 (about 720,000 gallons in 2027), rising to approximately 130,000 gallons per month by 2028,” within the existing permit.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “No revenue is guaranteed” and identified first task-order timing and PESI’s expected share as key questions; it called quantified 2027 Hanford revenue framing a potential bull trigger.

surprises.description: Perma-Fix Northwest’s location gives it a specific logistical advantage among the three master subcontract holders: it is about one mile from Hanford and can grout near the point of generation instead of requiring long-haul, out-of-state transport of liquid tank waste. The preview noted the three-awardee competition but not this advantage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Perma-Fix Northwest is the only one of three master subcontract holders located near Hanford (about one mile away), allowing grouting near the point of generation without long-haul transport of liquid tank waste out of state.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the $4.367B ceiling was “shared across three awardees” and highlighted the need for task-order timing and PESI’s expected share.

in_line: Treatment backlog reached $15.7 million, above the preview’s $15 million-plus corroboration threshold; the preview had identified $12.2 million at March 31 as the comparison point.
Nuclear Services revenue of $4.6 million was close to the preview’s roughly $4.5 million estimate for services revenue.

The H2C subcontract’s large shared ceiling did not translate into committed company volume: the call said no volumes were yet committed and task orders are eligible from 2027, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the award was a 2027-plus opportunity with no guaranteed revenue.

surprises.description: Solid Power reported Q2 revenue of negative $300,000 versus the preview’s approximately $1.55 million estimate. The shortfall included a $1.2 million non-cash reversal of Q1 revenue after assumptions about SK On milestone payments changed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was negative $300,000, hurt by a $1.2 million reversal of Q1 revenue tied to changed assumptions on SK ON milestone payments,” and the adjustment was “non-cash with no associated cost reversals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$1.55M (MarketBeat, 7/28/26)”

surprises.description: The preview focused on evaluation feedback from Samsung SDI and BMW, but the update was that the Phase 1 agreement expires at the end of September and continuation is still under discussion. That leaves the next framework unresolved rather than reporting evaluation progress.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Phase 1 Joint Evaluation Agreement with Samsung SDI and BMW is set to expire at the end of September,” and Solid Power is “in discussions to continue collaboration on a new framework.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Samsung SDI received electrolyte samples under the joint evaluation agreement with BMW — watch for evaluation feedback.”

surprises.description: The preview described Solid Power as evaluating partners for a commercial-scale facility, while management now expects to announce a South Korea electrolyte-production joint venture by year-end, with one prospective partner already discussing a draft term sheet. This is a step toward a concrete partnership, though no agreement is yet final.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects to announce a joint venture for commercial-scale electrolyte production in South Korea by the end of the year,” with “one of three prospective partners already in draft term sheet discussions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management is evaluating partners for a 500-metric-ton electrolyte facility, with demand focus in Korea rather than North America.”

surprises.description: The preview emphasized Korean demand and did not flag US customer interest, but management reported growing interest from humanoid-robotics companies and new interest from defense and aerospace. The opportunity remains early, with management noting that domestic cell manufacturing at scale is not yet available.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management noted growing US customer interest from humanoid robotics companies plus new interest from defense and aerospace,” while “no domestic cell manufacturing at scale” exists yet.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Demand focus in Korea rather than North America.”

in_line: Q2 GAAP EPS was a loss of $0.11 per share, close to the preview’s $0.12-per-share loss estimate.
The continuous pilot line’s commissioning is planned to start in Q4, broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation that commissioning would occur by year-end 2026.
Liquidity remained substantial at $419.3 million, consistent with the preview’s description of strong liquidity and significant runway.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $2.36, above the preview’s published $2.10–$2.20 consensus range and slightly above its $2.25–$2.35 whisper estimate. The beat was larger versus published consensus than versus the preview’s higher whisper bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EPS was $2.36, versus $1.76 a year ago.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS” consensus: “$2.10 – $2.20”; the preview also says the whisper was “likely closer to $2.25–2.35.”

surprises.description: Management raised full-year adjusted net income guidance, as expected, but the increase was smaller than the preview’s central expectation: the low end rose to $270 million while the high end stayed at $280 million, rather than reaching the preview’s expected $272–$286 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year 2026 adjusted net income guidance for the third time to $270-$280 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called a raise to “~$272–286M” the base case and said a 9th raise was expected.

surprises.description: The crop outlook moved well beyond the preview’s cited expectation of roughly 35% full-year growth: management raised the premium outlook from about $320 million to more than $400 million after Q2 crop premiums nearly doubled.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Crop franchise nearly doubled with gross written premium up 96% year-over-year,” prompting a raised outlook “to over $400 million (up from ~$320 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Crop GWP +82% in Q1 with FY guidance raised to +35% growth.”

surprises.description: The adjusted combined ratio came in at 76.7%, above the preview’s watch level of 76% and just outside its 74–76% base-case range, although it remained below the preview’s greater-than-78% bear-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted combined ratio of 76.7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “Watch: does adjusted CR hold ≤76%?” and gave a base case of “74–76%.”

surprises.description: Commercial earthquake pricing was weaker than the already-negative rate trend in the preview: average rate decreases exceeded 20%, and some new business was priced below technical levels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial Earthquake, now 36% of the earthquake book, saw average rate decreases exceeding 20% (over 20% on large layered/shared business), with some new business priced below technical levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported commercial EQ renewing at “~-18%” rates.

surprises.description: The quarter included a substantial favorable reserve release, an unanticipated earnings tailwind; the preview had instead highlighted potential crop-related reserve pressure as a risk to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 results included $14.3 million of favorable prior-year reserve development,” largely from Inland Marine/Property and crop, plus casualty from a legacy workers’ compensation fronting program.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Crop reserve commentary on OK/KS drought” as a potential negative surprise and said Q2 was about “reserve commentary.”

surprises.description: The crop year was currently booked near a 100% net combined ratio, indicating near-break-even underwriting on the expanded crop book. The preview anticipated crop growth and drought pressure but did not provide an expectation for crop underwriting profitability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2026 crop year [is] currently booked near a 100% net combined ratio.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described crop as “the first real test of the expanded book” and noted drought pressure on winter wheat in Oklahoma and Kansas.

surprises.description: Surety and Credit premiums grew much faster than the preview’s cited Q1 pace, reaching 236% year-over-year growth after the Gray Surety acquisition. The preview gave no Q2 segment consensus, so the acceleration is notable but not a direct consensus beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Surety and Credit gross written premium surged 236% year-over-year to ~$39 million following the Gray Surety acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 Surety & Credit GWP growth of “+131%” and said no verified segment-level Q2 consensus existed.

surprises.description: The company initiated a quarterly dividend, a new capital return measure not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board initiated a new quarterly dividend of $0.45 per share.”

surprises.description: Share repurchases accelerated from the $23.1 million bought back in Q1 to $41 million in Q2, exceeding the preview’s open question about whether buybacks would accelerate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased ~369,000 shares for $41 million at an average price of $111 during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “$23.1M repurchased in Q1” and asked, “did they accelerate?”

surprises.description: A new reinsurance treaty enabled Surety to write bonds up to $70 million while retaining $3.5 million net, a capacity expansion not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new reinsurance treaty enabling $70 million bond limits at a $3.5 million net retention.”

in_line: Gross written premium of $630.5 million was within the preview’s $615–$635 million base-case range, despite being above the approximately $616 million consensus estimate.

Management’s warning that the loss ratio would keep rising toward the mid-to-upper 30s was consistent with the preview’s expectation that mix shifts toward crop and casualty would drive continued loss-ratio pressure.

Earthquake and hurricane retentions remained at $20 million and $11 million, respectively, and earthquake coverage reached $3.92 billion after about $421 million of added limit, matching the reinsurance placement details stated in the preview.

surprises.description: Dario reported Q2 revenue of $5.2 million, about 14% below the $6.07 million consensus, and revenue fell from $5.6 million in Q1 instead of delivering the expected third consecutive sequential increase. Management said the decline was partly due to a strategic exit from pharmaceutical services.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue declined to $5.2 million,” down sequentially from $5.6 million, “partly due to a strategic exit from pharmaceutical services revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $6.07M”; the preview also expected “a third consecutive up-quarter” and said revenue below $5.8M would break the sequential-growth story.

surprises.description: The $13.1 million of contracted and late-stage ARR reported at quarter-end was well below the preview’s reference to approximately $30 million in contracted ARR. The figures may not be perfectly comparable, but the reported amount did not confirm the larger previously cited base.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Dario ended the quarter with approximately $13.1 million in contracted and late-stage annual recurring revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had flagged “~$30M in contracted ARR” on the Q1 call.

surprises.description: Management said the $13.1 million ARR would begin converting in the second half of 2026, with most of the contribution appearing in 2027. That is slower than the preview’s hoped-for confirmation that large accounts were live by July 1 and contributing in Q3, and leaves the expected roughly $14.3 million of second-half revenue less clearly supported.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects the contracted ARR “to convert into revenue starting in the second half of 2026,” with “the majority of contribution showing up in 2027” because of a typical four-to-five-quarter signature-to-full-run-rate cycle.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for confirmation that accounts “launch by July 1” and said the large accounts “land in Q3”; it also calculated “~$14.3M for H2.”

surprises.description: Gross margin rose to 62%, above the preview’s expected range of roughly 57–59%, even as revenue declined. This was a better margin result than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin rose to 62%,” up from 57% in Q1 and 55% a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “GAAP GM” of “~57–59%.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses fell 8% sequentially and operating loss improved 11% quarter over quarter, exceeding the preview’s benchmark of holding expenses at or below Q1’s $10.5 million while onboarding accounts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reduced operating expenses by 8% sequentially” and “improved operating loss by 11% quarter-over-quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s operating-leverage test was “Holding ≤$10.5M while onboarding large accounts.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed that about 75% of new accounts now come through channel partners, with shorter sales cycles and materially lower customer acquisition costs than direct sales. The preview had not identified this channel mix or its efficiency as a reported metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately 75% of new accounts now arrive through channel partners,” with “shorter sales cycles and materially lower customer acquisition costs than direct sales.”

surprises.description: Management said multi-condition expansion can generate two to five times more revenue per account. This was an additional potential growth lever beyond the preview’s discussion of DarioIQ’s expected uplift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Multi-condition expansion can generate two to five times more revenue per account.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed more than 180 signed employer and health-plan accounts, with roughly a quarter of the B2B2C client base drawn from the Fortune 500. The preview highlighted a fifth Fortune 50 client but did not provide these broader account-base figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: Dario has “more than 180 signed accounts across employers and health plans,” and “roughly 25% of its B2B2C client base” comes from the Fortune 500.

in_line: Pro forma cash was $36.8 million, in line with the preview’s estimated $35–36 million after the July raise.
B2B2C gross margin remained approximately 80%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that this margin line would hold.
Management’s estimate that DarioIQ could add approximately 10–15% in recurring revenue from existing customers matched the preview’s cited estimate.
The company reported five Fortune 50 clients, consistent with the preview’s reference to a fifth Fortune 50 client.

surprises.description: The preview expected Ferguson to reaffirm full-year sales growth at low-to-mid single digits. It instead raised the outlook to mid-single-digit growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ferguson raised full-year 2026 guidance,” now expecting “mid-single-digit sales growth (up from low-to-mid single digits).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance (unchanged since February): net sales growth low-to-mid single digit”; the base case also expected guidance to be “reaffirmed unchanged.”

surprises.description: Q2 sales were well above the preview’s estimate, including above the top of its stated range: $8.8 billion versus about $8.45 billion, with the range topping out at $8.6 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 sales rose 4.6% year-over-year to $8.8 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: ~$8.45bn (range $8.3–8.6bn).”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS exceeded the preview estimate and its high end: $3.39 versus about $3.25, with the preview range topping out at $3.35. The preview’s figure was adjusted EPS, while the call fact is labeled diluted EPS, so the comparison is not perfectly like-for-like.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS increased 5.3% to $3.39.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS: ~$3.25 (range $3.15–3.35).”

surprises.description: Q2 operating margin was above the preview’s roughly 10.4% expectation despite a 10-basis-point year-over-year decline. The call fact does not specify an adjusted margin, whereas the preview estimate is for adjusted operating margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating profit grew 2.9% to $932 million at a 10.7% operating margin (down 10 basis points).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating margin: ~10.4%.”

surprises.description: The preview worried that revenue might be flattered by pricing while volumes stayed soft. Instead, Ferguson said it returned to volume growth as inflation eased to low single digits.
surprises.fact_evidence: Sales growth included “3.8% organic growth” and management said the company was “returning to volume growth as inflation eased to low single digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “price is currently flattering the revenue line” and warned of “decelerating price with soft volume”; it also noted Q1 inflation was “mid-single-digit” and above the low-single-digit expectation.

surprises.description: Residential sales returned to growth at 2%, better than the preview’s base expectation of a 1%–2% decline. The recovery was uneven: HVAC grew strongly, while Ferguson Home and Fire & Fabrication declined.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. residential returned to growth, up 2%,” with HVAC up 11%, Ferguson Home down 1%, and Fire & Fabrication down 13%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “resi −1 to −2%”; it described a return to flat or positive as a “narrative unlock.”

surprises.description: The FloWorks acquisition was expected to be manageable for leverage, but the call said the deal would take net debt-to-EBITDA to about 1.8x. Management also tied resuming buybacks to leverage returning to the low end of its target range, indicating buybacks would wait for deleveraging.
surprises.fact_evidence: FloWorks “will raise net debt-to-EBITDA from 1.3x to approximately 1.8x upon closing”; management plans to “resume buybacks once leverage returns to the low end of its 1-2x target range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Ferguson had “ample capacity, so debt-funding should not pressure the buyback,” and warned that a buyback slowdown would be read negatively.

surprises.description: The preview sought evidence on the large-project pipeline, and management reported that backlogs were building faster than quarterly growth rates. That suggests demand visibility was strengthening beyond the current quarter’s reported growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Nonresidential growth was driven by large projects in data centers, pharma, and power generation, “with backlogs building above quarterly growth rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether management would provide “any backlog/large-project pipeline color” and whether the pipeline was broadening.

surprises.description: Management gave a stronger near-term trading signal than the preview quantified: it expected Q3 organic growth above Q2 and said July’s exit rate outpaced the second quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects “Q3 organic growth above Q2,” supported by “a July exit rate that outpaced the second quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the full-year guide required “a materially stronger back half,” but did not forecast Q3 organic growth or a stronger July exit rate.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a substantial first-half cash-flow decline tied to working capital and tax timing; the preview did not provide a Q2 or first-half cash-flow expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half operating cash flow fell ~$400 million year-over-year to $716 million” due to working capital investments in HVAC and large projects plus tax-payment timing; free cash flow was about $500 million.

in_line: U.S. nonresidential sales grew 8%, matching the preview’s expected 7%–8% range; commercial mechanical’s 15% growth remained double-digit, as the preview was watching for.

FloWorks’ approximately $1.6 billion enterprise value, roughly 10x EBITDA including about $45 million of expected synergies, immediate adjusted-EPS accretion, and expected Q3 close were consistent with the preview’s stated deal details and questions.
FloWorks’ expansion of Ferguson’s addressable market to about $400 billion matched the preview’s stated figure.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $124.5 million exceeded the $122.3 million top of the company’s guide and the preview’s $121.4 million live-consensus estimate. The beat was nevertheless within the preview’s $123–125 million whisper range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 total revenue reached $124.5 million” and was “above the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave a Q2 revenue guide of “$120.3–122.3M,” live consensus of “~$121.4M,” and said “Whisper is likely $123–125M revenue.”

surprises.description: ARR and net new ARR were stronger than the preview’s base case: total ARR reached $465.1 million versus an estimate of about $460 million, and net new ARR accelerated to a record $29.9 million. This landed around the preview’s bull scenario rather than its base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total ARR grew 27% year-over-year … to $465.1 million, an acceleration from Q1, with record net new ARR of $29.9 million up 35% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “~$460M (+25%),” while its bull scenario was “~$465M+ (+26–27%).”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating income beat the high end of guidance, and operating margin was above the preview’s expected range, rather than merely meeting the anticipated Q2 level.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company reported “non-GAAP operating income of $20.3 million (16.3% margin) beating guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 non-GAAP operating income guidance of “$18.7–19.7M,” consensus of “~$19.2M,” and expected non-GAAP margin of “15.5–16.1%” with consensus near “15.8%.”

surprises.description: The $100,000-plus customer cohort grew faster than the preview’s already-strong 25% expectation, with growth described as the fastest in over three years; larger customer cohorts also grew at least 30%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Customers with over $100,000 ARR grew 26% to 911, the fastest growth in over three years,” and cohorts above “$250K, $500K, and $1M grew at or above 30%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “863 in Q1, +25% y/y” for the $100,000-plus cohort.

surprises.description: Net retention slipped to 110% from the 111% level the preview hoped would stabilize, and AgentPulse bundle wins were still largely in the pipeline rather than booked. That leaves the anticipated expansion improvement not yet evident in booked results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net retention rate held at 110% (111% reported), still below the 115% long-term target, as AgentPulse bundle wins remain largely in pipeline rather than booked.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “NRR has drifted from 112% (Q2'25) to 111%,” and asked whether it would “stabilize at 111% or slip to 110%.” It also said investors wanted Agentic-AI “ARR attribution, not customer anecdotes.”

surprises.description: Control bundle demand showed stronger deal-size and customer-count traction than the preview had established: deals including AgentPulse were much larger and Control package customers roughly doubled quarter over quarter. However, the preview’s desired proof of booked ARR contribution had not yet arrived.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Control bundle deals including AgentPulse are averaging 2x-3x larger in dollar value, and the number of Control package customers roughly doubled quarter-over-quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “agentic-AI monetization evidence” and said investors wanted “ARR attribution, not customer anecdotes”; its bull scenario anticipated “early ARR contribution.”

surprises.description: Despite the Q2 operating-income beat, management said higher second-half technology and go-to-market spending would modestly pressure near-term operating income. That introduces some risk to the preview’s back-half-loaded margin ramp, though no cut to the full-year operating-income guide is stated in the provided facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is increasing H1 second-half spending on technology and go-to-market, which will modestly pressure near-term operating income.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the back half needed to deliver “~$53M (~19.7% margin)” and called for an “explicit 2H margin bridge”; its base case assumed the “2H ramp reaffirmed.”

in_line: The FY ARR range moved slightly lower on a reported basis despite an underlying raise, while the stated midpoint remained at 26% growth; the preview expected currency to affect the reported range while FX-adjusted growth held at 26%.
SaaS revenue growth was about as expected: the preview estimated roughly 27–30% growth, and reported growth was 27%.
The preview anticipated continued aggressive share repurchases as a possible confidence signal; the call reported $121.5 million of year-to-date buybacks and $108.6 million remaining in the program.

surprises.description: The preview derived a Q3 revenue bar of about $1.03–$1.06 billion and non-GAAP EPS of about $0.98–$1.05. TTM guided to $1.10–$1.14 billion and $1.21–$1.27, respectively, substantially above those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for net sales of $1.10–$1.14 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $1.21–$1.27, with further sequential growth expected in Q4.”

surprises.description: The preview used roughly $4.00 billion of FY26 sales and non-GAAP EPS of about $3.70–$3.80 as the expected framework. TTM raised its sales outlook to approximately $4.4 billion and said EPS was approaching $5, well above those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to approximately $4.4 billion in sales (above the prior $4 billion target) with non-GAAP EPS approaching $5.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 street revenue of ~$4.00B” and “the non-GAAP FY26 figure is closer to $3.70–3.80.”

surprises.description: The preview put Q2 non-GAAP EPS consensus at $0.92, already above the top of TTM’s $0.82–$0.88 guidance range. TTM reported $0.99, beating both consensus and its guidance ceiling.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS reached an all-time high of $0.99 per diluted share, a 71% year-over-year improvement, beating guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus” EPS was “$0.92”; the preview called out that it was “four cents above the high end of management's own guide ($0.88).”

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 revenue of $964.55 million, near the top of guidance. TTM reported a record $1.0 billion, exceeding that consensus estimate as well as guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “TTM delivered record Q2 2026 net sales of $1.0 billion, up 37% year-over-year and its first quarter surpassing the $1 billion threshold, exceeding guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 revenue consensus was “$964.55M,” described as “near the top of the $930–970M range.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged 42% of Q2 sales as the data-center-and-networking mix to watch. The reported share was 40%, two percentage points below that guide, even though the end market grew rapidly and became the largest share of sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Data Center and Networking sales surged 91% year-over-year to represent 40% of Q2 sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The Q2 end-market table listed Data Center & Networking at “42%,” and the preview identified the mix “vs. the 42% guide” as a key metric.

surprises.description: The preview highlighted yield and startup-cost risks from the capacity ramp. TTM instead said the N+M ramp’s yields were exceeding expectations and that margins were expected to improve, a more favorable ramp profile than the preview’s risk case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The N+M asymmetrical PCB ramp involves about $600 million of revenue in the second half (roughly one-third in Q3, two-thirds in Q4) with yields exceeding expectations and margins expected to improve.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “drag from Penang ramp (yields cited at 70–80%, improving)” and warned that flat-to-down gross margin could signal growth was “being bought, not earned.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the data-center mix shift to be evident in Q2, but TTM also indicated a further step-up ahead: data center and networking is expected to reach 49% of Q3 sales, alongside a decline in A&D’s share to 32%. That points to a faster next-quarter mix shift than the Q2 guide alone conveyed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Data Center and Networking “are expected to jump to 49% of net sales in Q3 as N+M production ramps”; A&D’s share “is guided to fall to 32% in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the Q2 data-center-and-networking guide as “42%” and identified its rise above A&D as “the narrative event of the print”; it gave no Q3 mix estimate.

surprises.description: The preview emphasized margin risk from the capacity build and cited a 15.7% Q1 adjusted EBITDA margin. TTM reported 16.6% in Q2, up 160 basis points year over year, with favorable product mix supporting the improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin rose to 16.6%, up 160 basis points year-over-year, driven by favorable product mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged the “non-GAAP gross margin trajectory” and warned that “flat-to-down QoQ gross margin alongside record revenue” would signal growth was being bought rather than earned.

surprises.description: The preview cited Q1 90-day backlog growth of 52% year over year but gave no Q2 backlog forecast. TTM reported 81% growth and a $901 million backlog, indicating stronger backlog growth than the prior-quarter pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 90-day cancellable backlog [was] up 81% year-over-year to $901 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed the Q1 “90-day backlog” as “$787M” and “+52%” year over year, without a Q2 forecast.

surprises.description: The preview anticipated discussion of the STG and ILFA acquisitions but did not flag a deal-related accounting loss. TTM disclosed a $14 million non-cash GAAP loss from a currency swap associated with the deals.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A deal-related currency swap created a $14 million non-cash GAAP loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the acquisitions “all-cash” and said their undisclosed purchase price would be scrutinized, but did not mention a currency-swap loss.

surprises.description: The preview discussed A&D’s $1.6 billion program backlog but did not anticipate a record qualified proposal pipeline above $7 billion. The reported pipeline adds a notably strong indicator of potential future A&D business.
surprises.fact_evidence: A&D had “a $1.7 billion backlog and a record qualified proposal pipeline exceeding $7 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited an A&D program backlog of “$1.6B” but provided no proposal-pipeline expectation.

in_line: Commercial book-to-bill remained strong: the preview said a result of at least 1.4 would sustain the demand case, and TTM reported 1.63 versus 1.65 in Q1.
The STG and ILFA acquisitions were still expected to close in Q3 and were described as moderately EBITDA-accretive, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a Q3 close and modest accretion.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $107 million, below the $121.85 million consensus and even the preview’s $116 million base estimate. The preview warned that revenue below $110 million would make the ramp story difficult to sustain; management attributed the shortfall to legacy work winding down faster than new awards ramped.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue was $107 million, down from $128 million in Q2 2025, as noncore and legacy projects wound down faster than new awards ramped up.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $121.85M” consensus; “My base” revenue estimate of “$116M”; and “sub-$110M makes the guide untenable.”

surprises.description: The FY2026 revenue range is $525–575 million, below the previously stated $550–600 million range—a $25 million reduction at both ends. That is more cautious than a reaffirmation, although the new midpoint remains above the preview’s $520 million full-year consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was raised to $525–575 million (about 12% growth at midpoint).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had “reaffirmed FY26 of $550–600M revenue / $15–30M adj. EBITDA” and framed the key scenarios as “reaffirmed or narrowed to the low end” or a cut toward “$520–545M.”

surprises.description: Liquidity ended at $33 million, materially below the preview’s roughly $45 million benchmark that included the May offering proceeds. The result falls below the preview’s $35 million bear-case threshold, even though management expects cash flow to improve after Tennessee project demobilization is complete.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Liquidity ended the quarter at $33 million, comprising $17 million unrestricted cash and $16 million of credit availability,” with cash flow expected to improve as legacy Tennessee project demobilization completes.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2-end liquidity materially below ~$45M means working capital consumed the raise”; the bear scenario specified “liquidity <$35M despite the raise.”

surprises.description: Management quantified the backlog-conversion challenge: less than 10% of backlog booked over the past 12 months had converted to revenue. The preview identified conversion speed as the central debate and expected the inflection to come later, but did not provide a conversion rate; management framed the low conversion as runway for future growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Less than 10% of backlog booked over the past 12 months has converted to revenue,” signaling “substantial runway for future revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the story was whether Shimmick could “convert [its] record backlog into revenue fast enough” and noted management had “explicitly pushed the inflection into ‘July, August and September.’”

in_line: Gross margin was 12%, matching the preview’s 12% expectation.
Adjusted EBITDA was $4 million, within the preview’s approximately $4–5 million estimate.
Backlog of $991 million was within the preview’s $0.95–1.05 billion range.
Adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed at $15–30 million, consistent with the preview’s prior guidance and expected treatment.
Noncore work was less than 3% of backlog, consistent with the preview’s expectation that noncore and legacy work would be effectively negligible.

surprises.description: EOG reported adjusted EPS of $5.07, slightly below the preview’s $5.08–$5.10 consensus range. The miss was small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS of $5.07.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS: $5.10” (Zacks) and “$5.08” (Barchart consensus).

surprises.description: EOG said its 2026 plan generates $8 billion of free cash flow at strip pricing, below the preview’s approximately $8.5 billion FY2026 FCF framing. The figures use different stated bases, so this is a qualified shortfall rather than a clear guidance reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “At strip pricing, the 2026 plan generates $8 billion in free cash flow.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management framing on the call: record ~$8.5B FY2026 FCF.”

surprises.description: Shareholder returns and remaining buyback capacity were stronger than the preview’s cited setup: EOG returned just over $1.8 billion in Q2, including $1.3 billion in repurchases, and reported $11.7 billion still available. The preview had said only $2.9 billion remained and identified accelerated repurchases as a potential positive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Returned just over $1.8 billion to shareholders in Q2 ($540 million in dividends and $1.3 billion in buybacks), with $11.7 billion remaining under its repurchase authorization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Only $2.9B remained on the buyback after Q1”; “An accelerated repurchase pace … would be the cleanest positive offset.”

surprises.description: EOG’s UAE exploration wells delivered more than 25,000 barrels of oil per well in their first 30 days, exceeding expectations and doing so before artificial lift. That is a better early well result than the company had expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company's UAE exploration wells produced an average of over 25,000 barrels of oil per well in their first 30 days, exceeding expectations while naturally flowing before artificial lift.”

surprises.description: EOG announced a new Austin Chalk sweet spot in Lavaca County and said its 60,000 net acres could add roughly a full year of drilling inventory, with about 125 remaining two-mile locations. The preview had not anticipated this new source of inventory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Announced a new Austin Chalk sweet spot in Lavaca County, organically leasing 60,000 net acres at $1,200/acre with ~125 remaining 2-mile locations adding roughly a full year of drilling inventory and payouts under one year at $65 WTI.”

surprises.description: Well costs fell materially in both the Delaware Basin and Eagle Ford, including a company-record low in the Eagle Ford. This ran counter to the cost-pressure concern raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Delaware Basin direct well costs fell $15 per foot year-to-date to under $710 per foot, while Eagle Ford well costs dropped to below $525 per foot, the lowest in company history.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Dallas Fed's Q2 survey flagged rising cost pressures.”

surprises.description: The Utica Encino acquisition exceeded its $150 million synergy target ahead of schedule, while also lowering direct well costs below $600 per foot and improving base production by 5%. The preview flagged Utica execution as important but did not anticipate this degree of delivery against the synergy target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Utica Encino acquisition exceeded its $150 million synergy target ahead of schedule, drove direct well costs below $600 per foot, and improved base production by 5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Utica/Encino execution. Encino is now EOG's third foundational play; +10 net Utica completions were added in Q1.”

surprises.description: EOG gave a new 2027 production-growth signal: low-single-digit oil growth, driven mainly by the Utica, with the Delaware Basin flat to moderate. The preview anticipated lower FY2027 EPS but did not give a production-growth expectation, so the production outlook is new rather than a clear beat or miss against a stated forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For 2027, EOG signaled a plan reflective of its 3-year scenario of low single-digit oil growth, with growth driven dominantly by the Utica while the Delaware Basin stays flat to moderate.”

surprises.description: EOG reported Janus running above 99% utilization and providing a netback uplift of more than $0.65/Mcf, alongside a forecast of 3%–5% annual U.S. natural-gas demand growth through decade-end. The preview focused on weak near-term gas economics and Dorado spending cuts, not this plant performance or demand outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EOG's Janus gas plant is running above 99% utilization delivering a netback uplift of over $0.65/Mcf, and the company forecasts U.S. natural gas demand growth of 3%-5% CAGR through the end of the decade.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dorado spending was cut on weak near-term Henry Hub; watch gas volume guidance and any LNG-linked commentary.”

in_line: EOG reaffirmed FY2026 guidance and kept capital expenditures at $6.5 billion, consistent with the preview’s report that capex was held at about $6.5 billion.
The commitment to return at least 70% of 2026 free cash flow was consistent with the preview’s stated payout commitment.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was negative $0.6 million, far worse than the preview’s estimated negative $0.05 million and below its base-case range of negative $0.15 million to positive $0.05 million. Management still said it aims for positive adjusted EBITDA in Q4, but the reported quarter was a much larger setback than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was negative $0.6 million in Q2 2026 versus negative $0.4 million a year ago”; management “reaffirmed its goal of reaching positive adjusted EBITDA in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates: Revenue $6.3M (–$0.1M vs. consensus, on procurement lumpiness), Adj. EBITDA –$0.05M”; the base scenario estimated “Adj. EBITDA –$0.15M to +$0.05M.”

surprises.description: The Q2 net loss was $1.4 million, substantially larger than the preview’s estimated $0.45 million to $0.70 million loss; the first-half loss also rose to $2.0 million from $0.2 million a year earlier. The preview cautioned that consensus EPS was unreliable, but its own Q2 loss estimate was still much less negative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $1.4 million in Q2 2026 from $1.1 million a year earlier,” and the six-month net loss “grew sharply to $2.0 million from just $0.2 million in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 net-income estimate was “(0.45)–(0.70)” million.

surprises.description: Core recurring Managed IT technology revenue grew only about 8%, well below the preview’s expected mid-to-high-teens growth and its stated threshold of +15%. This underperformed on the business line the preview identified as most important.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring managed IT technology revenue, the company's core, grew about 8% year-over-year and totaled $3.8 million in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “Managed IT +16–19%,” and said “Below +15% Y/Y breaks the re-rating thesis.”

surprises.description: Procurement revenue reached $2 million, up 64% year over year and roughly 18% sequentially from Q1’s $1.7 million, rather than being flat to down sequentially as the preview’s base case anticipated. The growth was AI-infrastructure-driven, but the preview warned that procurement carries lower margins, making the stronger revenue mix lower quality.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Procurement revenue jumped 64% year-over-year to $2 million in Q2… driven by AI-related server, storage and infrastructure sales, but carries lower margins and is project-based.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “procurement flat-to-down sequentially off a hot Q1,” and described procurement as “hardware pass-through” with “far lower gross margin.”

surprises.description: A large customer order spanning two reporting periods generated an outright loss because component and freight costs were higher than expected, compressing margins. The preview anticipated margin pressure from procurement mix, but did not flag a loss-making order.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A single large customer order fulfilled across two reporting periods incurred higher component and freight costs, producing an outright loss on that order that compressed margins.”

surprises.description: Memory, CPU and GPU supply constraints delayed shipments, leaving booked orders unrecognized as Q2 revenue and pushing them into future quarters. The preview did not anticipate component-driven shipment delays.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Supply chain constraints on memory, CPU and GPU components delayed shipments, leaving a portion of booked orders unrecognized as revenue and pushed into future quarters.”

surprises.description: Professional services revenue fell 47.3%, a steeper decline than the preview’s already-worrying expectation that the line might persist around a 30% decline. Management attributed the drop to customer timing rather than structural weakness.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Professional services revenue fell 47.3% to $363,000… which management attributed to customer timing rather than structural weakness.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “a persistent –30%” decline in professional services as a key issue.

surprises.description: Deferred revenue was $4.5 million, down $0.2 million from Q1’s $4.7 million, rather than roughly flat as the preview’s base case anticipated. It was nevertheless up $0.6 million from year-end 2025.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended the quarter with “$4.5 million in deferred revenue (up $0.6 million from year-end 2025).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected “deferred revenue roughly flat”; it identified a decline as a possible signal of a slowing funnel.

surprises.description: Revenue from related-party NewtekOne declined as it reduced IT spending, confirming a customer-concentration and captive-book risk that the preview identified but had not expected to show up in this result. Growth from new non-related-party customers partly offset the decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue from related party NewtekOne declined as it cut IT spending, a headwind partially offset by growth from new non-related-party customers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called “captive-book churn post-separation from NewtekOne” an “under-discussed risk” and flagged the related-party revenue concentration for monitoring.

in_line: Q2 revenue was $6.5 million, close to the $6.40 million consensus and within the preview’s $6.3–$6.6 million base-case range; 13% year-over-year growth also fit its expected 10–15% range.
Subscription revenue continued to decline, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the subscription/web-hosting line was shrinking.
Management’s acquisition appetite was consistent with the preview’s expectation that IPM remained open to acquisitions at reasonable valuations.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was a much larger loss than expected: Enviri reported a $0.63 adjusted loss per share versus the preview’s roughly $0.30 loss estimate (and $0.31 consensus).
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported an adjusted loss per share of $0.63.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS: ~$−0.30”; consensus “−$0.31.”
