surprises.fact_evidence: “The new K7 autonomous security robot passed its Alpha Prototype gate review and remains on track for initial deployments in Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided to K7 limited release by late summer 2026.”

surprises.description: KSCP reported roughly $1 million of expense tied to fair-value changes in acquisition contingent consideration, an item the preview did not anticipate. It added to reported expense, although it is distinct from the company’s underlying operating costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net expense included roughly $1 million tied to fair value changes in contingent consideration (earn-out) from the recent acquisition.”

in_line: Revenue was $9 million, matching the approximately $9 million preliminary figure already disclosed before the release; the preview explicitly said the revenue result was already known.
The company’s 434 clients across 42 states matched the client count already disclosed in the preview.

Cash ended at $8.2 million, within the preview’s $8–12 million base-case range, though below its roughly $10 million concern threshold. The call facts do not provide Q2 operating cash burn, so that part of the preview’s key cash debate cannot be assessed.

Operating expenses were $13.8 million, above the preview’s $12 million warning threshold; the preview had flagged that level as evidence that operating leverage was not yet visible and expected expense growth with headcount.

The preview anticipated that acquired guarding services would contribute substantially to revenue and that margin improvement could reflect a higher share of guarding. KSCP said the Security Force acquisition drove much of the growth; the call facts do not provide the segment split or legacy robotics revenue needed to resolve the preview’s organic-growth concern.

surprises.description: The preview cited management’s prior guidance that cash would fund operations into Q2 2027. The call instead disclosed substantial doubt about the company’s ability to continue as a going concern, with only about $4.8 million in cash and equivalents plus $1.5 million in restricted cash and securities at quarter-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company disclosed substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern,” ending Q2 with “approximately $4.8 million in cash and equivalents plus $1.5 million in restricted cash and securities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: On the Q1 call, management said existing cash would fund operations “into Q2 2027.”

surprises.description: Revenue was below the preview’s $0.99 million to $1.03 million consensus range: approximately $961,000, or about 3% to 7% short. The shortfall was small relative to the forecast, but it was a miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was approximately $961,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $0.99M (GuruFocus) / $1.03M (MarketBeat).”

surprises.description: The quarterly loss per share was $0.06, worse than the preview’s expected loss of $0.04 per share. Net loss also widened year over year to approximately $2.1 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss for Q2 2026 widened to approximately $2.1 million ($0.06 per share) from $1.8 million in Q2 2025.”

surprises.description: The preview identified Gates Foundation and CEPI as potential non-dilutive channels but did not give funding amounts. The call specified an approximately $3.9 million grant supporting the Gates-backed RSV and malaria antibody program; this is program funding, not stated as cash directly available for general company operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Gates Foundation-supported program is funded by an approximately $3.9 million grant for RSV and malaria antibodies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gates Foundation / CEPI program milestones — the credible non-dilutive channel.”

surprises.description: The call put a potential value on the CEPI collaboration that the preview had not quantified: Dyadic is eligible for up to approximately $2.4 million. The amount is an eligibility ceiling, not a committed payment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The CEPI-supported collaboration makes Dyadic eligible for up to approximately $2.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gates Foundation / CEPI program milestones — the credible non-dilutive channel.”

surprises.description: The preview had flagged an approximately 80% productivity gain in transferrin, but the call added a potential cost benefit: management expects the pilot result to reduce costs by roughly 40%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The animal-free recombinant human transferrin program achieved an approximately 80% productivity increase in its pilot run, expected to reduce costs by roughly 40%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~80% productivity gain in recombinant human transferrin.”

surprises.description: The preview’s financing debate focused on whether management would identify a path to address the cash shortfall. The call described a pursuit of non-dilutive sources—licensing, milestones, and royalties—and said the convertible notes remain covenant-compliant and do not mature until December 31, 2027, but did not report a completed financing transaction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Convertible notes remain in covenant compliance and do not mature until December 31, 2027,” and management is pursuing “non-dilutive capital such as licensing, milestones, and royalties,” citing “$30 million of prior non-dilutive industrial-side funding.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Financing plan / going-concern mitigation. The only question that matters. Does management name a path — ATM usage, strategic investment, partner prepayment, non-dilutive grant expansion?”

in_line: The preview flagged a grant-heavy revenue mix and margin pressure; the reported quarterly revenue included $837,000 of grant revenue, while cost of revenue rose 60% and exceeded revenue.

Commercial traction remained early and unquantified: Q2 included initial channel-filling shipments to IBT Bioservices and pilot sales, with no recurring-order ramp established, consistent with the preview’s concern about reorder rates and slow conversion to recurring sales.
The approximately 80% transferrin productivity increase was already flagged in the preview.

surprises.description: Q1 revenue was about $3.6 billion, below the preview’s $3.661 billion consensus and its $3.65–$3.70 billion base case. The 3% constant-currency decline was within the preview’s expected range, so the miss was modest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue was $3.6 billion, down 3% year-over-year on both a reported and constant currency basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $3.661B”; “My base case: revenue $3.66–3.70B (CC ~−3.5%).”

surprises.description: The adjusted pretax loss was less severe than the preview’s roughly $50 million base-case loss, and the $152 million workforce rebalancing charge was below the roughly $200 million charge the preview expected. The preview still expected Q1 to be the year’s earnings low point, so this was a modestly better trough than modeled.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported an adjusted pretax loss of $37 million, primarily driven by $152 million of workforce rebalancing charges that impacted adjusted pretax income margin by more than 4 points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base case: … adjusted PTI ≈ −$50M”; “Q1 is also the quarter management pre-announced as the earnings and cash-flow trough of FY27, absorbing a ~$200M workforce rebalancing charge.”

surprises.description: Q1 signings of $3.9 billion beat the preview’s $3.0–$3.3 billion base case and exceeded its $3.5 billion bull-case threshold. TTM signings were $14.2 billion, although still below the preview’s cited $18.3 billion year-ago level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month signings totaled $14.2 billion with $3.9 billion signed in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … signings ~$3.0–3.3B”; “Bull … Q1 signings >$3.5B”; “anything under ~$3.0B makes the back-half revenue ramp implausible.”

in_line: Kyndryl reaffirmed its FY27 adjusted pretax income, free cash flow, and constant-currency revenue outlook, as the preview expected.
The roughly 3-point adverse revenue headwind from evolving IBM purchasing patterns was expected to persist through FY27; the call said it is expected to persist through FY27.
The company reiterated expected FY28 workforce-rebalancing savings of $400–500 million annualized, matching the preview’s stated savings milestone.
The share of large-deal value from new scope and new logos was approximately 30%, consistent with the preview’s cited level of more than 30%, up from about 15% in FY25.
Ellen Johnson was set to start as CFO on August 6, in line with the preview’s expected CFO handoff timing.
Consult and hyperscaler-related revenue continued to grow at double-digit rates despite the hard comparisons the preview flagged; the preview had specifically warned of possible deceleration.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case called for Q2 revenue of $238–246 million, while Rocket Lab reported $234 million. That was still slightly above the cited $231.6 million consensus and within company guidance, but below the preview’s base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record Q2 2026 revenue of $234 million…landing within prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base…Revenue $238–246M”; consensus revenue was “$231.6M (Zacks) / ~$232M (LSEG).”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margins beat the preview’s expected guided step-down: non-GAAP margin was 41.5%, above the 38–40% guide, and GAAP margin was 36.1%, above the 33–35% guide. The beat was partly aided by a nonrecurring tariff refund, with an inventory reserve offsetting some of it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP gross margin of 41.5% and GAAP gross margin of 36.1% both exceeded guidance, aided by a nonrecurring tariff refund offset by an inventory reserve on the new light launch vehicle.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided down sequentially: GAAP 38.2% → 33–35%, non-GAAP 43.0% → 38–40%.”

surprises.description: Rocket Lab’s Q3 margin outlook is lower than its Q2 reported margins, with management citing unfavorable Space Systems mix. The preview discussed Q2 margin compression but did not give a Q3 margin forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for…GAAP 29–31%, non-GAAP 35–37%…due to unfavorable Space Systems mix.”

surprises.description: Q2 backlog ended at $2.36 billion, above the preview’s roughly $2.2 billion expectation, despite the preview noting that two large awards would land in Q3 backlog. Rocket Lab also reported over $1 billion of new contracts across Q2 and post-quarter, including the $266 million Space Force award.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed over $1 billion in new contracts across launch and Space Systems during Q2 and post-quarter, including a record $266 million Space Force contract”; “ended Q2 with $2.36 billion total backlog.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Backlog…~$2.2B”; “Q2 backlog holding roughly flat near $2.2B while burning ~$232M of revenue is a good outcome”; the $266M RSLP award was expected to land in Q3 backlog.

surprises.description: Management kept Neutron’s Q4 2026 pad-delivery plan on track, as the preview expected, but added that the year-end launch window is narrowing. That caveat increases schedule risk even though no slip was announced.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Neutron production remains on track for delivery to the pad in Q4 2026, though management acknowledged the year-end launch window is narrowing while prioritizing scaling to Flight 10.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether “the Neutron ‘Q4 2026’ language survives intact” and described the base case as “Neutron ‘Q4, tracking.’”

surprises.description: The pending Iridium acquisition is a major strategic development not anticipated in the preview: it would add a 66-satellite constellation and about $870 million in annual revenue, with management citing significant free cash flow. The deal is expected to close in mid-2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pending Iridium acquisition, expected to close mid-2027, adds a 66-satellite constellation with 2.5 million subscribers and roughly $870 million in annual revenue, providing significant free cash flow.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed Neutron pricing of $50–55 million per launch and said it is not offering significant early discounts, with potential pricing upside in a supply-constrained market. The preview discussed launch pricing for Electron but did not anticipate this Neutron pricing commentary.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Neutron is being sold at a $50-55 million ASP with no significant early discounting, and management sees more upside than downside to launch pricing given a supply-constrained market.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow use worsened to $110.1 million in Q2, and management said cash-flow positivity is expected only 18–24 months after Neutron’s first successful launch. The preview focused on adjusted EBITDA and breakeven but did not flag this level or timing of cash-flow use.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow deteriorated to a use of $110.1 million in Q2 (from $77.4 million in Q1), driven by Neutron tail production and Mynaric supply chain replenishment, with cash flow positivity expected 18-24 months after Neutron's first successful launch.”

surprises.description: Rocket Lab raised $1.08 billion through its ATM equity program, which has now terminated, and ended Q2 with about $2.4 billion in cash. That provides substantial funding for acquisitions and growth but was not anticipated in the preview and came through equity issuance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised $1.08 billion through its now-terminated at-the-market equity program, ending Q2 with roughly $2.4 billion in cash and equivalents to fund M&A and growth initiatives.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 “cash $1.48B (~$2.0B total liquidity)” but did not anticipate the ATM raise.

in_line: Q3 revenue guidance of $250–265 million was broadly in the preview’s expected base-case range of $250–260 million, with the midpoint at $257.5 million.
Neutron’s Q4 2026 pad-delivery timing remained on track, as the preview’s base case expected.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $22.2 million, below the preview’s $24–26 million realistic range and well below the $30 million published consensus. It was only slightly above the preview’s <$22 million “no recovery” threshold, not the sequential improvement the base case expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue fell to $22.2 million”; management said results came in “well below analyst expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base estimate: revenue $25M”; the preview said “$24–26M = on plan” and “<$22M = no recovery.” Published consensus was “$30M.”

surprises.description: Management said traffic headwinds continued rather than stabilizing, walking back the prior stabilization message. The preview identified whether “traffic volatility has subsided” as a key debate and expected Q2 seasonality and improving yields to support recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management acknowledged results were well below expectations “because traffic headwinds continued rather than stabilizing as previously guided.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview quoted management saying traffic volatility “has subsided” and asked whether that was “reaffirmed or walked back”; it also described Q2–Q4 as seasonally stronger.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $4.4 million, below the preview’s roughly $6 million base estimate, despite the preview expecting the one-time Q1 costs to largely disappear.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA dropped to $4.4 million in Q2 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base estimate: … adjusted EBITDA ~$6M”; the preview said Q1 one-time costs were “largely limited to the first quarter.”

surprises.description: Arena reported a $200,000 net loss rather than the return to profitability anticipated in the preview’s base case. The much higher year-ago net income included a one-time discontinued-operations gain, which the preview had explicitly cautioned investors to disregard.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported a net loss of $200,000 in Q2 2026”; Q2 2025 net income included “a $96.2 million gain from discontinued operations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “EPS ~$0.02–0.04” and described a “Return to profitability.” It also said the Q2’25 one-time benefit should not be treated as a meaningful comparison.

surprises.description: The debt facility was refinanced and extended by three years, removing near-term refinancing risk without dilution. The preview viewed a signed refinancing as a potential positive, but had looked for a lower-cost facility; the reported rate was unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: Arena “refinanced and extended its debt facility by three years with its existing lender at the same interest rate, avoiding dilution and removing near-term refinancing risk.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called a signed refinancing a “balance-sheet re-rating event” and its checklist looked for a “completed facility with a commercial bank at lower cost.”

surprises.description: Arena made an unpreviewed cash-funded acquisition of InfoSentience, an AI content-generation firm, and said it expects the deal to contribute immediately to cash flow and profit through existing B2B contracts.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “acquired InfoSentience, an AI content-generation firm, entirely with cash on hand” and “expects it to be immediately accretive to cash flow and profit via existing B2B contracts.”

surprises.description: Arena announced a rebrand to Pradium AI and a repositioning from traditional publishing toward an asset-light AI technology company, a strategic shift not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Arena is rebranding to Pradium AI, repositioning from a traditional publisher to an asset-light AI technology company empowering creators.”

surprises.description: The newly launched Cutter Studios targets about 1,000 video-first creators, turning long videos into five to ten articles each. The reported output is only about one-third as effective as handwritten articles, although monetization rates are comparable or better; the preview did not discuss this initiative or its productivity tradeoff.
surprises.fact_evidence: Cutter Studios targets “about 1,000 video-first creators,” converting long-form videos into “5-10 derivative articles each at roughly one-third the efficacy of handwritten articles but with comparable or better monetization rates.”

in_line: Cash remained at $11.2 million and the company generated over $2 million in operating cash flow in the first half, broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation that cash would hold up or build despite weak results.

surprises.description: The preview expected Q3 gross margin around 17.0%–17.5%, with roughly 17.3% needed for consensus. Management instead guided to 16.0%–16.5%, a clear step-down below that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for a sharp step-down to just 16%–16.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 GM guided 17.0–17.5%” in the base case; the catalyst checklist says “~17.3% needed.”

surprises.description: The preview treated $0.08 as the live Q2 EPS estimate and modeled about $0.05. Reported diluted EPS was only $0.03, with adjusted net income of $1.4 million versus $12.9 million a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income $1.8 million, or $0.03 per diluted share,” and “adjusted net income dropping to $1.4 million from $12.9 million a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (Class A, diluted) Consensus: $0.08”; the preview’s base case modeled “~$0.05 EPS.”

surprises.description: Orders substantially exceeded the preview’s expected range and roughly 800-order whisper: Q2 net new orders reached 970. That was also up 32% year over year, rather than merely continuing the expected pace-over-price growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net new home orders grew 32% year-over-year to 970.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “orders 750–820”; the catalyst checklist cited “~800 whisper.”

surprises.description: Closings and revenue came in well above the preview’s estimates: 839 closings exceeded both the derived 765–780 consensus range and the company’s 800-home guidance ceiling, while $273 million of revenue topped the cited $255.8–$258.1 million estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Home closing revenue rose 22% year-over-year to $273 million on 839 closings (up 25%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Home closings ~765–780 (derived)” and “Revenue $255.8M … · $258.1M.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin modestly beat the preview’s expectations: GAAP margin was 17.6%, above the 17.0%–17.5% company range and the roughly 17.3% consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP home closing gross margin was 17.6% (18.7% excluding $3.1 million of inventory impairments).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company guidance of “17.0%–17.5%” and consensus of “~17.3%.”

surprises.description: Incentive-related costs rose instead of stabilizing: they reached 780 basis points, above the 730 bps cited from Q1, and management expects them to rise further in Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Incentive-related costs … jumped to 780 basis points from 480 bps a year ago and 730 bps sequentially, and management expects them to rise further in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the key question whether “the 730 bps stabilized” and described a flat-to-down incentive load in its bull case.

surprises.description: The Q3 closing and price outlook points to revenue below the preview’s $291.1 million consensus: guidance is 825–900 closings at $315,000–$320,000, which falls short of that revenue estimate even at the top of both ranges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance projects 825–900 closings and a lower average sales price of $315,000–$320,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q3 consensus of “$291.1M” revenue and said that it required “~880 closings.”

surprises.description: The quarter included $3.1 million of inventory impairments across three communities, versus the preview’s reference to a $1.0 million impairment in Q1 and its concern about possible additional impairments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company took $3.1 million in inventory impairments across three communities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “impairments (Q1 had $1.0M in Southeast)” as a secondary item to watch.

surprises.description: The company also recorded $4.5 million in lot option abandonment charges, an additional land-related charge not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of lot counts and land spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$4.5 million in lot option abandonment charges during the quarter.”

surprises.description: The realized average sales price was $325,000, below the preview’s roughly $328,000 estimate and at the bottom of the company’s Q2 guidance range, even as closings exceeded expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An average sales price of $325,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed ASP consensus of “~$328K” and company guidance of “$325K–$330K.”

in_line: The company did not reinstate full-year guidance; the preview noted that the FY outlook had been withdrawn in April and described reinstatement only as a possible signal.

The land-light model remained in place: the company controls 22,319 unstarted lots, with only 3% owned on the balance sheet, consistent with the preview’s focus on controlled lots and limited balance-sheet land exposure.

surprises.description: Deluxe held adjusted EPS guidance at $3.60–$4.00 instead of raising it for Celero’s 2026 contribution. The preview expected roughly $3.70–$4.10 and said an unchanged EPS range would imply that financing or integration costs were absorbing the acquisition’s earnings contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS ($3.60–$4.00) and free cash flow (~$200 million) were held, as Celero's stub-period earnings roughly offset new interest and integration costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A revised guide of roughly $2.07–$2.14B revenue / $455–$480M EBITDA / $3.70–$4.10 EPS is the ‘as-advertised’ outcome”; “Anything that leaves EPS guidance unchanged or lower implies either core softness being papered over or heavier-than-expected financing/dis-synergy drag.”

surprises.description: Data Solutions grew to $82.3 million, well above the preview’s $70 million downside threshold and its $75 million bull-case marker, despite a tough comparison. That was stronger than the preview’s central concern about how sharply growth would moderate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Data Solutions segment grew revenue 21.4% to $82.3 million, marking its seventh consecutive quarter of 15%+ growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Below ~$70M (i.e. sub-3% growth) reads as one-time campaign timing”; the bull case required Data Solutions to be “>$75M.”

surprises.description: First-half free cash flow reached $85.9 million, substantially ahead of the $52.1 million generated in the first half of 2025 and stronger than the preview’s concern that the roughly $200 million full-year target required heavy second-half weighting.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-to-date free cash flow grew nearly 65% to $85.9 million, a $33.8 million improvement over the first half of 2025, driven by lower restructuring, SG&A, and cash taxes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FCF guide of ~$200M implies heavy 2H weighting off just $27.3M in Q1 (1H'25 was $52.1M).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was modestly above the preview’s modeled range, and comparable-adjusted growth was stronger than the preview’s roughly flat year-over-year baseline. The reported margin also expanded rather than merely holding near the prior-year level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA rose 5.3% on a comparable adjusted basis to $108.8 million, with margins reaching 21.8%, up 60 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$106–108M (my model, no published cons.)” and “~flat” year over year.

surprises.description: The Print segment’s margin improvement exceeded the preview’s expectation that margins would simply remain at 32% or better: management reported margins in the mid-30s, up about 110 basis points. The preview had anticipated some benefit from the Safeguard exit, but not this stated margin level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Print segment revenue declined 4.3% to $235.9 million but EBITDA margins expanded to the mid-30s (up ~110 bps)”; “the Safeguard exit added roughly 80 bps to enterprise margins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether core decline stays inside 4–6% and whether the 32%+ Print EBITDA margin holds.”

surprises.description: The reported Celero combination places Deluxe among the top 10 nonbank merchant acquirers, a positioning milestone not identified in the preview’s description of the deal’s expected scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[Celero] bring[s] combined processing volume to over $70 billion annually across more than 210,000 merchants and moving Deluxe into the top 10 nonbank merchant acquirers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a combined “~$70B annual gross transaction volume” and listed the acquisition as adding “+55,000 merchants,” but did not anticipate Deluxe entering the top 10.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue exceeded both cited consensus estimates, although it remained within the preview’s $490–$500 million base-case range. Comparable-adjusted growth was positive rather than the reported decline suggesting a weaker underlying quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $499.3 million, down 4.2% on a reported basis but up 2.6% on a comparable adjusted basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited revenue consensus of “$491.45M” and “$486.3M,” and described its base case as “$490–500M” with “revenue in line to slightly light.”

in_line: The revised revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance landed within the preview’s expected Celero-inclusive ranges: reported guidance was $2.095–$2.120 billion and $455–$475 million, versus preview ranges of roughly $2.07–$2.14 billion and $455–$480 million.
The approximately $200 million full-year free-cash-flow guide was maintained, as the preview expected.
Management’s warning that Data Solutions growth would moderate in later quarters was anticipated; the preview flagged moderation against tough Q3 and Q4 comparisons.

Merchant Services revenue growth of 6.1% was close to the preview’s ≥6% bull-case marker. However, the reported growth was aided by the December 2025 purchase of ISO residual commission rights, so it does not establish the clean organic momentum the preview wanted to see.
Print revenue declined 4.3%, within the preview’s expected 4–6% core-decline range; legacy Checks declined only 1.7%.
Payments and data represented 52% of revenue, broadly consistent with the preview’s 51% Q1 mix and its expectation that Celero would further increase the mix.

Pre-acquisition leverage was 2.9x, close to the preview’s 3.0x pre-deal reference. The preview expected leverage to rise after the July 31 Celero closing, which these pre-acquisition figures do not address.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $196.3 million, above the preview’s $184.7 million consensus and above its $175–185 million base-case range. The preview’s bull case began at $195 million, but the reported result cleared that threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenues rose 27% year-over-year to $196.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 FY26 revenue | Consensus | $184.7M”; the base case was “$175–185M” and the bull case “$195M+.”

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted operating income was $18.6 million, well above the preview’s $5–10 million base case and close to its $20 million bull-case threshold. This was a stronger recovery than the preview’s central case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income swing[ing] to $18.6 million from a $1.3 million loss in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “Q4 AOI +$5M to +$10M”; its bull case expected “+$20M or better.”

surprises.description: Theater bookings were weaker than the preview’s description of a contracted, largely de-risked FY27 calendar would suggest: MSGE was only about 60% toward its theater booking goal, with theaters pacing behind for both the September and December quarters. Garden bookings were much further along, at roughly 90%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is roughly 90% toward its Garden bookings goal but only ~60% toward its theater goal, with theaters pacing behind for both the September and December quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the “FY27 calendar” as “contracted and largely de-risked” and highlighted “Joe Hisaishi (7 nights, theater).”

surprises.description: Full-year revenue was about $1.061 billion, derived from the reported $1 billion-plus full year and the $196.3 million Q4 result, versus the preview’s $1.03 billion consensus. That is a modest beat, while reported 13% growth also exceeded the preview’s expected 9.4% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2026 full-year revenues exceeded $1 billion (up 13%).” Q4 revenue was reported as “$196.3 million.”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted operating income was $262 million, above the preview’s roughly $250 million base-case estimate, though below its roughly $265 million bull-case figure. The 18% increase was also stronger than the base case’s implied growth of about 12%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income of $262 million (up 18%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “FY26 AOI ~$250M (+12%)”; its bull case expected “FY26 AOI ~$265M (+19%).”

surprises.description: The Christmas Spectacular reported a record season—over 1.2 million tickets sold and the highest attendance in 25 years—whereas the preview discussed the upcoming 230-show season but did not anticipate a record attendance result for the season just completed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Christmas Spectacular set a record with over 1.2 million tickets sold across 215 performances (highest attendance in 25 years) generating approximately $195 million in revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “a 230-show Christmas Spectacular (+7% shows)” for FY27, but gave no expectation for attendance or revenue in the completed season.

in_line: The preview expected a significant increase in Garden concerts in Q4; the call reported that the number of concerts more than doubled, with most Q4 concerts sold out.
The preview highlighted Harry Styles’ 30-night residency and the 230-show Christmas Spectacular for FY27; the call confirmed the 30-date residency and the expansion to 230 shows.

The preview expected a championship-related Knicks monetization benefit and continued attendance support into FY27; the call cited a $7.4 million Q4 revenue increase from MSG Sports shared streams and expected continued benefit from strong arena attendance.

surprises.description: ESAB cut its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to $5.40–$5.50 from the prior $5.70–$5.90 range, even as it raised EBITDA guidance. Management said the new EPS range includes a $15 million drag from transitory price-cost neutrality tied to logistics and commodity inflation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EPS guidance is $5.40–$5.50,” incorporating “an assumed $15 million drag from transitory price-cost neutrality from logistics and commodity inflation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the standing FY26 adjusted EPS guide was “$5.70–5.90” and called for watching whether “core ex-Eddyfi” was held as guidance was recast.

surprises.description: Q2 core organic growth was 2.5%, a clear improvement on the preview’s near-flat to slightly negative base case and above the flat level it identified as the key threshold for keeping the full-year organic-growth bridge credible.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Core organic growth of 2.5%,” driven by “double-digit growth in automation and equipment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “Organic ~flat to −1%” and it said “Anything worse than flat organic” would make the full-year bridge implausible.

surprises.description: Q2 sales of $766 million exceeded the preview’s $747.3–$750.1 million consensus range by about 2–3%. The reported 13% year-over-year increase included only 2.5% core organic growth, so the headline beat was not all organic.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record Q2 total sales of $766 million, up 13% year-over-year, with core organic growth of 2.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview put revenue consensus at “$747.3M – $750.1M.”

surprises.description: ESAB raised full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $615–$625 million from the prior $575–$595 million range. The increase is positive, though it comes with the acquired business and offsets, rather than the preview’s clearest bull case of retaining the core outlook and adding the acquisition on top.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year 2026 guidance” to adjusted EBITDA of “$615–625 million”; DFI’s incremental contribution was “approaching $50 million,” including a $35 million net raise and $15 million of offsetting headwinds and investments.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed prior core adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$575–595M” and described the bull outcome as “core FY guide held, Eddyfi added on top (EBITDA → ~$625M+).”

surprises.description: The Middle East business was down roughly 10–11%, while logistics costs had tripled due to the conflict. The preview had already flagged the region’s conflict-related drag, but the reported contraction and cost escalation show a substantial ongoing impact; management said rebuilding could restore prior growth rates.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Middle East, “representing 7–8%” of the business, was “down double digits (~10–11%)” with logistics costs “tripling due to conflict”; rebuild efforts could restore prior “~20% growth rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the Middle East was “≈ 7% of sales,” noted an Iran-related regional drag, and highlighted whether management described the impact as “persisting” rather than “easing.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a cross-selling funnel with DFI approaching $450 million, but said conversion would take time and materialize mainly in 2027 and beyond. This adds a sizable opportunity not quantified in the preview, while indicating that it is not an immediate revenue driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DFI’s cross-selling funnel with ESAB is approaching $450 million,” but conversion is expected “to take time and materialize mainly in 2027 and beyond.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was $150 million, within the preview’s implied $146–$150 million range. The 19.5% margin was at the bottom of its implied 19.5–20.0% range, and the 90-basis-point year-over-year decline was within the preview’s expected 40–90-basis-point decline; price-cost neutrality had also been anticipated.
The full-year organic sales outlook remained 2–4%, consistent with the prior guidance and the preview’s stated range.
DFI’s high-single-digit growth, approximately 65% gross margin, and roughly 30% EBITDA margin were broadly consistent with the acquisition economics cited in the preview.

surprises.description: LVLU revenue was $67.8 million, down 17% year over year, versus the preview’s $76 million estimate and expected 6.8% decline. The company attributed the sharper drop to 17% fewer orders and higher return rates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net revenue declined 17% year-over-year to $67.8 million, driven by a 17% drop in total orders placed and higher return rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Q2 FY2026 estimate: $76.0M (-6.8% YoY)”; the preview also said “worse than -12% kills” the recovery story.

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 48.6%, far above the preview’s 45.8% estimate. Lower markdown sales and higher-margin mix helped drive the expansion, despite the preview’s concern that clearance markdowns could pressure margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 330 basis points to 48.6%, the company's highest Q2 gross margin since 2021, aided by higher-margin sales mix and freight cost savings”; “Total markdown sales fell 38%,” including a “65% decline in casual apparel markdowns.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Q2 FY2026 estimate: 45.8% (+50 bps)”; the bear scenario cited “casual/footwear clearance markdowns hit GM.”

surprises.description: The company reported that units transacted per new casual-apparel and footwear launch rose 28% year over year and 29% sequentially, even as it cut launches 48% year over year. The preview anticipated the assortment reset and fewer launches, but did not anticipate this improvement in productivity per launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Casual apparel and footwear new product launches were cut 48% year-over-year, while units transacted per new launch rose 28% versus Q2 2025 and 29% sequentially.”

surprises.description: LVLU secured a $4.5 million equity line of credit, with an option for an additional $5.5 million. The preview focused on liquidity and the ABL but did not anticipate this financing; it adds potential funding while also creating possible equity dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Secured new financing including a $4.5 million equity line of credit with an option for an additional $5.5 million.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was $1 million, matching the preview’s estimate and exceeding the preview’s cited $0.5 million guidance threshold; net loss was $1.5 million, also matching the estimate.
FY2026 adjusted EBITDA inflecting positive and improving revenue trends were reaffirmed, as the preview expected.
Wholesale continued expanding, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it was a growth vector and its focus on Nordstrom and Dillard’s door expansion.
Double-digit growth in occasion wear was consistent with the preview’s view that occasion and bridesmaid products were the company’s strongest category heading into the seasonal peak.
The strategic review remained part of the company’s situation, but the call facts provided no new development beyond the committee’s previously disclosed evaluation of strategic alternatives.
Lower inventory and fewer product launches were consistent with the reset and inventory-clearing effort described in the preview.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA of $93.3 million matched UBS’s published estimate of about $93 million, but came in below the preview’s $95–105 million buy-side whisper. The shortfall versus the whisper was small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $93.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Whisper: I'd put the buy-side bar at $95–105M adjusted EBITDA”; the preview also cited UBS’s “~$93M” mark.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS of $0.83 was well above the preview’s stated consensus range of $0.52–$0.65, exceeding even its high estimate by $0.18.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income attributable to Green Plains was $67.1 million or $0.83 per diluted share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted): $0.52”; the preview also gave an “EPS (alt.)” range of “$0.54 / $0.65.”

surprises.description: Green Plains had not monetized any of its 2026 45Z credits by the end of Q2, rather than providing the cash-conversion confirmation the preview identified as important. Management said it was waiting for a partner that could provide stable, predictable cash flows.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has not yet monetized any of its 2026 45Z credits, opting to stay patient to secure a partner offering stable, predictable cash flows.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “confirmation that credits are converting to cash on schedule” and said “EBITDA-to-cash lag is a real risk to the story.”

surprises.description: The Q3 margin outlook was more resilient than the preview’s concern that board crush would soften entering Q3: margins were said to be only slightly below Q2’s historically high levels, with the favorable structure expected to last into early Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 crush margins are only slightly below Q2's historically high levels, with the favorable margin structure expected to carry into early Q4 before seasonal declines.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “board crush [appears] to have softened from Q2 into Q3” and flagged Q3 crush commentary as a key debate.

surprises.description: Q2 operating cash flow and the ending cash balance were strong despite the preview’s concern about a lag between recognized 45Z EBITDA and cash collection. The reported $87 million of operating cash flow included a separate final $41 million payment for 2025 credits, so it does not establish that 2026 credits were monetized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Green Plains generated nearly $87 million of operating cash flow and ended June with over $243 million in cash”; it also received “a final $41 million cash payment for its 2025 45Z credits during Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “EBITDA-to-cash lag is a real risk to the story” and highlighted the timing of 45Z cash conversion; it cited Q1 cash of “$183.1M” including restricted cash.

surprises.description: The carbon platform generated nearly $59 million of net EBITDA, above the preview’s $45–55 million base-case range for net 45Z recognized value and close to its $60 million bull-case threshold. This was a modestly stronger credit contribution than the base case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The carbon platform contributed nearly $59 million of net EBITDA in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s operating scenarios used “net 45Z recognized” of “base $45–55M” and “bull ≥$60M.”

in_line: The final $41 million cash payment for 2025 45Z credits was consistent with the preview’s statement that 2025-vintage credits were fully collected in April 2026.
Full-year SG&A of about $90 million matched the preview’s stated FY target, and sustaining CapEx of about $25 million was within its $15–25 million annual frame.
Q2 utilization was reduced by planned spring maintenance, consistent with the preview’s expectation that maintenance would temper production volumes.

surprises.description: Revenue was expected to be roughly flat to slightly down at $142.9–$143.4 million, but SGC reported $148 million, up 3% year over year. That was about $5 million above the consensus range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 2026 revenue rose 3% year-over-year to $148 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $142.9M (MarketBeat) / $143.4M (Zacks)” with “Implied Y/Y” of “-0.5% to -0.8%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was expected at $0.09–$0.10, with even the preview’s discounted whisper only $0.12–$0.13; reported adjusted EPS was $0.21. This was a substantial upside gap, although GAAP EPS was $0.08 after the trade-name impairment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS more than doubled to $0.21”; “GAAP net income was $1.2 million or $0.08 per diluted share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS | $0.10 (MarketBeat) / $0.09 (Zacks)” and “A naive whisper is $0.12–$0.13.”

surprises.description: Branded Products revenue was expected to land roughly flat at $92–$93 million, with the preview warning that Q1’s pull-forward could weigh on Q2. Instead, the segment grew 6% to $98 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Branded Products, the largest segment, grew revenue 6% to $98 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus of ~$143M total effectively assumes BP lands flat, ~$92–93M”; the preview also said “Q1 2026 pulled revenue forward out of this quarter.”

surprises.description: Healthcare Apparel revenue was expected to grow 3–5%, but instead fell 4%. The decline was a clear miss against the preview’s segment outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Healthcare Apparel revenue fell 4% to $27 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “HA +3–5% but margin-pressured.”

surprises.description: Healthcare Apparel’s gross margin fell to 32.9%, with a $2.6 million inventory write-down weighing on the quarter. The preview anticipated margin pressure but did not flag a write-down or a decline of this reported size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Healthcare Apparel revenue fell 4% to $27 million with gross margin down 260 basis points to 32.9%, hurt by a $2.6 million noncash inventory write-down partially offset by a $1.8 million net tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Healthcare Apparel mix shift toward lower-margin customers” and expected the segment to be “margin-pressured.”

surprises.description: SGC recognized a $2.6 million noncash trade-name impairment in Healthcare Apparel, reducing GAAP EPS by $0.13 per share. The preview did not anticipate this charge, which helps explain why GAAP EPS of $0.08 was far below adjusted EPS of $0.21.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A pretax noncash trade name impairment of $2.6 million ($2 million net of tax, or $0.13 per diluted share) was recognized in the Healthcare Apparel segment.”

surprises.description: Contact Centers revenue declined 4%, a milder decline than the preview’s expected 5–8% drop; it also improved sequentially for a second consecutive quarter. However, its gross margin fell 170 basis points to 50.9% as onboarding investments weighed on results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Contact Centers revenue declined 4% year-over-year to $23 million but improved sequentially for the second consecutive quarter, with gross margin down 170 basis points to 50.9% due to onboarding investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “CC -5% to -8%”; the preview also said segment gross margin was “~52–53%.”

surprises.description: Management said Healthcare Apparel margin pressure would continue through the rest of 2026 under the assortment transition, with improvement anticipated in 2027. The preview identified ongoing pressure as a risk, but did not spell out this duration before improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects continued Healthcare Apparel margin pressure through the balance of 2026 during its assortment transition under new leadership, with improvements anticipated in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “Healthcare Apparel mix shift toward lower-margin customers” and asked “whether Healthcare Apparel mix has stabilized.”

surprises.description: Management signaled that a Contact Center acquisition or a Philippines call-center startup is likely this year. The preview anticipated M&A commentary broadly but did not identify either of these specific expansion paths.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “signaled a Contact Center acquisition or Philippines call center startup is likely this year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had positioned SGC “as a participant” in industry consolidation and listed “M&A commentary” as a narrative item to watch.

in_line: SGC reaffirmed its full-year 2026 sales and adjusted EPS guidance, as the preview’s base case expected the range to be reaffirmed or narrowed; the reported back-half-weighted cadence was also anticipated.
The preview flagged tariff-refund recognition as possible and as a one-time earnings-quality item; the quarter included a $1.8 million net tariff refund benefit in Healthcare Apparel.
Consolidated SG&A improved, consistent with the preview’s expectation that SG&A leverage would help absorb gross-margin pressure.

surprises.description: Revenue was expected at about $9.33–$9.54 million, with even the preview’s bull case at $12.5–$14.5 million. Satellogic reported $15.9 million, roughly 67% above consensus and above the bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 259% year-over-year to $15.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | $9.33M (Zacks) / $9.54M (Benzinga)”; bull case: “$12.5–14.5M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected an adjusted EBITDA loss of roughly $3.5–$4.5 million, with even its bull case calling for a loss of $1.5 million or better. Satellogic instead reported positive adjusted EBITDA of $2.8 million and its first positive quarterly operating income.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company achieved its first-ever positive quarterly operating income (~$300,000) and positive adjusted EBITDA ($2.8 million) in Q2 2026”; operating expenses “rose only 46%” while revenue grew 259%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~–$3.5M to –$4.5M”; bull case: “EBITDA –$1.5M or better.”

surprises.description: The preview modeled a large noncash fair-value gain because the stock had fallen, estimating a possible $40–$90 million gain. Instead, Satellogic reported a $19.7 million noncash fair-value charge and a $20 million GAAP net loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss was $20 million for the quarter, primarily due to a $19.7 million noncash fair value charge tied to stock price movements.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The stock fell roughly 40–45% between March 31 and June 30, which should drive a large non-cash gain … plausibly $40–90M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected a roughly 70/30 Data and Analytics/Space Systems revenue mix and flagged Space Systems at 35% or less as a quality test. Actual revenue was 45% Data and Analytics and 55% Space Systems, so the much larger-than-expected quarter was more weighted toward lumpy satellite deliveries than the preview’s preferred mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Data and Analytics revenue reached $7.1 million (45% of Q2 revenue)”; “Space Systems contributed $8.8 million (55% of Q2 revenue).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case: “a roughly 70/30 D&A/Space Systems split”; catalyst: “Revenue ≥ $9.33M and Space Systems ≤ 35% of the total.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Merlin’s first launch in October 2026 and full deployment in H1 2027. The October launch remains on track, but the call put full service in the second half of 2027, later than the preview’s stated deployment timetable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Merlin constellation's first satellite is fully integrated and on track for an October 2026 launch, with full service expected in the second half of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “First launch targeted October 2026, full deployment H1 2027.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated that the previously signed defense monitoring contract would push RPO higher, but did not anticipate the pilot converting into a full-scale program in under six months. The reported conversion and program value add a stronger signal of rapid pipeline conversion than the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A key defense pilot converted into a full-scale program valued at over $18 million in under 6 months, signaling faster-than-expected pipeline conversion amid a nearly $1 billion Space Systems pipeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $18M+ one-year international defense monitoring contract signed in May should push [RPO] materially higher.”

surprises.description: The company reduced secured convertible debt by $12 million through an equity conversion, a capital-structure change the preview did not anticipate. Lower debt is favorable, while the equity conversion also means dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reduced secured convertible debt from $30 million to $18 million via a $12 million equity conversion.”

in_line: RPO was $80.7 million, meeting the preview’s watch level of at least $80 million and falling within its $75–$85 million base-case range.
Cash ended at $112.8 million, within the preview’s expected $110–$118 million range and above its $110 million threshold.
CFO Rick Dunn’s departure effective August 21 and the possibility of Controller Dustin Greer serving as interim CFO matched the preview’s stated succession scenario.

Merlin’s October 2026 launch remained on track, and the call said it was funded to reach positive free cash flow in 2027, consistent with the preview’s expected October launch and fully-funded framing.

surprises.description: The preview’s working assumption was roughly 55–65 of 70 patients enrolled, but Talphera reported 75% enrollment, or about 53 patients. That is below the expected range, although all sites are now active and management said enrollment remains on track.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Talphera reached 75% enrollment in the registrational NEPHRO CRRT study with all clinical sites now activated,” and “remains on track to complete enrollment later in 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Enrollment number or LPO timing vs. the market’s assumption of ‘roughly 55–65 of 70 enrolled.’”

surprises.description: The preview expected management to reiterate a second-half 2026 topline. Instead, enrollment is expected to finish later in 2026 and topline data to follow roughly four to five weeks afterward, pointing to a possible early-2027 readout rather than a clear 2H26 result.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management said enrollment is expected to complete “later in 2026,” with “top-line data expected roughly four to five weeks after enrollment completion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reiteration (or not) of 2H26 topline”; the preview said the buy-side was listening for “‘second half of 2026’ topline reiterated verbatim.”

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate a larger estimated U.S. CRRT market: Talphera’s updated research put 2027 annual procedures at about 200,000, up 21% from its prior estimate of 165,000.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Updated market research raised the estimated 2027 annual U.S. CRRT procedures to approximately 200,000, a 21% increase from the prior estimate of 165,000.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag new guideline support for Nefamostat. The 2026 KDIGO guideline now references it as an acceptable regional anticoagulant alternative to citrate for the first time, although final publication is still pending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2026 KDIGO clinical practice guideline … now references Nefamostat as an acceptable regional anticoagulant alternative to citrate for the first time.”

surprises.description: Talphera reported an additional potential source of market access not anticipated in the preview: about three-quarters of U.S. institutions lack citrate, which management said could leave a large potential market for Nefamostat from launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately 75% of U.S. institutions do not have citrate available,” and citrate “is not FDA approved for CRRT and carries usage complexities, creating a large potential market for Nefamostat out of the gate.”

surprises.description: The preview did not describe Talphera’s specific commercial rollout plan. Management said CRRT procedures are concentrated in about 70 U.S. institutions, supporting a targeted rollout with account managers and educators rather than a traditional sales force.
surprises.fact_evidence: “About 70 U.S. institutions [represent] over 50% of CRRT procedures,” supporting “a targeted commercial rollout using account managers and educators rather than a traditional sales force.”

surprises.description: The preview mentioned partnering only as possible upside optionality; the call disclosed a specific post-readout negotiation right held by CoreMedix. This creates a concrete strategic-partner pathway, but no partnership was announced.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CoreMedix holds a right of first negotiation for 60 days post data readout, and its CEO Joe Tedisco sits on Talphera’s board, representing a potential strategic partnership consideration.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “commentary on PMA module pre-work, or on partnering/commercialization” as “upside optionality.”

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate disclosure of blinded-study dosing results. Talphera said most patients reached therapeutic range at the starting dose within about half an hour and that the independent safety committee recommended continuing without changes, a favorable interim signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly 80-85% of patients reached therapeutic range at the starting dose within about half an hour,” most were titrated to “20-25 mg/hour, well below the 50 mg maximum,” and the committee “recommended continuing without changes.”

in_line: Cash was $17.1 million at June 30, within the preview’s estimated $17.0–17.5 million range; the approximately $16 million in remaining conditional financing tranches also remained in place.
The PMA filing and potential approval timing remained within the preview’s expected 2027 window: Talphera plans to file in the first half of 2027 and targets approval around mid-2027.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.40, well above the preview’s $0.29 consensus and $0.30–$0.32 estimate. The preview expected adjusted EPS to decline year over year, whereas the reported figure was up $0.02 per share.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income was $25.3 million or $0.40 per diluted share, up only $0.02 per share year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS $0.29” consensus; “$0.30–0.32” estimate; the preview also described the consensus as “–19.4%” year over year.

surprises.description: Revenue of $543.7 million exceeded both the $526.2 million consensus and the preview’s $528–$532 million estimate, as well as the stated consensus range high of $539.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 16.9% year-over-year to $543.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $526.2M” consensus and “$528–532M” estimate; consensus range “$479.3–539.5M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA guidance was held at $473–$483 million even though the preview said a raise was the key question and that buyers expected one; the preview specifically warned that a hold could signal disappointment. The reported $30 million revenue-guidance increase was mostly fuel recovery fees, not a corresponding increase to EBITDA guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed at $473-$483 million”; revenue guidance rose by $30 million, “majority fuel recovery fees.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buy-side expects a raise given the Q1 outperformance”; “A hold after explicitly deferring the decision last quarter reads as a negative signal.”

surprises.description: The adjusted EBITDA margin fell to 22.7%, down 80 basis points, well below the preview’s roughly 23.3% estimate and its expectation that fuel would dilute margin by about 30 basis points. Resource Solutions added an unexpected 70-basis-point drag, despite the preview anticipating that recovering OCC prices could become a modest tailwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin declined 80 basis points to 22.7%, hurt by 40 bps from fuel and 70 bps from Resource Solutions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin … ~23.3%”; the preview modeled fuel “dilut[ing] optics ~30bps” and said the OCC year-over-year comparison would turn into a “modest tailwind.”

surprises.description: GAAP net income guidance was lowered again, from the existing $4–$10 million range to $0–$6 million, while the preview listed the $4–$10 million range as the standing guide. The company attributed the new reduction to higher amortization and taxes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income guidance lowered to $0-$6 million on higher amortization and taxes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Standing FY2026 guidance listed “Net Income (GAAP) $4–10M.”

surprises.description: Landfill volumes surged 8.4%, including a sharp increase in third-party tons. That was a strong positive datapoint against the preview’s central volume debate, which framed Q2 around whether solid-waste volumes would remain weak or improve only to around –1.0% to –1.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Landfill volumes surged 8.4% (86,000 tons) year-over-year, with third-party volume up 62,000 tons and internalized volume up 24,000 tons.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 is the quarter that proves or breaks that claim”; the preview’s base case expected “Volume –1.0 to –1.5%.”

surprises.description: Five acquisitions had been completed year to date, representing about $165 million of annualized revenue—more than the preview’s expectation of four deals totaling about $150 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Five acquisitions completed year-to-date represent approximately $165 million of annualized revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Four deals closed YTD (~$150M annualized revenue).”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA of $123.2 million was within the preview’s $120–$123 million implied range and $122–$124 million estimate.
Solid-waste pricing rose 5.5%, broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of roughly 5% pricing and above its stated 4.5% concern threshold.
The Mid-Atlantic cost plan remained on track: the preview expected $5 million of 2026 cuts and further synergies over the following years, and the call reported the $5 million plus $10 million plan.
Net leverage of 2.7x and approximately $500 million of liquidity were close to the preview’s roughly 2.75x pro forma leverage and $500 million liquidity expectations.
Revenue guidance was raised, as the preview said a raise was near-certain from fuel surcharges and acquisition rollover.

surprises.description: NCM announced a definitive $275 million acquisition of Captivate, a digital elevator and lobby advertising operator—an unanticipated expansion beyond its cinema network. Captivate reported $64 million of 2025 revenue and $19.3 million of adjusted EBITDA, and NCM expects at least $3.5 million in annual run-rate cost synergies; the deal will be debt-financed and bring net leverage to about 3.9x at close.
surprises.fact_evidence: NCM signed a definitive agreement to acquire Captivate for an enterprise value of $275 million, approximately 10x pro forma EBITDA including synergies. Captivate generated approximately $64 million revenue and $19.3 million adjusted EBITDA in 2025; management expects at least $3.5 million of annual run-rate cost synergies. The acquisition will be financed with $275 million of new committed term debt, resulting in net leverage of approximately 3.9x at close.

surprises.description: NCM provided no forward guidance because the Captivate transaction is pending, despite the preview identifying Q3 guidance as the key issue and deriving a roughly $68–71 million Q3 revenue bar. Investors therefore did not get the expected read on the second half or whether the FY revenue model remained achievable.
surprises.fact_evidence: No forward guidance was provided due to the pending transaction.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue/OIBDA guidance. This is the whole ballgame”; “implying a Q3 guide of roughly $68–71M.”

surprises.description: Attendance growth greatly exceeded the preview’s estimate, but the extra moviegoers did not translate into commensurate advertising yield gains. The preview expected attendance growth of 5.9%, while NCM reported approximately 19.3% growth and said lower-yielding horror films and FIFA-related budget shifts limited yield.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Network attendance grew approximately 19.3% year-over-year, but strong turnout from lower-yielding R-rated horror films (Backrooms, Obsession) plus a FIFA World Cup budget shift limited advertising yield gains.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus attendance: “122.15M” versus “115.30M,” or “+5.9%” year over year.

surprises.description: Total revenue came in below consensus, though it remained within the company’s guidance range. Revenue of $58.4 million was about 3% below the preview’s $60.4 million estimate, with year-over-year growth of 12.7% versus the 16.6% implied by consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue rose 12.7% year-over-year to $58.4 million … within guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $60.4M” consensus; “+16.6%” year over year; company guide “$57.0–63.0M.”

surprises.description: National advertising growth fell short of the preview’s already strong estimate: revenue rose 9% to about $45 million, versus consensus growth of 16.4% and an estimated $47.97 million. This was a weaker monetization result despite attendance growth far above the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “National advertising revenue rose 9% to about $45 million, supported by insurance, retail, automotive, and pharmaceutical categories despite a soft June film slate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “National advertising | $47.97M” consensus and “+16.4%” year over year; the preview said consensus required national growth of “+16.4% against attendance up only ~6%.”

surprises.description: NCM paused both its dividend and share repurchases to prioritize debt repayment, contrary to the preview’s expectation that the dividend would be maintained and its framing of buybacks as a possible confidence signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “NCM is pausing its dividend and share repurchase programs to prioritize debt repayment following the Captivate close.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “With a $347M cap and a 3.2% yield, dividend maintenance is table stakes; an upsized buyback at $3.70 would read as a confidence signal.”

surprises.description: Adjusted OIBDA was below the preview’s expected range, even though it remained inside company guidance. The $2.1 million result was below the preview’s implied $2.5–3.0 million consensus estimate and below the preview’s $2.5–4 million base scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted OIBDA tripled to $2.1 million, both within guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted OIBDA | ~$2.5–3.0M (implied)”; the base scenario expected “$2.5–4M.” Company guide was “$1.0–5.0M.”

surprises.description: Local advertising outperformed the preview’s aggressive growth expectation. Revenue reached $9.5 million, above the $9.1 million consensus estimate, with growth of 48.4% versus the expected 42.2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Local advertising revenue surged 48.4% year-over-year to $9.5 million, with average local revenue per attendee up 24% to $0.07.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Local/regional | $9.10M” consensus and “+42.2%” year over year.

in_line: The operational transformation remained on track with the preview’s cost-savings expectations: management said it was complete, reported $2.7 million of savings year to date, and remained on track for approximately $11 million of annualized run-rate savings, with up to $6 million by year-end 2026.

surprises.description: MP’s adjusted EBITDA was $28.5 million, below the preview’s $35–45 million base-case range. The preview’s wider discussion focused on whether EBITDA ex-PPA would turn positive, but the call facts do not state that figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated adjusted EBITDA to $28.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (50%) ... Adj. EBITDA $35–45M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was a $0.01 loss, worse than the preview’s base-case expectation of positive $0.02–$0.04 and below Zacks’ +$0.02 estimate. It did, however, match the preview’s cited alternative estimate of a $0.01 loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cutting adjusted diluted EPS loss to just $0.01.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS ... Consensus +$0.02”; “EPS (alt. compilers) $(0.01)”; base case “Adj. EPS $0.02–0.04.”

surprises.description: MP disclosed a new multiyear gadolinium oxide supply deal with a U.S. aerospace and defense manufacturer, with total value expected to reach nine figures and economics locked in rather than exposed to spot prices. The preview did not flag this contract.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new long-term gadolinium oxide supply agreement ... is expected to total nine figures over multiple years with locked-in economics unexposed to spot pricing.”

surprises.description: MP said precursor production generated adjusted EBITDA margins above 40%, a stronger unit-economics detail than the preview’s concern that downstream mix would bring higher costs. It also disclosed about $46 million of prepaid precursor revenue still to be recognized over the next 3–4 quarters, on a declining basis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Precursor production generated adjusted EBITDA margins exceeding 40%, with approximately $46 million of prepaid precursor revenue remaining to be recognized over the next 3 to 4 quarters on a declining basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cost of sales — guided higher on downstream mix (NdPr metal + magnetic precursor carry structurally higher unit costs than concentrate).”

surprises.description: MP said Independence magnet capacity is substantially committed between GM and Apple. The preview anticipated GM’s Independence sales starting in 2H26 but said it had excluded Apple agreement terms, so the Apple-related commitment is additional demand visibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Independence magnet capacity is substantially committed between GM and Apple.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Confirmation of Independence magnet sales starting 2H26”; “I did not verify the terms of MP's commercial magnet agreements (e.g. Apple) and have excluded them from the model.”

surprises.description: Management said the company’s $1.45 billion of cash and short-term investments fully funds its long-term capital plan. The preview discussed major 10X financing commitments but did not state that MP’s existing cash fully covered the long-term plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $1.45 billion of cash and short-term investments, which management said fully funds its long-term capital plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “10X commissioning targeted 2028, $1.0B JPM/Goldman commitment, $150M DoD loan for heavy separation.”

surprises.description: MP reported that the 10X facility had reached vertical construction during the call, an unanticipated construction milestone beyond the preview’s discussion of its 2028 commissioning target and contracted offtake.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 10X facility ... reached vertical construction during the call.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “10X commissioning targeted 2028.”

in_line: Total revenue and PPA income of $126.1 million was within the preview’s estimated consolidated revenue-plus-PPA range of roughly $125–140 million.

NdPr production of 840 metric tons was close to the preview’s implied 845–890 metric-ton range for the planned maintenance decline; Q3 production above 1,000 metric tons is consistent with the preview’s expectation of significant sequential growth resuming in Q3.
NdPr sales above 1,000 metric tons were within the preview’s expected range of 950–1,050 metric tons.
The Q3 high-$90s/kg realized-price guidance and roughly $10/kg of PPA income continue the price/PPA compression dynamic the preview anticipated, though the preview’s numerical estimate was for Q2.
GM commercial magnet shipments beginning in Q4, initially at modest volumes, are consistent with the preview’s expectation that Independence magnet sales would begin in 2H26.
The 10X facility being 100% contracted with the Department of War matches the preview’s description of 100% DoD-backstopped offtake.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $310 million, above the preview’s $301.5 million consensus and $300–303 million company-guide range. The beat was sizable against the preview’s main estimates, although the preview also noted a pre-guidance consensus figure of $309.77 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 GAAP revenue was $310 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “GAAP revenue | $301.5M” and company guidance of “$300–303M”; it also noted that “Pre-guidance consensus was $309.77M.”

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year revenue and unlevered free-cash-flow outlook instead of merely holding the prior guidance or trimming it. The revised revenue midpoint is about $17 million higher than the previous midpoint, while the adjusted operating margin target remains at 37%.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “raised full-year 2026 guidance to GAAP revenue of $1.207–1.217 billion” and “unlevered free cash flow of $403–423 million,” with “a 37% adjusted operating margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY26 guidance was “unchanged since May” at revenue of “$1.185–1.205B” and uFCF of “$400–420M”; it framed the question as whether the guide would hold or be trimmed.

surprises.description: A $651 million noncash goodwill impairment was recorded, an unanticipated charge that substantially affects reported GAAP results even though it does not use cash. The preview did not flag an impairment charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recorded a $651 million noncash goodwill impairment charge primarily driven by the decline in market capitalization following Q1 results.”

surprises.description: Downmarket ACV declined 12% year over year, somewhat worse than the roughly 10% decline the preview used for its base case. The preview already expected continued downmarket weakness, so the additional deterioration was limited rather than a wholly unexpected reversal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Downmarket ACV declined 12% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “downmarket still ~–10%.”

surprises.description: The primarily data-based operations business grew 20% year over year, and ACV from customers above $1 million rose 16%. These were unexpected areas of strength in a release where overall revenue was nearly flat; the preview did not provide an expectation for either metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The operations business (primarily data, not seat-based) grew 20% year-over-year, and ACV from $1 million-plus customers rose 16%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating margin reached 35%, modestly above the preview’s guide-implied estimate of about 34.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income margin reached 35%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed adjusted operating income at “~$104M (guide-implied)” and “~34.5% margin.”

surprises.description: The company retired $58.5 million of senior notes for $48 million and recognized an $11 million gain. The preview discussed leverage and capital allocation but did not anticipate a discounted debt retirement or its gain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retired $58.5 million of senior notes for $48 million, generating an $11 million gain.”

surprises.description: Net leverage improved to 2.3x, slightly better than the 2.4x level cited in the preview. The change is positive but small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage improved to 2.3x trailing-12-month adjusted EBITDA from 2.4x in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “2.4x net leverage.”

in_line: NRR fell to 89%, below the 90% consensus/flat expectation but within the preview’s stated 89–90% base-case range; the preview identified 88% or below as the bear trigger.
Upmarket ACV grew 3%, continuing the deceleration the preview warned about from the prior 5% growth rate.

Headcount reductions and restructuring charges were anticipated: the preview expected restructuring charges across Q2–Q3 and discussed a 600-head reduction, while the call reported a $35 million charge and further reductions as the restructuring completes.
The 37% full-year adjusted operating margin target was unchanged from the preview’s expected guidance.

surprises.description: Akamai disclosed a new U.S.-based technology customer’s commitment of over $600 million for cloud infrastructure over four years, with no material revenue expected in 2026 and a full ramp through 2027. Alongside more than $2.8 billion in multiyear CIS commitments signed this year, management now expects overall revenue growth to accelerate to the low teens in 2027; the preview identified a second large commitment only as a bull-case possibility and did not forecast this 2027 outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new U.S.-based technology company committed over $600 million over 4 years”; “Total multiyear cloud infrastructure services commitments signed this year now exceed $2.8 billion,” driving “overall revenue growth acceleration to low teens in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull scenario included “a second AI capacity commitment disclosed”; it also said “Anthropic only contributes $20–25M in Q4.”

surprises.description: The full-year 2026 CapEx outlook of about 40% of revenue remains within the preview’s expected 40–42% range, but the Q3 outlook is much heavier: $475–525 million, or 43–46% of revenue. Akamai also cited GPU shipments slipping from Q2 into July and up to $500 million of additional GPU CapEx, mostly in early 2027, implying greater near-term and follow-on investment than the preview’s expected Q2 ramp suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 CapEx stepping up to $475-$525 million (43-46% of revenue) driven by GPU build-outs and shipments that slipped from Q2 into July”; management also plans “up to $500 million in additional GPU CapEx (mostly hitting early 2027).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected Q2 CapEx of “$433–453M (40–41% of rev)” and flagged “capex ≤ 42% of revenue” as a catalyst threshold; it described the first materially negative FCF quarter as expected.
