surprises.description: CIS revenue was $99 million, below the preview’s $103.8 million consensus estimate, and its 39% growth was slower than the preview’s derived 46.2%. The call offered a partial offset: all GPU capacity is sold out and CIS is expected to accelerate meaningfully in Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cloud Infrastructure Services (CIS) revenue reached $99 million, up 39% year-over-year,” with “all GPU capacity currently completely sold out” and revenue expected to “meaningfully accelerate in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed CIS consensus of “$103.8M” and “+46.2%” YoY, and said to watch for “CIS ≥ $103.8M and reaffirmation of ‘at least 50%’ FY growth.”

surprises.description: Security exceeded the preview’s estimate and grew faster than expected: $604 million and 10% growth versus consensus of $597.7 million and 8.3%. Management also expects the full security portfolio to exceed $2.4 billion for the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Security revenue grew 10% year-over-year to $604 million,” with “the full security portfolio expected to exceed $2.4 billion in revenue for the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Security at “$597.7M” and “+8.3%,” and said double-digit growth would be a positive outcome.

surprises.description: Akamai described large-scale CIS contracts as take-or-pay commitments with non-GAAP cash gross margins in the mid-60s to mid-70s and operating margins from the low-to-mid 20s up to the low 30s. The preview focused on the cost of the AI build and company-wide margin pressure, but did not anticipate these contract-level economics or commitment protections.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Large-scale CIS contracts are structured with take-or-pay commitments delivering non-GAAP cash gross margins from mid-60s to mid-70s and non-GAAP operating margins ranging from low-to-mid 20s up to low 30s.”

surprises.description: Akamai is temporarily pausing share repurchases to redirect capital to its CIS pipeline, despite having spent about $616 million on buybacks so far this year. The preview discussed prior repurchases and the company’s AI investment needs but did not anticipate a suspension of buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is temporarily pausing share repurchases to reallocate capital to its high-growth CIS pipeline after spending approximately $616 million buying back roughly 5 million shares year-to-date.”

surprises.description: Revenue was slightly above consensus: $1.1 billion and 5% year-over-year growth versus the preview’s $1.091 billion estimate and 4.6% derived growth. This was a small beat rather than the larger headline beat contemplated in the preview’s bull case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $1.1 billion, up 5% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 revenue consensus of “$1,091M” and “+4.6%.”

in_line: Non-GAAP EPS of $1.59 was essentially in line with the preview’s $1.58 consensus; the 8% year-over-year decline was broadly consistent with the preview’s expected pressure from higher costs and margin compression.

Delivery and other cloud applications revenue declined 6% to $396 million, close to the preview’s $391.5 million estimate and derived 6.8% decline; the preview expected this line to remain a drag on growth.
Full-year 2026 CapEx guidance of approximately 40% of revenue remained within the preview’s expected 40–42% range.

surprises.description: TPC reported adjusted EPS of $1.74, far above the preview’s derived $1.20–$1.30 range; instead of the expected 8%–15% year-over-year decline, adjusted EPS rose 23%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS up 23% to $1.74.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS (derived, not sourced): ~$1.20–1.30” and “−8% to −15%” year over year.

surprises.description: Revenue was a modest beat: $1.6 billion versus the preview’s $1.565 billion consensus, or about 2% above expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 19% year-over-year to a record $1.6 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $1.565B” consensus.

surprises.description: Backlog ended at $19.9 billion with book-to-burn just over 1x, rather than the expected third consecutive decline and sub-1x bookings; it narrowly missed the preview’s $20 billion bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog stood at a near-record $19.9 billion with a book-to-burn just over 1x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “$19.2–19.8B” and expected “a third straight backlog decline”; its bull case required “>$20.0B, B:B >1.0.”

surprises.description: Civil margin reached 15.3%, exceeding the top of the segment’s 12%–15% target range; the preview expected 13% or better in its bull case, but not a result above the range’s ceiling.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Civil segment operating margin reached 15.3%, exceeding the top of its 12%-15% target range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “13%+ validates the mega-project mix shift” and flagged Civil margin of at least 12.6% as a catalyst.

surprises.description: TPC raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.15–$5.45. A raise was anticipated, but the new range is slightly above the preview’s bull-case range of roughly $5.10–$5.40.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.15-$5.45, up from the prior range of $4.90-$5.30.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case called for a raise “to ~$5.10–5.40,” while its catalyst checklist said the guide should be raised above $4.90–$5.30.

surprises.description: The Board raised the quarterly dividend 50% to $0.09 per share, a capital-return action not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board raised the quarterly dividend 50% to $0.09 per share.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a potential-opportunity pipeline exceeding $200 billion over the next three to four years, roughly triple its level two years ago, including $4.6 billion of near-term Guam bids; the preview discussed a dense bid calendar but did not anticipate this scale of opportunity pipeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A pipeline exceeding $200 billion in potential opportunities over the next 3-4 years (roughly triple the level of two years ago), including $4.6 billion of near-term Indo-Pacific bids for its Guam subsidiary.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to a “dense 2026–27 bid calendar” and named upcoming bids, but gave no comparable pipeline estimate.

in_line: Specialty Contractors returned to a positive 2.2% margin, within the preview’s 1%–3% 2026 guidance range.
The July refinancing’s replacement of $400 million of 11.875% notes with 6.625% notes, and the roughly $21 million annual interest savings, were anticipated in the preview.
The preview anticipated further slowing in buybacks as a possible soft negative; the company reported repurchasing $10 million of shares in Q2, after $20 million in Q1.
Management’s expectation of higher earnings in 2027 was consistent with the preview’s already well-socialized expectation of a strong 2027.

surprises.description: Against adjusted EPS consensus of $2.36, Constellation reported $2.55, a $0.19 per-share beat. That also exceeded the preview’s inferred buy-side range of roughly $2.40–$2.45.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted operating earnings were $2.55 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating EPS” consensus: “$2.36”; the preview also noted a buy-side whisper of “~$2.40–2.45.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the $11.00–$12.00 full-year range to be reaffirmed in the base case, or narrowed to $11.50–$12.00 in the bull case. Instead, Constellation raised the range by $0.50 at both ends, to $11.50–$12.50.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Constellation raised full-year 2026 adjusted operating earnings guidance by $0.50 to $11.50-$12.50 per share, with the new midpoint equal to the prior range's top end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “$11.00–$12.00” as the existing guide, with “flat reaffirmation” as the base case and “$11.50–12.00” as the bull-case narrowed range.

surprises.description: The preview said investors needed evidence that data-center contracting had resumed, ideally a named long-term PPA or explicit language that negotiations had restarted at scale. Constellation instead reported about 920 MW of new long-term nuclear deals, averaging 18.5 years, and said roughly 30% of clean baseload output is now contracted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed approximately 920 megawatts of new long-term nuclear deals with investment-grade customers averaging 18.5 years duration, bringing total contracted clean baseload output to roughly 30%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy side needs to hear that the pause has broken”; “A named new long-term PPA, or explicit language that negotiations have resumed at scale, is worth more than $0.20 of EPS upside.”

surprises.description: The preview looked for a possible buyback step-up from the prior quarter’s $335 million repurchase. Constellation reported about $2.2 billion deployed in four months, a much larger pace than that reference point, with $2.8 billion still authorized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Constellation deployed about $2.2 billion toward share repurchases in the four months since late March, with $2.8 billion remaining under authorization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “a step-up says management thinks the de-rating is wrong” and cited Q1 repurchases of “$335M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected nuclear capacity factor around 93% to be the key threshold, and the fleet met that level. Separately, the reported 23-day average refueling outage duration was 40% better than the industry average, an operational efficiency detail the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The nuclear fleet delivered a 93% capacity factor and 40 terawatt hours in the quarter, with a 23-day average refueling outage duration outperforming the industry average by 40% despite six planned outages.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything below ~93% invites questions”; the preview also noted that Q2 is refueling-outage season.

surprises.description: The preview discussed Calpine integration but did not flag the DOJ divestiture economics. Constellation reported that the Brazos Valley sale completes the final DOJ requirement and that the required divestitures are expected to yield about $5.9 billion at nearly $1,200/kW, above the stated $960/kW implied Calpine purchase price.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company agreed to sell the Brazos Valley Energy Center to LS Power for $860 million (about $1,420 per kW), satisfying the final DOJ requirement tied to the Calpine acquisition”; “DOJ-required divestitures are expected to generate approximately $5.9 billion in gross proceeds at nearly $1,200 per kW, a healthy premium to the implied $960 per kW Calpine purchase price.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a Q2 headwind from Illinois ZEC credits. The company said it recognized $85 million of bank credits versus $200 million in the prior year, reducing Q2 results, although it characterized the item as timing-related and already reflected in full-year guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 results were reduced by recognizing only $85 million of Illinois ZEC bank credits versus $200 million last year, a timing item already reflected in full-year guidance ahead of the program's May 2027 expiration.”

surprises.description: The preview did not discuss Crane’s restart approvals. Constellation reported NRC new-fuel licensing approval and a FERC waiver for transferring Eddystone capacity injection rights, while keeping the expected return-to-service timing in the second half of 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Crane restart progressed with NRC new fuel licensing approval and FERC's waiver to transfer Eddystone capacity injection rights, keeping the facility on track to return to service in the second half of 2027.”

surprises.description: The preview did not discuss the updated long-range earnings sensitivities. Constellation put a $0.20-per-share floor and greater-than-$0.75 upside on its 2029 capital-allocation sensitivity range, and said its updated PTC strike-price assumption adds about $0.30 per share to 2030 base earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2029 capital allocation sensitivity range was updated to a $0.20 per share floor with upside greater than $0.75 per share, while an updated PTC strike price assumption ($50.88/MWh in 2030) adds about $0.30 per share to 2030 base earnings.”

in_line: Nuclear capacity factor was 93%, matching the preview’s approximately 93% threshold for a normal Q2 fleet result.

surprises.description: Q2 GAAP revenue was $41 million, far above the preview’s modeled $13–17 million. The preview cautioned that revenue was low-signal, but the reported result was still a substantial upside gap to its estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 GAAP revenue was $41 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “my model implies $13–17M” and “Q2 FY26E Revenue $15M.”

surprises.description: Arcus raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $65–75 million from the prior $50–65 million range. That is an improvement on company guidance, although the new range remains below the preview’s cited sell-side estimates of $72–85 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “full-year 2026 guidance of $65-75 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company FY26 guide: Rev $50–65M”; the preview also says sell-side FY26 revenue estimates were “$72–85M” and flags “any FY revenue guide change.”

surprises.description: Quarterly R&D and G&A were each $5 million below the preview’s model, with R&D at $113 million versus $118 million expected and G&A at $24 million versus $29 million. Together, the two expense lines were $10 million lower than modeled.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D was $113 million net and G&A was $24 million for the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 model shows “R&D $118M” and “G&A $29M.”

surprises.description: The ARC-20 update is scheduled for an October investor event rather than being delivered with the results, consistent with the preview’s possible ESMO deferral. But the planned update is broader than the preview’s anticipated roughly 45-patient cabozantinib-focused cut: it will cover more than 200 patients across first-, second-, and late-line settings and include late-line overall-survival looks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In an October investor event before ESMO, Arcus will release ARC-20 data across first, second, and late-line settings from over 200 patients,” including “OS looks with ~28 months median follow-up” in the late-line cohort.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asks whether the “~45-patient ARC-20 casdatifan+cabo cut” will be disclosed that night or “point[s] to a medical meeting (ESMO, Oct 2026)”; it calls the latter “a mild disappointment.”

surprises.description: Arcus reported a 7% primary progression rate in the first-line casdatifan-plus-Zim cohort, well below the roughly 30% historical rate cited for anti-PD-1 monotherapy. The preview discussed first-line trial design and possible partners but did not anticipate this cohort result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The casdatafan plus Zim first-line cohort showed a 7% primary progression rate (2 of 30 patients) versus roughly 30% for anti-PD-1 monotherapy historically.”

surprises.description: The company identified Ipi-Nevo as the combination for its registrational frontline Phase 3, resolving the preview’s open question about which backbone would be selected. The preview had suggested an ipi/anti-PD-1 approach as a possibility, so the specific choice is more a resolution of uncertainty than a wholly unexpected direction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A registrational frontline Phase 3 trial called PEAK-20, evaluating casdatafan plus Ipi-Nevo, is on track to be initiated by the end of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asks “Which backbone gets picked” and says an “ipi/anti-PD-1 bedrock” had been hinted at.

surprises.description: Management said casdatafan could become a $5–10 billion drug and the backbone therapy across all lines of clear cell RCC treatment. The preview framed Arcus as a casdatafan-centered story with first-line potential, but did not cite an expectation of this scale or an across-all-lines role.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management believes casdatafan has potential to become a $5-10 billion drug and expects it to become the backbone therapy across all lines of clear cell RCC treatment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview describes RCUS as “a single-asset story on casdatifan” and discusses expanding the opportunity to the “full 1L opportunity,” without stating a $5–10 billion potential or a backbone role across all lines.

surprises.description: Management said casdatafan now has no competition in the frontline HIF-2-alpha inhibitor space following Merck’s LightSpark 012 failure. The preview discussed the first-line opportunity and partner options but did not anticipate this competitor exit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Following Merck's LightSpark 012 failure, management states casdatafan now has no competition in the frontline HIF-2-alpha inhibitor space.”

in_line: PEAK-1 remains on track to complete enrollment by the end of 2026, as the preview expected.

Cash of $775 million at June 30 matched the preview’s estimate of approximately $775 million; the expected roughly $600 million year-end cash balance and runway into at least the second half of 2028 were also reaffirmed.
The PEAK-20 frontline trial remains on track to start by the end of 2026, consistent with the preview’s expected year-end initiation timing.
AB102’s clinical entry this month is consistent with the preview’s Q3 2026 clinical-entry milestone.
The PRISM-1 pancreatic cancer Phase 3 readout remains expected in the first half of 2027, as previewed.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $0.91 was well above the preview’s $0.70 working consensus and even the $0.62–$0.68 whisper range, rather than merely delivering the large sequential rebound already expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EPS more than doubled to $0.91” from $0.43 a year ago.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working consensus for this note: $0.70 EPS”; “the effective whisper likely sits in the $0.62–$0.68 band.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $4.3 billion substantially exceeded the preview’s $3.90 billion working estimate, instead of coming in around the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue up 9% to $4.3 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working consensus for this note: $0.70 EPS / $3.90B revenue”; published estimates were “$3.92–3.94B” and “$3.80B.”

surprises.description: Fluor lowered its adjusted EBITDA guidance to $500–$525 million, below the prior $525–$560 million range and contrary to the preview’s central expectation that guidance would be reaffirmed or raised. The reduction is a negative offset to the strong quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revised adjusted EBITDA guidance of $500 million to $525 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described prior guidance as “$525–$560M” and said the key question was whether Fluor would “reaffirm, narrow again, or cut”; its base case expected the “FY guide simply reaffirmed,” while the bull case expected it “raised to top half.”

surprises.description: Quarterly awards exceeded $6.1 billion, far above the preview’s $3.0–$3.8 billion base range and even its greater-than-$4 billion bull case. Management also upgraded its full-year book-to-bill outlook to well above 1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New awards for the quarter exceeded $6.1 billion”; management upgraded full-year book-to-bill guidance to “well above 1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “awards $3.0–3.8B,” its bull case called for “new awards >$4B,” and it said Q2 needed about “$3.1B/quarter” to support 2026 awards exceeding 2025.

surprises.description: Ending backlog reached $26.9 billion, above the preview’s expected $25.5–$26.5 billion range, despite the Mexican JV sale removing more than $650 million from backlog.
surprises.fact_evidence: Awards grew backlog to “$26.9 billion”; the JV sale “remov[ed] over $650 million from backlog.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected ending backlog of “~$25.5–26.5B” and described a flat “$25.5–26.0B” base case.

surprises.description: Urban Solutions earned $38 million, well below the preview’s roughly $75 million base-case profit, and it absorbed another large project loss. The $44 million Gordie Howe bridge losses contradict the preview’s expectation that the earlier mining charge would remain isolated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Urban Solutions profit of $38 million included $44 million in additional losses on the Gordie Howe bridge project” from currency swings, a subcontractor bankruptcy, and client-driven changes.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case estimated “~3% margin, ~$75M profit” and warned that “a second lump-sum charge here breaks that narrative”; it described the $37 million mining charge as framed as isolated.

surprises.description: Energy Solutions profit rose to $88 million, rather than clearly normalizing after the preview cautioned against extrapolating Q1’s closeout-boosted results. Management attributed much of the strength to favorable mega-project closeouts, while warning that benefit will diminish in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Energy Solutions segment profit surged to $88 million from $15 million” and was “driven largely by favorable closeout of completing mega projects,” which “will diminish in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 profit of $74 million was “flattered by favorable closeouts,” advised “Do not extrapolate 10.5%,” and called a normalized 6–7% the “honest run-rate.”

surprises.description: The adjusted EPS guidance floor rose to $2.70 from $2.60, while the high end stayed at $2.80. That improves the low-end outlook even as the EBITDA range was lowered.
surprises.fact_evidence: Revised guidance “imply[ies] adjusted EPS of $2.70 to $2.80 at current repurchase pace.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said adjusted EPS guidance was “$2.60–$2.80” and flagged whether that range “survives.”

surprises.description: The anticipated $175 million Mexican JV divestiture generated an additional $90 million pretax gain that was excluded from guidance. The sale itself was expected; the gain was not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Fluor sold its equity in the 30-year Mexican JV for “$175 million, triggering a $90 million pretax gain (excluded from guidance).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “the $175M ICA-Fluor JV divestiture” as a secondary item and called it a “modest risk-reduction positive.”

surprises.description: Quarterly operating cash flow was negative $317 million, an unexpected reported outflow, though a $357 million NuScale-related tax payment explains it and normalized cash flow would have been positive $40 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow was negative $317 million due to a $357 million NuScale-related tax payment, but would have been positive $40 million normalized.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 operating cash flow was “$110M” and “running ahead” of the maintained “$300M FY26 OCF” guide, and flagged cash flow against that annual target.

surprises.description: Fluor raised full-year adjusted operating cash flow guidance to $300–$320 million instead of simply maintaining the preview’s $300 million target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted OCF guidance was slightly raised to $300 million to $320 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the “maintained $300M FY26 OCF guide.”

surprises.description: The remaining legacy problem-project exposure is close to resolution: only $120 million remains in backlog, with $94 million of remaining loss-project funding potentially concluded in Q3. The preview highlighted charge risk but did not anticipate this specific wind-down status.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Legacy problem-project backlog has fallen to $120 million,” with “only $94 million in remaining loss-project funding expected, potentially all concluded in Q3.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA of $149 million was within the preview’s $145–$165 million base range and close to its roughly $155 million quarterly implication, though below the preview’s $160 million level for an especially strong ramp signal.
The $175 million Mexican JV sale itself was anticipated in the preview.
The company continued to model $1.4 billion of 2026 buybacks, matching the preview’s annual target.

surprises.description: Q2 net sales were $160.1 million, below the preview’s $162.9 million working consensus and $162 million guidance midpoint, though still within the $160–164 million guidance range. The shortfall was modest rather than a miss of the company’s range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales were essentially flat year-over-year at $160.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Consensus | $162.9M”; “guidance midpoint ($162M) as the true bar”; Q2 company guidance was “$160–164M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 61.1%, about 110 basis points above the preview’s approximately 60% expectation. Lower tariffs and more full-price selling in streetwear brands contributed to the expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 360 basis points to 61.1%, with roughly 240 basis points from lower tariffs and 120 basis points from higher full-price selling in streetwear brands.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~60% | Guidance”; the preview said to watch Q2 adjusted gross margin “vs. the ~60% guide.”

surprises.description: Management reported high-single-digit Q3-to-date sales growth overall, with the US up double digits, and guided Q3 sales to $160–164 million. That is a constructive sign for the H2 acceleration needed to deliver full-year guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3-to-date net sales growth in the high single digits overall, with the US running up double digits”; Q3 guidance was “$160-164 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said full-year guidance required “H2 revenue growth of ~+5.6% to +10.1%” and called for “a July quarter-to-date comment that is unambiguously positive.”

surprises.description: Australia/New Zealand sales fell 13%, a sharp reversal from the region’s Q1 growth and worse than the preview’s description of a pressured Australian consumer suggested. This contrasts with modest US growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Australia/New Zealand region net sales declined 13% to $39.8 million due to macro pressure”; US sales grew 2.1% to $110.7 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 Australia/NZ sales of “$36.9M, +3.8%” and said the Australian consumer was “probably a little bit more pressured than the U.S.”

surprises.description: The rest-of-world region grew 50.5% to $9.6 million, driven by the new UK distribution center. The preview did not identify this as a revenue driver, although the region is a relatively small part of sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rest-of-world growth of 50.5% to $9.6 million driven by the new UK distribution center.”

surprises.description: Princess Polly outlined a larger, longer-term US store opportunity than the preview discussed: up to 10 new US stores in 2027, with five leases already signed, and potential for at least 100 US stores over time.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Plans up to 10 new US stores in 2027 (five leases signed), and sees long-term potential for at least 100 US stores.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed a near-term target of “17 US + 2 Australian by year-end” and “8 executed leases,” but did not mention the 2027 plan or the 100-store potential.

surprises.description: Culture Kings will resume opening US stores for the first time since 2022, with two Q4 2026 openings planned in smaller formats. The preview did not flag a Culture Kings US store restart.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Culture Kings will open its first new US stores since 2022 in Q4 2026 (Puerto Rico and a major metro), targeting 4,500-6,000 sq ft formats smaller than the Las Vegas flagship.”

surprises.description: The Q3 gross-margin outlook is approximately 59%, below the Q2 result of 61.1%, with management citing tariffs and elevated air freight. The preview discussed freight headwinds but did not give a Q3 margin forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for ... gross margin of approximately 59% reflecting tariffs and elevated air freight.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “freight and air-freight cost headwinds,” but provided a roughly 60% expectation for Q2, not a Q3 margin forecast.

surprises.description: A roughly $3 million one-time distribution-center relocation charge will hit Q3 selling expenses, creating an unflagged expense headwind, though it is excluded from adjusted EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A one-time charge of approximately $3 million will hit Q3 selling expenses (excluded from adjusted EBITDA) related to a planned distribution center relocation.”

surprises.description: Active customers rose 4.4% to 4.31 million and AOV held at $78, both better than the preview’s expected customer growth and declining AOV. This suggests customer growth and AOV held up better than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month active customers rose 4.4% to 4.31 million while average order value held steady at $78.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited active customers at “4.26M (+3.1%)” and AOV at “$77 (–1.3%),” and said to watch whether AOV stabilizes.

surprises.description: Total orders dipped 0.5%, versus the preview’s expectation of 4.2% order growth. The customer and AOV improvement therefore did not translate into more orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total orders dipped 0.5% to 2.04 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited orders at “1.73M (+4.2%).”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $8.7 million, in line with the preview’s implied $8.7–8.9 million expectation.
Management reiterated full-year net sales guidance of $625–635 million and adjusted EBITDA guidance of $30–32 million, as the preview’s base case expected the revenue range to be reaffirmed.

surprises.description: Backlog rose to $271 million, well above the preview’s expectation that it would stay near $246 million and above the $260 million step-up it identified as the bull-case marker. The 10% sequential increase materially strengthens the reported order coverage versus the preview’s concern that coverage was thinning.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total backlog grew to $271 million, up 10% sequentially and up 16% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Rosenblatt expects ‘stable at $246M.’” The preview also said to “watch for a step-up toward $260M+.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin was 73%, below the preview’s roughly 76% estimate and below its 75% concern threshold. Management attributed the decline from Q1 to higher perpetual software licenses and expects a recovery next quarter, while retaining the 77% long-term target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin fell to 73% in Q2 (down from Q1 due to higher perpetual software licenses), but management expects recovery next quarter and maintains a 77% long-term target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin ~76% (est.).” The preview also said “Sub-75% would raise questions about the 77% target.”

surprises.description: Operating margin reached 22%, below the preview’s estimated 24–25% for the quarter. It was still about 300 basis points higher year over year, and management reaffirmed its 27% target model, but the reported margin was weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin reached 22%, roughly 300 basis points higher year-over-year, with a reaffirmed 27% target operating margin model.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin ~24–25% (est.).”

surprises.description: PDF Solutions reported EPS of $0.27, a small beat against the $0.26 consensus cited in the preview, but it fell short of the preview’s stated realistic buy-side whisper of $0.29–$0.31. Thus the result was better than published consensus but weaker than the preview’s higher informal bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 EPS was $0.27.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS $0.26”; the preview also said “A realistic buy-side whisper is $0.29–$0.31.”

surprises.description: The company signed unusually large contracts, including 8-figure secureWISE and DirectScan deals and multiple 7-figure Exensio deals. The preview anticipated bookings and renewals as potential backlog drivers, but did not anticipate contracts of this scale or the largest secureWISE contract in company history.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured 8-figure contracts for both secureWISE and DirectScan systems, plus multiple 7-figure Exensio deals with hyperscalers and photonics companies.” The “largest secureWISE contract in company history” extends “across virtually all 300mm fabs with upside expansion expected.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected backlog to build on “Exensio/secureWISE renewals and DFI bookings.”

surprises.description: The company placed three new eProbe machines, including two with new customers, putting it at two-thirds of its six-machine annual goal. That is stronger progress than the preview’s one Q1 shipment and provides new-customer placements, although the preview had described two to three Q2 units as part of its bull scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company placed 3 new eProbe e-beam inspection machines (2 with new customers, one a 5-year subscription), reaching two-thirds of its annual goal of 6 machines.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Target is six systems in 2026”; “one shipped in Q1.” The preview’s bull scenario called for “2–3 eProbe units incl. a non-Intel name.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of $61.5 million was close to the preview’s roughly $61 million consensus anchor and within its stated $60–63 million live band.
Management reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue growth guidance of 20%, as the preview identified a clean 20% reaffirmation as the bar.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $4.37 beat the $3.77 consensus by about 16%, well above the preview’s $3.85–$4.00 bull-case range. The preview expected just 6.8% year-over-year EPS growth; reported growth was 24%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $4.37, up 24% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS $3.77”; the preview’s bull case was “$4.00+,” and its stated consensus growth was “+6.8%.”

surprises.description: Revenue was about $1.7 billion, roughly 2.5% above the $1.659 billion consensus, and grew 3% reported year over year rather than declining as the preview’s consensus implied. This was a clear reversal from the expected revenue trend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $1.7 billion, up 3% year-over-year as reported and 2% FX neutral.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue ~$1.659B”; the preview listed implied year-over-year growth of “−2.4%.”

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year EPS floor to at least $14, above the preview’s $13.61 street EPS and its bull-case guide of at least $13.60. EBITDA and free-cash-flow floors also rose, though the preview already expected those measures to be raised.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance was raised, with EBITDA now at or above $1.57 billion (up $40 million operationally), adjusted EPS at or above $14, and free cash flow at or above $1.185 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 street EPS $13.61”; the bull case anticipated “EPS to ≥$13.60.” The preview’s base case expected EPS/EBITDA/FCF to be raised.

surprises.description: Contract value accelerated, but not to the level the preview said would validate the expected Federal-lap-driven step-up: total CV grew 2% versus a 3% bar, and ex-Federal CV grew 3.3% versus a 3.5% bar. The positive acceleration was therefore weaker than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total contract value reached $5.3 billion, growing 2% year-over-year—a second consecutive quarter of acceleration and a 70-basis-point improvement from Q1—while ex-U.S. federal CV grew 3.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bar: total CV ≥3% and ex-Fed ≥3.5%”; the catalyst checklist also called for “Total CV growth ≥3% FX-neutral AND ex-Fed ≥3.5%.”

surprises.description: Conferences revenue significantly outpaced expectations: it was $244 million, versus $218.9 million consensus, and grew about 12% FX neutral rather than the expected 3.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Conferences revenue grew about 12% FX neutral to $244 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Conferences $218.9M”; implied year-over-year growth was “+3.5%.”

surprises.description: Consulting revenue declined less than expected, reaching $142 million versus the $134.5 million consensus and a preview-implied 13.5% year-over-year decline. Bookings rose 17% and backlog grew 9%, adding evidence of improvement beyond the expected revenue decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consulting revenue declined to $142 million but bookings rose 17% and backlog grew 9% year-over-year for the first increase since Q1 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consulting $134.5M”; implied year-over-year growth was “−13.5%.” The bear case warned of “Consulting worse than −13.5%.”

surprises.description: New-business results showed a split rather than a clearly broad-based turnaround: GTS new business rose 2% year over year, but GBS new business fell 5%. Total new-business dollars did improve about 10% sequentially, but the reported figures do not establish whether net new CV returned above zero as the preview hoped.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GTS new business rose 2% year-over-year while GBS new business fell 5%, though total new business dollars increased about 10% sequentially to roughly $240 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “Net new CV back above zero (Q1: −$56M)” and said “Sequential improvement here matters more than the revenue line.”

surprises.description: GBS wallet retention improved to 99%, above its 98% Q1 level, while GTS retention stayed at 97% (99% ex-Federal). The preview focused on retention holding steady, so the GBS improvement and reported stabilization in downsells were better than that baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GTS retention improved to 97% (99% ex-Fed) and GBS wallet retention was 99%, with downsell activity stabilizing and in-quarter retention rates rising as leading indicators of future growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1: GTS 97% (99% ex-Fed), GBS 98%”; the preview said retention holding “≥97.5% blended” was the key threshold.

surprises.description: Management described a previously unflagged split by client size: midsized enterprise clients had mid-single-digit CV growth, while larger, more global enterprises faced greater budget pressure and uncertainty. The preview discussed broad demand and AI concerns but did not identify this divergence.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Midsized enterprise clients delivered mid-single-digit CV growth as their lower complexity enabled easier AI adoption, whereas larger, more global enterprises faced greater budget pressure and uncertainty.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed its target of adjusted EPS growth above 12% on a compound annual basis over the next three years, as the preview said to watch for any hedging of that commitment.
GTS retention was 97% (99% ex-Federal), consistent with the preview’s Q1 GTS levels and its expectation that retention remain near the stated threshold.

The $547 million of Q2 repurchases was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of further buyback deployment; the preview had noted $535 million repurchased in Q1 and a roughly $1.2 billion authorization.

surprises.description: BYND reported Q2 revenue of $68.8 million, about $4 million above the high end of its $60–65 million guide and well above the preview’s $60.8–62.4 million consensus range. The year-over-year decline was also much narrower than the preview’s expected 17%–19% decline, at 8.2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net revenues fell 8.2% year-over-year to $68.8 million but beat the high end of the $60-65 million guidance range by roughly $4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net revenue | Consensus: $60.8M–$62.4M”; “Company guidance | $60M–$65M”; implied Y/Y decline “−17% to −19%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA loss was $27.7 million, worse than the preview’s modeled loss range of $20–24 million. The loss was also 40.2% of revenue, rather than roughly flat with the prior-year margin as the preview modeled.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $27.7 million (-40.2% of net revenues) from a $24.7 million loss (-33%) a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~−$20M to −$24M (modeled)”; the preview’s implied year-over-year comparison was “roughly flat.”

surprises.description: Cash use was about $18 million, above the preview’s hoped-for $10–12 million if Q1’s low burn held. It remained below the preview’s $20 million level that would reopen the financing concern, so the miss was meaningful but not a worst-case outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash used excluding financing activities fell 44% (about $14 million) to roughly $18 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If Q2 burn holds near $10–12M, the runway story is genuinely intact”; “Any re-acceleration above ~$20M reopens the financing question.”

surprises.description: The $11 million arbitration-settlement credit helped drive the 19% year-over-year drop in operating expenses, making that reduction less clearly representative of recurring cost savings. The preview had treated roughly $14 million of year-over-year opex reduction as potentially sticking, but did not anticipate this settlement credit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses dropped 19% year-over-year to $36.7 million, aided by an $11 million credit from an arbitration settlement with a former co-manufacturer.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pair that with the ~$14M of Y/Y opex reduction sticking”; no arbitration-settlement credit was mentioned.

surprises.description: Management’s Q3 revenue guide of $60–65 million implies a sequential decline from Q2’s $68.8 million, despite the Q2 beat and improving year-over-year trend. The preview did not give a Q3 estimate, but its stabilization framing and bull case assumed the Q1 green shoots would compound.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 net revenue guidance of $60-65 million implies a sequential decline from Q2's $68.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the bull case as needing “the Q1 green shoots to compound” and called for evidence that “the category is stabilizing.”

surprises.description: International retail accelerated to 16.5% growth, with both volume and price contributing, compared with Q1’s 8.1% growth. That was stronger than merely preserving the preview’s “only grower” among the four channels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International retail up 16.5% to $18.5 million (volume +8.2%, price +7.7%) driven by double-digit retail growth in Europe and Canada.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said international retail was “the only grower” at Q1, at “$13.7M (+8.1%),” and flagged that turning negative would remove the last growth pocket.

surprises.description: The call facts provided do not report a Nasdaq compliance action, reverse-split ratio, or Capital Market transfer application, despite the preview identifying a compliance plan as the highest-signal issue and saying silence would be negative.
surprises.fact_evidence: No Nasdaq compliance action, reverse-split ratio, or Capital Market transfer application is reported in the supplied call facts.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Nasdaq compliance plan (highest signal). Does management announce a reverse split, name a ratio, or disclose a Capital Market transfer application?” The preview added: “Silence here is itself a negative signal.”

surprises.description: The preview said management had promised additional detail on foodservice portfolio changes for this call, but the supplied call facts report channel revenue declines without any portfolio changes or exits. That leaves the expected detail unreported.
surprises.fact_evidence: The supplied call facts report U.S. foodservice revenue and its decline, but no foodservice portfolio changes or exits.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management explicitly promised ‘additional detail’ on foodservice portfolio changes on this call. Expect exits.”

surprises.description: The preview looked for Beyond Immerse velocity and repeat-rate commentary, but the call facts only identify the launch as a new growth pillar and provide no evidence on consumer traction. The launch therefore remained unvalidated on the specific measures the preview said mattered.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call facts say management is “expanding into functional beverages via its Beyond Immerse launch as a new growth pillar,” but give no velocity or repeat-rate figures.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Only ~4 weeks fall inside the quarter, so revenue is immaterial — velocity and repeat-rate commentary is the asset, not the dollars.”

surprises.description: Management cited industry-funded “misinformation” campaigns as a continued drag on domestic demand, an explanation not raised in the preview. It adds a specific external demand headwind to already weak U.S. sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “cited industry-funded ‘misinformation’ campaigns as a continued drag on domestic demand.”

surprises.description: Management said Q2 was the final quarter with an approximately two-point gross-margin drag from accelerated depreciation tied to the China shutdown, implying that this drag will no longer weigh on margin in the following quarter. The preview noted the China exit target but did not flag this timing or the prospective margin relief.
surprises.fact_evidence: “This was the final quarter carrying the ~2-point drag from accelerated depreciation tied to the China operations shutdown.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the China exit was “targeted for completion by year-end,” but did not mention the accelerated-depreciation drag ending after Q2.

in_line: Gross margin was 8.5%, within the preview’s expected ~8–11% range.
U.S. retail and foodservice revenue both declined, consistent with the preview’s concern about weak domestic channels; their year-over-year declines narrowed versus Q1.

surprises.description: CRA reported $210.8 million of revenue, above both the $198.9 million consensus and the preview’s seasonality-adjusted $203–206 million bar. The result was a 12.8% year-over-year increase, rather than the preview’s published estimate of 6.4% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record quarterly revenue of $210.8 million in Q2 2026,” representing “12.8% year-over-year growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY26 Consensus” revenue of “$198.9M”; the preview also said “$203–206M [is] the real one.”

surprises.description: EBITDA growth substantially exceeded the preview’s implied 5–9% increase: CRA reported 15.3% growth. Using the preview’s $23.3 million prior-year EBITDA, that implies about $26.9 million of Q2 EBITDA, or roughly a 12.7% margin—above the preview’s 12.5% catalyst threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EBITDA grew 15.3% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Non-GAAP EBITDA was “implied” at “~$24.5–25.5M” and “+5–9%”; the preview’s catalyst checklist called for “Non-GAAP EBITDA margin ≥12.5%.”

surprises.description: Management raised full-year revenue guidance to $805–820 million, a stronger increase than the preview’s minimum expectation of a raise to at least $795 million. The EBITDA margin range, by contrast, was reaffirmed rather than raised.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $805-820 million from the prior $785-805 million range, while reaffirming non-GAAP EBITDA margin guidance of 12.0%-13.0%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s catalyst checklist said “FY26 revenue guidance raised to ≥$795M”; its base case expected guidance “nudged to $790–810M.”

surprises.description: International operations grew 32.9% organically, far faster than North America’s 8.7% growth. The preview did not set a geographic growth expectation, so this was an unanticipated area of strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International operations surged 32.9% year-over-year (all organic) while North American operations grew 8.7%.”

surprises.description: The non-GAAP effective tax rate rose to 32.6% from 29.0% a year earlier because of nondeductible executive compensation, an unflagged headwind to earnings. Management expects the elevated 32–33% rate to continue for the full year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The non-GAAP effective tax rate increased to 32.6% from 29.0% a year ago due to nondeductible executive compensation, with full-year rate expected at 32%-33%.”

surprises.description: Days sales outstanding rose to 113 days from 100 days in Q1, an unanticipated sequential deterioration in collections and working capital.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DSO rose to 113 days from 100 days in Q1.”

surprises.description: CRA repurchased $27.8 million of shares in Q2, up from the $21.5 million repurchased in Q1, leaving just $16.6 million under the authorization. That was a faster buyback pace than the preview’s last reported quarter suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company returned $31.4 million to shareholders in Q2,” including “$27.8 million repurchasing ~193,000 shares,” with “only $16.6 million remaining under its buyback program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported “$44.5M remained on the buyback authorization after Q1” and “~116k shares / $21.5M repurchased.”

in_line: Non-GAAP EPS growth of 14.9% was broadly in line with the preview’s implied 14.4% growth from the $2.15 consensus estimate versus $1.88 a year earlier; the call facts do not provide the reported EPS amount.

Utilization was 77%, matching the preview’s estimate of approximately 77%. Consultant headcount was up 3.3% year over year, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the hiring cycle would continue to build.

Energy and Life Sciences both grew over 20%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that those practices would maintain double-digit growth; Antitrust & Competition Economics’ sixth consecutive record quarter continued the record performance the preview expected to repeat.

surprises.description: Evergy’s weather-normalized demand grew just 1.8% in Q2 and 3.3% year to date, below the preview’s 4–5% Q2 base-case expectation and its warning that growth below about 4% would raise questions about the 7–8% load-growth outlook. Industrial demand was up 6.2%, rather than holding the double-digit pace the preview highlighted, although commercial demand reached 4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Weather-normalized demand grew 1.8% in Q2 and 3.3% year-to-date, with commercial demand up 4% and industrial demand up 6.2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “WN demand 4–5%” in the base case; “Anything below ~4% total invites questions”; and watch whether “industrial holds double-digit growth.”

surprises.description: The identified expansion potential around existing customer sites grew to 2.0–2.5 GW from 1–1.5 GW last quarter, alongside 1–2 GW of Tier 2 opportunities and a pipeline of more than 10 additional GW. The preview focused on the existing 3 GW of contracted demand and a possible additional ESA, but did not anticipate this larger set of uncontracted opportunities, which management said is outside the current five-year plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expansion opportunities at or adjacent to existing customer sites grew to 2.0-2.5 GW (up from 1-1.5 GW last quarter), plus 1-2 GW of Tier 2 opportunities and a remaining pipeline of over 10 additional GW, none of which is included in the current 5-year financial plan.”

surprises.description: Management said annual EPS growth is expected to exceed 8% beginning in 2028 through 2030. That is more specific and stronger than the preview’s 6–8%+ long-term growth framing and its 7.1% FY2027 growth estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Evergy reaffirmed its long-term adjusted EPS growth target of 6% to 8%+ through 2030 off a 2026 midpoint of $4.24, and expects annual EPS growth to exceed 8% beginning in 2028 through 2030.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the long-term guide as a “7–8% retail load CAGR” and the EPS algorithm as “6–8%,” and listed FY2027 adjusted EPS growth of 7.1%.

surprises.description: Evergy’s preferred generation additions through 2032 include less natural gas and more solar and battery storage than the preview’s cited 4.7 GW Missouri gas pivot and 465 MW solar plan suggested: the call described roughly 3.9 GW of gas, nearly 800 MW of solar, and 450 MW of batteries. This is a different generation mix, though the financial implications are not specified in the provided facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The IRP preferred plans through 2032 include more than 5 GW of new additions, comprising roughly 3.9 GW of natural gas, nearly 800 MW of solar, and 450 MW of battery storage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “the pivot to 4.7 GW of Missouri gas” and solar “cut from 2,415 MW to 465 MW.”

surprises.description: Management added a customer-bill outlook: most residential customers’ rate increases are expected to stay at or below inflation, while Missouri West customers may see above-inflation increases. The preview flagged the Metro rate case as a key issue but did not give this customer-rate expectation; the exception for Missouri West makes the outlook uneven.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expect[s] most residential customers’ rate increases to remain at or below inflation, though Missouri West customers may see above-inflation increases.”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EPS of $0.88 was within the preview’s $0.86–$0.90 effective whisper range and the dispersed published estimates; the preview’s base case was $0.87–$0.90.
Evergy reaffirmed its $4.14–$4.34 FY2026 adjusted EPS range and said it remains on track for the midpoint, consistent with the preview’s expected plain reaffirmation.

The five data-center ESAs and approximately 3 GW of total contracted peak demand matched the preview’s reported baseline; the preview also already expected at least one additional ESA in 2026, and management reiterated confidence in executing one.
The $21.6 billion five-year CapEx plan and approximately 12% rate-base CAGR were already in the preview’s expectations.
The $425 million of ATM forward equity sales, no plan for a block issuance, and 14–15% FFO-to-debt target were consistent with the preview’s financing discussion and guidance.
The $25 million reduction in the Missouri Metro rate-case request had already been disclosed in the preview.

surprises.description: SEG reported adjusted EPS of positive $0.02, versus the preview’s expected loss of $0.25 per share; adjusted net income was $320,000. The common-stockholder loss also narrowed to $0.82 per share, better than the preview’s approximate $1.05 GAAP loss estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP adjusted net income per share improved to positive $0.02”; “net loss per share to common stockholders narrowed to $0.82.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS (non-GAAP) $(0.25)”; “GAAP EPS: ~$(1.05).”

surprises.description: SEG achieved its first positive operating EBITDA, $4.5 million, while the preview framed post-G&A profitability as a milestone and described its base case as near breakeven. The result clears that near-breakeven baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Seaport Entertainment achieved its first-ever positive operating EBITDA of $4.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Post-G&A positive is the milestone the equity story needs”; the base case anticipated “EBITDA near breakeven post-G&A.”

surprises.description: Management said the next three quarters will improve year over year but likely will not match Q2’s 103% per-share gain, with a more meaningful earnings inflection expected in 2027 and 2028. That is more measured and later-dated than the preview’s bullish scenario of positive consolidated EBITDA in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The next three quarters will show year-over-year improvement but likely not match Q2's 103% per-share gain,” and “a more meaningful earnings inflection” is expected “in 2027 and 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case called for management to “guide[] to positive 2H EBITDA”; it also described the re-rating case as depending on the “2H EBITDA inflection.”

surprises.description: Entertainment EBITDA fell despite the preview’s expectation that entertainment would carry the quarter and that the rooftop expansion would support the segment. Higher rooftop repair and operating costs and the loss of founding sponsor Chase weighed on results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The entertainment segment's operating EBITDA declined $1 million (23%) year-over-year,” due to “higher rooftop repair/operating costs and lost sponsorship revenue after founding sponsor Chase declined to renew.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said entertainment was expected to “carry the quarter” and highlighted the rooftop’s “expanded premium offerings”; its estimate for sponsorships, events and entertainment revenue was $22.0 million.

surprises.description: Rental revenue rose 67% rather than falling as the preview’s rental estimate implied, but most of the increase came from the one-time Nike lease termination. The remaining termination fee and most remaining rent were received during the quarter, making the reported lift less recurring than it might appear.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rental revenue rose $2.8 million (67%) year-over-year, driven largely by the early Nike lease termination that added $2.7 million net,” with “the remaining termination fee and majority of remaining rent received during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated rental revenue of $3.6 million versus $4.2 million a year earlier, noting “Nike gone.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Balloon Museum rent to have commenced and called for confirmation of the start date and early attendance. The call facts instead place Balloon Museum among non-income-producing space still opening within the next 18 months and provide no attendance or rent-start confirmation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company has “over 194,000 square feet of non-income-producing space opening within 18 months,” including “Balloon Museum,” with incremental EBITDA “yet to materialize.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the museum “opened July 15, 2026” and that “Three weeks of operating data will exist by the call”; it identified rent commencement and early attendance as key items to watch.

surprises.description: SEG substantially reduced available seaport leasing space, from roughly 150,000–200,000 square feet to under 50,000 square feet. This is progress beyond the preview’s focus on the roughly 20,000-square-foot One Seaport Plaza vacancy, although management cautioned that the remaining smaller spaces may take longer to lease.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Available seaport leasing space fell from roughly 150,000-200,000 square feet to under 50,000 square feet,” while “remaining smaller footprints are expected to take longer to lease.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted One Seaport Plaza as “~20,000 sf, the last material vacancy” and said a signed anchor there would effectively complete lease-up.

surprises.description: The company had cut trailing 12-month G&A by more than 20% over nine months, even though the preview said management had warned that the pace of reductions would moderate. That indicates stronger cost reduction over the period than that expectation suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month G&A was reduced more than 20% over nine months to under $27 million from $34 million in Q3 2025”; management is “targeting further cuts as legacy contracts expire.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “management warned the pace of reduction moderates from here.”

surprises.description: Remaining capital expenditures were estimated at $50–70 million over the next two years, below the preview’s $70–90 million estimate for remaining capex through 2028.
surprises.fact_evidence: SEG “expects $50-70 million in remaining capital expenditures over the next two years to reach 2028 stabilization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$70–90M of remaining capex through 2028.”

surprises.description: Sadie’s Garden Bar grew revenue 125% year over year in its first full quarter under company management, a strong operating result not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of the hospitality segment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sadie's Garden Bar grew revenue 125% year-over-year in its first full quarter under company management.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled hospitality at $9.8 million versus $15.2 million a year earlier, attributing the expected decline to the Tin Building closure, but did not flag this growth at Sadie’s.

in_line: Quarterly G&A was $6.6 million, close to the preview’s approximately $6.7 million estimate.

surprises.description: GEN’s Q1 revenue was $1.34 billion, above the preview’s $1.300–$1.312 billion consensus range and the $1.325 billion top of company guidance. Revenue growth of 11% also exceeded the preview’s 8–10% pro forma growth guide; bookings grew 11% as well.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 bookings and revenue both grew 11% year-over-year to $1.28 billion and $1.34 billion respectively, the fastest revenue growth rate since Gen was created.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Company Guide … $1.300–1.325B | Street Consensus ~$1.300B … / $1.312B …”; “management guided Q1 to ‘+8–10% pro forma.’”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS reached $0.71, above both the preview’s $0.69 consensus and the $0.68–$0.70 guided range. That was a stronger result than the preview’s base case of $0.69–$0.70.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS reached $0.71, up 19% year-over-year and beating the guided range of $0.68-$0.70.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS … Street Consensus $0.69 …”; “Base … Non-GAAP EPS $0.69–0.70.”

surprises.description: Rather than maintaining FY27 guidance as the preview’s base case anticipated, GEN raised its revenue and EPS ranges. The new midpoints are $5.425 billion in revenue and $2.92 EPS, versus prior midpoints of $5.375 billion and $2.90.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year FY2027 guidance to 9%-11% revenue growth (to $5.375-$5.475 billion) and 14%-18% non-GAAP EPS growth (to $2.87-$2.97), up from prior guidance of 8%-10% revenue and mid-teens EPS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base … FY27 maintained”; “With Street pinned to the $2.90 midpoint, maintaining FY27 is a de facto disappointment.”

surprises.description: Cyber Safety did not reaccelerate to the 6–8% bookings growth the preview said to watch for: bookings and revenue each grew 4%, below that target and below the segment’s 5% bookings exit rate. This contrasts with the much faster growth in Trust-Based Solutions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cyber Safety bookings and revenue each grew only mid-single digits (4%), while Trust-Based Solution bookings grew 25% and revenue grew 24%, showing the growth is concentrated in the Trust segment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Exited FY26 at only +5% bookings … Watch for mid-single-digit → 6–8%.”

surprises.description: Engine’s annual network inquiries exceeded the preview’s roughly $400 million reference point, reaching more than $425 million; the marketplace also surpassed a $0.5 billion annual revenue run rate. The preview discussed Engine expansion but did not give an expected revenue run rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Engine embedded marketplace surpassed a $0.5 billion annual revenue run rate with over 30 new partnerships added and total network inquiries exceeding $425 million annually.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Engine ~400M annual inquiries”; the preview also noted “Engine expansion” as part of the expected H2 contribution.

surprises.description: MoneyLion connected accounts exceeded the preview’s 107 million figure, reaching more than 110 million. The call also reported that 35% of the paid base engages with financial wellness, for which the preview gave no specific benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Connected financial accounts grew to over 110 million from 75 million at MoneyLion's acquisition, with 35% of the paid base now engaging with financial wellness.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “connected accounts 107M (+36%).”

in_line: Trust-Based Solutions revenue grew 24%, within the preview’s expected 22–28% range; its 25% bookings growth is consistent with the preview’s expectation that TBS would carry the quarter.

Cyber Safety and Trust-Based Solutions operating margins were 61% and 30%, respectively, matching the preview’s stated framework of Cyber Safety at 60%+ and TBS around 30%. Blended operating margin remained stable sequentially at 50%, despite lower-margin marketplace mix.
Norton cross-sell penetration reached 27%, above the preview’s stated level of more than 26%; higher-tier Norton 360 annualized bookings were nearly $0.5 billion.
Net leverage of 2.95x was essentially in line with the preview’s 3.0x reference.

surprises.description: Instead of revising its full-year sales outlook downward, Heron withdrew its $173–183 million net product sales guidance altogether. The preview expected a cut, with its base case at $155–168 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company withdrew its full-year 2026 guidance of $173–183 million in net product sales, citing generic uncertainty, spending cuts, and strategic review.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “I assign ~70% probability to a guidance cut on this print”; base case: “FY guide cut to $155–168M.”

surprises.description: Heron also withdrew its $10–20 million adjusted EBITDA guidance rather than providing a lower or revised target. The preview identified withdrawal of this guidance as a bearish possibility, but its base case anticipated a reduction toward breakeven.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company withdrew its full-year 2026 guidance of $10–20 million in adjusted EBITDA, citing generic uncertainty, spending cuts, and strategic review.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base case anticipated “adj. EBITDA guide cut toward breakeven”; it also called withdrawal of this guide “the bear trigger.”

surprises.description: Heron disclosed a strategic-alternatives process with no timetable and no assurance of a transaction. The preview named this kind of review as a bear-case signal, but it was not part of its base-case outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is exploring strategic alternatives with no set timetable and no assurance a transaction will result; the process is also reflected in the amended credit agreement.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a bear-case signal would be management “evaluating strategic alternatives” or capital-structure options.

surprises.description: The Hercules amendment requires up to $17.5 million of principal reduction, including $13.5 million paid immediately, and could leave cash at about $24.3 million after a further payment. The preview flagged Hercules covenant status and possible amendments as issues to watch, but did not anticipate this size of cash outflow.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company agreed to a principal reduction of up to $17.5 million ($13.5 million paid at execution plus a potential further $4 million by September 15); pro forma cash falls to roughly $28.5 million and then about $24.3 million, from $42.7 million at quarter-end.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “cash vs. the $44.8M base” and “Hercules covenant compliance” as balance-sheet issues to watch, and noted “any amendment, waiver, or forward-looking covenant caution.”

surprises.description: Heron paused its planned second-half Salesforce expansion and tightened spending after the court decision. The preview focused on whether Zynrelef could sustain growth, but did not anticipate this specific commercial pullback.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company paused its planned second-half Salesforce expansion and tightened spending following the June court decision.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called Zynrelef “the only genuine growth asset” and said it “needs >$11.5M to keep the acute-care story intact.”

surprises.description: Zynrelef sales were $11.1 million, slightly below the preview's $11.5 million threshold, and average daily unit growth was 19% year over year rather than the 22% demand growth cited in the preview. The sales shortfall was modest, though the preview also expected strong growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Zynrelef net sales were $11.1 million, up 9% sequentially and 35% year-over-year, with average daily units growing 19% year-over-year but below internal targets.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Zynrelef “needs >$11.5M to keep the acute-care story intact” and cited “demand units +22% YoY.”

surprises.description: Aponvy reached $4.2 million in sales, above the preview's $3.9 million base-case build, and its share of the surgical NK1 segment rose to 23%.
surprises.fact_evidence: Aponvy net sales reached $4.2 million, up 74% year-over-year, capturing 23% of the surgical NK1 segment, up two points sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base-case build estimated Aponvy at “$3.9M.”

in_line: Q2 net revenue of $37.7 million was within the preview's independent $36–39 million estimate and above its $36.8 million base-case build, although below the $42.2 million consensus that the preview explicitly described as stale.

Cinvanti sales of $21.8 million were close to the preview's roughly $21 million estimate, and its 25% market share matched the preview's stated 25% Q1 share. The year-over-year decline was consistent with the expected continued erosion.

surprises.description: The preview put Q2 revenue consensus at $9.43–9.45 billion and described a bull case of $9.65 billion or more. Amgen reported revenue above $10 billion, a substantially larger beat than either the consensus or the preview’s bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenues exceeded $10 billion in Q2 2026, a 10% year-over-year increase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Q2'26 Consensus | $9.43–9.45B”; bull scenario: “Revenue | $9.65B+.”

surprises.description: The preview said a raise was important and framed a narrow-and-raise as the guide to watch. Amgen raised both full-year guidance ranges, with the revenue range moving to $38.2–39.4 billion and the EPS range to $22.30–23.50; the revenue midpoint is above the preview’s $37.8 billion consensus, while the new EPS midpoint is roughly in line with its consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Amgen raised full-year 2026 guidance to total revenues of $38.2 billion to $39.4 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $22.30 to $23.50.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Prior guidance was “$37.1B – $38.5B” revenue and “$21.70 – $23.10” non-GAAP EPS; consensus was “~$37.8B” revenue and “~$22.90” EPS. The preview called a “narrow-and-raise” the action to watch.

surprises.description: Repatha exceeded the preview’s $904.4 million estimate by about 5%, and its reported 37% growth was also above the preview’s roughly 30% growth expectation. The preview’s bull case had identified sales above $950 million as upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repatha delivered $953 million in sales growing 37% year-over-year, with new-to-brand prescriptions growing more than 50% in the U.S.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Repatha — total | $904.4M | +29.9%”; bull scenario: “Repatha >$950M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected margins to hold around 45–46%. Q2 non-GAAP operating margin was 48%, above that expectation, although full-year margin guidance remained roughly 45–46% of product sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin was 48%”; full-year operating margin was guided to “roughly 45%-46% of product sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected non-GAAP operating margin of “~45–46%” and said the base case was that “margins hold ~45–46%.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted UPLIZNA’s 188% Q1 growth and warned that deceleration in a growth driver could weaken the growth-portfolio thesis. UPLIZNA still grew rapidly, but its reported Q2 year-over-year growth rate was 90%, well below that highlighted Q1 rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “UPLIZNA sales surged 90% year-over-year to $335 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 UPLIZNA sales growth of “+188%” and said “Any one of these decelerating undermines the ‘new portfolio outruns the cliff’ thesis.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on MariTide’s planned Phase III readouts and dosing cohorts but did not anticipate that Amgen would discontinue a separate Phase I obesity asset. Ending development of AMG 513 removes that program from the obesity pipeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Amgen discontinued development of AMG 513, a Phase I obesity asset.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed that a Q3 business-development transaction will bring a $100 million upfront R&D payment and a meaningful sequential increase in operating expenses, an expense item and near-term cost increase not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A Q3 business development transaction will trigger a $100 million upfront R&D payment, contributing to an expected meaningful sequential increase in Q3 operating expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed cyber remediation, legal costs, and the MariTide R&D ramp as potential cost pressures, but did not mention this transaction or its payment.

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a CFO transition. The call reported that Peter Griffith is departing and Thomas Dittrich is taking over, an unanticipated management change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CFO Peter Griffith departs as Thomas Dittrich takes over.”

surprises.description: Amgen reported that MariTide is being advanced across nine ongoing and three planned Phase III studies, with a target of as few as four to six doses per year. The preview expected Phase III progress and early-2027 readouts, but did not anticipate this breadth of studies or the stated dosing target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Advancing MariTide through 9 ongoing and 3 planned Phase III studies targeting as few as 4-6 doses per year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described two Phase III studies reading out “early 2027” and advised watching for maintenance-dosing information; it gave no expectation of nine ongoing and three planned studies or a four-to-six-dose annual target.

in_line: Prolia and XGEVA combined sales declined 33% to $1.1 billion, in line with the preview’s expected roughly $1.05–1.10 billion run-rate and its focus on approximately 33% XGEVA erosion.
The six growth drivers grew 26% and represented nearly 70% of product sales, broadly matching the preview’s expectation that the drivers would remain around 70% of sales and grow at least 20%.
Full-year operating margin guidance of roughly 45–46% of product sales matched the preview’s stated margin guide.
The $2.52 quarterly dividend was already declared before the release, as the preview noted.

surprises.description: The preview modeled Q2 retail adjusted EBITDAR at about $505–515 million and expected a roughly 33.5% margin amid the Aurora disruption and new-property costs. PENN reported $517.2 million at a 34.4% margin, above the estimate range and the anticipated margin softness.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retail segment achieved record quarterly revenues of $1.5 billion and adjusted EBITDAR of $517.2 million,” with “margins of 34.4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Retail adj. EBITDAR ~$505–515M”; the base case expected “~$500–515M, margin ~33.5%,” while the preview said the Aurora closure and opening-period costs “argue for a soft optical margin.”

surprises.description: The preview’s existing retail guidance midpoint was $5.795 billion of revenue and $1.93 billion of adjusted EBITDAR, with a raise viewed as a possible catalyst. PENN raised the 2026 midpoints to $5.87 billion and $1.963 billion, respectively.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PENN raised its full-year 2026 retail guidance to $5.87 billion revenue and $1.963 billion adjusted EBITDAR at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The guidance in force was “Retail revenue | $5.73B–$5.86B” and “Retail adj. EBITDAR | $1.88B–$1.98B”; the preview said “any FY guidance revision” was worth watching and called a second consecutive retail raise a catalyst.

surprises.description: The preview described the year-end lease-adjusted net leverage outlook as 5.3x–5.7x. Management now says PENN is deleveraging faster than expected and is targeting leverage below 5x.
surprises.fact_evidence: PENN’s 2026 outlook includes “faster-than-expected deleveraging”; management is “targeting lease-adjusted net leverage below 5x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “YE lease-adj. net leverage | 5.3x–5.7x (>1 turn improvement).”

surprises.description: The preview expected Interactive revenue of about $355–375 million, based on roughly $1.6 billion of full-year guidance. Q2 revenue was $349.4 million, and PENN cut its 2026 Interactive revenue guidance to $1.57 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Interactive segment posted revenues of $349.4 million”; PENN “lowered its 2026 Interactive revenue guidance to $1.57 billion from $1.6 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Interactive revenue | ~$355–375M”; full-year guidance was “Interactive revenue | ~$1.6B (incl. ~$820M tax gross-up).”

surprises.description: The preview knew Aurora had opened but identified the prior riverboat shutdown as a Q2 retail drag and sought early ramp data. The new Aurora roughly doubled admissions, slot volumes, table volumes, and non-gaming revenue versus the prior year; rated guests staying at the hotel had 21% higher daily worth, and 20% of guests were new to the property.
surprises.fact_evidence: Hollywood Casino Aurora “roughly doubled admissions, slot volumes, table volumes and non-gaming revenue versus prior year,” with “rated guests generating 21% higher daily worth when staying at the hotel and 20% of guests being new to the property.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “a ~2-week shutdown of the legacy riverboat in late May/early June — a known drag on Q2 retail” and said to watch for “Early Aurora / Columbus ramp data points.”

surprises.description: The preview noted Columbus’s hotel tower opening but gave no expectation of an immediate record or the share of hotel revenue coming from outer-market guests. In July, its first full month with the tower, Hollywood Columbus set an all-time net revenue record, with outer-market guests generating 85% of hotel cash revenue.
