surprises.fact_evidence: “Hollywood Columbus set an all-time net revenue record in July, its first full month with the new hotel tower, with outer-market guests accounting for 85% of hotel cash revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview stated that the “203-room, ~$100M hotel tower opened June 12” and flagged early Columbus ramp data as something to watch.

surprises.description: The preview expected total 2026 CapEx of $420 million, including $200 million of project CapEx. PENN reduced project CapEx to $180 million and total CapEx to $400 million, and said the $31 million retail EBITDA guidance increase flows fully into improved cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PENN reduced 2026 project CapEx to $180 million from $200 million (total CapEx cut to $400 million), and the $31 million retail EBITDA guidance increase flows fully into improved cash flow.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Capex | $420M ($200M project / $220M maintenance).”

surprises.description: The preview discussed leverage and buybacks but did not anticipate the specific debt transactions PENN reported. The company extended major debt maturities and repaid $106.7 million of convertible notes, eliminating 4.5 million potentially dilutive shares.
surprises.fact_evidence: PENN “refinanc[ed] its $1 billion revolver and Term Loan A to 2031, extend[ed] Term Loan B to 2033, and repay[ed] $106.7 million of convertible notes to eliminate 4.5 million potentially dilutive shares.”

surprises.description: The preview said investors wanted to see sports-betting hold nearer 9.0% after 8.4% the prior quarter. Instead, PENN said customer-friendly sports outcomes reduced quarterly hold by roughly $3 million, indicating an adverse outcome rather than the anticipated hold improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Customer-friendly sports outcomes creating roughly a $3 million hold impact for the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street is looking for hold nearer ~9.0% vs. 8.4% last quarter.”

surprises.description: The preview described M&A as something PENN might pursue opportunistically. Management instead emphasized a high bar: a deal must outperform returns from deleveraging, buybacks, and internal growth projects, while also saying the 2027 consensus implies a nearly 20% free cash flow yield that makes buybacks attractive.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cited “a nearly 20% free cash flow yield on 2027 consensus making buybacks attractive, and a high bar for M&A that must beat returns on deleveraging, buybacks, and internal growth projects.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said PENN had “said it would act opportunistically” on M&A and listed buyback pace and capital return as items to watch.

in_line: Interactive adjusted EBITDA was a $9.5 million loss, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a small Q2 loss; management maintained its $20 million full-year loss guidance, inclusive of the $20 million Alberta launch investment.
Management continued to expect Interactive to turn positive in Q4, as the preview’s guidance and key-metrics section anticipated.

surprises.description: Q2 loss per share was $0.33, better than the preview’s $0.44 loss consensus and its base-case range of $0.40–$0.50. The loss also improved 32% sequentially, although net loss was still 6% worse year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss was $3.97 million in Q2 2026, a 32% sequential improvement from $5.83 million but a 6% worse result year-over-year, with loss per share improving to $0.33 from $0.71 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 Consensus” EPS: “$(0.44)”; the base scenario also projected EPS of “$(0.40)–$(0.50).”

surprises.description: Q2 operating cash outflow fell to $3.4 million, below the preview’s $5 million level of concern and sharply down from Q1. This was a better quarterly cash-burn result than the preview’s key risk framing implied, though cash burn and going-concern concerns remain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash used in operating activities improved 58% sequentially to $3.4 million in Q2 2026 from $8.2 million in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything above ~$5M undermines the ‘cash-flow positive in 2026’ claim outright”; management had said Q1 working-capital use would “not repeat at the same magnitude.”

surprises.description: NEXUS was already generating meaningful sales soon after launch: it reached $1 million in cumulative sales in about 10 weeks, with another $1.5 million in orders in July. The preview expected a first disclosed contribution but said NEXUS had not contributed meaningfully in Q1 and did not anticipate this scale or pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The new NEXUS tonneau cover reached $1 million in cumulative sales within about 10 weeks of its April 13 production launch and generated approximately $1.5 million in sales orders in July alone.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “first disclosed revenue contribution from SOLIS, COR (UL/CSA certified April), and NEXUS” and that “none contributed meaningfully in Q1.”

surprises.description: Management put a sizable gap between current revenue and operating cash-flow breakeven: at a 35% margin, it says roughly $12.9 million in quarterly revenue is needed to cover the current cost structure, versus Q2 sales of $5.2 million. That makes the preview’s 2026 cash-flow-positive expectation look more demanding than the preview’s already difficult H2 revenue math alone suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit covered only about 32% of the quarter's recurring cash operating requirements, with roughly $12.9 million in quarterly revenue at 35% margins needed to fully cover the current cost structure absent expense cuts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Company-guided FY2026 included “operational cash-flow positive during 2026”; the preview described the low end of revenue guidance as requiring “~$26.6M in H2.”

surprises.description: The cash-flow-positive goal remained for 2026, but management would not give a calendar target for sustained breakeven and described only a possible momentary positive quarter in Q3. That is less definite than the preview’s expectation of operational cash-flow positivity during 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management believes it may reach momentary operating cash flow positivity in Q3 2026 but declined to provide a specific calendar target for sustained breakeven, which it still aims to achieve in 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Company guidance, “reaffirmed May 13, 2026,” was “operational cash-flow positive during 2026.”

surprises.description: Inventory had increased by $2.5 million from year-end and included $4.6 million of finished goods, even as the preview expected inventory to convert to revenue and reduce working-capital use. Management’s identification of inventory as its largest internal liquidity source also underscores reliance on selling down stock to fund operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory stood at $12.1 million (up $2.5 million from year-end), including $6.6 million raw materials, $4.6 million (roughly 6,800 covers) finished goods, and $845,000 work-in-progress, which management targets as its largest internal liquidity source.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management said Q1 working-capital use would “not repeat at the same magnitude as inventory converts to revenue.”

surprises.description: Worksport reported two distributor additions, including Meyer as its first multinational partner, and discussions with three more major distributors. The preview expected distribution activation but did not flag a first multinational partner or this specific pipeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added two distributors in Q2, including its first multinational partner Meyer Distributing, is in talks with three additional major distributors.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “distribution activation” and said to watch for a hard number of dealer locations, with a target of 1,500+ by year-end.

surprises.description: AetherLux certification is expected in fall 2026, with product available 45–60 days afterward, bringing a product milestone forward relative to the preview’s framing of Terravis/AetherLux as a 2027+ story.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added two distributors in Q2 … and expects AetherLux heat pump certification in fall 2026 with product available 45-60 days thereafter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called Terravis/AetherLux “a 2027+ story” and said “no 2026 revenue is projected.”

in_line: Q2 net sales of $5.2 million were within the preview’s estimated $5.0–$5.3 million range and close to its ~$5.1 million expectation; the preview said the revenue beat was already largely pre-released, despite the result exceeding the listed $4.50 million consensus.

Gross margin of approximately 32% was close to the preview’s estimated ~31% blended Q2 margin and its expectation of ~30%+; the rise to 35% by June was consistent with the preview’s focus on durability above 35%.

The June 30 cash balance of $1.2 million plus $820,000 of remaining credit availability, and continued substantial-doubt going-concern disclosure, were broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of roughly $1–2 million in cash and ongoing liquidity risk.

surprises.description: The preview's base case was EPS of $1.88–$1.92, with a ~$1.90 whisper, but TXRH reported $1.85. That was slightly above the $1.83 consensus cited in the preview, yet below its higher expected bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS declined 0.7% to $1.85.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base estimate: revenue ~$1.69B, EPS ~$1.90”; the base scenario gave EPS of “$1.88–1.92.” The preview also cited consensus EPS of “$1.83.”

surprises.description: Comps were strong but came in a little below the preview's 6.5% base and buy-side expectation. They also eased from 6.7% in May to 5.7% in June, though the preview's implied-consensus comp estimate was lower, at about 5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable sales rose 6.2%”; monthly comps were “6.2%, 6.7% and 5.7% for April, May and June.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base case was “+6.5%” comps and said the buy side expected “comps 6.5%+”; it also said published consensus implied roughly “5.0%.”

surprises.description: TXRH cut full-year commodity inflation guidance to about 5%, a larger cut than the preview's bull-case range of 5–6% and a contrast with its base case of holding at 6–7%. The preview expected Q2 to be the peak; management also described a sharp Q3 easing before inflation rises again in Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 commodity inflation guidance was lowered from 6%-7% to approximately 5%,” with Q3 inflation “just 2%-3% (versus 7% in Q2)” before returning to “about 5% in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the guide was “currently 6–7%,” with a “second cut to 5–6%” as the bull catalyst; its base case was that management “reiterates 6–7%” and calls Q2 the peak.

surprises.description: Restaurant margin was better than the preview's expected range despite still declining year over year: 16.4% versus the preview's 16.0–16.3% estimate, with a 66-basis-point decline rather than the expected 80–110 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Restaurant margin as a percentage of sales fell 66 basis points to 16.4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “~16.0–16.3%” margin and expected a decline of “−80 to −110bps.”

surprises.description: The average check rose 3.2%, below the 3.6% menu pricing the preview cited, suggesting some check or mix dilution even as traffic grew. Traffic was up 3%, below the prior-quarter 4.5% figure discussed in the preview, though the preview did not give a specific Q2 traffic forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: Comps were driven by “3% traffic growth and a 3.2% higher average check.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “3.6% menu pricing” and flagged “mix erosion” if check underperformed that pricing; it described Q1 as “+4.5% traffic / +2.6% check.”

surprises.description: Management announced a 1% menu price increase for the start of Q4, resolving the preview's open question in favor of additional pricing rather than relying only on the existing carryover. That supports margin defense, though the preview also noted the possible traffic-confidence trade-off.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company will implement a 1% menu price increase at the start of Q4, bringing effective pricing to 2.9% in both Q4 2026 and Q1 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said pricing was “currently 1.9% carryover ‘plus any additional’” and flagged the “Q4 pricing decision” as an important unknown.

surprises.description: Management newly quantified a holiday-calendar headwind to Q4 same-store sales, which the preview did not flag: shifted Halloween and Christmas calendars are expected to reduce comps by about 75 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “flagged an estimated ~75 basis point negative impact to Q4 same-store sales from Halloween and Christmas holiday calendar shifts.”

surprises.description: Labor costs improved by 40 basis points even though traffic grew 3%, with labor hours up only 0.8%. The preview did not identify this labor leverage, while wage inflation guidance remained at 3–4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Labor costs improved 40 basis points to 32.5% of sales as labor hours grew only 0.8% against 3% traffic growth,” while “wage inflation of 3.9%” kept the “3%-4% full-year guidance intact.”

surprises.description: Weekly sales reached a company record, exceeding $175,000 for the first time in TXRH's 33-year history. The preview discussed revenue and comps expectations but did not anticipate this sales-per-week milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 average weekly sales exceeded $175,000 for the first time in the company's 33-year history,” including over $183,000 at company-operated Texas Roadhouse, over $129,000 at Bubba's 33, and over $76,000 at Jaggers.

surprises.description: To-go sales exceeded $25,000 per week and dining-room mix turned positive during the quarter. The preview did not forecast these channel-mix developments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “To-go sales reached over $25,000 per week, representing 14.3% of total weekly sales while dining room mix turned positive during the quarter.”

in_line: Revenue growth of 11.1% was modestly ahead of the preview's cited 10.7% consensus growth, though short of the preview's roughly 12% revenue-growth estimate.
The company remained on track for approximately 35 company-owned openings in 2026, in line with the preview's ~35-opening expectation.

surprises.description: Contract momentum was far stronger than the preview’s recent weekly data suggested: Opendoor said it was signing over 500 purchase contracts a week, reached roughly 700 in the latest week, and had 6,908 acquisition contracts. That points to a much stronger forward pipeline than the preview’s report of weekly contracts up 12% in mid-July.
surprises.fact_evidence: “signing over 500 purchase contracts weekly,” hitting “a multi-year high of roughly 700 last week,” with acquisition contracts “reaching 6,908.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Weekly contract data showed +12% in the week ended July 18”; the preview warned that if contracts stalled, Q3/Q4 revenue could re-accelerate downward.

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook combines stronger growth language with a lower contribution-margin forecast: revenue is guided up at least 20% year over year and contribution profit more than doubles, but margin is expected to fall to 4%-4.5%. The margin decline is less severe than Opendoor’s historical seasonal pattern, but it does not match the preview’s preference for Q3 growth with contribution margin held.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For Q3, the company guided to revenue up at least 20% year-over-year, contribution profit more than doubling year-over-year, and contribution margin of ~4%-4.5%, reflecting seasonal decline better than its historical 470 bps Q2-to-Q3 average.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the buy-side wanted “sequential growth and CM held,” and described the base case as Q3 revenue “roughly flat-to-up modestly.”

surprises.description: Q2 contribution margin and contribution profit came in a little below the preview’s midpoint expectations: margin was 5.8% versus about 6%, and contribution profit was $51 million versus about $54 million. The margin was still within Opendoor’s 5%-7% guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Contribution margin climbed to 5.8%” and contribution profit was “$51 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed contribution margin consensus at “~6% (guide midpoint)” and contribution profit at “~$54M.”

surprises.description: Opendoor described substantial operating-productivity improvements that were not quantified in the preview: per-acquisition operations expense fell to $3,000 from $8,400 a year earlier, while project managers and underwriters are handling many more homes. These gains reinforce a leaner cost structure than the preview’s profitability discussion captured.
surprises.fact_evidence: “home project managers now handling ~10 renovations each (up from 3, targeting 20), underwriters doing 50+ per day (up from 20), and per-acquisition operations expense falling to $3,000 from $8,400 a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted fixed OpEx of “$33M, −$6M Y/Y” and estimated a roughly “$63M below-the-line bridge,” but did not anticipate these productivity figures or the per-acquisition expense decline.

surprises.description: The company said it built inventory largely with nonrecourse asset-backed financing, rather than the preview’s stated expectation that inventory growth would be funded from its cash balance. This is a meaningful difference in how the expansion was financed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “grew inventory by over $700 million funded largely by nonrecourse asset-backed facilities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “Growth funded from the $999M cash balance with no equity raise.”

surprises.description: Mortgage attach appears to be gaining traction quickly, with more than half of scheduled Colorado closings and nearly one in five in Texas financed through Opendoor just six weeks after launch. However, the stated plan to reach 35-40 states by year-end is later than the preview’s target of 20-plus states by Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “over half of scheduled closes in Colorado and nearly 1 in 5 in Texas (just 6 weeks post-launch) are financed through Opendoor, with plans to be licensed in 35-40 states by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “20+ states targeted by Q3” and listed mortgage expansion and attach rates as items to watch.

surprises.description: Marketing spend dropped sharply to $5 million, from $19 million in Q1, taking marketing from 1.6% to 0.3% of acquisition GMV. The preview did not forecast a cut of this size, so the lower spend is an unexpected cost reduction, though its effect on future acquisition momentum is not specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marketing spend fell dramatically to just $5 million in Q2 (from $19 million in Q1), lowering marketing as a percent of acquisition GMV from 1.6% under Opendoor 1.0 to 0.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed fixed OpEx and profitability but did not give an expected Q2 marketing-spend level.

in_line: Q2 acquisitions were 4,378 homes, within the preview’s estimated range of roughly 3,500-4,500.
Contribution margin remained within the company’s guided 5%-7% range.
Management reaffirmed its end-2026 adjusted-net-income breakeven target, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the target would be reaffirmed.

surprises.description: Ibsrela came in well below the preview’s $95–100 million build at $86.2 million, and Ardelyx cut its 2026 Ibsrela outlook from $410–430 million to $350–370 million. Management attributed slower new-patient starts to stricter prior authorizations and step edits, which are delaying rather than blocking prescriptions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ibsrela Q2 revenue was $86.2 million”; management “lowered full-year 2026 Ibsrela guidance to $350-$370 million”; “Payers implemented more stringent prior authorizations and step edits that slowed new patient starts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s build estimated “IBSRELA $95–100M” and said current FY guidance was “$410–430M IBSRELA.”

surprises.description: Xphozah revenue of $31.9 million substantially exceeded the preview’s $24–26 million estimate, and Ardelyx kept its 2026 outlook at $110–120 million despite the preview identifying that range as vulnerable to a cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Xphozah revenue was $31.9 million (up 27% YoY), driven by strong demand”; the company “reiterated full-year 2026 Xphozah guidance of $110-$120 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “XPHOZAH $24–26M” for Q2 and called it “where the cut risk sits,” with a trim identified as the most likely messy-print outcome.

surprises.description: Ardelyx withdrew its $750 million long-term Xphozah revenue guidance rather than framing the 2027 opportunity as an upside case. Management cited uncertainty around the end of TDAPA, a proposed phosphorus QIP measure, and competing binders in development.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company pulled its $750 million long-term Xphozah revenue guidance,” citing “uncertainty from the end of the TDAPA period, a proposed phosphorus QIP quality measure, and competitive binders in development.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “2027 XPHOZAH framing post-TDAPA cliff” as an “under-owned upside” and said management’s framing of the opportunity was a “free option.”

surprises.description: The company lowered its 2026 operating-expense outlook to below $500 million, better than the preview’s expectation of roughly $520 million. This is a more favorable cost outlook even though SG&A and R&D were higher year over year in the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revising 2026 OPEX guidance to below $500 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY26 opex was “guided to ~$520M” and flagged spending above that level as a bear trigger.

surprises.description: Ardelyx drew $50 million from its SLR arrangement, a financing step not identified in the preview, which had highlighted the cash balance and undrawn facility. The draw supported a higher reported cash balance, but also means more borrowing rather than an improvement funded solely by operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $281.8 million in cash and equivalents and drew down $50 million from its SLR arrangement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Cash fell $26.6M in Q1 to $238.1M against $234M of debt” and noted “$100M undrawn.”

in_line: Xphozah’s full-year 2026 guidance remained at $110–120 million, as previewed.
Management continued to project a path to profitability in 2027, consistent with the preview’s discussion of the expected 2027 profitability path.

The company affirmed the CMS appeal loss and said it would pursue no further litigation, consistent with the preview’s statement that the legal option was closed; the Ibsrela patent protection through 2042 was also anticipated.

surprises.description: Free-cash-flow guidance was cut by about $200 million to $150–$200 million, rather than being held at the preview’s expected $350–$400 million. That is roughly a 50% reduction at the midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow guidance was cut by roughly $200 million… now expected at $150-$200 million for the year versus a prior forecast of $350-$400 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management called it AP-timing ‘noise’ reversing in Q2–Q3 and held FY FCF.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 4.9%, below the preview’s 6.0%–6.5% estimate, and Energy margin was slightly negative rather than the modeled 2%–4%. The reported margin damage was therefore worse than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin collapsed to 4.9% in Q2 from 12.3% a year earlier”; renewables overruns pushed “Energy segment margins slightly negative versus 10.8% prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin (my est.) ~6.0–6.5%”; Energy segment “Q2 2026E GM 2–4%.”

surprises.description: The expected Energy margin recovery is arriving more slowly: management guided to 6%–8% in Q3 and 8%–10% in Q4, rather than the preview’s expectation that Q3 would gravitate toward normal and Q4 would reach 10%–12%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Energy segment gross margins are guided to 6%-8% in Q3 and 8%-10% in Q4, before returning to the normal 10%-12% range in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 ‘gravitating back toward normal,’ Q4 reaching the 10–12% target.”

surprises.description: Revenue came in slightly below consensus: just under $1.7 billion versus the preview’s $1.734 billion estimate. The gap was modest, and the Energy decline was broadly in line with the preview’s modeled decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was just under $1.7 billion, down 10.7% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $1.734B.”

surprises.description: The renewables close-out had slightly less progress completed than the preview’s near-term expectation: two projects were complete, while three were still expected to reach substantial completion in Q3. The final project remained on a year-end completion path.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Six renewables projects drove the margin pressure, with two now complete, three expected to reach substantial completion in Q3, and the final project…by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Three complete ‘within the next month,’ one in Q3, one in Q4 2026.”

surprises.description: Backlog and awards exceeded the preview’s expected range: backlog reached nearly $13.9 billion versus an expected $12.5–$13.0 billion, with more than $3.9 billion in new awards. Natural-gas generation contributed about $1.4 billion of bookings, supporting a stated revenue ramp to $800 million–$1 billion in 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record total backlog of nearly $13.9 billion, up ~$2.2 billion sequentially,” with “more than $3.9 billion in new awards”; natural-gas generation contributed “approximately $1.4 billion of new bookings” and is expected to grow from “$500-$600 million in 2026 to $800 million-$1 billion in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Backlog should print ~$12.5–13.0B”; the company had flagged “~$2.0B of Q2 Energy awards” and the gas funnel was “$7.1B, with ~$800M of verbal awards described as imminent.”

surprises.description: Pain Crest was described as performing better than expected, adding about $200 million of acquired backlog and securing another $250 million of bookings in the quarter. The preview noted the acquisition and its data-center contribution but did not anticipate these backlog and booking figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Pain Crest acquisition is exceeding expectations, adding ~$200 million of acquired backlog plus $250 million of new bookings in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Utilities includes ~1 stub quarter of PayneCrest Electric ($399.5M, closed May 1; ~$112M annualized hyperscaler data-center revenue).”

surprises.description: Leverage rose to 1.6x net debt-to-EBITDA and is expected to approach just under 2x in Q3 before improving. The preview highlighted cash and liquidity risk but did not anticipate this leverage trajectory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt-to-EBITDA rose to 1.6x following the Pain Crest acquisition and lower Q2 EBITDA,” with a Q3 increase “toward just under 2x.”

in_line: Management maintained FY2026 GAAP EPS guidance of $1.30–$1.85, adjusted EPS of $2.05–$2.60, and adjusted EBITDA of $275–$325 million, matching the preview’s expected reaffirmation. Management also identified Q2 as the low point for the year, consistent with the preview’s focus on a second-half recovery.

surprises.description: Revenue growth was 28% year over year, below the preview’s $371.1 million consensus estimate: applying 28% growth to the preview’s $282.3 million prior-year revenue implies roughly $361 million. That also falls just below the preview’s $364 million low end of its revenue bridge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total omnichannel revenue increased 28% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $371.1M”; the preview’s revenue bridge estimated “Total revenue” of $364M–$392M.

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was a substantially larger loss than expected: –$0.53 versus consensus of about –$0.33 and the preview’s –$0.30 to –$0.35 base-case range. Management attributed the decline to acquisition integration costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS was a loss of $0.53 (a $0.31 decline), reflecting acquisition integration costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS” consensus: “–$0.33 (range –$0.33 to –$0.34)”; the base scenario expected “–$0.30 to –$0.35.”

surprises.description: The company broke the year-over-year adjusted EBITDA improvement streak the preview viewed as a key test: adjusted EBITDA worsened by $4 million from Q2 2025, despite the preview’s expectation that a seventh consecutive year-over-year improvement was a possible outcome. The $12 million loss itself was within the preview’s estimated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $12 million (a $4 million decline versus Q2 2025).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called a “seventh consecutive improvement with TBHC consolidated” the “single most bullish outcome” and said the bear case would “break[]” the streak; its estimate was “–$10M to –$14M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was stronger than the preview’s guided range: Q2 margin reached 26.8%, above the 24–26% band, with the acquired business’s mix helping rather than dragging on margin. Management also forecast Q3 margin near 30%, materially above that band.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 310 basis points to 26.8%, aided by favorable mix shift” from the merger; Q3 margins are expected to improve “close to or potentially touching 30%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited company guidance of “24–26%” and flagged gross margin “vs. the 24–26% guided band” as a key metric.

surprises.description: The base e-commerce business returned to year-over-year growth for a second quarter in a row, reversing a 19-quarter run of declines. That is a more encouraging underlying-business trend than the preview’s concern that legacy organic growth might slow to roughly flat–3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The base e-commerce business grew year-over-year for a second consecutive quarter, reversing 19 straight quarters of revenue decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the revenue estimate implied legacy organic growth of “roughly flat–3%” and warned that growth built on fewer customers could be fragile.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a planned rebrand and exchange/ticker change that the preview did not anticipate: the parent will become Neighborhood Intelligence and move from the NYSE to NASDAQ under NXH.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The parent company will rebrand as Neighborhood Intelligence and begin trading on NASDAQ under ticker NXH effective August 17, transitioning from the NYSE.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a pending acquisition pipeline valued at over $2.5 billion, a scale not discussed in the preview’s review of announced and contemplated deals. The growth opportunity is accompanied by additional deal-execution and funding uncertainty.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management described “total pending acquisitions valued at over $2.5 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed the Container Store, F9 Brands, and Fathom transactions and estimated “~30%+ potential dilution from announced/LOI deals,” but did not cite a pending-acquisition total of this size.

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA of –$12 million was within the preview’s estimated –$10 million to –$14 million range, even though the year-over-year improvement streak broke.
The revenue step-up was primarily acquisition-driven, as the preview expected the full-quarter consolidation of The Brand House Collective to be the main source of the year-over-year increase.
Cash and restricted cash of $126 million was broadly within the preview’s $110–$125 million cash scenario and above its cited roughly $110 million liquidity threshold.

surprises.description: Avient reported Q2 organic sales growth of 4.3%, well above the preview’s expectation that organic growth could remain flat to negative. Growth was still mostly price-led—about 75% price and 25% volume—rather than the volume-driven inflection the preview emphasized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Organic sales grew 4.3% year-over-year, composed of roughly 25% volume and 75% price.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said organic sales “could still be ~flat-to-negative” and highlighted “Organic sales growth ex-FX vs. ~+1% whisper” as a key catalyst.

surprises.description: Avient raised its FY2026 adjusted EPS and EBITDA ranges instead of simply reaffirming the prior outlook: EPS guidance moved to $3.10–$3.25 from $2.93–$3.17, and EBITDA guidance to $575M–$603M from $555M–$585M. The new EPS range also exceeds the preview’s bullish scenario, which called for narrowing to $3.05–$3.17.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year 2026 guidance to adjusted EBITDA of $575M-$603M [and] adjusted EPS of $3.10-$3.25.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 guidance of “$2.93–$3.17” EPS and “$555–585M” EBITDA, and said a simple reaffirm was the base case while the bullish outcome was “$3.05–$3.17.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS was $0.96, substantially above the preview’s anticipated $0.90–$0.91 result, not merely a small beat of the $0.89 consensus. The call attributed the beat primarily to volume growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EPS came in at $0.96, beating expectations by $0.09, driven primarily by volume growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “$0.90–0.91 is the expected beat,” with consensus and company guidance both at $0.89.

surprises.description: Specialty Engineered Materials EBITDA rose 20% and its margin expanded 310 basis points, overcoming the preview’s highlighted risk of continued SEM margin pressure. About 100 basis points of the expansion came from lapping prior-year maintenance expense, so not all of the improvement was underlying.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Specialty Engineered Materials adjusted EBITDA rose 20% to $76 million with margins up 310 basis points, though about 100 bps came from lapping ~$3M of prior-year maintenance expense.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged SEM as “the one to check” after its margin “contracted 160bp y/y last Q2,” and included SEM margin compression in its bear case.

surprises.description: Asia delivered unusually strong growth that the preview did not identify as an expected driver: organic sales rose 18% year over year and 20% sequentially, led by electronics, high-performance computing, and functional additives.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Asia was a standout with organic sales up 18% year-over-year and 20% sequentially, driven by electronics, high-performance computing, and functional additives.”

surprises.description: Management described a larger data-center and electronics business and a stronger growth trajectory than the preview’s stated tracking level: related business is near $100M today, including about $60M in electronics, and is expected to double over two to three years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A directly addressable data center/electronics opportunity of roughly $2 billion, with current related business near $100 million (electronics ~$60M) and expectations to double over the next 2-3 years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said electronics/HPC was “tracking >$40M FY26 sales, +$10M incremental.”

surprises.description: Avient lowered its 2026 capex guidance to $120M–$130M from $140M because of project timing, a change not anticipated in the preview. The call attributes the reduction to timing rather than a stated cancellation or permanent cost saving, so its shareholder implication is unclear.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capex guidance was lowered to $120M-$130M from $140M due to project timing.”

in_line: Volume was roughly +1%, consistent with the preview’s “~+1% whisper” and its expectation of flat-to-slightly-positive Q2 volume.
FY2026 free cash flow guidance of $210M–$230M cleared the preview’s expectation of more than $200M.
Management’s caution about having less visibility for Q4 was consistent with the preview’s expectation of limited H2 certainty.

surprises.description: Radian reported adjusted operating EPS of $1.14, well below the preview’s $1.38 consensus and the $1.36–$1.44 base-case range. The revenue result was stronger, but it did not offset the sizeable earnings miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net operating EPS grew to $1.14.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating EPS $1.38”; the base case expected “$1.36–1.44.”

surprises.description: Specialty’s Q2 combined ratio was 98%, worse than the preview’s 85–90% base case and above its 95% bear-case threshold. The preview identified storm losses and reserve strengthening as risks, but the reported roughly $30 million reserve charge included Middle East conflict claims and updated inflation assumptions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Radian took roughly $30 million in reserves in the Specialty segment for expected and potential Middle East conflict claims plus updated inflation assumptions, pushing the Q2 specialty combined ratio to 98% (versus mid-to-high 80s excluding the item).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “Specialty CR 85–90%”; it described “north of 95%” as a bear-case outcome.

surprises.description: Management said a low-90s Specialty combined ratio now better reflects the softening market, above the mid-80s to high-80s historical levels cited for Inigo and above the preview’s 85–90% base-case range. This signals a less favorable expected run-rate beyond the quarter’s reserve charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A specialty combined ratio in the low 90s is now more reflective of the softening market environment, up from the mid-80s to high-80s seen historically for Inigo.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Specialty CR 85–90%” in its base case and described Q1’s 85.3% as the key reference point.

surprises.description: Revenue reached $575 million, above the preview’s $537–$557 million estimate range and its $540–$565 million base case. The preview cautioned that revenue estimates were unreliable because analysts used different definitions, so the beat is less definitive than the EPS miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenues grew 93% year-over-year to $575 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed revenue estimates of “$556.5M” and “$537.2M,” and a base-case range of “$540–565M.”

surprises.description: Radian raised expected 2026 dividends from Radian Guaranty to at least $650 million, above the preview’s expectation of at least $600 million. This is a higher expected capital return to the holding company than the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Increasing expected 2026 dividends from Radian Guaranty to at least $650 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Radian Guaranty is committed to ≥$600M of dividends to the holdco in 2026.”

surprises.description: The company had repurchased $176 million year-to-date and moved full-year buyback guidance toward the upper end of the $200–$250 million range. The preview expected the program to remain on pace and noted $115 million deployed through April, but did not expect a move toward the top of the range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Radian repurchased $176 million (5 million shares) year-to-date and raised full-year buyback guidance toward the upper end of the $200-$250 million range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$115M (3.3M shares) already deployed through April” and described the base case as “buyback on pace.”

surprises.description: Radian reduced holding-company leverage to 19% after repaying $75 million of its revolver draw, reaching below the preview’s sub-20% year-end target earlier than that target implied. Another $75 million is still expected to be repaid in 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reduced holding company leverage to 19% by repaying $75 million of its revolver draw (with $75 million remaining to be repaid in 2026).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said debt/capital was 20.2% with a target “below 20% by year-end.”

surprises.description: The PMIERs cushion was $1.5 billion, below the $1.6 billion cushion cited in the preview. The difference is modest, but the reported cushion was smaller than the stated reference level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Maintained a $1.5 billion PMIERs cushion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “PMIERs cushion $1.6B (41%).”

surprises.description: Book value per share was $36, below the preview’s approximate $37 expectation. The company still reported 8.5% year-over-year growth, but the reported level was lower than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Grew book value per share 8.5% year-over-year to $36.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “BVPS ~$37.”

surprises.description: Mortgage defaults were better than the preview’s expected normalization: new defaults fell quarter-over-quarter and the default rate was 2.47%, below the preview’s 2.50–2.60% base-case range. This contrasts with the expected upward drift in defaults.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New defaults declined 9% quarter-over-quarter to 12,400” and “the default rate fell to 2.47%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected a mortgage default rate of “2.50–2.60%” and said Radian’s rate “should drift similarly” to MGIC’s increase.

in_line: Mortgage insurance in force reached $284 billion, matching the preview’s expectation of approximately $284 billion.
New mortgage insurance written was $16.3 billion, within the preview’s expected range of approximately $16–17 billion.

The Specialty ratio excluding the roughly $30 million reserve item was in the mid-to-high 80s, broadly within the preview’s 85–90% base-case range. The reported 98% headline ratio and management’s lower forward outlook were not in line.

surprises.description: Q1 revenue was $166 million, about 10.8% above the $149.8 million consensus, and management said it exceeded company expectations. This was a materially stronger result than the preview’s expected double-digit growth bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 revenue reached $166 million, up 27% year-over-year, exceeding company expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $149.8M Zacks consensus, +14.4% YoY”; the preview said the bar was to “sustain double-digit growth.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS of $0.19 beat the preview’s $0.14 consensus by about 36%. The preview also cited a lower analyst estimate of $0.10, which the reported result exceeded by more.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net income more than tripled to $24.1 million ($0.19 per share) from $7 million ($0.06) a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS: $0.14 Zacks consensus”; “Craig Hallum ... is below consensus at $0.10 for the quarter.”

surprises.description: Instead of merely reiterating FY2027 guidance, Digital Turbine raised both ranges: revenue by $20 million at each end and adjusted EBITDA by $10 million at each end. That was a clear upside to the preview’s stated likely outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised FY2027 guidance to revenue of $650-670 million (from $630-650 million) and adjusted EBITDA of $145-155 million (from $135-145 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bar: ... at least reiterate FY27 guidance”; “reiteration vs. raise is likely the key swing factor.”

surprises.description: On-Device Solutions accelerated to 15% year-over-year growth from 5% in the prior quarter, despite the preview highlighting soft U.S. device volumes. International ODS was especially strong, with nearly 80% growth and more than 40% RPD expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On-device solutions revenue rose 15% year-over-year to $110 million, with international ODS growing nearly 80% driven by both higher device volumes and 40%+ RPD expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged On-Device Solutions growth of “+5% in Q4” amid “soft U.S. device volumes,” while highlighting international carrier expansion and revenue-per-device trends.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA rose 69% and its margin expanded about 640 basis points to 25.6%, a strong increase in profitability alongside revenue growth. The preview did not provide a quarterly EBITDA estimate, so the scale of the margin improvement was not quantified in its expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 69% year-over-year to $42.5 million, with margin expanding roughly 640 basis points to 25.6%.”

surprises.description: Gross margin improved 210 basis points year over year to 49.4%, while cash operating expenses rose only 7% against 27% revenue growth. That indicates stronger operating leverage than the preview’s open-ended question about the gross-margin trajectory had specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin improved to 49.4% from 47.3% a year earlier on favorable AGP-weighted mix, while cash operating expenses rose only 7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “AI monetization ... and gross-margin trajectory” as issues to watch but gave no margin estimate.

surprises.description: Leverage was down to 2.5 turns, and a post-quarter threshold triggered a 50-basis-point rate reduction on the largest loan tranche. The preview had highlighted the roughly $354 million debt load and deleveraging, but the reported leverage level and resulting borrowing-cost reduction were favorable specifics it had not forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage improved dramatically from over five turns a year ago to 2.5 turns, and a post-quarter leverage threshold triggered a 50 basis point reduction on the largest loan tranche.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “the ~$354M debt load / deleveraging” as a key issue to watch.

surprises.description: Management reported a sharp productivity gain: revenue per employee rose from about $800,000 to over $1 million, attributed to AI-driven automation and operating leverage. The preview discussed AI monetization but did not anticipate or quantify this workforce-productivity measure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue per employee rose from about $800,000 a year ago to over $1 million, reflecting AI-driven automation and operating leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview raised “AI monetization (DTiQ, Ignite Graph)” as a topic to watch but did not mention revenue per employee or an automation productivity target.

in_line: AGP grew 56% year over year, sustaining growth above 50% and broadly matching the preview’s expectation of continued strong App Growth Platform momentum; Q4 growth had been 57%.

surprises.description: Q2 free cash flow reached $751 million, well above the preview’s $600–670 million bogey and even above its $650 million threshold for a new record. The preview expected record FCF, but the reported result cleared the top of its range by $81 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “record Q2 2026 free cash flow of $751 million, up nearly 50% quarter-over-quarter”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$600–670M is the bogey”; “Anything above $650M is a genuinely new record”

surprises.description: Management raised full-year oil production guidance to 199,000 barrels per day, above the preview’s 190,000–195,000 range and contrary to its base case of reaffirmed guidance. Most of the production increase was attributed to higher working interest rather than acquired volumes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “raised full-year 2026 oil production guidance to 199,000 barrels per day”; “only 1,000 bbl/d of the 6,500 bbl/d production increase came from acquired volumes … with the majority from higher working interest”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “190–195 MBbl/d oil”; base case: “FY guidance reaffirmed with H2 flexibility language intact”

surprises.description: Permian Resources disclosed about $1.05 billion of year-to-date Delaware acquisitions, exceeding the preview’s stated $600–800 million historical sweet spot. The transactions added about 55,000 net acres and 330 high-NRI drilling locations, including a $520 million Ward County bolt-on.
surprises.fact_evidence: “acquired ~55,000 net acres … for ~$1.05 billion across roughly 190 separate transactions, adding ~330 high-NRI drilling locations”; “largest deal was a … Ward County bolt-on for $520 million”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “targeting their historical $600–800M sweet spot”; “any confirmed bolt-on in the $600–800M range”

surprises.description: Despite funding substantial acquisitions, leverage ended Q2 at about 0.5x and is expected to stay there through year-end, below the preview’s 0.8x figure. That indicates a stronger balance-sheet position than the preview led investors to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Leverage stood at approximately 0.5x at the end of Q2 and is expected to remain around 0.5x at year-end, giving the company an investment-grade balance sheet while funding acquisitions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Leverage 0.8x”

surprises.description: Gas curtailments were substantial, at about 20% quarter over quarter, but the company still reported positive realized gas pricing and more than $75 million of incremental gas revenue from curtailments, firm transportation, and hedging. The preview anticipated Waha-related volume and revenue pressure but did not anticipate this level of revenue mitigation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “curtailed natural gas production by ~20% quarter-over-quarter amid WAHA prices averaging negative $3.14 per Mcf”; “still realized $0.38 per Mcf and captured over $75 million of incremental gas revenue through curtailments, firm transportation, and hedging.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Expect total BOE/d to look soft … even if oil beats”; “Gas/NGL volume disclosure and curtailment quantification”

surprises.description: The call described a $100 million CapEx increase, including $25 million of Ward County takeover costs, whereas the preview’s base case expected the existing CapEx range to be reaffirmed. The reported $1.95 billion figure was within the preview’s stated range, but the increase itself was not what the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$25 million of the $100 million CapEx increase was Ward County takeover costs”; full-year CapEx was reported at “$1.95 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “capex $1.75–1.95B”; base case: “FY guidance reaffirmed”

surprises.description: Q2 oil production was about 198,000 barrels per day, slightly above the preview’s implied 196,000 barrels per day and its bull-case threshold of 197,000. The beat was modest, and the call attributed production strength in part to higher working interest in completed wells.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Oil production reached approximately 198,000 barrels per day in Q2”; completed wells had “higher working interest of ~82% … versus the original 75% expectation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s derived revenue math assumed “~196 MBbl/d oil”; its bull case cited oil volumes “at/above 197 MBbl/d.”

surprises.description: Management cited several specific operating changes—including water-based mud, slimmer New Mexico wellbore designs, water recycling, and surfactant trials—as offsets to diesel and casing inflation, while keeping LOE near $5 per BOE. The preview highlighted cost efficiency as a key watch item but did not anticipate these measures or their stated cost-control role.
surprises.fact_evidence: “water-based mud (~$5-$7/ft savings), slimmer New Mexico wellbore designs (saving nearly a day per well), record water recycling, and surfactant trials (up to 100+ bbl/d uplift) are offsetting diesel and casing inflation, keeping LOE near $5 per BOE.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cost per lateral foot” was a key metric to watch; the preview cited “$685/ft in Q1” and a “$675/ft year-end target.”

in_line: The preview expected severe Waha pricing pressure and anticipated gas curtailments or soft gas/NGL volumes; the call confirmed deeply negative Waha prices and substantial curtailments, even though revenue mitigation was stronger than anticipated.

surprises.description: SoHo revenue was $30.9 million, with the year-over-year decline slowing to 4.7%, versus the preview’s modeled Q2 range of roughly $29.0–$29.4 million and an expected decline around 10%. Management also expects declines of only 5%–7% over the next two quarters, better than that trajectory implied by the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SoHo revenue declined only 4.7% year-over-year to $30.9 million,” and management expects declines of “5% to 7% over the next two quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case is ~$29.0–29.4M” and the base scenario expected SoHo of “~$29.2M (−10.2%).”

surprises.description: CCSI reported $91.4 million of revenue, above the $89.63 million Street consensus and the preview’s $89.6–$90.0 million base case. The result was near the top of the preview’s bull-case range, so the beat was positive but not wholly unexpected under that scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated revenue grew 4.1% year-over-year to $91.4 million in Q2 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 Street Consensus” revenue was “$89.63M”; the base scenario forecast “$89.6–90.0M,” while the bull scenario forecast “$90.8–91.5M.”

surprises.description: The full-year ranges were reaffirmed rather than narrowed upward or raised, despite the preview’s expectation of at least a narrowing toward the top half. Management did indicate that revenue should land between the midpoint and high end, with EBITDA and EPS slightly above midpoint, tempering the disappointment from leaving the ranges unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reaffirmed rather than raised full-year guidance ($350M-$364M revenue, $5.55-$5.95 EPS), but now expects revenue between the midpoint and high end and EBITDA/EPS slightly above midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The base expectation is at minimum a narrow to the top half”; the preview also said a flat reaffirm would be “a de facto disappointment at this price.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was near expectations, but the 52.9% margin came in just below the preview’s expected 53%–54% range. Management’s full-year margin outlook toward the lower end of the 50%–55% range also points to more margin pressure than the preview’s clean-case expectation, though hiring-related margin declines were already anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was essentially flat year-over-year at $48.3 million (0.5% growth) with a 52.9% margin,” and management guided full-year margins “toward the lower end of the 50%-55% range as hiring ramps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called “53–54%” the “clean outcome” and said margins were expected to step down as hiring ramped.

surprises.description: Corporate customers grew faster than the preview’s reference level: approximately 67,000 customers and 9.4% year-over-year growth versus the preview’s roughly 65,000 and 7% growth. Corporate ARPA, by contrast, was essentially at the preview’s stated level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The corporate customer base grew 9.4% year-over-year to approximately 67,000, while corporate ARPA rose about 1% to $305.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Corporate customer count (~65k, +7% y/y)” and “Corporate ARPA ($305.59/mo in Q1).”

surprises.description: Net revenue retention reached 103.1%, up about 110 basis points sequentially. That was stronger than the preview’s reference point of NRR above 102%, although the preview did not provide a specific Q2 target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net revenue retention rate rose to 103.1%, up approximately 110 basis points sequentially from 102% in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “NRR (>102% in Q1)” among the secondary metrics to watch.

in_line: Corporate revenue reached $60.5 million, essentially matching the preview’s ~$60.5–$60.7 million estimate; 9.3% growth was close to the implied ~9.6%, though short of the preview’s 10%-plus bull trigger.

Free cash flow of $25.5 million was within the preview’s stated normal Q2 range of approximately $20–$25 million; management’s expectation for full-year FCF to approximate 2025’s $106 million had no specific preview comparator.
The $48.3 million adjusted EBITDA result was close to the preview’s roughly $48 million expectation.
A new or expanded buyback authorization was identified as a live catalyst in the preview; the company raised the authorization to $200 million and reported about $118 million remaining.
The VA contribution was expected to be around $9 million in 2026, with management confident it would meet or exceed that level; the reported expectation of north of $9 million was broadly consistent.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $258.8 million, well above the preview’s $240.3 million consensus estimate. The roughly 7.7% beat was much stronger than the preview’s expected low-single-digit year-over-year growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 10.6% to $258.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $240.3M” and “YoY | +2.7%.”

surprises.description: Energy Storage revenue reached $42.8 million, far exceeding the preview’s implied Q2 range of about $17–22 million, and its 56.2% gross margin was above the preview’s stated 35–40% full-year guide. The preview specifically identified a Q2 margin above 50% as upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Energy Storage revenue nearly tripled, increasing 195.1% to $42.8 million at a 56.2% gross margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied Q2 segment bridge … Storage ~$19M (+31%).” “Storage gross margin … guided FY to 35–40%.” “A repeat above 50% is upside.”

surprises.description: Product revenue was within the preview’s implied dollar range, but the segment’s gross margin was only 9.7% amid higher European construction costs and FX. The preview focused on the expected sales decline and backlog, and did not flag this degree of margin pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Product segment revenue fell 21.6% to $46.7 million with gross margin compressing to 9.7% due to higher European construction costs and FX.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied Q2 segment bridge … Product ~$44M (–26%).”

surprises.description: Product backlog declined further to about $203 million from the preview’s cited $239 million, rather than rebuilding as the preview said was important for supporting the out-year Product ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog declined to about $203 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Backlog fell to $239M … backlog rebuild is what tells you whether 2027 Product is fundable.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a $6.6 million write-off for a storage project it chose not to pursue, an unanticipated expense that contributed to Q2 net income falling despite revenue growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net income fell to $27.1 million ($0.43/share) from $28 million ($0.46/share), reflecting a $6.6 million write-off of a storage project the company decided not to pursue.”

surprises.description: Re-contracted and blend-and-extend PPAs, including Blue Mountain, are expected to add about $14 million in annual revenue through 2030 with minimal incremental capital. The preview did not anticipate this quantified revenue contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Re-contracted and blend-and-extend PPAs, including Blue Mountain, are expected to add roughly $14 million in annual revenues through 2030 with minimal incremental capital investment.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed about 190 megawatts of contracted capacity for 2031–2034 at roughly $86/MWh, below current market pricing above $100/MWh, creating potential repricing upside that the preview had not identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has approximately 190 megawatts under contract from 2031–2034 priced at about $86/MWh, below current market pricing of over $100/MWh, representing embedded repricing upside.”

in_line: Management raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $1.15–$1.2 billion and adjusted EBITDA guidance to $630–$650 million from the prior $1.11–$1.16 billion and $615–$645 million ranges. The preview identified August as a scheduled guidance-update quarter and said the bar for a raise was relatively low.
Product revenue of $46.7 million was within the preview’s implied Q2 range of roughly $41–48 million and declined less than the preview’s implied 26% year-over-year decline.

Management expects Energy Storage merchant pricing to normalize in the second half; the preview already described storage gross-margin normalization to a 35–40% full-year level and warned that Q1’s strong merchant pricing was not expected to repeat.
The company reaffirmed its 2028 portfolio target of 2.6–2.8 gigawatts, as the preview specifically identified reaffirmation of that target as a narrative item to watch.
The declared $0.12 quarterly dividend matches the preview’s stated $0.48 annual dividend.

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EPS was $9.27, well above the preview’s $8.30 consensus and even its $8.40–$8.50 whisper range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 sales rose 10% (8% organic) with adjusted EPS up 21% to a record $9.27.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS: $8.30”; “A realistic whisper is $8.40–$8.50.”

surprises.description: Q4 sales growth was stronger than the preview’s expected 6.9% year-over-year revenue growth: reported sales rose 10%, with 8% organic growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 sales rose 10% (8% organic).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $5.61B (+6.9% y/y)”; the company-implied Q4 guide was “~$5.53B (+5.5% rptd, +4% organic).”

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted segment margin reached 28.0%, above the preview’s roughly 27.3%–27.5% consensus and 27.4% implied guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted segment operating margin reached a record 28.0%, the first time above 28%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. segment op margin: ~27.3–27.5%”; company implied Q4 guide: “~27.4%.”

surprises.description: FY27 adjusted EPS guidance came in above the preview’s $34.03 consensus, at a $34.75 midpoint, although the implied 8% increase was a little below the preview’s expected 8.9% growth rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 guidance calls for … adjusted EPS of $34.75 at midpoint, an 8% increase.”

surprises.description: FY26 free cash flow exceeded the preview’s $3.3–$3.6 billion guide, reaching $3.9 billion with 107% conversion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow of $3.9 billion at 107% conversion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 FCF guided $3.3–$3.6B.”

surprises.description: Parker raised its long-term margin ambition after reaching its prior goal early: it now targets 30% adjusted segment margin by FY31, 300 basis points above the previous 27% target for FY29.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its adjusted segment operating margin target by 300 basis points to 30% by FY31, after achieving its prior FY29 target of 27% early.”

surprises.description: The FY27 aerospace growth outlook is only 8.5%, a step down from the sustained double-digit growth the preview said the aerospace story needed; the call noted four consecutive prior years of double-digit growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Aerospace & Defense guided to high single-digit (8.5%) growth after four consecutive years of double-digit growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the aerospace print needed “double-digit organic” growth to keep the multiple intact and identified aerospace as “carrying the story.”

surprises.description: Parker said it is guiding positive organic sales growth across every market vertical for the first time, addressing the preview’s concern that industrial growth might remain too weak to support FY27.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For the first time ever, Parker is guiding positive organic sales growth across all market verticals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY27 could not work “on 3% industrial organic forever” and called for looking for a short-cycle turn in Diversified Industrial North America.

surprises.description: Demand indicators were stronger than the preview’s last reported levels: orders were up 12% on a rolling 12-month basis and 19% on a 3-month basis, while backlog reached a new record of $12.8 billion versus the previously cited $12.5 billion record.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 total orders were up 12% on a rolling 12-month basis (19% on 3-month), with backlog up 16% to a record $12.8 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Record $12.5B backlog” and company orders “+9% in Q3.”

surprises.description: The pending acquisition commitment includes CIRCOR aerospace as well as Filtration Group, a second large deal not anticipated in the preview, with roughly $12 billion allocated to the pending transactions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company deployed nearly $15 billion in capital in FY26, including the $1 billion Curtis acquisition, ~$12 billion for pending Filtration Group and CIRCOR aerospace deals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on the “$9.25B Filtration Group deal” and its close, accretion, and leverage implications; it did not mention CIRCOR.

surprises.description: Management expects leverage to peak near 3x after the pending deals close, above the preview’s roughly 2x pro-forma leverage reference, before returning to 2x within about six quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt to adjusted EBITDA fell to 1.4x from 1.7x a year earlier, and management expects it to peak near 3x after the pending deals close, returning to 2x within about 6 quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “pro-forma net leverage vs. the ~2x target” as a key issue.

surprises.description: Parker will switch all Industrial businesses to rolling 12-month order reporting starting in FY27, an unanticipated reporting change that will alter how industrial order trends are presented.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Beginning in FY27, Parker will convert all Industrial businesses to rolling 12-month order reporting.”

in_line: FY26 adjusted segment operating margin was 27.3%, in line with the preview’s 27.3%–27.5% consensus range.
FY27 guidance excludes the impact of pending acquisitions, consistent with the preview’s base-case expectation that Filtration Group would be excluded pending close.

surprises.description: LINC’s Q2 student-start growth was only 1%, far below the preview’s 8–12% estimate and its expectation that a high-single-digit slowdown would mostly reflect calendar effects. Management attributed the shortfall to weaker AI-driven lead generation, financial-aid packaging delays, and student loan defaults.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Student start growth slowed dramatically to just 1% in Q2 versus nearly 20% in Q1”; a lower percentage of enrollments converted to starts due to “weaker AI-driven lead generation, financial aid packaging delays, and student loan defaults.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Student starts +8–12% (house est.; comp-distorted)” and “headline decelerating from Q1's +19.5% to high-single-digits is likely mechanical, not fundamental.”

surprises.description: Despite the weak Q2 starts, management reaffirmed rather than raised FY26 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance. The preview’s base case anticipated a raise to roughly $595–605 million revenue and $78–82 million adjusted EBITDA, and said an unchanged reaffirmation would be a negative departure from that expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “reiterated full-year guidance of $590–$600 million revenue” and “$76–$80 million adjusted EBITDA,” along with the other existing guidance ranges.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case is a guidance raise to roughly $595–605M revenue / $78–82M EBITDA”; “an in-line reaffirm would read as a negative.”

surprises.description: FY26 capital expenditure guidance rose to $95–100 million from $70–75 million, a substantial increase beyond the preview’s stated capex plan. The spending is tied partly to property and campus investment, with management saying about 75% of capex supports growth initiatives.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year capital expenditure guidance was raised from $70–$75 million to $95–$100 million,” reflecting the “$18.8 million Melrose Park property purchase and Suitland, Maryland campus spend”; “~75% of CapEx” is tied to growth initiatives.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 capex guidance of “$70–75M” and said management had guided “~half of FY26 capex (~$35M) into Q2.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA of $12.7 million came in below the preview’s $13–15 million house-estimate range and $14.0 million base case, even as revenue exceeded its estimate. This was a modest shortfall against the expected quarterly EBITDA level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 42.4% to $12.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$13–15M (house est., no published consensus found)” and “Our numbers (base case): … adj. EBITDA $14.0M.”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $0.06, above the preview’s $0.03 base case and well above the roughly breakeven consensus estimate. Net income was $1.9 million, with management noting that higher depreciation from recent capital investment kept net-income growth below EBITDA growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income increased 25% to $1.9 million ($0.06 diluted EPS), though net income grew slower than EBITDA due to higher depreciation from recent capital investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS ~$0.00 (≈$0.001; some feeds show a fractional loss)” and “Our numbers (base case): … EPS $0.03.”

surprises.description: Revenue reached $142.6 million, modestly above the preview’s $139.49 million consensus and $141 million base case. The beat was small relative to the expected level, rather than a major upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 22.4% to $142.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $139.49M” consensus; “Our numbers (base case): revenue $141M.”

surprises.description: Management projected Q3 student starts returning to low double-digit year-over-year growth and said the August class is expected to be the largest in company history, including high school starts up more than 15%. That outlook was not anticipated in the preview and contrasts with Q2’s sharp start slowdown.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Q3 student starts to return to low double-digit year-over-year growth, projecting the largest August start class in company history, with high school starts alone expected to be up more than 15%.”

surprises.description: The call described a Suitland focused-campus model with substantially lower capital needs and ambitious return and mature-campus targets. The preview anticipated possible expansion news, but did not set expectations for this model’s economics.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Suitland “focused campus” model requires “only ~$10 million in capital (vs. ~$25 million for traditional campuses), targets a 30%+ IRR, and is expected to generate over $50 million revenue and $5 million EBITDA at full ramp.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “expected to announce more expansions by Q2 results,” but gave no focused-campus cost, return, revenue, or EBITDA targets.

surprises.description: Student attrition improved by about 150 basis points year over year, helping keep the student population more than 10% higher despite weak starts. The preview discussed population growth but did not anticipate this retention improvement as a specific offset to the starts shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Student attrition improved approximately 150 basis points year-over-year,” boosting retention and helping keep the student population “up over 10% (roughly 1,800 students) across 22 campuses, offsetting weak starts.”

in_line: The preview had already expected roughly $10 million of FY26 new-campus losses to be included in adjusted EBITDA; the call likewise said approximately $10 million of full-year new-campus losses are included in guidance and are no longer added back.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $31.5 million, below the preview’s roughly $34.1–$34.4 million consensus, though it remained above $30 million and within the preview’s base-case range. The shortfall was about 8% versus consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $31.5 million (over $30 million)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $34.13M (Zacks) / $34.42M (Investing.com); street range ~$34.4–35M”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating expense excluding cost of revenues was at the very top of the preview’s $85–$95 million guide, and Q3 guidance rose to $105–$115 million, with 2026 averaging about $100 million per quarter. That points to a higher near-term expense run rate than the preview’s existing quarterly guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP adjusted OpEx excluding cost of revenues rose to $95.9 million in Q2 from $79.8 million in Q1, with Q3 guided to $105-115 million and full-year 2026 averaging ~$100 million per quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. opex ex-COGS | $85–95M (company guide)”

surprises.description: AST disclosed three new U.S. government awards with more than $100 million of funded near-term value expected during 2026–2027. The preview discussed government milestones and backlog but did not anticipate these specific new awards.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AST received 3 new U.S. government contract awards with funded near-term value of over $100 million expected during 2026-2027”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue here is not subscriber revenue — it is gateway equipment deliveries and government contract milestones.”

surprises.description: AST reported a preliminary J-LEO award with Rakuten that could bring up to approximately $1 billion in nondilutive, non-debt government capital. This sizable potential source of funding was not flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A preliminary award from Japan's J-LEO project with partner Rakuten carries a total expected value of up to approximately $1 billion in nondilutive, non-debt government capital.”

surprises.description: The company raised $1.15 billion through convertible notes and said pro forma cash exceeded $3.7 billion, easing the preview’s near-term financing concern. The 1.625% coupon was described as AST’s lowest ever, although the notes also introduce potential conversion dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company issued $1.15 billion of 1.625% convertible senior notes due 2034 (its lowest-ever coupon) with a capped-call conversion price of $149.20, bringing pro forma cash to over $3.7 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any hint of an equity or convert raise is a live risk into an ~$28B market cap.”

surprises.description: Management reaffirmed a target of approaching $1 billion in revenue in the first full year of commercial service and said government could contribute up to half. The preview did not provide this quantified commercial-year target or government contribution range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reaffirmed a target of approaching $1 billion in revenue in the first full year of commercial service, with government potentially contributing up to half of that figure.”

in_line: AST reiterated FY2026 revenue guidance of $150–$200 million, as the preview expected a reaffirmation; the call also described the expected back-half weighting.
Q2 CapEx of approximately $610 million was within the preview’s $575–$650 million company guide.

The target of approximately 45 satellites by early 2027 was consistent with the preview, which said the 45-satellite continuous-coverage milestone had already moved to early 2027. The stated $21–$23 million per-satellite cost also matched the preview’s cited target.

surprises.description: The preview treated the Brook Mine update as a near-term financing catalyst, with an update expected in 2H26. The call instead put major refinery capital disbursements more than two years away and the pre-feasibility study in spring 2027, pushing the project timeline further out.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Major capital disbursements for the refinery are still more than two years away,” with a “pre-feasibility study expected in spring 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “This is that window” for updates on non-dilutive financing and offtake arrangements, which management had said would come in 2H26.

surprises.description: Ramaco cut its full-year production and sales ranges below the preview’s expected ranges: production is now 3.6–3.9 million tons versus 3.7–4.1 million, and sales are 4.0–4.3 million versus 4.1–4.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 production guidance was cut to 3.6-3.9 million tons and sales guidance to 4.0-4.3 million tons.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 production guidance of “3.7 – 4.1M tons” and sales guidance of “4.1 – 4.5M tons,” and said to watch for a reaffirmation or trim.

surprises.description: Class A EPS was a larger loss than consensus: a $0.26 loss per share versus the preview’s $0.23 loss estimate. The gap was small, but it was worse than the preview’s expectation that EPS would be nearly a formality.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Class A EPS loss of $0.26” in Q2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 FY26 consensus EPS was “−$0.23”; the preview also called the EPS line “nearly a formality.”

surprises.description: The coal cash margin came in at $17 per ton, above the preview’s roughly $12-per-ton base case and the expected compression from Q1’s $16. Realized prices rose to $116 per ton rather than declining, while costs stayed below $100 per ton.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 cash margins fell to $17 per ton from $20 per ton a year ago,” as realized prices “dropp[ed] 6% to $116 per ton” and cash costs held at “$99.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario estimated a “~$12/t” cash margin and said realizations were “guided lower” from Q1’s $114/t.

surprises.description: The company bought back far more shares than the preview’s prior-period figures suggested, repurchasing almost 5 million shares—more than 8% of Class A shares—for about $66 million. This is a strong continuation of buybacks at a time when the preview specifically questioned whether management would keep buying at $9–11.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased more than 8% of its Class A shares (almost 5 million shares) for about $66 million,” reducing shares outstanding to less than 52 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “2.6M shares/$37M repurchased at ~$14.50,” asked “Did they keep buying at $9–11?” and said aggressive buying below $11 would be “a genuine confidence signal.”
